acts.title: Which side of the thing
acts.milestone: You have watched a conversation switch to English over one word order.

acts.title: The six words
acts.milestone: Six words, each one attached to a sentence somebody has already written.

acts.title: Her form
acts.milestone: Three of them follow the rule you had, three replace the word, and you can hear all six.

acts.title: Before a vowel
acts.milestone: bel and vieil, which almost nothing else in the language has and everybody uses.

acts.title: Say it, write it, use it
acts.milestone: You have read them on a real board and said all fourteen out loud.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete. Adjective placement is next, and it starts where this one stopped.

recorded.desc: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT NOTE IN THIS LESSON. EVERY MASCULINE / FEMININE PAIR IS ONE TAKE, one voice, one pace, the plain form immediately followed by its feminine with no gap and no reset: grand / grande, petit / petite, mauvais / mauvaise, bon / bonne, beau / belle, vieux / vieille. The ONLY difference the learner may hear is the ending. Recorded apart these become two performances and the learner compares the performances instead of the forms. UNLIKE a1.13, ALL SIX OF THESE PAIRS GENUINELY DIFFER, so there is no silent pair to protect here and the risk runs the other way: do not EXAGGERATE the difference to make it audible. It already is. Read every pair at ordinary conversational pace. bon / bonne is the one to get right. bon is a nasal vowel with NO n sound behind it at all, and bonne is a plain oral o followed by a clearly pronounced n. That is a vowel change and a consonant arriving in one step, it is the largest change in the set, and it must not be softened into a half-nasal. This is the brun / brune shape from sons.03 and should be read the same way. beau / belle and vieux / vieille are not endings and must not be read as though they were: they are two different words and should sound like two different words.

THE THREE-FORM SETS, AND EACH IS ONE TAKE. « beau / bel / belle » read straight through as one continuous take by one voice, then « vieux / vieil / vieille » the same way. The three-form set is this lesson's unique content and it only reads as a set if it is heard as one. bel and belle are the same sound and vieil and vieille are the same sound, and the learner has to hear that rather than be told it, so do not differentiate them: read the second and third members of each set identically. THEN THE PHRASES, AND THESE ARE NEVER BARE. « un bel homme », « un bel arbre », « un vieil ami » and « un vieil immeuble » are recorded AS FULL PHRASES, never as isolated words. The form exists ONLY because of the vowel that follows it, so a lone bel clip teaches nothing and a lone vieil clip is actively misleading. Record each vowel phrase immediately after its consonant partner, in the same take, so the contrast is inside one performance: « un beau jardin » then « un bel arbre », « un vieux château » then « un vieil immeuble ». There is NO liaison to perform in any of these. Do not add one.
clipIds: Mon grand-père a un vieil ami à Lyon.

recorded.desc: THE WORD ORDER PAIR, AND IT IS THE HARDEST THING IN THIS BRIEF TO READ CORRECTLY. « une maison grande » and « une grande maison » are recorded as ONE TAKE, one after the other, with an even beat between them and NOTHING ELSE DIFFERENT. Both must be read as ordinary confident French. Do NOT read the first one hesitantly, do not put a question in the voice, do not mark it as wrong in any way. The entire teaching of this lesson is that the wrong one sounds completely fine, and a reader who performs the error destroys it. Same instruction for « un appartement grand » against « un grand appartement » and for the same reason. Also record the two-order phrases as whole units at conversational pace, with no pause between the noun and either describing word: « une petite robe rouge », « un petit chien blanc », « une belle robe bleue ». The pattern being absorbed is that both words belong to the same phrase, and a pause in the middle would break it into two.
clipIds: Elle porte une petite robe rouge.
Elle porte une belle robe bleue.
Elle habite dans une grande maison.

recorded.desc: The six as ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE by one voice at one speed, in the deck order: grand, petit, beau, vieux, bon, mauvais. Six words recorded in six sessions are six performances, and any drift in pace or pitch teaches a difference between the recordings rather than a difference in French. Read them straight through with an even beat, then again slowly in the same take. grand and bon are NASAL and must be read with no n sound behind the vowel at all. petit and mauvais both end in a silent consonant and must end on the vowel, with nothing after it. THE MASCULINE PLURALS ARE NOT RECORDED IN ISOLATION AND MUST NOT BE. vieux and mauvais are identical in the singular and the plural, and a lone clip of a plural implies a difference that is not there. Where a plural is needed it is recorded as the second half of a pair with its own singular, in one take, so the learner hears that nothing changed: grand / grands, petit / petits, bon / bons, vieux / vieux, mauvais / mauvais. If a reader cannot resist marking the plural somehow, record the singular twice and use it for both, because that is a more truthful clip than a performed difference.

The four-form grid, read ACROSS THE ROW in one take: « Ce garçon est très grand, cette fille est très grande, les garçons sont grands, les filles sont grandes. » Reading a row in one take is the entire point: the learner has to hear that the row changes ONCE, at grande, and never again, because the two plurals are the same sound as the two singulars. Do not record these four sentences separately. Do not vary the pace between them. There is no s sound anywhere in the third or fourth sentence and there must be no hint of one: no lengthening, no release, no breath.

The five written traps, wrong version then right version, with a clear beat between them. Read EVERY wrong version plainly and at ordinary pace rather than comically. THREE OF THE FIVE ARE ACOUSTICALLY IDENTICAL TO THEIR CORRECTION: « des vieuxs vélos » and « des vieux vélos » are the same sound, and so is the vieuxe pair once the reader stops trying to mark it. Do not try to make the wrong one sound wrong. Read both members identically and let the screen carry the difference, because a reader who performs a distinction that does not exist teaches the learner to listen for something that will never be there. THE FIRST TRAP IS THE OPPOSITE CASE AND IS THE MOST IMPORTANT CLIP IN THE LESSON. « une maison grande » against « une grande maison » differs audibly, because word order is the one thing that is never silent, and it must still be read WITHOUT any hint that the first is wrong. That combination is the whole lesson: audibly different, and nobody ever mentions it. Only the « un beau homme » / « un bel homme » pair and the « bone » / « bonne » pair genuinely differ in a way the reader should let through, and both should be read straight.

The opening scene. Nadia is an estate agent in her forties with a folder open and twenty minutes, reading at an ordinary working pace rather than a teaching pace. THE BEAT THAT MATTERS IS THE ONE WHERE SHE SWITCHES TO ENGLISH. « Ah, a big one. No problem, I have three. » must be read as HELPFUL AND SLIGHTLY BRISK, never as corrective, never as pointed, and above all never as unkind. She is not marking anybody. She heard a sentence, understood it completely, made a snap judgement about which language would be faster, and moved on. The whole lesson depends on the learner feeling that nothing bad happened, because nothing bad did. Any edge on that line turns it into a telling-off and loses the point entirely. Her final line, where she stays in French and starts describing a street, is where warmth is allowed to show, because that is the reward for having fixed it.
clipIds: Alors, qu'est-ce que vous cherchez exactement ?
Ah, a big one. No problem, I have three.
Un petit jardin, d'accord. J'ai exactement ça, dans une vieille rue très calme.

lessons.intro: Six describing words you will use every day, and the first thing to know about them is that they do not go where the colours went. This is how to put them in front of the thing, get the feminine right on all six, and use the two extra shapes that appear in front of a vowel.

theFeminine.body: You already know the rule from last lesson: for the une kind of thing, add an e. Grand becomes grande, petit becomes petite and mauvais becomes mauvaise, and nothing new is being asked of you there. Bon doubles its n first and becomes bonne. Beau and vieux do not add anything at all: they turn into belle and vieille, which are different words to look at. Nothing about the plain form tells you which of the three will happen, so these are six shapes to know rather than one rule to apply.
theFeminine.title: Three of them follow the rule and three do not

examples.note: The plain rule, doing what it did all last lesson.
And the one that replaces the word instead of adding to it.

beforeAVowel.body: Beau and vieux each have a form nothing else in this lesson has. In front of a word starting with a vowel sound they become bel and vieil: un bel homme, un vieil ami. It is the same pressure you met in the elision lesson, where two vowel sounds meeting each other is something French will not do. Beau homme and vieux ami both put two vowels together, so the word in front changes shape to stop it. These two are used constantly and they are worth having now.
beforeAVowel.title: A third shape, in front of a vowel

examples.note: Homme starts with a vowel sound, so beau cannot stand there.
Ami does the same thing to vieux.

whereTheySit.body: Colours go after the thing they describe, and you have just spent a lesson on that. These six go in front of it instead. Une grande maison, not une maison grande. That is the English order, which makes it easy to say and easy to forget, because the habit you built last lesson pulls the other way. Nobody will correct you if you get it wrong, since the sentence is perfectly understandable either way, and that is exactly why it is worth fixing now rather than later.
whereTheySit.title: Not where the last lesson put them

examples.note: A colour, sitting behind the thing, which is where every colour sits.
One phrase carrying both: the size in front, the colour behind.

alwaysAudible.body: Last lesson four of the twelve colours changed sound for the une kind and the rest did not, and on bleu and noir there was nothing to hear at all. These six are the other way round: every one of them sounds different. Grand wakes a d, petit wakes a t, mauvais wakes an s as a z, bon collapses its nasal into a plain n, and beau and vieux become other words entirely. So on these six your ear is worth listening to. The plural is still completely silent, exactly as it was.
alwaysAudible.title: The opposite of the colours

examples.note: The biggest change of the six, and the nasal lesson already taught why.
The silent letters lesson authored this one: the d arrives with the e.

noPluralChange.body: For more than one thing you add an s, and it is silent, which you know. But vieux already ends in an x and mauvais already ends in an s, and French does not stack a second one on top. Un vieux vélo and des vieux vélos are the same word on the page as well as in the air. Vieuxs and mauvaiss are not words and never have been. This is the one place in the lesson where the careful thing to do is nothing.
noPluralChange.term: vieux and mauvais, for several things
noPluralChange.title: Two of them already end in the plural letter

examples.note: One old grandfather.
Several old friends, and the word has not moved.

lessons.title: Les adjectifs de base

drills.coach: Say the whole phrase out loud before you turn the card. If the word is one of these six it goes in front, and if it is a colour it goes behind.
drills.title: Which side does it go on?

drills.q: A big house. Which one?
drills.why: une grande maison. In front of the house, which is not where the colours went, and nobody will ever tell you if you get it wrong.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: The English is on the left. Say the French out loud before you turn the card, and put it in front of something.
drills.title: English in, French out

drills.q: Which one means bad?
drills.why: mauvais. bon and beau both start with a b and mean nothing like each other, which is what makes this trio worth saying out loud as a group rather than reading.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Say the feminine out loud before you place each one. If you added an e it is the first group; if you doubled a letter first it is the second; and if you said a completely different word it is the third.
drills.title: What does the feminine do?
buckets: Adds an -e, exactly like last lesson

drills.q: What is the feminine of vieux?
drills.why: vieille. It replaces the word rather than adding to it, and so does belle. Those two are the ones there is no way to work out.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Ignore the describing word entirely and look at the word after it. If it starts with a vowel sound the describing word had to change, and if it starts with a consonant nothing happened.
drills.title: Which shape, in front of this word?

drills.q: un ___ ami. Which one?
drills.why: vieil. ami starts with a vowel sound. It sounds exactly like vieille and it is not the feminine: the word in front is still un.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Look at the last letter of the plain form. If it is already an s or an x, French will not put another one behind it, and the word for several things is the word you are looking at.
drills.title: Does the plural add anything?

drills.q: Several old friends, all the un kind. Which one?
drills.why: de vieux amis. The x is already there and nothing goes behind it. mauvais does the same, and they are the only two of the six.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Say each one, then say it again with the plain form of the describing word. If the two versions sound different it goes on the left. If you said the same thing twice it goes on the right.
drills.title: Heard, or only written

drills.q: How much of the plural can you hear on these six?
drills.why: None of it. The plural s is silent on every one of these six, exactly as it was on every colour. The feminine is the half you can hear, and that part is new.
opts: some of it, on some words
drills.title: One more time

sheets.title: All six, in every shape

What the feminine does to each

rows.v: beau becomes bel. Never un beau homme: two vowel sounds would collide.
The same thing on a thing rather than a person. It is only ever about the next sound.
vieux becomes vieil. One of the most common phrases in the language.
Same again. bel and vieil sound exactly like belle and vieille and are not the feminine.
The feminine is unaffected by any of this: belle is belle in front of anything.

sections.title: In front of a vowel sound

rows.k: Adds an -e, exactly like last lesson
rows.v: grand, petit, mauvais. Add an e, and on all three of them you can hear the last letter wake up.
bon. bonne doubles the n, which is what makes the vowel plain and the n audible.
beau, vieux. belle and vieille replace the word. There is nothing to work out and nothing that would have told you.

rows.k: vieux and mauvais for several things
rows.v: Both already end in the letter the plural would add, so the un kind never changes: un vieux vélo, des vieux vélos.
rows.say: un vieux vélo, des vieux vélos

rows.v: In front of the thing they describe, which is the opposite of where a colour goes. That is the one thing a listener hears immediately.
rows.say: une grande maison, une jupe verte

How this differs from the colours

sections.title: Can you hear the feminine?

sections.body: The colour lesson spent an act teaching that most of agreement is invisible, and it was right about colours. Four of the twelve already ended in an e and were the same word for either kind of thing. Two more, bleu and noir, added an e that changed nothing you could hear. Only four of the twelve did anything audible at all, and the practical advice was to stop listening for the ending and work it out from the thing instead. That advice was correct and it does not transfer here. Every one of these six changes sound for the une kind, and they do it in three different ways. grand, petit and mauvais all end in a consonant that is silent while it is last in the word, and the feminine e stops it being last, so the d, the t and the s all come back. That is the silent letters lesson doing exactly what it said it would. bon is a different mechanism and a bigger change: the n on the end of bon is not a consonant at all, it is a mark telling you the vowel is nasal, and doubling it in bonne puts a vowel behind the first n, which makes it a real consonant and makes the vowel plain. You met that in the nasal lesson with brun and brune. beau and vieux do not do anything to their ending because they do not keep it: belle and vieille are different words and sound like it. So on these six the ear is a reliable guide to the feminine, which is worth knowing because a learner who took the last lesson at its word will have stopped listening. The plural is the part that has not changed at all. The s on grands, petits, bons and beaux is never pronounced, in any position, on any word, and grand and grands are the same recording. Nothing about listening more carefully will separate them, and a native speaker cannot do it either. So the rule is now in two halves and both of them are short: listen for the feminine and work out the plural.

sections.title: One Word, Four Shapes

sections.say: Tap any row to hear both halves. Every single one of these six changes sound, which the colours did not.

detail.say: Ce garçon est très grand. Cette fille est très grande. Les garçons sont grands. Les filles sont grandes.
detail.body: [GRAHⁿ] becomes [GRAHⁿD], so the d at the end wakes up. Ce garçon est très grand. Cette fille est très grande. Les garçons sont grands. Les filles sont grandes.
detail.title: grand to grande

detail.say: Elle a un petit chien. Il a une petite voiture. Nous avons de petits problèmes. Elle porte de petites chaussures.
detail.body: [pə-TEE] becomes [pə-TEET], so the t at the end wakes up. Elle a un petit chien. Il a une petite voiture. Nous avons de petits problèmes. Elle porte de petites chaussures.
detail.title: petit to petite

detail.say: C'est un beau jardin. C'est une belle maison. Ce sont de beaux tableaux. Ce sont de belles fleurs.
detail.body: [BOH] becomes [BEL], so the word is replaced outright. C'est un beau jardin. C'est une belle maison. Ce sont de beaux tableaux. Ce sont de belles fleurs.
detail.title: beau to belle

detail.say: Mon grand-père est vieux. Ma grand-mère est vieille. Ce sont de vieux amis. Ce sont de vieilles photos.
detail.body: [VYUH] becomes [VYEY], so the word is replaced outright. Mon grand-père est vieux. Ma grand-mère est vieille. Ce sont de vieux amis. Ce sont de vieilles photos.
detail.title: vieux to vieille

detail.say: Le repas était très bon. La soupe est bonne. Les résultats sont bons. Les nouvelles sont bonnes.
detail.body: [BOHⁿ] becomes [BON], so the nasal collapses into a plain n. Le repas était très bon. La soupe est bonne. Les résultats sont bons. Les nouvelles sont bonnes.
detail.title: bon to bonne

detail.say: Ce film est mauvais. Cette idée est mauvaise. Les temps sont mauvais. Les odeurs sont mauvaises dans la cuisine.
detail.body: [moh-VEH] becomes [moh-VEHZ], so the s wakes up as a z. Ce film est mauvais. Cette idée est mauvaise. Les temps sont mauvais. Les odeurs sont mauvaises dans la cuisine.
detail.title: mauvais to mauvaise

sections.title: All Six, Both Shapes

sections.say: The six, split by what the feminine actually does. Two of last lesson's four groups are empty here, which is worth noticing.
sections.title: Three Groups, Not Six Rules

check.q: These three add an e and nothing else. On how many of them can you HEAR it?
check.why: All three. grande says its d, petite says its t, mauvaise says its s as a z. That is the difference from last lesson, where four of the twelve colours changed sound and the rest did not.

groups.label: Adds an -e, exactly like last lesson

check.q: bon does not become bone. What is the feminine?
check.why: bonne, with two n letters. The doubled n has to be there because a single one would leave the vowel nasal, which is the thing that stopped being true. You met this in the nasal lesson: an n followed by a vowel blocks it.

check.q: The feminine of beau is belle. What happened to beau?
check.why: It was replaced. belle shares almost nothing with beau and vieille shares almost nothing with vieux, so these two are not the rule going wrong, they are two shapes to know. There is no way to work them out.
opts: It was replaced by a different word

sections.say: One word, and the vowel itself changes. Slow the audio down on this one.
sections.hint: Four cards on the biggest sound change of the six.

cards.body: One sound, and there is no n in it at all. The n on the page is there to tell you the vowel is nasal, and it is never itself pronounced.
cards.head: bon
cards.label: the plain form

cards.body: Two n letters and now you say one of them. The vowel stops being nasal and becomes a plain o. This is the largest change any of these six makes and it is impossible to miss.
cards.head: bonne
cards.label: the une kind

cards.body: The nasal lesson taught this exact mechanism: an n with a vowel behind it stops making the vowel nasal and starts being a consonant you say. Doubling the n is how the spelling gets a vowel behind the first one.
cards.head: A single n would not work
cards.label: why it doubles

cards.body: bone with one n would be a different sound and is not a word. The doubling is not decoration and it is the only one of the six that does this, so it is worth writing out by hand once.
cards.head: Never bone
cards.label: what not to write

sections.title: The One That Changes Most

sections.say: Six pairs, and something changes in every single one. That is not what happened last lesson.

lines.en: you hear a difference: the d at the end wakes up
you hear a difference: the t at the end wakes up
you hear a difference: the s wakes up as a z
you hear a difference: the nasal collapses into a plain n
you hear a difference: the word is replaced outright

sections.title: You Can Hear All Six

questions.q: How many of those six pairs sounded identical?
questions.why: None. Every one of these six changes sound for the une kind, which is the opposite of the colours: bleu and bleue were the same word twice and four others already ended in an e. Here your ear is telling you the truth.

questions.q: On grand, petit and mauvais, what is making the sound?
questions.why: The consonant. The e is not itself a sound: it stops the letter in front of it being last in the word, so that letter gets said again. grand hides its d and grande says it, which is the silent letters lesson doing its job.
opts: The e itself is being pronounced
A letter that was silent is now being said
The speaker is stressing the ending

questions.q: None of those six pairs was a plural. Why not?
questions.why: There is nothing to hear. The plural s is silent on all six, exactly as it was on every colour, so grand and grands are one sound. Your ear separates the two kinds here and can do nothing about the number.
opts: Plurals were covered in an earlier lesson
Plural forms of these words are rare
The plural s is never pronounced, so there would be nothing to hear
The recording only had singular forms

sections.say: Same decisions, nothing to look at. This is the one that tells you whether it landed.
sections.title: Now Without The Table

check.q: Ma grand-mère, and the word is vieux. What do you write?
check.why: vieille. It is one of the two that get replaced rather than added to, so there is nothing to work out and nothing that would have told you. vieuxe is not a word and never was.

groups.label: One thing of the une kind

check.q: Several old friends, all of them the un kind. What do you write?
check.why: de vieux amis, unchanged. vieux already ends in an x and French will not stack a plural on top of it, so the singular and the plural are the same word on the page as well as in the air.

check.q: Les temps, and the word is mauvais. What do you write?
check.why: mauvais, exactly as it was. The s is already there, so there is nothing to add. This is the same situation as vieux and they are the only two of the six it happens to.

groups.label: The other one that does not move

check.q: Les filles, and the word is grand. What do you write?
check.why: grandes. The une kind, so an e, and more than one, so an s, in that order. You can hear the e and not the s, so half of that decision came from your ear and half from the girls.

sections.say: Two of the six have a shape you have not met, and it only exists in front of a vowel sound.
sections.hint: Five cards. These two are used constantly.

cards.sub: [BOH] · a vowel sound at the start of the next word
cards.body: beau ends in a vowel sound and homme starts with one, and French will not run two of them together like that. You met the same pressure in the elision lesson, where le became l' for exactly this reason.
cards.head: Two vowels, touching
cards.label: the problem

cards.body: beau becomes bel, and the l gives the vowel something to land on. It sounds exactly like the feminine belle, and it is not the feminine: this is a man, and the word in front of him is un.
cards.head: bel
cards.label: the answer

cards.fr: Mon grand-père a un vieil ami à Lyon.
cards.sub: [VYEY] · My grandfather has an old friend in Lyon.
cards.body: vieux becomes vieil for the same reason, and it sounds exactly like vieille. un vieil ami is one of the most common phrases in the language and almost every course leaves it until much later.
cards.head: vieil
cards.label: the same thing again

cards.body: arbre starts with a vowel, so the same thing happens. Nothing here is about whether the thing is a person: it is only ever about the first sound of the word that comes next.
cards.head: It is not about people
cards.label: on a thing rather than a person

cards.body: Colours follow the noun. These six come first. And when one of them lands in front of a vowel, it changes shape again. These two forms are worth more than anything else in this lesson because you will need them today.
cards.head: un vieil immeuble
cards.label: and the other one

sections.title: A Third Shape, Before A Vowel

sections.say: Two rows, four real sentences, and the same opening on all four. Only the next word changed.
cols: next word starts with a consonant
next word starts with a vowel

rows.say: C'est un beau jardin. C'est un bel arbre.

detail.say: C'est un beau jardin. C'est un bel arbre.
detail.body: C'est un beau jardin. C'est un bel arbre. Identical up to the describing word, and then one of them has to change because of a letter in the word after it. It's a beautiful garden. It's a beautiful tree.
detail.title: beau and bel

rows.say: C'est un vieux château. C'est un vieil immeuble.

detail.say: C'est un vieux château. C'est un vieil immeuble.
detail.body: C'est un vieux château. C'est un vieil immeuble. Identical up to the describing word, and then one of them has to change because of a letter in the word after it. It's an old castle. It's an old building.
detail.title: vieux and vieil

sections.title: The Same Sentence, One Sound Apart

sections.say: Colours follow the noun. These six come first. Five things an English speaker writes in their first month, one per screen.
sections.title: Five Traps

errors.why: The highest-value one here, and the only one nobody will ever mention. It is understood perfectly, so it survives for years and marks every sentence you say. These six go in front, and the colours you learned last time do not.
errors.wrong: Writing « une maison grande ».

errors.why: vieux already ends in an x, so there is nothing to add and vieuxs has never been a word. mauvais does the same thing with its s. These two are the only place in this lesson where the careful move is to leave it alone.
errors.wrong: Writing « des vieuxs vélos ».

errors.why: homme starts with a vowel sound, and beau ends in one, so the two would collide. bel exists to stop that. It sounds identical to belle and it is not the feminine: the word in front is still un.
errors.wrong: Writing « un beau homme ».

errors.why: bonne doubles its n, and the doubling is doing real work: a single n would leave the vowel nasal, which is what bon is. Two n letters is what makes the o plain and the n audible.
errors.wrong: Writing « la soupe est bone ».

errors.why: vieux is one of the two that get replaced rather than added to. Applying last lesson's rule to it produces something that is not a word, and there is nothing about vieux that would have warned you. It has to be learned.
errors.wrong: Writing « ma grand-mère est vieuxe ».

sections.say: Four notices, and one of them has the describing word where English would have left it.
sections.text: The board inside the bakery door is where this part of town advertises itself, and most of it is people trying to let a room. « Grande chambre dans une vieille maison. » Whoever wrote that got both words into the right place, and the room has almost certainly gone already. Under it somebody is selling a bicycle and the whole notice is five words long. « Un vieux vélo, bon état. » Nothing on the end of either word, and nothing needed: one bicycle, and both words are the un kind. A third card is looking for a flatmate, and the writer has left the describing word exactly where English would put it. « Je cherche une personne calme dans un appartement grand. » Everybody who reads that will understand it, nobody will correct it, and every French reader will notice. The last one is the shortest thing on the board and it is selling the flat above the bakery. « Belle vue, petit loyer. »
sections.title: The Board At The Bakery

glossary.note: In front of the room, which is where these six go. The d is pronounced here because of the e.
The une kind, so vieux is replaced by vieille rather than gaining an ending.
The un kind and one of it, so the plain form. A second bicycle would change nothing at all.

glossary.en: a big flat, with the words the wrong way round
glossary.note: This should be un grand appartement. It is understood, and it is the thing this lesson exists to stop.
The une kind, so beau becomes belle. In front of the view, as always.

questions.a: The flatmate notice says « un appartement grand ». It should say « un grand appartement ». All six of the words in this lesson go in front of the thing, and this one has been left where English would put it.
questions.q: Three of the four notices put the describing word in the same place. Which one does not, and what should it say?

questions.a: Exactly the same thing: « de vieux vélos ». vieux already ends in an x, so the plural adds nothing to it. Only the word for bicycle changes, and even that change is silent.
questions.q: The bicycle notice says « un vieux vélo ». What would it say for two bicycles?

questions.a: Yes, and this is the one error in the lesson you can hear, because word order is the one thing that is never silent. Every other mistake here is about an ending, and endings are half inaudible. An order is always audible.
questions.q: Would a French reader notice the mistake in the flatmate notice if somebody read the board out loud?

cards.back: Elle est grande. grande, and the silent d wakes up so you can hear it.
petite, and the silent t wakes up.
mauvaise, and the silent s comes back as a z.
C'est une bonne idée. bonne, with two n letters, and the vowel stops being nasal.
Ils achètent une belle maison. belle. It is not beau with an ending, it is a different word.
vieille. Also a different word, and vieuxe has never existed.
C'est un bel homme. bel, because homme starts with a vowel sound.
cards.front: un ___ homme, and the word is beau.

cards.say: Mon grand-père a un vieil ami à Lyon.
cards.back: Mon grand-père a un vieil ami à Lyon. vieil, for the same reason.
cards.front: un ___ ami, and the word is vieux.

cards.back: Ce sont de vieux amis. vieux does not change, because the x is already there.
cards.front: Several old friends, all the un kind.

cards.back: Never. The s is silent on all six, exactly as it was on every colour.
cards.front: Can you hear the plural on any of these six?

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched a conversation quietly switch to English over one word order, learned six describing words you will use every day, and found out that three of their feminine forms follow the rule you already had and three of them replace the word instead. You have met a third shape that beau and vieux take in front of a vowel and that almost nothing else in the language has, and you have discovered that unlike the colours, every one of these six can be heard changing. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.
sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: Word order, which is the one thing in this lesson that is never silent.
rounds.label: Which side of the thing

questions.q: Your sister has a big house. Which line do you write?
questions.why: Elle a une grande maison. The word goes in front of the house, and it takes an e because a house is the une kind. The first option is the one a listener understands perfectly and never corrects.

questions.q: A green skirt, and a small dog. Which pair puts both words where French wants them?
questions.why: The colour goes behind the skirt and the size goes in front of the dog. Those are two different rules operating at once and both of them are already yours: one from last lesson and one from this one.
opts: une jupe verte, un petit chien
une verte jupe, un chien petit
une jupe verte, un chien petit
une verte jupe, un petit chien

questions.q: Write the French for a big house. The word for house is maison, and it is the une kind.
questions.why: une grande maison. In front of the house and carrying an e. Word order is the half of this that a French listener hears immediately, and the ending is the half they only see.

questions.q: In « Elle porte une petite robe rouge », why is one word in front of the dress and one behind it?
questions.why: Colours follow the noun. These six come first. Both words describe the same dress and neither is competing for the other's place. That sentence is a published one, not an invented example, which is what makes it worth remembering.
opts: Because petite is one of the six that come first and rouge is a colour
Because rouge has more letters than petite
Because petite matches the dress and rouge does not
Because the two could be swapped without changing anything

rounds.say: The names, quickly.
rounds.label: The six words

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: mauvais. Its final s is silent, so it ends on the vowel and sounds like moh-VEH. It is the least frequent of the six and the one most likely to slip away, which is why it is here.

questions.q: Which one means the opposite of bon?
questions.why: mauvais. These six come in opposite pairs and it is worth using that: grand against petit, and bon against mauvais. Two of them are already the other one's answer, which halves what there is to remember.

questions.q: Write the French for old. Use the form for one thing of the un kind.
questions.why: vieux, ending in an x. That x is why the plural adds nothing to it later, and it is one of only two words in this lesson that behaves that way.

questions.q: Le repas était très bon. What is being said about the meal?
questions.why: It was good. bon is the plain form because a meal is the un kind, and here it sits after the verb rather than in front of a noun, which is the one position where all six behave like any other describing word.

rounds.say: Three of the six follow the rule you already have. Three do not.
rounds.label: The feminine

questions.q: Ma grand-mère, and the word is vieux. Write the word.
questions.why: vieille. It replaces vieux rather than adding to it, which is the half of this lesson that cannot be worked out from the plain form. vieuxe is what the rule from last lesson would have produced and it is not a word.

questions.q: Cette idée, and the word is mauvais. Write the word.
questions.why: mauvaise. This one is the plain rule doing its job: add an e. The reward is that the sleeping s wakes up as a z, so unlike most of last lesson you can hear that you got it right.

questions.q: Fix this. « La soupe est bone. »
questions.why: bonne, with two n letters. The doubling is what stops the vowel being nasal, so bone would be a different sound as well as a misspelling. This is the same mechanism the nasal lesson taught with brun and brune.

questions.q: Which of these feminines is NOT the plain form with an e added?
questions.why: belle. grande, petite and mauvaise are all their plain form plus an e, exactly as the colours were. belle is a different word from beau, and so is vieille from vieux, and there is nothing in either plain form that says so.

rounds.say: The shape almost nothing else in the language has.
rounds.label: In front of a vowel

questions.q: Un ___ homme. Which one goes in the gap?
questions.why: bel. homme starts with a vowel sound and beau ends in one, so the two would collide and French will not have it. bel sounds exactly like belle, and belle would be wrong here because the word in front is un.

questions.q: Un ___ ami. Write the word for old that fits.
questions.why: vieil. Same pressure as bel, same solution, and un vieil ami is one of the most common phrases you will hear. It sounds identical to vieille and it is not the feminine.

questions.q: C'est un beau jardin, but C'est un bel arbre. What decided which one to use?
questions.why: The first sound of the next word. jardin starts with a consonant and arbre starts with a vowel, and that is the whole of it. Nothing about gardens or trees comes into it, and nothing about people does either.
opts: The first sound of the word that comes next
Whether the thing is the un kind or the une kind
Whether the speaker is being polite

questions.q: Fix this. « C'est un vieux immeuble. »
questions.why: vieil immeuble. immeuble starts with a vowel sound, so vieux changes shape in front of it. This is the same thing the elision lesson showed you when le turned into l' before a vowel.

rounds.say: Two of the six already end in the letter a plural would add.
rounds.label: What does not move

questions.q: Several old friends, all of them the un kind. Which one do you write?
questions.why: de vieux amis. vieux already ends in an x and French does not stack a plural on top of it, so the word is spelled the same for one friend and for six. vieuxs has never existed.

questions.q: Fix this. « Les temps sont mauvaiss. »
questions.why: mauvais, unchanged. The s is already on the end of the word, so the plural adds nothing. mauvais and vieux are the only two of the six this happens to, and it happens for the same reason both times.

questions.q: Les garçons, and the word is grand. Write the word.
questions.why: grands. It sounds exactly like grand, because the plural s on a describing word is never pronounced, so the only reason to write it is that there is more than one boy. That much is unchanged from last lesson.

questions.q: Now the same thing about les filles. Write the word.
questions.why: grandes. An e for the girls being the une kind and an s for there being several, in that order. You can hear the e clearly and you cannot hear the s at all, which is the split this whole lesson turns on.

rounds.say: The last round, and this is the half that is different from the colours.
rounds.label: Heard, or only written

questions.q: Listen to these two: « bon » then « bonne ». What changed?
questions.why: The n arrives and the vowel stops being nasal. This is the biggest change any of these six makes, and it is the opposite of bleu and bleue last lesson, which were the same sound twice.
opts: Nothing, they are the same sound
The n is now pronounced and the vowel is plain

questions.q: Listen. Is the speaker describing one thing of the un kind, or one thing of the une kind?
questions.why: The une kind. You can hear the d on the end, and the d only arrives when the e is there. On these six the ear genuinely answers this question, which it could not do for bleu or noir.

questions.q: Say this out loud: my grandmother is old.
questions.why: vieille sounds nothing like vieux, so this is one of the few places in either lesson where getting it right out loud proves you also know what to write. Most agreement is not like this.

questions.q: You hear « Les garçons sont grands » and « Le garçon est grand ». What tells you the first one is about several boys?
questions.why: Nothing in the describing word. grand and grands are one sound, so les and garçons and sont are carrying the whole message. The feminine you can hear on these six; the plural you never can, on any word, ever.
opts: The way the speaker stresses the ending
The e sound at the end
Nothing in the describing word, only the words in front of it

sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can put six of the most useful describing words in the language in front of the thing they describe, get the feminine right on all six including the three that do not follow the rule, and use bel and vieil in front of a vowel, which most courses leave for much later. You also know that on these six your ear is worth trusting for the feminine and worth ignoring for the plural. Adjective placement is next, and it takes the fact this lesson stated and turns it into the system behind it.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Colours follow the noun. These six come first. That is the sentence to keep.
Three of the six add an e. bon doubles first, and beau and vieux are replaced outright.
In front of a vowel sound, beau becomes bel and vieux becomes vieil.
vieux and mauvais already end in the plural letter, so for several things they do not move.

errorTriggers.description: Puts one of the six behind the noun, the way a colour goes. The default error on this lesson, because a1.13 taught the opposite order on every screen and nobody ever corrects this one out loud.
Reaches for the wrong one of the six, most often between bon and beau, which start the same way and mean nothing like each other.
Applies a1.13's rule to the half of this set it does not reach: writes vieuxe for vieille, beaue for belle, or bone for bonne.
Writes un beau homme or un vieux ami. Not a mistake a learner can hear themselves make, because both are perfectly pronounceable, and the correct forms are almost never taught this early.
Writes vieuxs or mauvaiss. The learner has just internalised "add an s" and applies it to the two words that already end in the letter.

Carries a1.13's conclusion across unchanged and stops listening, or listens for the plural and concludes their ear is at fault. Costs confidence rather than accuracy, which is why it gets its own drill.

grammarAssumed: Noun gender, and that un and une follow it, introduced in a1.03
le, la, l' and les, introduced in a1.04
un, une and des, introduced in a1.11
The full present of être, introduced in a1.06
The full present of avoir, introduced in a1.07
mon, ma and mes, introduced in a1.05
Adjective agreement, the four forms, and the silent plural -s, introduced in a1.13

The nasal vowels and the fact that a following vowel blocks them, introduced in sons.03
That French avoids two vowel sounds meeting, introduced in sons.07
grammarIntroduced: The prenominal position of a closed set of six common adjectives, stated as a fact about these six and not as a system
Irregular feminine formation by suppletion: beau to belle, vieux to vieille
Feminine formation with consonant doubling: bon to bonne, and the denasalisation it produces
The third masculine form before a vowel: bel and vieil
Invariance of the masculine plural on adjectives already ending in -s or -x: vieux, mauvais
That the feminine of all six is audible, in contrast with a1.13, while the plural remains silent

recorded.desc: The station break beat: « ou » read flat as an English reader writes it, then « où » in the agent's own delivery. Both must be acoustically identical, which is the point of the beat.
café, été, école, métro, télé, clé, thé, santé, idée, désolé, préféré, cinéma, étudiant. Isolated, 900ms gaps, the é clearly /e/ with no glide onto an English AY diphthong.

père, mère, frère, très, après, élève, chèvre, bière, première, collège, sincère. Isolated, 900ms gaps, the è audibly wider than the é set above. Record back to back with rec-aigu-nine in one session so the contrast is real.
fête, tête, forêt, hôpital, être, château, île, goût. Isolated, 900ms gaps. No trace of an s anywhere, which learners expect to hear once told the mark replaced one.
des/dès, métro/mètre, mais/maïs, a/à, ou/où, sur/sûr. Each pair twice: separately, then back to back with a 400ms gap. The last three pairs must be indistinguishable, and that is the take to keep.
a/à, ou/où, sur/sûr, gâteau. The three pairs must be identical takes in every measurable way. If the two halves differ the recording teaches the opposite of the mission.
mais, maïs, Noël, naïf, égoïste, Haïti. The split syllables audibly separated with a light glottal break, so ma-EESS never collapses into MEH.
français, garçon, ça, leçon, reçu, déçu, carte, ceci. The first six on a clean /s/, carte on a hard /k/ and ceci on a soft c with no tail, so the whole contrast is on one tape.

All 10 example sentences, normal and 0.65 speed, natural connected delivery rather than word by word.
All 16 dictation words, normal speed only, one clean take each. No slow pass: the dictation caps replays at three and a slow version would defeat the exercise.
The 5-line weekend message, normal and slow, plus per-line stems. Read as a voice note from a friend, not as a newsreader.

lessons.intro: French writes five marks over its letters, and none of them is decoration. Two change which vowel comes out of your mouth, one splits a syllable in two, one changes a consonant, and several change nothing you can hear at all while still deciding which word you have written. This lesson gives you the one question that sorts them, so a marked word you have never seen comes out close to right on the first try.

ipa.body: Sounds appear two ways in this course. IPA sits between slashes and is exact, the same alphabet linguists use worldwide: /ka.fe/. The respelling sits between brackets and is a reading aid for an English speaker, with the stressed syllable capitalised: [ka-FAY]. When the two disagree, trust the IPA. A small raised n, as in [frahⁿ-SEH], marks a nasal vowel: the vowel is sent through the nose, and it does NOT mean you should say an N.
ipa.title: The two notations, and what each is for

trema.body: Two dots, and the only French mark that is an instruction about SYLLABLES rather than about a sound. French normally fuses neighbouring vowels into one sound: ai is a single /ɛ/, oi is a single /wa/. A tréma on the second vowel cancels that and forces both to be said separately. mais is one syllable, MEH. maïs is two, ma-EESS, and it means corn rather than but. The dots are the entire difference between those two words, on the page and in the mouth.
trema.title: The tréma: two dots that pull two vowels apart

examples.note: maïs, two syllables
mais, one syllable
Noël, noh-EL

cedille.body: The hook under a c, and the only mark in this lesson that goes on a consonant. French c follows the same rule English c does: before e or i it is soft, an /s/, and before a, o or u it is hard, a /k/. The cédille overrides that. It appears only before a, o or u, and it forces the soft /s/ where a /k/ would otherwise be. That is why it is never needed before e or i, where the c is already soft: a word like ceci has no tail because it does not need one. Without the tail, français would be read frankay and garçon would be gar-KOHN.
cedille.title: The cédille: the tail that keeps a C soft

examples.note: français, soft c before a
garçon, soft c before o
carte, no tail, hard c

accentAigu.body: The rising stroke, and the one you will meet most. It appears on the letter e and on no other letter in the language, which makes it the easiest mark to read: é is always the same sound, /e/, the vowel in the English word day with no glide at the end. It is on the past participle of every regular verb in French, so you will see it in almost every sentence you ever read. When you meet an é, you do not have to work anything out. Say AY.
accentAigu.title: The accent aigu: the mark that only ever goes on an e

examples.note: café, the final vowel sounds
two marks, one sound, twice
three é in one word

accentGrave.body: The falling stroke, and the one mark in French that does two unrelated things depending on which letter it sits on. On an e it changes the sound: è is /ɛ/, the vowel in the English word bed, wider and flatter than é. On an a or a u it changes nothing you can hear at all: à sounds exactly like a, and où sounds exactly like ou. There it is doing grammar rather than sound, separating two words that would otherwise be spelled identically. So the question to ask is not what the mark is, it is which letter it is on.
accentGrave.title: The accent grave: two completely different jobs

examples.note: père, the è is /ɛ/
où, same sound as ou
à, same sound as a

circonflexe.body: The little hat, and the most useful mark on the page for an English reader, because it is usually a receipt. Where French now writes a circumflex, the word almost always used to carry an s that has since dropped out, and English very often borrowed the word while the s was still there. So hôpital is hospital, forêt is forest, fête is feast, île is isle. Cover the hat, imagine an s after the vowel, and you can often read a word you have never seen. On an e it also opens the vowel to /ɛ/, the same sound as è. On an a, i, o or u it makes no difference a beginner needs to hear.
circonflexe.title: The circumflex: a receipt for a letter that left

examples.note: hôpital, hospital
forêt, forest
île, isle

minimalPair.body: Two words spelled identically except for one thing, where that one thing changes the meaning. They are the sharpest tool for learning a mark, because they remove every other clue: if ou and où are different words, the mark is carrying the difference by itself and nothing else can be doing it. This lesson uses five of them. Two of the pairs sound identical and are told apart only on the page, and three of them sound genuinely different, which is the distinction worth holding on to.
minimalPair.title: A minimal pair: two words, one difference

examples.note: des, DAY
dès, DEH
sûr, identical to sur

drills.q: The é in « café » is:

drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Six words. Sort them by whether the mark changes anything you can hear.
drills.title: Which one belongs here

drills.q: Compared to « ou », the word « où » sounds:
drills.why: A grave on a u changes nothing you can hear.
drills.title: One more time

drills.title: One syllable or two

drills.q: How many syllables in « maïs »?
drills.why: The tréma splits ai apart: ma-EESS.

sections.say: Tap any row to open it.
sections.title: All twelve marked letters

letters.memo: The rising stroke rises to the front of your mouth.
letters.name: e accent aigu
letters.rule: Changes the vowel. Only ever appears on an e, and always sounds the same.
letters.sound: the vowel in day, with no glide on the end

letters.memo: The falling stroke drops your jaw.
letters.name: e accent grave
letters.rule: Changes the vowel. On an e only. On a or u the same mark is silent.
letters.sound: the vowel in bed, wider and flatter than é

letters.memo: The hat is a headstone for a letter that died.
letters.name: e accent circonflexe
letters.rule: Changes the vowel, and usually marks a lost s: fête was feste, and English kept feast.
letters.exception: On a, i, o and u the hat changes nothing a beginner needs to hear.

letters.memo: Two dots, two syllables.
letters.name: e tréma
letters.rule: Changes the syllable count, not the vowel. Two dots mean say both vowels separately.
letters.sound: forces its own syllable rather than fusing with the vowel before it

letters.memo: The tail hooks the hard sound out.
letters.name: c cédille
letters.rule: Changes the consonant. Appears only before a, o or u, where a bare c would be /k/.
letters.sound: a soft c, an s sound
letters.exception: Never appears before e or i, where c is already soft.

letters.memo: Same sound, different word.
letters.name: a accent grave
letters.rule: Changes nothing you can hear. It separates à (to) from a (has) on the page.
letters.sound: exactly the same as a plain a

letters.memo: One word, one job.
letters.name: u accent grave
letters.rule: Changes nothing you can hear, and appears in exactly one French word: où.
letters.sound: exactly the same as a plain u in ou

letters.name: a accent circonflexe
letters.rule: Marks a lost s (gâteau, and English gateau kept the shape). The sound difference is not one to chase.
letters.sound: a slightly darker a, and most speakers no longer distinguish it

letters.name: i accent circonflexe
letters.rule: Marks a lost s and nothing else: île was isle.
letters.sound: exactly the same as a plain i

letters.name: o accent circonflexe
letters.rule: Marks a lost s: hôpital was hospital. It also closes the o slightly.
letters.sound: a closed o, the vowel in boat

letters.name: u accent circonflexe
letters.rule: Changes nothing you can hear. It separates sûr (sure) from sur (on).
letters.sound: exactly the same as a plain u

letters.name: i tréma
letters.rule: Splits ai apart: mais is one syllable, maïs is two.

sections.say: There are two kinds, and they fail in different ways.
sections.body: Some pairs sound identical and are told apart only on the page: a and à, ou and où, sur and sûr. Getting those wrong is a writing error, and no amount of listening will help you. Other pairs genuinely differ in sound: des and dès, métro and mètre, mais and maïs. Getting those wrong is a speaking error, and the fix is your ear. Knowing which kind you are looking at tells you which skill to use.
sections.title: Two kinds of pair

sheets.title: The circumflex and the missing s
contains: the ones that are not lost-s

sections.say: This is the single most useful reading trick in the lesson.
sections.body: French dropped an s from a large number of words between the eleventh and eighteenth centuries and marked the gap with a circumflex. English borrowed many of those same words from French BEFORE the s left, and kept it. So the hat is frequently a pointer at an English word you already know. Cover the mark, imagine an s directly after the vowel, and read what you get.
sections.title: Why the hat is a gift to an English reader

sections.say: It is a strong pattern, not a law.
sections.body: Some circumflexes mark a lost vowel rather than a lost s (âge was aage), and some simply distinguish two words (sûr from sur, dû from du). être has no s in its history at all. Try the s first, because it works far more often than not, and drop it when the result is not a word.
sections.title: When the trick does not work

sheets.title: How to read the sounds in this course

sections.say: When the two disagree, trust the IPA.

The respelling sits between brackets and is a reading aid for an English speaker, with the stressed syllable capitalised: [ka-FAY]. When the two disagree, trust the IPA. A small raised n, as in [frahⁿ-SEH], marks a nasal vowel: the vowel is sent through the nose, and it does NOT mean you should say an N.

overview.introFr: En français, cinq accents peuvent se poser sur une lettre. Certains changent la voyelle, un sépare deux syllabes, un change une consonne, et d'autres ne changent rien à l'oral. Dans cette leçon, vous apprenez ce que chaque accent modifie.
overview.titleEn: Accents: what each mark actually changes

say.text: Six things. Every one of them is something you do, not something you know about.

goals.s: Read café, été and désolé with a clean /e/, the vowel in day, and no glide on the end of it.
Tell des from dès and métro from mètre by ear alone, with nothing else in the sentence to help.
Meet hôpital and forêt cold, put the missing s back, and recognise the English word underneath.
Say maïs as two syllables and mais as one, and know which of them means corn.
Say français and garçon with a soft c, and explain why ceci never needs the tail.
Say à, ou and sur without hunting for a sound that is not there, because some marks change nothing you can hear.

say.text: Five ideas. The rest of the lesson is these five, slowed down.

sections.hint: Swipe through. Nothing to answer yet.

cards.body: That is the whole lesson in one line. In English a mark is a flourish you can drop when typing. In French it is a letter, and dropping it can give you a different word.
cards.head: The mark is part of the letter, not decoration on it.

cards.body: The names are useful later. What you need at reading speed is one question: does this mark change the vowel, the syllable, the consonant, or nothing at all? Four answers, and every mark in French is one of them.
cards.head: Ask what it changes, not what it is called

cards.body: It only ever sits on an e, it is always the same sound, and it is on the past participle of every regular verb in the language. One mark, no exceptions, enormous coverage.
cards.head: é is the one you will meet most

cards.body: à sounds exactly like a. sûr sounds exactly like sur. The mark is still part of the letter: it is telling two words apart on the page rather than in the mouth.
cards.head: Some marks are silent, and that is not a loophole

cards.body: Four of the five sit on vowels. The cédille is the odd one out, and it does one job: it keeps a c soft in front of a, o or u.
cards.head: Only one mark touches a consonant

sections.title: Five things to hold on to

say.text: Tap any mark to open it. The full table is behind the button at the top.

letters.memo: The rising stroke rises to the front of your mouth.
letters.name: e accent aigu
letters.rule: Changes the vowel. Only ever appears on an e, and always sounds the same.
letters.sound: the vowel in day, with no glide on the end

letters.memo: The falling stroke drops your jaw.
letters.name: e accent grave
letters.rule: Changes the vowel. On an e only. On a or u the same mark is silent.
letters.sound: the vowel in bed, wider and flatter than é

letters.memo: The hat is a headstone for a letter that died.
letters.name: e accent circonflexe
letters.rule: Changes the vowel, and usually marks a lost s: fête was feste, and English kept feast.
letters.exception: On a, i, o and u the hat changes nothing a beginner needs to hear.

letters.memo: Two dots, two syllables.
letters.name: e tréma
letters.rule: Changes the syllable count, not the vowel. Two dots mean say both vowels separately.
letters.sound: forces its own syllable rather than fusing with the vowel before it

letters.memo: The tail hooks the hard sound out.
letters.name: c cédille
letters.rule: Changes the consonant. Appears only before a, o or u, where a bare c would be /k/.
letters.sound: a soft c, an s sound
letters.exception: Never appears before e or i, where c is already soft.

letters.memo: Same sound, different word.
letters.name: a accent grave
letters.rule: Changes nothing you can hear. It separates à (to) from a (has) on the page.
letters.sound: exactly the same as a plain a

letters.memo: One word, one job.
letters.name: u accent grave
letters.rule: Changes nothing you can hear, and appears in exactly one French word: où.
letters.sound: exactly the same as a plain u in ou

letters.name: a accent circonflexe
letters.rule: Marks a lost s (gâteau, and English gateau kept the shape). The sound difference is not one to chase.
letters.sound: a slightly darker a, and most speakers no longer distinguish it

letters.name: i accent circonflexe
letters.rule: Marks a lost s and nothing else: île was isle.
letters.sound: exactly the same as a plain i

letters.name: o accent circonflexe
letters.rule: Marks a lost s: hôpital was hospital. It also closes the o slightly.
letters.sound: a closed o, the vowel in boat

letters.name: u accent circonflexe
letters.rule: Changes nothing you can hear. It separates sûr (sure) from sur (on).
letters.sound: exactly the same as a plain u

letters.name: i tréma
letters.rule: Splits ai apart: mais is one syllable, maïs is two.

say.text: Three steps. The rule first, then the pairs, then you prove it.

rule.body: A grave on an e changes the vowel. On an a or a u it changes nothing you can hear. Same mark, different letter, different job. The mark is part of the letter, not decoration on it.
rule.title: On a, u and i, the mark is doing grammar

cards.tip: a is the verb, he has. à is the preposition, to or at. No sound tells them apart.
ou means or. où means where. The grave on a u appears in this one word and nowhere else.
sur means on. sûr means sure. The hat marks the lost s of the old spelling seur.
The hat on an a is a receipt for a lost s, not an instruction. Most speakers make no difference at all.

check.why: The tail forces a soft c where a hard one would be, and that only happens before a, o or u. Before e or i the c is soft already, so a cédille there would have no work to do.

say.text: Six mistakes, each one common enough that you will make at least two of them this week.

errors.why: Leaving the mark off is not a typing shortcut. The mark is part of the letter, not decoration on it, and a French reader sees a misspelling exactly as you would see cafe written cofe.
errors.wrong: writing cafe, ecole, etudiant

errors.why: é is narrow, the vowel in day with no glide. è is wide and flat, the vowel in bed. des and dès are different words and this is the only thing separating them.
errors.wrong: reading é and è as the same vowel

errors.why: The circumflex marks where the s used to be, so the s is gone from the mouth as well as the page. Put it back to recognise the word, never to pronounce it.
errors.wrong: saying an English hospital for hôpital

errors.why: The tréma is an instruction about syllables. It cancels the fusion of ai, which is why maïs is corn and mais is but.
errors.wrong: reading maïs as one syllable

errors.why: Without the tail the c sits before a or o, where French c is a hard /k/. You would be saying gar-KOHN and frankay.
errors.wrong: garcon, francais

errors.why: Some marks change nothing you can hear. On an a or a u the grave separates two words on the page, and listening harder will never reveal a difference that is not there.
errors.right: they are identical to a and ou
errors.wrong: hunting for a sound in à and où

say.text: Four rounds. Fail one and you get its drill before the next round starts.
Round one. é against è, and the hat that sounds like è.

questions.q: How is « café » pronounced?
questions.why: The é is /e/, the vowel in day. Without the mark the final e would be silent and the word would be /kaf/.

questions.q: Which letter can carry an accent aigu?
questions.why: e and nothing else. That is what makes é the most reliable mark in French: one letter, one sound, no exceptions to learn.

questions.q: Which word contains the /ɛ/ vowel, the one in bed?
questions.why: père /pɛʁ/. The grave on an e opens the vowel wide. The other three all carry é, which is the narrower /e/.

questions.q: Type the IPA vowel that « è » makes.
questions.why: è is /ɛ/, wide and flat, the vowel in the English word bed. é is /e/, narrower, the vowel in day.

questions.q: What does the circumflex in « forêt » tell you?
questions.why: forest lost its s and gained a hat. The trick works on hôpital, fête and île too, which is why a circumflex is often a free translation.
opts: the word is borrowed from English
an s used to sit after the vowel

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a lost-s circumflex?
questions.why: être is simply spelled that way and has no English cousin with an s. hospital, forest and feast all kept theirs, which is what makes the trick worth trying first.

questions.q: You hear /de/. Which word is it?
questions.why: des is /de/, the narrow vowel, and it means some. dès is /dɛ/, wide, and it means from. Here the grave really does change the sound.

questions.q: Spot the error: « Je prends le mètro. »
questions.why: The underground is métro, with an é: /me.tʁo/. mètre with a grave is the unit of length, /mɛtʁ/. One mark apart, two unrelated words.

say.text: Round two. The marks that change nothing in the mouth.

questions.q: How does « où » sound compared to « ou »?
questions.why: Identical. The grave on a u changes nothing you can hear: it exists only to separate where from or on the page.
opts: with a w at the front

questions.q: Il ___ trente ans.
questions.why: a with no mark is the verb, he has. à with the grave is the preposition, to or at. They sound the same, so only the grammar chooses.

questions.q: Je vais ___ Paris.
questions.why: Going TO somewhere takes à. The bare a is the verb form of avoir, which would make this sentence say I go has Paris.

questions.q: What is the difference between « sur » and « sûr » when spoken?
questions.why: Nothing. Both are /syʁ/. The hat marks the s that dropped out of the old spelling, and it separates on from sure on the page only.

questions.q: Type the word that means where.
questions.why: où, with the grave. It is the only French word that uses a grave on a u, and writing ou instead gives you the word for or.

questions.q: If two spellings sound identical, the mark is:
questions.why: It is doing grammar. The mark is part of the letter, not decoration on it. Leaving it off does not write the word less carefully, it writes a different word.

questions.q: Say the pair: « sur, sûr ».
questions.why: Both halves must come out identical. Any audible difference means you are inventing a sound the mark does not make.

questions.q: Which mark does « gâteau » carry, and what does it change?
questions.why: A circumflex on an a. It marks a lost s, and most speakers make no audible difference at all. A cédille never goes on a g, and there is no tréma here.
opts: a grave, and it changes the vowel
a circumflex, and it changes almost nothing
a tréma, and it splits the vowels
a cédille, and it softens the g

say.text: Round three. Two dots, and what they do to a syllable.

questions.q: How many syllables in « maïs »?
questions.why: Two: ma-EESS. The tréma cancels the fusion of ai into a single sound, which is the whole reason the dots are there.

questions.q: How many syllables in « mais »?
questions.why: One: /mɛ/. With no dots, ai behaves normally and fuses into a single vowel. This is the word that means but.

questions.q: What is a tréma an instruction about?
questions.why: Syllable count. Every other mark in this lesson is about a sound or about telling words apart. The tréma alone is about how many vowels you actually say.

questions.q: How is « Noël » said?
questions.why: Two syllables, noh-EL. Without the dots the oe would fuse, which is exactly what the tréma is there to prevent.

questions.q: Type the French word for corn.
questions.why: maïs, with the dots on the i. Spelling it mais gives you the word for but, and drops the word to one syllable.

questions.q: Which word carries a tréma?
questions.why: égoïste, on the i: ay-goh-EEST. It carries two marks doing two different jobs, since the é makes a sound and the ï splits one.

questions.q: Say it: « maïs ».
questions.why: Two clean syllables with a break between them. If it comes out as one, you have said but rather than corn.

questions.q: Tap the letters in « Noël » that carry a mark.
questions.why: Only the ë. The two dots sit on the e and force it into its own syllable, away from the o in front of it.

say.text: Round four. The only mark in the lesson that is not on a vowel.

questions.q: What does the cédille do in « français »?
questions.why: It forces the soft /s/. The c sits before an a, where a bare c would be /k/, so without the tail the word would open frankay.
opts: makes the c a soft s
makes the c a hard k

questions.q: Before which letters can a cédille appear?
questions.why: a, o and u, the three that make a c hard. Before e or i the c is already soft, so the tail would have nothing to do.

questions.q: Why does « ceci » never take a cédille?
questions.why: c before e or i is soft with no help. The cédille exists only to override a HARD c, and there is no hard c here to override.
opts: the c is already soft before e
the cédille only goes on capitals

questions.q: How would « garcon », written without the tail, be read?
questions.why: gar-KOHⁿ. The c sits before an o, so with no cédille it is a hard /k/. The tail is what makes the word sound like the one you say to a waiter.

questions.q: Type the French word for boy.
questions.why: garçon, with the tail under the c. Writing garcon changes the consonant, not just the look of it.

questions.q: Which word does NOT need a cédille?
questions.why: ceci. Its c comes before an e, so it is soft already. The other three all have a c before a or o and would go hard without the tail.

questions.q: Spot the error: « Je parle francais. »
questions.why: The c needs its tail before the a. Without it the word reads frankay, which is not a word in any language.

questions.q: Say it: « Je parle français ».
questions.why: The last word must land on a soft /s/ and a wide /ɛ/. A hard k anywhere in it means the cédille did not reach your mouth.

say.text: One idea and four rules. That is the whole lesson.

sections.body: The mark is part of the letter, not decoration on it. Every mark in French is answering one of four questions: does it change the vowel, the syllable, the consonant, or nothing at all? You now have all four answers, which means you can read a marked word you have never seen and get it close to right on the first attempt.
sections.title: What you take with you
points: é is /e/, always. è and ê are /ɛ/, wider and flatter.
A circumflex usually marks a lost s, so put one back and look for the English word.
A tréma splits two vowels into two syllables: maïs is corn, mais is but.
A cédille keeps a c soft before a, o or u, and is never needed before e or i.

segments.text: I am Liam, and this lesson is the five accent marks French uses, and what each one actually changes.
Here is the idea the whole lesson hangs on. The mark is part of the letter, not decoration on it.
café
That mark is not a flourish on the e. It is the reason you hear the last syllable at all.
Four questions cover every mark in the language. Does it change the vowel, the syllable, the consonant, or nothing at all?
Start with the vowel. The rising stroke, on an e, is always the same sound.
été
Two marks, one sound, twice. Now the falling stroke, which is wider and flatter.
père
Listen to the two of them side by side. Narrow first, then wide.
métro
mètre
One mark apart, and two unrelated words: the underground, and the unit of length.
The hat is different again. It usually marks an s that dropped out, and English often kept it.
hôpital
Cover the hat, put an s back, and there is your English word.
Your turn. Say each one after me.
Two dots next. They are not about a sound, they are about how many syllables you say.
maïs
Now without me. How do you say the word for boy, with the tail under the c?
And the word for school.
One more. The word for Christmas, and remember it is two syllables.
Two checks. First, one of these two sounds different from the other. Say the one that means from, rather than some.
Now the harder kind. These two sound identical, so say the one that means where.
Four rules worth keeping. é is narrow, è and ê are wide.
A hat usually means a lost s, so put one back and look for the English word.
Two dots mean two syllables. A tail under a c keeps it soft before a, o or u.
And when a mark changes nothing you can hear, it is still doing a job. The mark is part of the letter, not decoration on it.

recorded.desc: THE MOST IMPORTANT NOTE IN THIS LESSON. « le fils » AND « fil » ARE ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, one pace, said one immediately after the other with no gap and no reset: le fils, fil, le fils, fil. The whole point is that the SPELLING PREDICTS THE WRONG SOUND, and two separate recordings let the speaker drift so the learner hears two performances instead of two words. le fils is FEES: the l is completely silent and the final s IS pronounced. fil is FEEL: the l is pronounced and there is no s. Do not lean on either one, do not slow the fils down to make the point, and do not aspirate the s. Read them as two ordinary words that happen to sit next to each other, because that is what a learner will meet. Then « le fils de Marie » as a whole phrase in the same take, so the trap is heard inside a sentence rather than only in isolation.

« la femme » RECORDED SLOWLY IN ISOLATION ONCE, and then again at ordinary pace, in the same take. It is FAM: the vowel is the one in the English word calm, and it is the only common French word where the letter e says that. This is the pronunciation the learner will get wrong and the deck is the only place it is heard alone, so the slow reading matters more here than anywhere else in the lesson. Then « la femme » and « une femme » AS A PAIR IN ONE TAKE, read IDENTICALLY apart from the little word in front. The teaching is that the two are acoustically the same and only the article separates them, so any difference the reader performs on the noun teaches something untrue. Finally the scene lines: « Voici la femme. » and « Voici une femme. », also one take, also identical on the noun.

EVERY MASCULINE AND FEMININE PAIR IS ONE TAKE, one voice, the masculine immediately followed by its feminine with no gap: le père / la mère, le frère / la sœur, le fils / la fille, l'oncle / la tante, le cousin / la cousine, le neveu / la nièce. Recorded apart, the learner compares two performances instead of two forms, and the whole teaching of this act is that the two members of each pair differ only in the article and the person. LE COUSIN / LA COUSINE IS THE ONE TO WATCH AND IT IS THE ONLY PAIR WHERE THE NOUN ITSELF CHANGES SOUND. le cousin ends in a NASAL VOWEL with NO n consonant behind it at all; la cousine has a REAL n, because a vowel follows it. Read the masculine with nothing after the vowel and the feminine with the n clearly sounded. Do not nasalise la cousine and do not put any n at the end of le cousin. Every other pair should sound identical on the noun.

EVERY de PHRASE IS RECORDED AS A WHOLE PHRASE, NEVER AS THREE WORDS. The rule being taught is about the ORDER, so a clip of de on its own teaches nothing and a phrase assembled from three separate clips teaches the learner to pause where a French speaker does not. « la mère de Paul », « le père de Marie », « le frère de Paul », « la sœur de Marie », « la fille de Paul », « le fils de Marie », each one continuous, with the de completely unstressed and swallowed into the phrase the way it really is. THE MINIMAL PAIR IS ONE TAKE: « Marie est la sœur de Paul. » immediately followed by « Paul est le frère de Marie. » Same voice, same pace, same everything, because the two sentences differ only in which name lands after de and the learner has to hear that as the only change. Do not emphasise either name.
clipIds: Marie est la sœur de Paul.
Paul est le frère de Marie.

recorded.desc: The rest of the household as one continuous take at an even pace: la famille, les parents, la grand-mère, le grand-père, les grands-parents, le petit-fils, la petite-fille, le mari, la femme, le beau-père, la belle-mère, le demi-frère, la demi-sœur. THE NASALS MUST BE CLOSED, WITH NO n SOUND BEHIND THEM AT ALL: les parents, la grand-mère, le grand-père and les grands-parents all carry a genuine nasal vowel and the app respells them with a superscript n deliberately. A reader who sounds the n contradicts the card. In les grands-parents the d of grands is silent and the liaison does NOT happen. In le petit-fils the t of petit is silent and the s of fils IS sounded, which is the same trap as the fils clip.

The three possessives, each attached to its noun and NEVER bare: « mon père », « ma mère », « mes parents ». A bare mon teaches nothing, because the whole question is which noun it goes in front of. One take, in that order. mon carries a nasal vowel with no n sound behind it; mes parents has NO liaison between mes and parents in ordinary speech at this level and should be read without one. Then the avoir lines, also one take: « J'ai un frère et deux sœurs. », « Je n'ai pas de frère. », « Tu as des frères et sœurs ? ». The last one is a question by INTONATION ONLY, with the voice rising at the end and the words in statement order, which is how it is really asked.

Tu as des frères et sœurs ?

recorded.desc: The opening scene, French lines only, in the voice of a woman in her thirties at an ordinary conversational pace rather than a teaching pace. The beat where Salomé congratulates the learner on a marriage that has not happened (« Ah, tu es marié ? Félicitations ! ») must be WARM AND GENUINELY PLEASED, with no hint of correction, teasing or a raised eyebrow. The entire teaching depends on the learner hearing that NOTHING WENT WRONG as far as she is concerned: she has simply understood something that was not said, and any edge on that line turns an invisible error into a visible one and loses the point. The final line, « Ah d'accord ! Et lui, c'est le frère de Paul, non ? », should be equally unremarkable, because it is the rest of the lesson arriving in somebody else's ordinary speech.

lessons.intro: Twenty-two words for the people in a family, and one rule for saying whose they are that runs the opposite way round from the one your own language gave you. This is how you say who is who, name everybody, and introduce your own family out loud.

deOwner.body: English marks the owner with an apostrophe and puts them first: Paul's mother. French has no apostrophe at all, so it names the relationship first and hangs the owner off the back of it with de: la mère de Paul. The two names come out in the opposite order, and that is the whole mechanism. Whatever sits immediately after de is the one who owns, and whatever sits in front of de is the relationship. That is why la sœur de Paul and le frère de Marie can describe the same two people and still say different things. You have met de before, in a bottle of water and a lot of water, where it was doing a different job: there it measured out a quantity, and here it names a person. The order rule is the same in both, which is the useful part. Say the thing, then de, then whose it is.
deOwner.term: de, and who it points at
deOwner.title: De marks the owner, and the owner comes second.

examples.note: De points at Paul, so Paul is the one with a sister.
