rounds.say: The forms, quickly.
rounds.label: Which of the three

questions.q: You want a book. Any book. You have not said anything about books yet.
questions.why: Nothing about books is in the conversation yet, so the listener has no way of knowing which one. That is exactly what un is for.

questions.q: Which article does voiture take the first time you mention it?
questions.why: Voiture is feminine, which you settled in the gender lesson. This lesson only decides indefinite against definite; the noun decides the rest.

questions.q: Fix this. « J’achète pommes. »
questions.why: English has nothing in front of apples so nothing reminds you. French has no bare plural noun: des is the plural of un and une and it is not optional.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: Un and une are one vowel apart and there is no consonant to hold on to. Slow it down and the rounded ü of une separates cleanly.

questions.q: Write the plural of « un croissant ».
questions.why: Both halves change: the article becomes des and the noun takes its s. English would give you croissants and nothing in front of it.

rounds.say: The rule the whole lesson is about.
rounds.label: First mention, second mention

questions.q: You are new in town and you stop a stranger. « Excusez-moi, je cherche ___ hôtel. »
questions.why: They have no way of knowing which hotel you mean, and you do not mean a particular one. Ask for the hotel and you get asked which one.

questions.q: She has just told you there is a hotel behind the station. You ask: « ___ hôtel est loin ? »
questions.why: She named it one sentence ago, so you are both thinking of the same building. Le and la become l apostrophe in front of a vowel sound.

questions.q: Fix the second sentence. « Il reste une chambre. Je prends une chambre. »
questions.why: Une a second time introduces a second, different room. The room is already in the conversation, so it is the room now.

questions.q: The croissants are on the plate between you. Complete: « ___ croissants sont pour moi ? »
questions.why: You can both see them, so you can both point at the same ones. Des would be asking about croissants in general.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: Des and les are the same pair of problems as un and une: one vowel, no consonant, and the whole meaning riding on it.

rounds.say: Where English leaves the slot empty.
rounds.label: The whole of it

questions.q: Fix this. « J’aime café. »
questions.why: You are talking about coffee as a whole, and French names the whole of it. A category is the most known thing there is, so it takes le.

questions.q: "I like coffee" in French is:
questions.why: Le café here is not "the coffee". It is coffee itself, which is what English says with no article at all.

questions.q: Which of these is about coffee in general rather than one cup of it?
questions.why: The other three are all one cup or several places. Only the fourth is a statement about coffee itself, and that is the one that takes le.
opts: Il y a des cafés ici.

questions.q: You hate tomatoes. All of them, always. Complete: « Je déteste ___ tomates. »
questions.why: Hating, liking, loving and preferring all name the whole category, and a whole category takes le, la or les. Des would be some particular tomatoes.

questions.q: Fix this. « Elle aime un thé. »
questions.why: Un thé is one cup, which nobody likes in general. Aimer takes the whole of the thing, so le.

rounds.say: Two rules English gives you no help with.
rounds.label: Jobs and negatives

questions.q: Fix this. « Je suis un professeur. »
questions.why: After être a job goes in bare. English needs the article and French forbids it, so a correct English instinct is wrong every time here.

questions.q: Which one is right?
questions.why: Nothing between est and the job. The third would mean she is the lawyer you have both already been talking about.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je n’ai pas une voiture. »
questions.why: Un, une and des all collapse to de under a negative. De agrees with nothing, so there is only one form to remember.

questions.q: « J’aime le café. » Now say you do not.
questions.why: Le does not move under a negative. That asymmetry is what lets you work out afterwards which article you had used.

questions.q: You are pointing at someone across the room and telling a friend what they do.
questions.why: C'est points at a person and takes the article back. Il est describes one and takes nothing. Those are the only two shapes.

rounds.say: All of it, mixed.
rounds.label: Put it together

questions.q: You have mentioned no hotel and neither has she. Fix this. « Je cherche l’hôtel. »
questions.why: L apostrophe claims the two of you already have the same building in mind. She does not, so the question has no answer and she has to stop and ask.

questions.q: « J’ai une voiture. » Write it again, saying you do not.
questions.why: Une goes to de, not to pas une and not to pas la. The car never entered the conversation, so there is nothing for la to point at.

questions.q: Say it out loud, to a stranger in a town you do not know.
questions.why: Un runs straight into hôtel and the two become one three-syllable block. A gap between them is what makes it sound like two separate words.

questions.q: Fix this. « Il y a livres sur la table. »
questions.why: The books are new to the listener so they take des. The table is one you can both see, which is why la is already right.
accept: Il y a des livres sur la table.
questions.answer: Il y a des livres sur la table.

questions.q: What does the choice between un and le actually depend on?
questions.why: It is a fact about the conversation rather than about the noun. Gender decides un against une; this decides un against le, and it is the part that stays hard.
opts: Whether the noun is masculine or feminine
Whether the thing is one or many
Whether the sentence is a question
Whether the person listening already knows which one you mean

sections.say: Five things you did not have this morning.
sections.body: You can bring something into a French conversation and hand it over properly, which is most of what an article is for. The four traps below are worth more to you than the forms are: the forms take a morning and the traps take a year, and you have just had them all named.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Un introduces it. Le assumes you already know it.
Des is the plural of both, and English puts nothing where French puts des.
Talking about a thing in general takes le, la or les. J’aime le café.
After être a job takes nothing at all. Je suis professeur.
Under a negative un, une and des become de. Le, la and les do not move.

errorTriggers.description: Leaves the plural bare, because English has nothing in front of it to translate.
Uses le, la or les on a first mention, so the listener is asked to know something they do not.
Drops the article when talking about a thing in general, the way English does.
Puts un or une in front of a job after être, because English requires it there.
Keeps un, une or des under a negative instead of collapsing all three to de.

grammarAssumed: Every noun carries a gender, and the article in front of it is the choice that gender makes
Elision of le and la to l apostrophe in front of a vowel
grammarIntroduced: The indefinite article un, une and des, including the plural English has no equivalent for
First mention against second mention: which article a sentence wants is decided by what the listener already knows
Generalisation takes the definite article in French where English takes none
No article at all after être in front of a profession, and its exception after c’est
Under negation un, une and des all reduce to de, while le, la and les are unchanged

recorded.desc: The tens, then seventy through ninety-nine, then cent. Each number said alone with a clear pause after it, ONE TAKE straight through so the pace does not change between the seventies and the nineties. Do not splice. Also supplies the tapTable rows, the card decks and the flashcard deck.

The contrast pairs, ONE TAKE PER PAIR with both members inside it and no pause longer than a beat: soixante-douze / soixante-seize, then quatre-vingt-deux / quatre-vingt-douze, soixante-treize / quatre-vingt-treize, soixante-quinze / quatre-vingt-quinze, quatre-vingts / quatre-vingt-un, soixante / soixante-dix. Same voice, same speed. Across two takes the members are not comparable and the learner hears the difference between the recordings rather than between the numbers.

The eight listening lines, each read straight through as a whole sentence at natural pace and again at 0.65 from the same take. Never assembled from separately recorded words: the number sits mid-sentence in every one of them and the joins are exactly where the teaching lives.

lessons.intro: Eighty numbers, and above sixty-nine French stops naming them and starts calculating them out loud. Ninety-seven is four words and three operations. The skill this lesson builds is not doing the sum faster, it is not doing it at all.

theS.body: Quatre-vingts takes an S when it stands as exactly four twenties, and loses it the moment another number follows: quatre-vingts euros, but quatre-vingt-un and quatre-vingt-dix. Nothing about the sound changes either way, so this is a rule you will only ever meet on paper: a form, an address, a cheque.
theS.title: A letter that appears and disappears in writing only

arith.body: Up to sixty-nine every ten has its own word. From seventy it does not. Seventy is sixty-ten, eighty is four-twenties, ninety is four-twenties-ten, and the language expects you to hear the total rather than the parts. The cost is not difficulty, it is time: a listener who computes ninety-two has already missed the next thing the speaker said.
arith.title: Where French stops naming numbers and starts adding them

chunks.body: A French phone number is said as five two-digit numbers, not as ten digits. Zéro six, quatre-vingt-douze, soixante-quinze, and so on. Someone who cannot catch quatre-vingt-douze at speed cannot write down a number in France, which makes this range the difference between taking a contact and asking for it in writing.

etRule.body: A number ending in one takes the word et, and loses its hyphens with it: vingt et un, trente et un, quarante et un, cinquante et un, soixante et un. Seventy-one takes it too, as soixante et onze, because eleven is standing where one would. Eighty-one and ninety-one do not: quatre-vingt-un, quatre-vingt-onze. That inconsistency is the most common written error in this range.

regional.body: Belgium and Switzerland use septante for seventy and nonante for ninety, and parts of Switzerland use huitante for eighty. They mean exactly what they look like and they are standard where they are used. You do not need to produce them. You do need to have been told they exist, because meeting one with no warning sounds like a word you misheard.

sections.title: Two Numbers, One Job

sections.say: Five tens, and only four of them are new. Everything from twenty-one to sixty-nine is one of these plus a number you already have.

detail.body: The one you arrive with. Twenty-one to twenty-nine are built on it, and it is the only ten in this lesson you were already taught.
detail.title: vingt

detail.body: Thirty. The vowel is nasal, so no N is pronounced: one sound made through the nose, then a T. Thirty-one to thirty-nine follow the same pattern as the twenties.
detail.title: trente

detail.body: Forty. Two syllables, stressed on the second, with the same nasal vowel and final T as thirty. Nothing about it echoes quatre, which is the trap an eye makes and an ear does not.
detail.title: quarante

detail.body: Fifty. Two nasal vowels in one word, and a K between them. Cinq is inside it and so is the sound of quinze, which is why fifty and fifteen get mixed up in prices.
detail.title: cinquante

detail.body: Sixty, and the last ten in French with a word of its own. Everything above it is built out of this one, which is why it is worth more attention than the four before it.
detail.title: soixante

sections.title: The Tens

sections.say: One rule, six numbers, and the single most common written mistake in the whole range.
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.

cards.body: Twenty-one is three separate words with et in the middle and no hyphens anywhere. Thirty-one, forty-one, fifty-one and sixty-one all do the same thing.
cards.head: Numbers ending in one
cards.label: The rule

cards.body: Every other unit joins straight on with a hyphen and no et. That covers forty-three of the forty-nine numbers between twenty-one and sixty-nine, so the rule is the exception.
cards.head: Two to nine
cards.label: Everything else

cards.body: Seventy-one keeps the et, as soixante et onze. Eighty-one and ninety-one drop it. There is no reason underneath that you can use, and it is the error people make most.

detail.body: Seventy-one. The et is here because onze stands where un would stand. It is the only number above sixty-nine that takes one.

detail.body: Seventy-two. Douze is built with a Z that never leaves, so this one is easier to catch than most of its neighbours.
detail.title: soixante-douze

detail.body: Seventy-six. Seize ends on a Z and six ends on an S, so seventy-six and sixty-six are told apart by the last sound and nothing else.

detail.body: Seventy-seven. Three words and two operations. The S of dix says nothing here, exactly as it says nothing in dix-sept.

detail.body: Ninety-one. No et, where seventy-one took one. This and eighty-one are the two exceptions worth writing down.

detail.title: quatre-vingt-douze

detail.body: Ninety-five. Quinze ends on a Z and cinq ends on a K, so this and eighty-five are separated by the last sound alone.

sections.text:
It is half past eight and Claire is checking into a small hotel in Dijon.

« Bonjour. J’ai une réservation au nom de Lefèvre. »
« Bonjour. Chambre quatre-vingt-douze, au quatrième étage. »
« Quatre-vingt-douze. Et le petit déjeuner ? »
« De sept heures à dix heures. Ça fait quatre-vingts euros la nuit. »

Claire pays and takes the key. The lift has a sign on it.

« Le code de la porte ? »
« Soixante et onze, puis la touche verte. »
« Soixante et onze. Merci beaucoup. »

sections.body: You have counted to a hundred out loud, taken a phone number in two-digit chunks, and written the two rules that only exist on paper. What is left is the part that tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts.

sections.say: Four rounds. Miss too many in one and you get its drill before the next round starts.

rounds.say: The regular half, and the one written rule inside it.
rounds.label: Twenty-one to sixty-nine

questions.q: Which of these is twenty-one?
questions.why: A number ending in one takes et and drops its hyphens with it. Both hyphenated spellings are wrong and both are written constantly.

questions.q: Listen. Which number is it?
questions.why: Quarante-cinq is forty then five. Quarante alone stops at forty, and cinquante starts on an S rather than a K.

questions.q: Sixty-two is:
questions.why: Only numbers ending in one take et. Everything from two to nine hyphenates straight on to the ten in front of it.

questions.q: Listen. Which number is it?
questions.why: Trente-huit is thirty then eight. Trente stops short and treize is a single word with no second half at all.

questions.q: Someone has written fifty-one as « cinquante-un ». Write it properly.
questions.why: Fifty-one ends in one, so it takes et and loses its hyphen. So do twenty-one, thirty-one, forty-one and sixty-one.

questions.q: How many tens in French have a word of their own?
questions.why: Vingt, trente, quarante, cinquante and soixante. After sixty the language stops inventing words and starts adding them together.

questions.q: Listen. Which did you hear?
questions.why: One is the only number with a gender, so twenty-one becomes vingt et une in front of a feminine noun. Nothing above it does.

rounds.say: The seventies, where the arithmetic starts.
rounds.label: Sixty plus ten

questions.q: Seventy is written as:
questions.why: Seventy is sixty and ten. Septante is real and standard in Belgium and Switzerland, and it is not what France uses.

questions.q: Listen. Which number is it?
questions.why: Quinze ends on a Z and cinq ends on a K. Seventy-five and sixty-five are separated by that one sound.

questions.q: Which of these takes et?
questions.why: Seventy-one is the last number in the language to take et, because onze stands where un would. Eighty-one and ninety-one refuse it.

questions.q: Listen. Which number is it?
questions.why: Seventy-eight is sixty, ten, eight. Sixty-eight has no dix in the middle, and that syllable is the only thing between them.

questions.q: Write seventy-two in French.
questions.why: Sixty and twelve. The second half is a word you already had, which is true of every number from seventy-one to seventy-nine.

questions.q: What is the second half of soixante-seize?
questions.why: Seize is sixteen, so soixante-seize is seventy-six. Six would make it sixty-six, and a Z on the end is what tells the two apart.

questions.q: Listen. Which did you hear?
questions.why: Seventy-one is sixty and eleven, with et between them. Sixty-one ends on un, which is one nasal syllable rather than two.

rounds.say: The eighties and nineties, and the two rules that only exist on paper.
rounds.label: Four twenties

questions.q: Which is eighty, standing on its own?
questions.why: Eighty takes an S when it is exactly four twenties and nothing follows. The other three spellings are all things people write.

questions.q: Someone has written eighty-one as « quatre-vingts-un ». Write it properly.
questions.why: A number after quatre-vingt takes the S away. Eighty-one, eighty-two and ninety all lose it, and only eighty standing alone keeps it.

questions.q: Ninety-one is:
questions.why: No et, no S, and onze rather than ten plus one. Ninety-one is four twenties and eleven, hyphenated straight through.

questions.q: Listen. Which number is it?
questions.why: Douze ends on a Z and deux ends on a vowel. Ninety-two and eighty-two are one syllable apart, and this is the pair that loses people phone numbers.

questions.q: Ninety-seven decomposes as:
questions.why: Four twenties, ten, seven, in four words. Working that out is worth one reading; recognising the shape without it is worth the whole lesson.

questions.q: Someone has written ninety as « quatre-vingts-dix ». Write it properly.
questions.why: Dix is a number, and any number after quatre-vingt removes its S. Ninety therefore never carries one.

questions.q: Listen. Which did you hear?
questions.why: The S on quatre-vingts is written and never said, so eighty and eighty-one are told apart by the un on the end and by nothing else.

rounds.say: Where all of this actually happens.
rounds.label: At speed, and out loud

questions.q: Listen to the whole number. Which pair comes straight after zéro six?
questions.why: Five two-digit chunks, said once at speed, and the second one ends on douze. Nothing repeats it and nothing is written down, which is why the chunk has to be a shape you know.

audio.clip: zéro six, quatre-vingt-douze, soixante-quinze, quatre-vingt-un, trente-trois

questions.q: Say it out loud: ninety-two.
questions.why: Four syllables run together, with no pause where the arithmetic would be. A pause in the middle is the sound of somebody adding up.

questions.q: A landlord says « quatre-vingt-quinze euros ». What do you owe?
questions.why: Quatre-vingt-quinze is four twenties and fifteen. Quatre-vingt-cinq would have ended on a K sound rather than a Z.

questions.q: Listen. Which room are you in?
questions.why: Douze on the end, so ninety-two. A room number is said once and there is nothing written in front of you to check it against.

questions.q: Count out loud: seventy, eighty, ninety, a hundred.
questions.why: Three of these four are sums and the last one is not. Cent is the ceiling of this lesson and the only round word left in it.

questions.q: You will hear nonante in Belgium. It means:
questions.why: Nonante is ninety and septante is seventy. They are standard where they are used, so recognise them on sight and keep saying quatre-vingt-dix.

questions.q: The fastest way to catch a number at speed is to:
questions.why: Learn the shape, not the sum. A number you recognise costs nothing. A number you compute costs you the next sentence.
opts: learn each one as one shape

sections.say: Seven things you did not have this morning, and one line about where the numbers go next.
sections.body: You can count to a hundred, and more usefully you can catch a two-digit number inside a sentence at the speed somebody actually says it. That second thing is what a phone number, a price and a room number all require, and it is the thing no written list of the numbers can hand you.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Learn the shape, not the sum. A number you recognise costs nothing, and a number you compute costs the next sentence.
Twenty-one to sixty-nine is a ten and a unit, hyphenated. Forty-nine numbers, one pattern.
Seventy is sixty-ten, eighty is four-twenties, ninety is four-twenties-ten. Three sums, learned as three shapes.
et appears on 21, 31, 41, 51, 61 and 71, and nowhere else. Eighty-one and ninety-one refuse it.
quatre-vingts keeps its S only when nothing follows. quatre-vingt-un and quatre-vingt-dix have none.
Seventy-one to seventy-nine and ninety-one to ninety-nine reuse onze through dix-neuf unchanged, so twenty of the thirty hard numbers were already yours.
In Belgium and Switzerland you will hear septante for seventy and nonante for ninety. They mean exactly what they look like.
The next lesson takes the ceiling off: prices, years and quantities above a hundred.

segments.text: I am Camille. Today is twenty-one to a hundred, and the part of it that is arithmetic rather than vocabulary.
You could learn eighty words from a list. Catching one of them at speed is a different skill, and above sixty-nine it is the only one that matters.
Quatre-vingt-douze.
Ninety-two. Four twenties and twelve, and if you had to work that out just now, we have found the thing to fix.
Quarante-cinq.
Forty, then five. Nothing to work out, and most of this range behaves like it.
Soixante-dix. Quatre-vingts. Quatre-vingt-dix.
Sixty-ten, four twenties, four twenties and ten. Three sums, and none of them is worth doing twice. Learn the shape, not the sum.
The tens first. Say each one after me.
Trente, quarante, cinquante, soixante.
Sixty is the last one with a word of its own. After that the language adds.
Soixante-dix, quatre-vingts, quatre-vingt-dix.
And the ceiling, which is the last round word in the language until a thousand.
Cent.
Two numbers one syllable apart. Listen to the end of each.
Quatre-vingt-deux. Quatre-vingt-douze.
Deux ends on a vowel and douze ends on a Z. Eighty-two and ninety-two, and a phone number will hand you both.
Soixante-douze. Soixante-seize.
Now the written rule. Twenty-one takes et. Eighty-one does not, and neither does ninety-one.
Your turn, with nothing in front of you. Say ninety-two.
And seventy-one, which is the one that takes et.
And eighty on its own, where the S is written and never said.
One question. I will give you a number the way somebody would give it to you, and you tell me the middle pair.
Mon numéro est le zéro six, quatre-vingt-douze, soixante-quinze, quatre-vingt-un, trente-trois.
Ninety-two. Said once, at speed, with nothing written down to check it against, which is the only way you will ever get one.
Three things to keep. Seventy is sixty-ten, eighty is four-twenties, ninety is four-twenties-ten.
et appears on twenty-one through seventy-one, and never on eighty-one or ninety-one.
And quatre-vingts keeps its S only when nothing follows it.
À bientôt.

errorTriggers.description: Decomposes the number instead of recognising it, and loses the rest of the sentence while doing the arithmetic.
Puts et where it does not belong, or leaves it out where it does: quatre-vingt-et-un, or cinquante-un.
Keeps the S on quatre-vingts when a number follows it, or drops it when nothing does.
Hears one number and takes another, usually a pair one syllable apart: eighty-two for ninety-two, seventy-six for seventy-two.

A final consonant sounding, dropping or changing according to the word that follows it

recorded.desc: IL FINIT AND ILS FINISSENT, ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE, ONE VOICE, RECORDED ADJACENTLY AND IN THAT ORDER, WITH NO TEACHING PAUSE BETWEEN THEM. This is the single most important instruction in this lesson. The two are one sound apart and that sound is a final S, not a syllable: eel fee-NEE, then eel fee-NEES. Do not lengthen the plural, do not lean on the ending, do not add the faintest vowel after the S, and do not slow down for the second one. The difference must be exactly the size it is in ordinary speech, because the whole claim of the lesson is that a learner can catch it at conversational pace. RECORDED APART, IN TWO SESSIONS, THE LEARNER COMPARES TWO PERFORMANCES INSTEAD OF TWO FORMS and the teaching is lost: any drift in pace, pitch or emphasis between the halves will be heard as the difference, and the real difference will not be. The same instruction applies to every pair in this clip list, and each pair is one take.

All six forms as one continuous take, in the order the table shows them (je, tu, il, ils, nous, vous), by one voice at one speed, then the six full sentences in the same take. The first three must be INDISTINGUISHABLE from each other, because they are: three spellings and one sound. The fourth adds one S and nothing else. The last two add a whole syllable each and should sound ordinary rather than emphasised: -issons ends on a nasal vowel with no N sound on the end of it. Do not stress the verb anywhere; the weight belongs at the end of the phrase.

THE SINGULAR TRIPLE, IN ONE TAKE, AND THE THREE MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE. je finis, tu finis, il finit, then je remplis, tu remplis, il remplit. This is the opposite instruction from the usual one and it is the same instruction the contrast clip carries from the other side: do not help. Do not differentiate them, do not touch the final letter, do not let the t of finit surface. If a listener can tell any of these three apart from the audio alone, the recording has taught the opposite of what the lesson teaches. Read them at conversational pace, one after another, with no pause for teaching.

The three number pairs, EACH PAIR IN ONE TAKE BACK TO BACK, singular then plural: Elle choisit / Elles choisissent, Il réussit toujours / Ils réussissent toujours, Elle grandit vite / Elles grandissent vite. In every pair the PRONOUN must sound identical on both sides, because it is: elle and elles are one sound and so are il and ils. The only difference the learner may hear is the S at the end of the verb. Any difference in the pronoun, in pace or in emphasis destroys the pair, because the learner will use it instead of the S.

The ten naming forms, read as a flat list at conversational pace, one voice. Every one of them ends in the same EER sound and that sameness is the teaching: the learner should come away hearing -ir as one ending rather than ten word-endings. Do not vary the intonation to keep the list interesting. Keep roughly a second between them so a learner can repeat into the gap.

The opening scene, French bubbles only, one man in his forties at an ordinary shift-desk pace, mildly hurried and entirely unbothered. The last line (« D'accord. Une place à six heures. ») must be brisk and final rather than pointed: the whole scene turns on nobody minding and nobody checking, so any hint of doubt or of correction in his voice would destroy it. He is writing while he speaks and he has already moved on.
clipIds: Le bus est là à six heures.
Alors, qui finit à six heures ce soir ?
D'accord. Une place à six heures.

lessons.intro: The second of the three regular patterns, and the first verb in this course whose ending tells your ear something. Six endings, three of which arrive as a sound, and one of those three is the difference between one person and several.

stem.body: finir gives fin-. choisir gives chois-. remplir gives rempl-. Take the last two letters off the naming form and what is left does not move, whoever is speaking. That is the same machine a2.01 gave you for -er verbs, and nothing about it has changed. What has changed is the six things you put on the end of it.
stem.title: What is left when -ir comes off

examples.note: fin- with the je ending on it.
The same fin-, with the nous ending, which is longer than you expect.

nousOn.body: nous parlons is what you write. on parle is what you say. Both are correct and both mean we. on takes the same form as il, which on an -ir verb means on finit and never on finissons: the spoken we takes the short form and puts no sound on the end at all. That is the one place this lesson's rule will not help you, and it is the form you will hear most.
nousOn.title: The we that sounds singular

examples.note: The written one, with the ending you can hear.
The spoken one, taking the il form, and sounding like one person.

theSound.body: The three plural forms all have -iss- in the spelling and all three reach the ear, but not in the same way. ils finissent adds one sound, an S, right at the end of the verb: fee-NEE becomes fee-NEES and the word is still two syllables. nous finissons and vous finissez add a whole syllable each. What matters at the moment of listening is not which of those you got, it is that you got something at all, because the singular gives you nothing.
theSound.title: What the plural puts on the end

examples.note: One sound more than the singular, and nothing else.
A whole syllable more, and you would not mistake it for anything.

notThisFamily.body: partir, sortir, dormir, servir, sentir, venir, tenir, ouvrir, offrir and courir all end in -ir and not one of them takes -iss- anywhere. Several are more common than any verb in this lesson, so you will meet them early and often. They are not exceptions to this pattern; they are a different pattern, and running the machine on them produces something no French speaker says. Recognising that a verb is not in this family is worth as much as building the ones that are.
notThisFamily.title: Ending in -ir is not enough

examples.note: This one is in the family, and the plural says so out loud.
And this one is too, even though on makes it sound singular.

singularThree.body: Three spellings and one sound. -is, -is and -it all arrive as nothing, exactly the way -e, -es and -ent did on an -er verb in a2.01, so in the singular the pronoun is still carrying the person on its own. This half of a2.01 has not been taken back and it never will be. What is new is that the plural no longer joins them.
singularThree.title: je finis, tu finis, il finit

examples.note: Ends in -is.
Ends in -it, and is said exactly the same way.

sections.title: finir, all nine pronouns, in the usual order

sections.body: The singular hides the person. The plural announces itself. In the singular, je finis, tu finis and il finit are three spellings and one sound, exactly as je parle, tu parles, il parle and ils parlent were four spellings and one sound in a2.01. Nothing there has been withdrawn: out loud the singular of an -ir verb still tells you nothing about who is speaking, and the pronoun in front is still carrying it. What has changed is that the plural stopped joining them. ils finissent puts one S at the end of the verb, and the word is still two syllables, so it is a consonant that arrives rather than a beat. nous finissons and vous finissez each add a whole syllable, which nobody could miss. So three of the six now reach the ear, and one of those three is the first singular against plural pair in this course that a learner can settle without reading the page. The one place this does not hold is on. It means we, it takes the il form, and it is what almost every French speaker actually says, so the commonest spoken plural in the language sounds exactly like one person. That is not an exception to the rule so much as a reminder of what the rule is about: the rule is about the FORM, and on is grammatically singular.
sections.title: The two halves, and where the line falls

sections.body: The method has not changed since the last unit and it will not change in the next one: find the stem, add the person. What each unit gives you is a different short set of endings to add. The one after this takes the third and last regular pattern, and after it there is no regular set left to learn, only verbs that had to be memorised outright. The habit worth carrying out of this lesson is a listening habit rather than a spelling one. You have now met a verb whose ending tells you something, so from here on the question at the end of a French verb is not whether you heard anything, it is what you heard. And you have met the reason that question has a limit: the naming form of a verb does not tell you which family it is in, so ten of the commonest verbs in the language end in -ir and take none of this.
sections.title: What carries forward

sheets.title: The ten verbs
contains: The ten that end in -ir and are not here

sections.body: Every verb here builds all six of its present-tense forms from one stem plus the six endings on the other sheet, so one pattern gives you ten verbs and sixty forms, and it keeps working on verbs nobody has shown you: rougir, punir, salir, bâtir, agir and vieillir all behave identically. That is not true of every verb ending in -ir, and the exceptions are not rare ones. partir, sortir, dormir, servir, sentir, venir, tenir, ouvrir, offrir, courir all end in -ir and not one of them takes the extra sound anywhere in its present tense. Several of them are more frequent than anything on the list above, which is the awkward part: you will meet the exceptions before you have finished practising the rule. Nothing in the naming form separates the two groups, so this is the one thing in the lesson that is learnt verb by verb rather than worked out. venir and tenir have a unit of their own at a2.02. The others are worth treating as individual words for now: recognising that a verb is not in this family is most of the benefit, because it stops you producing a form that does not exist.

sections.say: Four things, and then the lesson that finishes the set.
sections.body: You can build the present tense of any regular -ir verb, including ones nobody has shown you. More than that, you can do something with your ears that a2.01 could not ask of you: hear one person against several from the verb alone, with no pronoun to help. The half of that lesson that still holds is the singular, where three spellings are one sound and the page is the only place they differ. The singular hides the person. The plural announces itself. The next unit takes the third and last set of endings, and after it there is no regular pattern left to learn.

lessons.intro: You order « un café » with confidence, but the barista pauses for half a second. Most French consonants are exactly like English. This lesson isolates the handful that are not: the throaty R, the soft J, the two-sound C and G, and the CH, GN, QU, PH, TH spellings, so you can read any word and already know which sound to make.
lessons.title: Les consonnes françaises

overview.subFr: Les consonnes : ce qui change vraiment
overview.introFr: La plupart des consonnes françaises ressemblent à l’anglais. Ce cours isole celles qui diffèrent vraiment : le R du fond de la gorge, le J adouci, la règle à deux sons du C et du G, et les groupes CH, GN, QU, PH, TH.
overview.titleEn: French Consonants: The Sounds That Actually Differ

sections.say: Picture this. You order a coffee with total confidence, but the barista pauses for half a second before understanding you. Here is the reassuring part: most French consonants are nearly identical to English. B, D, F, L, M, N, P, T, V, Z, say them the way you already do. This lesson is a short, closed list of exceptions, not a whole new system.
sections.body:
You say « un café, s’il vous plaît » with confidence, but the barista hesitates before understanding you. Your C slipped toward an S, and your R never left the tip of your tongue.

The good news: most French consonants are nearly identical to English. B, D, F, L, M, N, P, T, V, Z sound the way you already say them. This lesson is not a new consonant system, it is a short, closed list of exceptions to the one you already have.
sections.title: Why this matters

sections.say: By the end of this lesson you can produce the throat R and soft J, apply the C and G rule from spelling alone, read every forced-spelling override, and handle CH, GN, QU, PH, TH and silent H on sight.
sections.title: What you’ll master
points: Produce the throat R instead of an English or Spanish-style R.
Produce soft French J, and hear why soft G makes the identical sound.
Apply the C rule (hard before a, o, u, soft before e, i, y) on sight.
Apply the matching G rule, plus the three forced-spelling overrides: ç, gu, ge.
Read CH, GN, QU, PH, TH and silent H correctly, every time.
Tell which ten consonants need zero new muscle memory.

sections.say: Three buckets. Bucket one is unchanged from English, nothing to learn. Bucket two is a new but fixed sound: R, J, CH, GN, QU, PH, TH, H. Bucket three is a letter that switches sound depending on what follows it: C and G. Today lives almost entirely in buckets two and three.
sections.body:
Every French consonant sorts into one of three buckets. Bucket one: unchanged from English, no new skill, that’s B D F L M N P T V Z. Bucket two: a genuinely different but fixed sound, no ambiguity once learned, that’s R, J, CH, GN, QU, PH, TH, H. Bucket three: a letter that switches between two sounds depending on the next letter, that’s C and G.

This lesson spends almost all its time in buckets two and three, because that’s where every real mistake lives.
sections.title: The three buckets

sections.say: Five letters, one grid. Tap any letter to open its card: its French name, the sound it makes inside words, and an example. C and G each carry two sounds, that’s worth extra attention, and it’s exactly what the next few cards go deep on.

letters.memo: Not the American tongue-curl, not the Spanish trill. Build it from a relaxed hard G.

letters.memo: A pure hiss, voiced. No hidden d at the front.

sections.say: Building the throat R, one step at a time. Start from a relaxed hard G, drop the scrape in front of a vowel, then try it in a cluster and at the end of a word. The last card stacks five R’s into one sentence.
sections.hint: One step per card

cards.body: Say an English hard g, back of the mouth. Now let a little air rasp through instead of closing fully. That controlled scrape is R.
cards.head: Start from a hard G
cards.label: STEP 1

cards.body: Same scrape, now leading into a vowel. Hold it, don’t rush past it.
cards.head: Drop it in front of a vowel
cards.label: STEP 2

cards.body: The throat R shows up in clusters too: tr, pr, gr. Same sound, no different.
cards.head: Try it after a consonant
cards.label: STEP 3

cards.body: French never drops a final R the way some English accents do. Say it fully, twice, in this one word.
cards.head: End a word on it
cards.label: STEP 4

cards.fr: Le professeur regarde trois roses rouges.
cards.sub: The teacher looks at three red roses.
cards.body: Five throat R’s, four different positions. If this feels smooth, the sound is yours.
cards.head: Say the sentence
cards.label: CHECK

sections.say: J is always soft in French, and soft G is the exact same sound wearing a different spelling. Swipe through and say each one, feeling for that buzzy measure sound with no hard stop at the front.

cards.body: Isolate the buzzy sound in the middle of the English word measure. That, at the start of a word, is French J.

cards.label: THE SOUND

cards.body: No hard d at the front, just the buzz.
cards.head: je

cards.body: Same buzz, straight into the throat R.

cards.body: G before e, i, y makes the identical sound to J. One sound, two spellings.

cards.body: G before i, the same soft buzz again.

sections.say: The single most useful rule in this lesson. C and G both flip sound depending on the very next letter. A, o, u keeps them hard. E, i, y makes them soft. Tap any row for the detail, and watch the third and sixth rows: ç and gu are how French forces the “wrong” sound on purpose.

detail.body: A hard k. Café, comme, cuir.
detail.title: C before a, o, u

detail.body: A soft s. Ce, ici, cycle.
detail.title: C before e, i, y

detail.body: The cedilla forces a soft s even in front of a, o, u: garçon, français.
detail.title: Ç overrides the rule

detail.body: A hard g. Gare, gomme, aigu.
detail.title: G before a, o, u

detail.body: A soft zh, identical to J. Gel, gilet, gym.
detail.title: G before e, i, y

detail.body: A silent u forces a hard g even before e or i: guerre, guitare.
detail.title: GU overrides the rule

sections.frSub: C et G : la double porte
sections.title: C and G: the two-sound gate

sections.say: Three override spellings do all the work: ç forces a soft sound before a, o, u. Gu forces a hard sound before e, i. Ge forces a soft sound before a, o. Once you see them as a permission slip rather than an exception, they stop needing memorization word by word.
sections.hint: Same rule, deliberately broken

cards.body: Both hard g. The silent u in guerre exists for one reason: to keep the g hard in front of e.
cards.head: gare vs guerre

cards.body: Gel is the regular soft g before e. Guitare is the forced hard g, thanks to that same silent u.
cards.head: gel vs guitare

cards.body: Café is the regular hard c before a. Garçon needs the cedilla to force the c soft in front of o.
cards.head: café vs garçon

cards.body: GE keeps a G soft in front of a or o, by inserting a silent e. Same idea as gu, opposite direction.
cards.head: The mirror trick

sections.title: The forced-spelling trap

sections.say: CH and GN behave as single, indivisible units. CH is always the plain sh sound. GN is always one merged nasal sound, never a hard g followed by a separate n.
sections.hint: One sound each, no exceptions today

cards.body: Never the English hard ch of chair. Always the plain sh of shoe.
cards.head: CH is just sh

cards.body: Same sh, three syllables in.
cards.head: le chocolat

cards.body: Not g, then n. One merged sound, tongue on the roof of the mouth, like the ny in canyon.
cards.head: GN is one sound, not two

cards.body: Hard g at the start, GN at the end. Two rules in one small word.
cards.head: gagner

sections.frSub: CH et GN : deux sons fixes
sections.title: CH and GN: two fixed digraphs

sections.say: The vocabulary bank, sorted by sound rather than by topic: throat R words, soft J and soft G words, hard C and hard G words, then CH and GN. Tap a theme to open its own mini deck.

sections.say: A simple scanning habit turns this rule from a guess into a reflex. Spot every C and G, check the next letter, watch for the three override spellings, then speak. A few days of doing this on short phrases and it becomes automatic.
sections.frSub: Lire un C ou un G avant de le dire
steps: Spot every C and G in the phrase before you speak it.
Check the very next letter. A, O, U or a consonant means hard. E, I, Y means soft.
Watch for the three overrides: ç forces soft, gu forces hard, ge forces soft.
Say the phrase once in your head, then say it out loud.
sections.title: Read any C or G before you say it

sections.say: Four borrowed spellings, each simplified to one clean sound. QU is k, never a kw glide. PH is f. TH is t. And H, no matter where it sits, makes no sound at all.

detail.body: Never the English “kw”. Quatre is [KATR], not koo-AT-ruh.
detail.title: QU is just k

detail.body: No exceptions worth learning yet. Pharmacie, photo.
detail.title: PH is always f

detail.body: French has no equivalent of the English th in think. Thé, théâtre.
detail.title: TH is always t

detail.body: Whether at the start or mid-word, H is silent. The word opens on the next letter.
detail.title: H makes no sound

cards.body: Curling the tongue back or rolling it is the fastest signal of a foreign accent. R lives at the back of the throat.
cards.head: Using an English or Spanish R

cards.body: French J never starts with a hard d stop. It’s a pure buzz, like the middle of measure.
cards.head: Saying J like English jump
cards.label: MISTAKE 2

cards.body: Café is hard, ce is soft. The rule is fully predictable, there’s never a real reason to guess.
cards.head: Guessing the C sound

cards.body: Gare is hard, gel is soft. G follows the identical rule as C, one letter later in the alphabet.
cards.head: Guessing the G sound

cards.body: French almost never uses the hard English ch sound. It’s the plain sh of shoe.

cards.body: It looks like g then n, but it functions as a single consonant, like the ny in canyon.

sections.say: Bravo. Before the quiz, your key takeaways. Ten letters need nothing new. R is a throat scrape. J and soft G are the same buzzy sound. C and G both flip on the next letter, and ç, gu, ge are the built-in overrides. Ready? The quiz is one tap away.
sections.body: Bravo. You just isolated the handful of French consonants that genuinely differ from English, and left the other ten alone. R lives in the throat, J and soft G buzz like measure, and C and G both flip on the very next letter. One short quiz stands between you and the finish line.
sections.title: Round-up
points: Ten letters transfer free: B, D, F, L, M, N, P, T, V, Z.
R is a throat scrape, never the tongue tip.
J and soft G are the exact same buzzy sound, two spellings.
C and G both flip on the next letter: a, o, u is hard, e, i, y is soft.
Ç forces soft, GU forces hard, GE forces soft. The rule’s built-in overrides.
CH is sh, GN is one merged sound, QU is k, PH is f, TH is t, H is silent.

segments.text: Bonjour !
Welcome back to Sons. Today, French consonants, the ones that actually differ from English.

You already know ten of them by heart: B, D, F, L, M, N, P, T, V, Z. This lesson isolates the handful that don’t transfer: the throaty R, the soft J, the two-sound C and G, and four borrowed spellings.
One useful reframe before we start. You are not learning a new consonant system. You are learning a short, closed list of exceptions to the one you already have.
Today’s focus: R, J, the C and G rule, and CH, GN, QU, PH, TH, H.
Start with R. Say an English hard g, back of the mouth. Now let a little air rasp through instead of closing fully. That controlled scrape is the French R.
la rue
The street. All throat, no tongue tip. Now the soft J: isolate the buzzy middle sound of the English word measure.
je
I. No hard d at the front, just the buzz. And that same buzz is exactly what soft G sounds like too.
le gel
The gel. Now the rule that runs all of this: C and G each carry two sounds, and the very next letter decides which. A, o, u keeps them hard. E, i, y makes them soft.
le café, ce
Coffee, this. Hard, then soft. Same letter, two jobs.
Your turn. Repeat after me, slowly. The street:
la rue
Now the boy, where the cedilla forces the c soft even before o:
le garçon
And the cat, a plain sh, never the English ch:
le chat
Now say this sentence on your own, slowly. Watch the G twice, hard, then soft.
Un grand garçon regarde la guitare.

segments.expected: Un grand garçon regarde la guitare.

segments.text: Now the mountain, one merged sound for GN, not two:
Quick check. Before a, o or u, is C hard or soft?
And what does the cedilla, ç, force?

Your cheat sheet. Ten letters transfer free: B, D, F, L, M, N, P, T, V, Z. R lives in the throat. J and soft G buzz like measure. C and G both flip on the very next letter: a, o, u keeps them hard, e, i, y makes them soft, and ç, gu, ge are the overrides. CH is sh. GN is one sound. QU is k. PH is f. TH is t. H is always silent.
Bravo, à bientôt !

recorded.desc: Two readings of "Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît." First with ENGLISH rhythm: stress on VOU and CA, unstressed syllables reduced to schwa, uneven lengths. Second with French rhythm: every syllable equal length, one lengthening on PLAIT only. Same voice, same speed, back to back with a 600ms gap. The contrast IS the scene, so the two must be recorded in one take.

Six short statements, 3 to 5 syllables, read with strictly even syllable lengths and a single final lengthening: Il fait froid. / Le chat dort. / Tu lis trop. / C'est trop chaud. / Il neige beaucoup. / Je pars bientôt.. 900ms between items. Metronome-flat is the target, do not perform them.

Eight medium statements read TWICE each: first with the push on the correct group-final syllable, then with the push wrongly placed on the first content word (the English instinct). 400ms between the two readings, 900ms between pairs. Both readings must be the same speed and the same voice or the contrast is unreadable.

Eight questions and eight statements, alternating, so the rise and the fall sit next to each other: Tu viens demain ? / Vous partez déjà ? / Il pleut encore ? / C'est trop tard ?. The rise is on the final syllable only; the rest of the phrase stays flat and even.

THE MOST IMPORTANT BRIEF IN THIS LESSON. Eight pairs of sentences with identical words and different grouping. Each pair MUST be recorded in one take, back to back, 500ms apart, so the two readings are directly comparable. Pair 1 for example: "On mange, les enfants." said as TWO groups (break after mange, push on MANGE and on FANTS) then "On mange les enfants." said as ONE group (no break, single push on FANTS). If these are recorded separately or on different days the lesson loses its central argument.

The eight three-group phrases, each read with two clear breaks and three pushes, at conversational speed: Le matin, je me lève, et je pars. / Ce soir, on mange tôt, puis on sort. / En été, il fait chaud, même la nuit.. The breaks are short (roughly 200ms), not dramatic pauses.

Ten phrases for the dictée, read once at natural speed with correct even rhythm. The learner writes the phrase AND marks where the break falls, so the break must be audible: a real 200ms group boundary, not a swallowed one.

A 45-second monologue at natural conversational speed, using the long phrases (11 to 15 syllables). Rhythm fully natural, not slowed for teaching. This is the only place in the lesson where the learner hears French rhythm at real speed without a beat row on screen.

Six long phrases that stack the whole track: a silent letter, an elision, a liaison AND even rhythm in the same sentence. Read at natural speed. These are the "this is what French actually sounds like" clips and they close the lesson.

lessons.intro: You have spent this track getting individual sounds right. This lesson is about the shape they make together. French gives every syllable the same length and saves its one push for the end of the group, which is the opposite of what English does. Get this and sentences you already know start sounding French.

push.body: The slight lengthening on the last syllable of a group. Nothing gets louder: it is held, not stressed.
push.title: The push

group.body: A run of words said in one breath. The push lands at the end of each one, not once at the end of the sentence.
group.title: Rhythm group

contour.body: Whether the voice rises or falls on that final syllable. Up is a question, down is a statement.
contour.title: Contour

syllable.body: One beat of a word. French gives every one the same length, which is why nothing gets swallowed.
syllable.title: Syllable

overview.introFr: Vous avez passé ce parcours à perfectionner chaque son individuel. Cette leçon porte sur la forme qu'ils prennent ensemble. Le français donne la même durée à chaque syllabe et garde sa seule poussée pour la fin du groupe, l'inverse de l'anglais. Maîtrisez cela, et les phrases que vous connaissez déjà commencent à sonner vraiment françaises.

setting.place: A café counter

say.text: Six things, and every one of them is something you do out loud, not something you know about.

goals.s: Say a five-syllable phrase with all five syllables the same length, with nothing swallowed and nothing stretched.
Put the one lengthening on the last syllable of the group, not on the word you think matters most.
Tell a two-group phrase from a one-group phrase by ear, with no comma on the page to help you.
End a question upward and a statement downward without changing a single word.
Carry a twelve-syllable sentence without speeding up in the middle or trailing off at the end.
Read a sentence with a silent letter, an elision, a liaison and even rhythm all at once, and sound like one person saying one thing.

say.text: Five cards. The whole lesson is in these, and the rest is practice.

sections.hint: Swipe through. Five cards.

cards.body: That is the entire system. Everything else in this lesson is a consequence of it.
cards.head: Even syllables, then one push at the end.
cards.label: THE RULE

cards.body: English has strong and weak syllables: PHO-to-graph, pho-TO-gra-pher. The weak ones collapse to uh. French does not do this. Every syllable keeps its full value, which is why French can sound fast: nothing is being skipped.
cards.head: No syllable is more important
cards.label: EVEN

cards.body: It is not a stress in the English sense. Nothing gets louder. The final syllable of the group is simply held a little longer, and that is what marks the end.
cards.head: One lengthening, at the end of the group
cards.label: THE PUSH

cards.body: The push lands at the end of the GROUP, not at the end of the sentence. A long sentence has several groups, and several pushes. This is the part learners get wrong.
cards.head: A group is a breath, not a word
cards.label: THE GROUP

cards.body: Through this lesson: even chips are even syllables, the bigger outlined chip is the push, and a new row is a new group. In the respelling, the CAPS syllable is the pushed one and the | mark is the break.
cards.head: Chips, rows, and CAPS
cards.label: READING IT

say.text: One question before you move on.

check.q: In "Il fait froid", which syllable is longest?
check.why: The last one, and only slightly. The first two are exactly equal; froid is held a little longer because it ends the group. That single lengthening is the push, and it is the only thing marking the end of the phrase.

say.text: This one is different. You are not learning to add something. You are learning to stop doing something you cannot hear yourself doing.

sections.intro: English stress is automatic and it runs before you have decided anything. You do not choose to stretch the important word, you simply do, and you cannot hear it because it is what normal sounds like. So this cannot be fixed by knowing the rule. It has to become a reflex, and reflexes are built by doing.
sections.title: Training the flat line

closing.text: Do this on one French phrase a day, out loud, anywhere. Even syllables, then one push at the end. Thirty seconds a day beats an hour once.

targets.sub: For any phrase you are about to say too English
targets.label: The flat hand
steps: Hold your hand flat, palm down, in front of you.
Say the phrase while moving your hand straight sideways, at a constant speed.
If your hand wants to bounce on a syllable, that is the English stress trying to get in.
Say it again and keep the hand moving evenly all the way to the last syllable.
On the last syllable only, let the hand slow down and stop. That is the push.

targets.sub: For when a phrase keeps collapsing in the middle
targets.label: The syllable count
steps: Count the syllables on your fingers before you speak.
Say the phrase and put down one finger per syllable.
If you run out of phrase before you run out of fingers, you swallowed one.
Say it again slower, and make the swallowed syllable as long as the others.

say.text: Tap once per syllable as you say it. Keep the taps evenly spaced, and land the last one a little later than the rest.

Longer phrases now, six to eight syllables, and each one is still a single group. So there is still exactly one push, on the final syllable. Notice it does not move to the word carrying the meaning: it does not care what the sentence is about.

sections.title: The push lands at the end

items.en: The cold air bites hard outside.
He stays standing for a very long time.
The wind is finally picking up.

say.text: One question.

check.q: An English speaker says a French sentence and pushes the most important word. What has gone wrong?
check.why: French places the push by POSITION, not by meaning. It goes at the end of the group no matter which word carries the sense. Pushing the important word is the single most recognisable English accent in French.
opts: Nothing, that is also correct in French
The push belongs on the last syllable of the group, not on the important word
French has no push at all
The push should be on the first syllable

say.text: The push tells you where the group ends. The direction tells you what kind of sentence it was.

sections.hint: Six cards. Same words, different endings.

cards.body: It carries the push, and it carries the direction. Up means a question. Down means a statement. Everything before it stays flat and even either way.
cards.head: The last syllable does two things
cards.label: THE SECOND JOB

cards.body: Are you coming tomorrow? The voice goes up on the final syllable only. The rest of the phrase is as flat as a statement.
cards.head: Tu viens demain ?
cards.label: RISING

cards.body: Are you leaving already? The voice goes up on the final syllable only. The rest of the phrase is as flat as a statement.
cards.head: Vous partez déjà ?
cards.label: RISING

cards.body: Is it still raining? The voice goes up on the final syllable only. The rest of the phrase is as flat as a statement.
cards.head: Il pleut encore ?
cards.label: RISING

cards.body: Is it too late? The voice goes up on the final syllable only. The rest of the phrase is as flat as a statement.
cards.head: C'est trop tard ?
cards.label: RISING

cards.body: French can turn a statement into a question with nothing but the direction of the last syllable. No inversion, no est-ce que, no extra word. If you keep the contour flat, a question lands as a statement and gets answered as one.
cards.head: This is the whole question form
cards.label: NO WORD CHANGES

sections.frSub: Monte pour une question, descend pour une phrase

say.text: Two readings of each phrase. One is French. One is what your mouth wants to do. They are recorded back to back so you can hear the difference rather than read about it.

rule.body: English marks the important word by stretching it and shortening everything around it. In French that stretches one syllable in the middle and collapses the rest, which is the one shape French never makes.
rule.title: What English does to a French sentence

sections.title: Where an English speaker puts it

say.text: Everything so far has been one group and one push. Real sentences are longer than that.

sections.hint: Swipe. This is where the push stops being simple.

cards.body: A long sentence does not get one push at the very end. It breaks into groups, and each group gets its own. This is the part that separates a learner who knows the rule from one who can use it.
cards.head: The push is per GROUP, not per sentence
cards.label: THE CORRECTION

cards.sub: [zhay troh frwa suh ma-TAⁿ | zhuh rehst soo lay DRA]
cards.body: I'm too cold this morning, I'm staying under the covers. Two pushes, one at the end of each group. The break is where the phrase breathes.
cards.head: J'ai trop froid ce matin, je reste sous les draps.
cards.label: 2 GROUPS

cards.sub: [eel eh TAR | luh puh-tee vee-lazh dohr soo la NEHZH]
cards.body: It's late, the little village sleeps under the snow. Two pushes, one at the end of each group. The break is where the phrase breathes.
cards.head: Il est tard, le petit village dort sous la neige.
cards.label: 2 GROUPS

cards.body: In the evening, I read a little. Two pushes, one at the end of each group. The break is where the phrase breathes.
cards.head: Le soir, je lis un peu.
cards.label: 2 GROUPS

cards.sub: [luh ma-TAⁿ | zhuh bwa mohⁿ ka-fay trahⁿ-keel-MAHⁿ]
cards.body: In the morning, I drink my coffee calmly. Two pushes, one at the end of each group. The break is where the phrase breathes.
cards.head: Le matin, je bois mon café tranquillement.
cards.label: 2 GROUPS

cards.sub: [a-preh luh ruh-PA | ohⁿ marsh dahⁿ luh PARK]
cards.body: After the meal, we walk in the park. Two pushes, one at the end of each group. The break is where the phrase breathes.
cards.head: Après le repas, on marche dans le parc.
cards.label: 2 GROUPS

cards.body: A written comma usually marks a group boundary, which is why these are easy to see. But French breaks phrases where the sense breaks, and plenty of boundaries have no comma at all. The ear is the real guide.
cards.head: The comma is a clue, not the rule
cards.label: ON THE PAGE

sections.title: A comma is a breath

say.text: This is the argument for the whole lesson. Identical words. The only difference is where the phrase breaks, and it changes what the sentence means.

sections.hint: Eight pairs. Listen to both before you swipe on.

cards.body: If rhythm were only an accent thing, getting it wrong would make you sound foreign and nothing worse. It is not. Where you break a phrase can change what you said.
cards.head: Grouping is not decoration
cards.label: WHY THIS MATTERS

cards.body: He is here, my brother. Two groups: someone is here, and I am telling my brother.
cards.head: Il est là, mon frère.
cards.label: TWO GROUPS

cards.body: There is my brother. One group, no comma: my brother is the one who is here.
cards.head: Il est là mon frère.
cards.label: ONE GROUP

cards.body: We are eating, children. Two groups: I am calling the children to the table.
cards.head: On mange, les enfants.
cards.label: TWO GROUPS

cards.body: We are eating the children. One group: the children are the meal. The comma is the difference.
cards.head: On mange les enfants.
cards.label: ONE GROUP

cards.body: She is waiting, her husband. Two groups: she waits, and I am addressing her husband.
cards.head: Elle attend, son mari.
cards.label: TWO GROUPS

cards.body: She is waiting for her husband. One group: the husband is what she waits for.
cards.head: Elle attend son mari.
cards.label: ONE GROUP

cards.body: I drink, some milk. Two groups: an afterthought, tacked on.
cards.head: Je bois, du lait.
cards.label: TWO GROUPS

cards.body: I drink milk. One group: the ordinary sentence. One push, at the end.
cards.head: Je bois du lait.
cards.label: ONE GROUP

cards.body: Are you coming, with us? Two groups: the question is whether you come. With us is added.
cards.head: Tu viens, avec nous ?
cards.label: TWO GROUPS

cards.body: Are you coming with us? One group: the whole thing is one question.
cards.head: Tu viens avec nous ?
cards.label: ONE GROUP

cards.body: He talks, my neighbour. Two groups: he talks, and my neighbour is who I mean.
cards.head: Il parle, mon voisin.
cards.label: TWO GROUPS

cards.body: He is talking to my neighbour. One group: the neighbour is who he talks to.
cards.head: Il parle à mon voisin.
cards.label: ONE GROUP

cards.body: We are leaving, tomorrow morning. Two groups: we are leaving. When, is a second thought.
cards.head: On part, demain matin.
cards.label: TWO GROUPS

cards.body: We leave tomorrow morning. One group: a single plan, said in one breath.
cards.head: On part demain matin.
cards.label: ONE GROUP

cards.body: She sings, very well. Two groups: she sings. And then: very well.
cards.head: Elle chante, très bien.
cards.label: TWO GROUPS

cards.body: She sings very well. One group: one statement about how she sings.
cards.head: Elle chante très bien.
cards.label: ONE GROUP

sections.title: Same words, different meaning

say.text: One question about the pairs.

check.q: You say "On mange les enfants" as one group, with one push at the end. What have you just said?
check.why: One group makes les enfants the object of mange: they are the meal. Breaking after mange makes it a separate group and turns les enfants into who you are talking TO. Same five syllables, and the break is the only thing carrying the difference.
opts: Both readings mean the same thing

say.text: Ten phrases. Write the words, and put the comma where you hear the phrase breathe. The break is audible even when you cannot see it.
Natural speed, no beat row, nothing on screen to help. This is the first time you hear the rhythm without a picture of it.

lines.fr: Le petit garçon joue devant la grande maison.

questions.q: How many groups does the third sentence break into?
questions.why: You can hear it without counting words: the voice holds a syllable, breathes, then starts flat again. Each of those holds is the end of a group.

questions.q: Where did the speaker put the push in the last sentence?
questions.why: Position, not meaning. However long the sentence is and whatever it is about, the push lands at the end of each group.
opts: On the last syllable of each group

say.text: Ten of them, and they are long. Tap, speak, and a model plays straight after. If the middle sped up, say it again with the model.
These stack the whole track. A silent letter, an elision, a liaison and even rhythm, in the same sentence. This is what French actually sounds like.

questions.a: Rhythm. The other rules decide which sounds are there; rhythm decides how they are spaced once they are. That is why it is the last lesson before the Masterclass: it sits on top of everything else.
questions.q: Of everything this track has taught, which rule applies last, after all the others?

questions.a: One per group. Count the rows in the respelling: each | is a break, and each group ends on the CAPS syllable.
questions.q: Read the last sentence aloud. How many pushes did you make?

say.text: Not the sentences, the system. If you keep four things, keep these.

cards.back: Even syllables, then one push at the end.
cards.front: What is the rule, in one line?

cards.back: At the end of each GROUP, not once at the end of the sentence. A three-group sentence has three pushes.
cards.front: Where does the push go in a long sentence?

cards.back: Stretch the important syllable and collapse the rest to uh. French keeps every syllable at full value, which is why it can sound fast.
cards.front: What does English do that French does not?

cards.back: Take the final syllable upward instead of downward. No word changes.
cards.front: How do you turn a statement into a question?

cards.back: Yes. "On mange, les enfants" and "On mange les enfants" are the same five syllables and are not the same sentence.

say.text: Six things that go wrong, in the order you are likely to hit them.

errors.why: The English instinct: push the words that carry meaning. French pushes by position, always at the end of the group.
errors.wrong: JE voudrais un CA-fé

errors.why: English reduces unstressed syllables to uh and drops them. French does not reduce, so the syllables you would swallow in English have to stay.
errors.right: seel voo PLEH, all three syllables at full value
errors.wrong: Swallowing the middle: "s'il vous plaît" as "svouplé"

errors.why: This is the most common half-learned version of the rule. It makes a long sentence sound like one enormous word.
errors.right: One push at the end of every group
errors.wrong: One push at the very end of a long sentence

errors.why: The break is a boundary, not a silence. Too long and the sentence sounds like two sentences.
errors.right: A short breath, about two tenths of a second
errors.wrong: A dramatic pause at the comma

errors.why: In French the contour can be the only thing marking a question. Flat means statement, and it gets answered as one.
errors.wrong: Ending a question flat

errors.why: Rushing the middle is English rhythm reappearing under pressure. Even means even the whole way, including the boring parts.
errors.right: The same syllable length from the first to the last
errors.wrong: Speeding up in the middle of a long phrase

say.text: Before the quiz, a quick look at what you have covered.

sections.body: Five acts done. You have gone from three-syllable phrases to fifteen, and from one group to three. The quiz is mostly listening and speaking, because that is the only way to test something you cannot see.

stats.v: Short phrases, said flat, with nothing swallowed
At the end of the group, not on the important word
Heard by ear, and it can change the meaning
Up for a question, down for a statement

sections.title: Where you are

say.text: Five rounds. Most of them ask you to listen or to speak, because rhythm is not something you can prove on paper.
Eight on the basic shape. Two of them ask you to speak, so find somewhere you can talk out loud.

questions.q: What does French do to the syllables in a phrase?
questions.why: Every syllable keeps its full value. That is why nothing gets reduced to uh the way it does in English, and it is why French can sound fast without anything being skipped.
opts: Gives every one the same length
Stretches the important ones, shortens the rest

questions.q: Listen. How many syllables did you hear?
questions.why: Three, and all three the same length. Counting them is the first skill: an English ear tends to hear the stretched one as "the" syllable and lose the others.

questions.q: Say it: "Il fait froid."
questions.why: Three syllables, all the same length, and the last one held slightly longer. [eel feh FRWA]

questions.q: In English, what happens to an unstressed syllable?
questions.why: English reduces unstressed vowels to schwa: the second syllable of photograph is not the vowel it is spelled with. French does not reduce, so every syllable you would swallow in English has to survive.

questions.q: Listen. Which syllable was held the longest?
questions.why: The last, and only slightly. If you heard a middle syllable stand out, that was an English ear supplying a stress the speaker did not make.

questions.q: Say it: "Tu lis trop."
questions.why: Flat and even, then hold the last one. [tü lee TROH]

questions.q: Which of these is the rule, in one line?
questions.why: Even syllables, then one push at the end. That is the whole system, and everything else in the lesson follows from it.
opts: Even syllables, then one push at the end.
Stress the word that matters most

questions.q: Listen to the four-syllable phrase. How many syllables were held longer than the others?
questions.why: Exactly one, the last. If you heard two, one of them was an English stress arriving early.

say.text: Eight on placement. This is the round that catches the English instinct.

questions.q: Where does the push go in a French rhythm group?
questions.why: By position, never by meaning. French does not move the push to the important word, which is exactly what English does and why the English version is so recognisable.
opts: On the last syllable of the group
On the word that carries the meaning

questions.q:
This reading is WRONG: [EEL pluh boh-koo duh-ohr]

"Il pleut beaucoup dehors."

Type the word that should carry the push instead.
questions.why: The push goes on the last word of the group, not on the word that carries the meaning. [eel pluh boh-koo duh-OHR]

questions.q: Listen. Which word did the voice hold at the end?
questions.why: The last word of the group, every time. French marks the end by position and lets the words carry their own weight, where English would lean on whichever word it thought mattered.

questions.q: Say it, with the push at the end: "L'air froid pique fort dehors."
questions.why: Everything even, then hold the final syllable only. [lehr frwa peek fohr duh-OHR]

questions.q:
This reading is WRONG: [LUH grahⁿ lee eh kohⁿ-fohr-tabl]

"Le grand lit est confortable."

Type the word that should carry the push instead.
questions.why: The push landed early, on the first content word. That is the English instinct. It belongs on the group-final syllable: [luh grahⁿ lee eh kohⁿ-fohr-TABL]

questions.q: Does the push make the syllable louder?
questions.why: It is a lengthening, not a stress. Nothing gets louder and nothing else gets quieter, which is why it sounds so different from English emphasis.
opts: Yes, and the others get quieter
No, it is held slightly longer

questions.q: Listen. Where did the push land?
questions.why: At the end of the group, as always. Whatever the sentence is about, the position does not move.

questions.q: Say it: "Je bois un chocolat chaud."
questions.why: Resist the urge to lean on the word that matters. [zhuh bwa uhⁿ shoh-koh-la SHOH]

say.text: Eight on direction. Same words, different endings.

questions.q: How does French mark a question with no extra word and no inversion?
questions.why: The contour alone can carry it. That is why a flat question gets answered as a statement: nothing else in the sentence marked it.
opts: By taking the final syllable upward

questions.q: Listen. Was that a question or a statement?
questions.why: The final syllable went up. Everything before it was as flat as a statement, which is exactly the point: the direction is the only clue.

questions.q: Say it as a question: "Tu viens demain ?"
questions.why: Flat and even all the way, then up on the last syllable only. [tü vyaⁿ duh-MAⁿ]

questions.q: Listen. Was that a question or a statement?
questions.why: The final syllable fell. Same rhythm as the question, opposite direction on one syllable.

questions.q: What happens to the syllables BEFORE the final one in a question?
questions.why: The rise is on the last syllable only. Learners often ramp the whole phrase upward, which sounds like surprise rather than a question.
opts: They stay flat, exactly as in a statement

questions.q: Say it as a question: "Vous partez déjà ?"
questions.why: Do not ramp the whole phrase. Flat, flat, flat, then up. [voo par-tay day-ZHA]

questions.q: Listen. Does this want an answer, or agreement?
questions.why: It rose on the last syllable, so it is a question and it wants an answer. A falling ending would be a statement, wanting agreement, with not one word changed.
opts: An answer: it is a question

questions.q: Listen. The speaker meant it as a question. Did it land as one?
questions.why: A flat ending reads as a statement whatever the speaker intended. This is the single most common way a French question fails to be heard as one.

say.text: Eight on grouping. This is where the push stops being simple, and where it can change what you said.

questions.q: A sentence breaks into three groups. How many pushes does it get?
questions.why: One per group. The half-learned version of this rule puts a single push at the end of the sentence, which makes a long sentence sound like one enormous word.

questions.q: "On mange les enfants." said as ONE group. What does it mean?
questions.why: One group makes les enfants the object: they are the meal. Breaking after mange turns them into who you are speaking to. Five syllables either way, and the break is the only difference.

questions.q: Listen. How many groups did the voice break this into?
questions.why: Two, breaking after mange. That break is what turns les enfants into who you are speaking TO rather than what you are eating. One group would mean the other thing.
opts: Two, with a breath in the middle

questions.q:
"J'ai trop froid ce matin je reste sous les draps."

The voice breathes once. Type the LAST WORD before the break.

sections.body: That is the last rule in the sound track, and it is the one that ties the others together. The silent letters, the elisions and the liaisons all decide which sounds are there. Rhythm decides how they are spaced. Even syllables, then one push at the end. Say that to yourself before you speak and most of the English will fall out of your French on its own.
sections.title: What you take with you
points: Even syllables, then one push at the end.
The push is per group. A long sentence breathes several times, and each breath ends on a push.
Nothing gets louder. The final syllable is simply held a little longer.
Up is a question, down is a statement, and no word has to change.
Where you break a phrase can change what you said.

segments.text: Hi, I am Camille. This lesson is about the music of French, and the whole of it fits in one line. Even syllables, then one push at the end.
You already know the sounds. What we are fixing today is the shape they make together, because that is the part that still says English.
Il fait froid.
Three syllables, all the same length, and only the last one held. Say it with me.
Here is the whole rule, and I am going to say it the same way every time. Even syllables, then one push at the end.
English stretches the syllable it cares about and swallows the rest. French does neither. Nothing is swallowed, and the only thing marking the end is a slight hold.
Le chat dort.
Now longer. Six to eight syllables, still one group, so still one push at the very end. Listen for how flat the middle stays.
Il pleut beaucoup dehors.
L'air froid pique fort dehors.
Notice the push did not move to the important word. It does not care what the sentence is about.
Your turn without me leading. I will give you the English, you give me the French, and keep it flat until the last syllable.
Now a sentence that breaks in two. Two groups means two pushes: one at the end of each. Do not run them together.
J'ai trop froid ce matin, je reste sous les draps.

segments.expected: J'ai trop froid ce matin, je reste sous les draps.

segments.text: And one more, three groups this time. One sentence that breathes twice, not three sentences.

segments.expected: Le matin, je me lève, et je pars.

segments.text: One check. I am going to say this two ways, and only one of them is French.
If you heard the break after mange, you heard someone calling the children to the table. Without it, the children are the meal.
Three things to keep. Even syllables, then one push at the end.
The push is per group, not per sentence. A long sentence breathes several times and each breath ends on a hold.
And up is a question, down is a statement, with no word changing.
À bientôt.

errorTriggers.description: The push landed early, on the word carrying the meaning. That is the English instinct, and it needs the stop drill again.
The group boundary was missed, so a multi-group phrase came out as one long group.
