lessons.intro: Three words scale every number in French, and all three behave differently. cent takes an S in one position and loses it in the next, mille takes one nowhere, and million takes one everywhere and needs a de as well. None of it is audible, and all of it is on the form.

centS.body: cent takes an S in exactly one situation: a number stands in front of it AND nothing stands after it. deux cents, trois cents, cinq cents. Put any number behind it and the S is gone, as in deux cent cinquante and trois cent trente. Leave the front empty and there was never one to lose, as in cent mille. Nothing about the sound changes in any of the three, so this is a rule you will only ever meet on paper.
centS.title: A letter that appears only when cent is both multiplied and last

examples.note: Multiplied and final, so the S is there.
Multiplied, but cinquante follows, so the S has gone.
Not multiplied at all, so there was never one.

bareCents.body: French names the currency and then says the cents as a plain number with nothing in front of them. vingt-deux euros cinquante is 22,50. There is no word for centimes in ordinary speech and no et joining the halves, so the whole price arrives as one run at one speed. Somebody waiting for "euros and fifty cents" will still be waiting when the sentence is over.
bareCents.title: How a French price says the part after the comma

examples.note: 124,80. Six words, one price, no pause anywhere in it.

invariable.body: mille is spelled the same in every position and every quantity. deux mille, dix mille, cent mille, and a year like mille huit cent quarante. There is no situation, none at all, in which it takes an S. Learners over-generalise the S they just learned on cents and write it anyway, which is the single most common written error in this range, and it is the one thing here that has to be memorised rather than worked out.
invariable.title: mille, which has never taken an S in the history of the language

examples.note: Two thousand, and no S.
Ten thousand, and still no S.
A hundred thousand, and neither word carries one.

multiplier.body: cent, mille and million are the only words in French that scale a number. Everything else you have learned counts up to ninety-nine and stops. These three take that ninety-nine and make it a hundred times, a thousand times or a million times larger, and the number in front of them says how many of the multiplier there are. Two of them behave one way and the third behaves another, which is the entire difficulty of this lesson.
multiplier.title: The three words that decide the size of everything in front of them

examples.note: Two hundreds.
Two thousands.
Two millions, and this one is a noun.

nounNumber.body: million and milliard are nouns, not number-adjectives, so they behave like any other French noun of quantity. They take an S in the plural and they need de before the thing they count: huit millions de visiteurs, deux milliards de bouteilles. In front of a vowel that de becomes d’. cent and mille attach straight to their noun with nothing in between, which is why deux cents habitants has no de in it and huit millions de visiteurs must.
nounNumber.title: Why million needs a word to reach what it counts, and cent does not

examples.note: The de, elided to d’ before a vowel.
Eight millions, and then de before what they are.
milliard does exactly the same thing.

decimalComma.body: French writes the decimal point as a COMMA and separates thousands with a space or a narrow gap. So 1 234,56 is one thousand two hundred thirty-four point five six, and 1,25 is one and a quarter rather than a thousand two hundred fifty. An English speaker reading a shelf label straight off gets the size wrong by a factor of a thousand, in the direction that makes cheap things look expensive. This is reading knowledge and there is nothing to practise: see it once, and check the comma before you check the digits.
decimalComma.title: The punctuation mark that means the opposite of what you expect

examples.note: Written 124,80 and said with no comma in it at all.

sheets.title: The three rules, on one screen
contains: Every case of the S on cent

cols: Why it is spelled that way
rows: Nothing multiplies it, so no S.
Nothing multiplies it, and un follows. No S twice over.
Multiplied, and nothing follows. The S.
Multiplied, but cinquante follows. No S.
Multiplied, but trente follows. No S.
Multiplied, and still no S. There is no case where it has one.
mille takes the S off quatre-vingts and adds none itself.

A noun, so it reaches its noun through de, elided to d’.
A plural noun: the S is unconditional and the de is required.
milliard is a noun too, with exactly the same two habits.
sections.title: Every case, side by side

sections.body: Read the third column down the page once, then cover it and work down the first. Two of the fourteen rows carry an S on cent and both of them end on cent, which is the whole rule in a sentence: the S needs a number in front and nothing behind. Not one row carries an S on mille, and every million and milliard row carries both an S and a de. If you remember only one thing from this sheet, make it that mille is invariable, because it is the rule with no logic underneath it and the only one you cannot reconstruct from the reframe.
sections.title: What to do with this

sheets.title: What the page says and the voice does not

sections.body: French writes the decimal point as a COMMA and separates thousands with a space, often a narrow gap. English does exactly the reverse, so the same figure is 1 234,56 in France and 1,234.56 at home. That gap is never a typing error, and that comma is never a thousands mark. Reading it the English way moves the size by a factor of a hundred or a thousand, in the direction that makes a cheap thing look expensive and an expensive thing look like a bargain. It is the one convention on this sheet that costs real money, and there is nothing to practise: check the comma before you check the digits.
sections.title: The comma and the space

sections.body: 124,80 € is said cent vingt-quatre euros quatre-vingts. The comma has no spoken form at all in a price: the currency is named once and the cents follow it as a bare number, with no word between them and no et. The word centimes does exist and is used on official documents and almost nowhere else, so nobody at a till will say it and you never need to. The euro sign goes AFTER the figure with a space in front of it, as in 12,50 €. In front of the figure is the English habit.
sections.title: Saying a price

sections.body: Outside a price the comma IS said, and the word for it is virgule. 1,25 litre is un virgule vingt-cinq litre, and 1,25 % is un virgule vingt-cinq pour cent. So the same written mark is silent on a price tag and spoken on a fuel pump, a set of scales or a weather forecast. If what follows the figure is money, say nothing; if it is a unit, say virgule.
sections.title: Saying a measurement

sections.body: Any year before 2000 has two spoken forms and both are correct: mille neuf cent quatre-vingt-quinze, or dix-neuf cent quatre-vingt-quinze. The mille form works for every century and is the one to reach for when you are not sure; the century form is what most people say for the twentieth. From 2000 the second form stops existing and there is only deux mille sept, deux mille dix, deux mille vingt-six. There is no vingt cent and nobody has ever said one. On a contract or a cheque you will also see years spelled mil neuf cent, with one L. It is an old legal convention, it is not wrong, and that is the only place you will meet it.
sections.title: Both forms of a year

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do

sections.say: Three words do all the scaling in French. Two of them behave one way and the third does not, and that is not a detail.
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.

cards.body: Two hundred inhabitants, with nothing between the number and the thing counted. cent and mille sit straight against their noun the way an English number does, and there is no extra word to remember.
cards.head: They attach directly
cards.label: The first two

cards.body: Eight million visitors, and the de is not optional. Take it out and the sentence is wrong in the way a missing preposition is wrong: understood, and audibly not French.
cards.head: It needs a word to reach
cards.label: The third one

cards.body: cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun. An adjective attaches to what it counts. A noun needs de to reach it, and pluralises like any other noun. Everything else in this lesson falls out of that one line.

sections.title: Three Words, Two Kinds

sections.say: One letter, three situations, and you will never hear it in any of them.
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.

cards.body: A number stands in front of cent and nothing stands after it. That is the only situation in which the S exists. trois cents and cinq cents behave the same way.
cards.head: Multiplied, and last
cards.label: It has one

cards.body: Put anything behind cent and the S goes, whatever the number in front is doing. deux cent cinquante, trois cent trente, six cent cinquante. Same word, same sound, no letter.
cards.head: A number follows
cards.label: It loses it

cards.body: One hundred thousand. There is no number in front of cent, so there is nothing to make it plural and no S to lose. A bare cent is always spelled cent.
cards.head: Nothing multiplies it
cards.label: It never had one

sections.title: The S On Cent

sections.say: Read the third column down the page before you read anything else. The pattern is in it and it takes about four seconds.

detail.body: A hundred on its own. Nothing multiplies it, so there is nothing to agree with and never an S.
detail.title: cent

detail.body: Two hundreds, and nothing after them. Both conditions are met, so this is one of the few forms that carries the letter.
detail.title: deux cents

detail.body: Still two hundreds, but cinquante is behind it now. The S goes the moment any number follows, and nothing about the sound changes.
detail.title: deux cent cinquante

detail.body: The height of the Eiffel Tower in metres, and the form people write with an S more often than any other. trente follows, so there is none.
detail.title: trois cent trente

detail.body: Five hundreds, nothing after them, so the S is back. Add one euro to it and it becomes cinq cent un, with none.
detail.title: cinq cents

detail.body: A hundred thousand. Here cent is the multiplier rather than the thing multiplied, which is the third situation and the one people forget.

sections.title: Six Rows, One Rule

sections.say: Four lines, and the spelling of cent is different in three of them. You will not hear a single one of those differences, which is the point of doing this now.

sections.title: Cent, Inside Sentences

questions.q: How many people live in the village?

sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.

cards.body: Two thousand. Multiplied, final, both at once, neither: mille is spelled the same way in every situation there is. There is no case to learn because there is no exception.

cards.label: Never

cards.label: Not even here

cards.body: Eighteen forty. cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun. An adjective may agree, and mille is the one that never does. You have just learned an S on cents, and this is where it will follow you.

detail.body: A thousand. Said as one syllable, with no un in front of it: French does not say a thousand, it says thousand.
detail.title: mille

detail.body: Two thousand, and the form every year from 2000 onward is built on. Written with no S and no hyphen.
detail.title: deux mille

detail.body: Ten thousand. The X of dix goes silent in front of the M, so this is said dee MEEL and not deeks MEEL.
detail.title: dix mille

detail.body: Eighty thousand. quatre-vingts drops the S it would carry alone, because mille is a number and follows it. mille adds none of its own.

sections.title: Five Sentences, Five Sizes

sections.say: cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun. Six rungs, and the last two are the ones that behave like things rather than like numbers.

detail.body: The rung you arrived with. a1.27 taught it as a ceiling and this lesson uses it as a floor.
detail.title: cent

detail.body: A thousand, said with no article in front of it and spelled the same way for ever.
detail.title: mille

detail.body: Ten thousand. French has no single word for it, which English does not either, so nothing new is being asked of you here.
detail.title: dix mille

detail.body: A hundred thousand, and the last rung before the words change class. Everything up to here is an adjective.
detail.title: cent mille

sections.say: One per rule, and all three are written mistakes. Nobody will ever hear you make any of them.
sections.title: Three Traps

errors.why: mille has no plural form. The S you just learned belongs to cent and only to cent, and this is the first place it will follow you across.
errors.right: Writing it as « deux mille », which is how it is spelled in every position.
errors.wrong: Writing two thousand as « deux milles », with the S carried over from cents.

errors.why: cent keeps its S only when nothing follows it. trente follows, so it goes. This is the exact shape of the quatre-vingts rule you already met.
errors.right: Writing it as « trois cent trente », with no S at all.
errors.wrong: Writing three hundred thirty as « trois cents trente », with the S left on.

errors.why: cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun. A noun reaches what it counts through de, and dropping it is the one mistake in this lesson a listener actually notices.
errors.right: Saying « huit millions de visiteurs », with the de in place.
errors.wrong: Saying « huit millions visiteurs », with nothing between the two.

sections.title: Four Prices, Said Once

questions.q: What does the train ticket cost?
questions.why: quatre-vingts on the end is the cents, said as a bare number with no word in front of it. Nothing in the sentence marks where the euros stop and the cents start except the word euros.

questions.q: Which of the four is the largest?

questions.q: A baguette at un euro vingt costs:
questions.why: The bare number after the currency is always the cents. Read as digits it is 1,20, and the comma is what an English reader has to remember not to treat as a thousands mark.

sections.say: Nothing to practise here. Read it once, then check the comma before you check the digits for the rest of your life.

detail.body: Where English puts a comma, French puts a space or a narrow gap. A gap in a price is never a decimal point and never a typing error.
detail.title: The space is the thousands mark

detail.body: This is the misreading that costs real money, because it moves the size by a factor of a hundred in the direction that makes a bargain look like a mistake.
detail.title: The comma is the decimal point

detail.body: Written with the comma, said with nothing in its place. The comma has no spoken form at all in a price, only in a measurement.
detail.title: A price with cents

detail.body: No thousands gap because there are no thousands, and a comma because there are cents. This is the price from the last two missions, on paper.
detail.title: The two conventions together

rows.say: mille deux cent trente-quatre euros cinquante-six

detail.say: mille deux cent trente-quatre euros cinquante-six
detail.body: A space for the thousands and a comma for the cents, in the same number. Once you have read this one, every French price tag is readable.
detail.title: Both marks in one figure

sections.title: What The Label Actually Says

sections.say: Anything before 2000 has two spoken forms and both are correct. Anything after it has one.

detail.body: Both forms are current. The mille form works for every year in every century, which is why it is the one to reach for when you are not sure.
The dix-neuf cent form is the one most people use in speech for the twentieth century, and it is the one you will hear from anyone born in it.
cent has no S in either form, because quinze follows it both times. The two forms differ only in how the century is named.
From 2000 the second form stops existing. There is no vingt cent, and nobody has ever said one.
Three words, and mille sits bare in the middle of them as it always does. English says twenty ten and French does not.
This year. Every year of your life from here is deux mille plus a number you learned in the last two lessons.

sections.text:
It is a Tuesday in October and Marc is buying tickets at a museum in Paris.

« Bonjour. Deux billets, s’il vous plaît. »
« Bonjour. Ça fait trente-quatre euros cinquante. »
« Trente-quatre euros cinquante. Vous prenez la carte ? »
« Bien sûr. Le musée reçoit huit millions de visiteurs par an. »

Marc pays and looks at the leaflet she gives him.

« Le bâtiment date de mille cinq cent quarante-six ? »
« Oui. Et la pyramide, de mille neuf cent quatre-vingt-neuf. »
« Mille neuf cent quatre-vingt-neuf. Merci beaucoup. »

sections.body: You have said every multiplier out loud, read five quantities that climb by a factor of ten, and written the three rules that only exist on paper. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Four rounds, one per rule and one for where they get used. Miss too many in a round and you get its drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: One letter, three situations, and no sound at all.
rounds.label: The S on cent

questions.q: Which of these carries the S?
questions.why: deux cents is multiplied by deux and nothing follows it, which is the only situation the S survives. The other three each fail one half of that.

questions.q: Someone has written five hundred as « cinq cent ». Write it properly.
questions.why: cinq multiplies cent and nothing comes after it, so the S belongs. Add anything at all behind it, as in cinq cent un, and it goes again.

questions.q: Three hundred thirty is written:
questions.why: trente follows cent, so there is no S, and French numbers below a hundred take hyphens while the multipliers above them do not.

questions.q: Listen. Which did you hear?
questions.why: Two hundred, with the S nobody can hear. The other three are the same opening followed by another word, and each of them is a different order of magnitude.

questions.q: Write two hundred fifty in French.
questions.why: No S, because cinquante follows cent. This is the form the corpus had no card for until this lesson, and the one people write with an S.

questions.q: cent mille has no S on cent. Why?
questions.why: There is no number in front of cent here, so it was never made plural and had no S to lose. cent is multiplying mille rather than being multiplied.

questions.q: Someone has written a hundred fifty euros as « cents cinquante euros ». Write it properly.
questions.why: Nothing multiplies cent here, so there is no S even before you notice that cinquante follows it. Both halves of the rule refuse it.

rounds.say: The shortest rule here, and the one you are most likely to break.
rounds.label: Mille, which never moves

questions.q: In how many situations does mille take an S?
questions.why: None at all. mille has no plural form, which makes it the one thing in this lesson that has to be memorised rather than worked out.

questions.q: Someone has written ten thousand as « dix milles ». Write it properly.
questions.why: The S came across from cents, which is where it belongs and the only place it does. dix mille is spelled this way whatever comes before or after it.

questions.q: Write the year 1840 out in words, the form that works for any century.
questions.why: mille takes no S and cent loses its own because quarante follows. dix-huit cent quarante is also correct, and the mille form is the one that never lets you down.

questions.q: Listen. How many spectators?
questions.why: Eighty thousand. Without mille the same opening is eighty, and the syllable that separates them is the only thing standing between the two figures.

questions.q: quatre-vingt mille has no S on quatre-vingt. Why?
questions.why: mille is a number and it follows quatre-vingt, which takes the S off exactly as un does in quatre-vingt-un. That is a1.27 rule meeting this one on a single line.

questions.q: As a quantity, 1 999 is written:
questions.why: mille bare, cent with no S because a number follows, and quatre-vingt with none for the same reason. The dix-neuf cent form exists but it is for years, not quantities.

questions.q: Say it out loud: two hundred fifty thousand.
questions.why: Four words with no S anywhere in them, because a number follows cent and mille never carries one. Said as one run, the way a figure is given.

rounds.say: One word class, two habits, and both of them are visible.
rounds.label: Million, and the word after it

questions.q: Eight million visitors is:
questions.why: The S because millions is a plural noun, and de because a noun cannot touch what it counts. des would make it some of the visitors rather than that many.

questions.q: Someone has written « trois millions utilisateurs ». Write it properly.
questions.why: The de is missing, and in front of the vowel of utilisateurs it elides to d’. This is the one mistake in the lesson a French listener actually hears.

questions.q: Why does deux cents habitants have no de in it?
questions.why: An adjective attaches straight to its noun and needs nothing in between. Only million and milliard, which are nouns, have to reach across a de.

questions.q: Write two billion in French.
questions.why: milliard is a noun, so the plural S is unconditional: it does not wait for the word to be final the way cent does. A French milliard is the English billion.

questions.q: Listen. How many bottles?
questions.why: Two billion. million and milliard open on the same two syllables and separate only at the end, which is a thousandfold difference decided by one sound.

questions.q: A French milliard is:
questions.why: A thousand million, which is what English calls a billion. The French word billion means a thousand times more again and is almost never the one you want.

questions.q: Which two words attach straight to what they count, with nothing in between?
questions.why: cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun. That is the whole prediction: two of them behave like adjectives and need no de, and the third behaves like a thing and does.

rounds.say: Where all of this actually happens, which is a counter and a shelf.
rounds.label: Prices, years and the page

questions.q: The label says 1,25 €. That is:
questions.why: The comma is the decimal point in France and the space is the thousands mark. Read the other way round, a bargain looks like a mistake.
opts: one thousand two hundred fifty euros

questions.q: Listen. What does the ticket cost?
questions.why: The bare number after euros is the cents. There is no word marking the boundary, so the word euros itself is the only signal that the second half has started.

questions.q: « vingt-deux euros cinquante » means:
questions.why: Twenty-two euros and fifty cents, said with no word for the cents and no et. A speaker expecting either is still waiting when the price is over.

questions.q: Someone wrote « sept euros et cinquante centimes ». Write it the way it is actually said.
questions.why: Understandable and not what anybody says. The currency is named once and the cents follow it as a bare number, which is what makes a price one run rather than two.

questions.q: 2010 said aloud is:
questions.why: From 2000 there is one form and it is built on deux mille. There is no vingt cent, and no et in any number above a hundred.

questions.q: Write the price 124,80 the way it is said, in words.
questions.why: cent with no S because a number follows, then the cents as a bare number, and quatre-vingts keeps its own S because nothing comes after it.

questions.q: Say the price out loud: 124,80 euros.
questions.why: One run at one speed, with no pause where the comma is. A pause in the middle is the sound of somebody reading the label rather than saying the price.

sections.say: Eight things you did not have this morning, and one of them is a comma.
sections.body: You can say any number in French up to a billion, which sounds larger than it is: the numbers were never the difficulty. What you actually have is the three spelling rules that separate a form filled in correctly from one that has to be done again, and a way of reading a price tag that does not put the decimal point in the wrong place.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun. An adjective attaches to what it counts and a noun reaches it through de.
cent takes an S only when a number multiplies it and nothing follows: deux cents, but deux cent cinquante and cent mille.
mille never takes an S, in any position, in any quantity. This is the one to memorise outright.
million and milliard are nouns: an S in every plural, and de before what they count. huit millions de visiteurs, and d’ before a vowel.
A price names the currency and then says the cents as a bare number: vingt-deux euros cinquante is 22,50.
French writes a space for thousands and a comma for the decimal, so 1 234,56 and never 1,234.56.
Years before 2000 have two spoken forms, mille neuf cent and dix-neuf cent. From 2000 there is only deux mille.
A French milliard is the English billion. The French word billion is a thousand times larger and rarely what you want.

segments.text: I am Camille. Today is the numbers above a hundred, and the part of them that is grammar rather than size.
Three words do the scaling in French, and all three spell themselves differently. None of that is audible, which is why it is worth twenty minutes.
Deux cents. Deux mille. Deux millions de.
One of those has an S you cannot hear, one has none anywhere, and one needs a word after it. That is the lesson.
Deux cents habitants.
Two hundred inhabitants. cent is multiplied and nothing follows it, so it takes an S.
Deux cent cinquante euros.
Same word, and the S has gone, because cinquante is behind it now. cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun.
The hundreds first. Say each one after me.
Deux cents. Trois cents. Cinq cents.
Now the thousands, and listen for a letter that is not there.
Mille. Deux mille. Cent mille.
And the two that are nouns, which need a word before what they count.
Un million d’habitants. Deux milliards.
Two figures three noughts apart. Listen to the middle of each.
Cent mille. Un million.
A hundred thousand and a million. In a sentence they open on the same sound and separate at the end.
Now a price, which arrives as one run. There is no word for the cents.
Cent vingt-quatre euros quatre-vingts.
A hundred twenty-four euros eighty, written with a comma you will never hear.
Your turn, with nothing in front of you. Say two hundred fifty.
Now a hundred thousand, where neither word takes an S.
And a million inhabitants, with the word that reaches them.
One question, and it is the only rule here a listener can hear you break. I will say a quantity and you tell me the word that sits between the number and the thing.
Le musée du Louvre reçoit huit millions de visiteurs par an.
de. Leave it out and the sentence is still understood and audibly not French, which is the only mistake in this lesson anybody will notice out loud.
Three things to keep. cent takes an S only when a number multiplies it and nothing follows.
mille never takes one, in any position. That is the one to memorise rather than work out.
And million and milliard take an S and a de, because they are nouns.
À bientôt.

errorTriggers.description: Keeps the S on cent when a number follows it, or drops it when nothing does, or adds one to a cent that was never multiplied.
Writes mille with an S, carrying the plural across from cents. The corpus contains no example of this, so the lesson has to stage it.
Drops the de after million or milliard, or leaves the plural S off it, treating a noun as if it were a number-adjective.
Hears a price as two separate numbers, or reads a written decimal comma as a thousands separator and gets the size wrong by a factor of a hundred.

grammarAssumed: Every number from un to cent, including the S on quatre-vingts and where et appears
A final consonant sounding, dropping or changing according to the word that follows it
grammarIntroduced: The agreement of cent when multiplied and final, and its loss before a following number
The invariability of mille in every position
million and milliard as nouns of quantity: plural agreement, and de before the noun counted
The French decimal comma and space-separated thousands, and how a price is said aloud

acts.title: A word you already own
acts.milestone: You have watched one syllable decide what somebody handed you.

acts.title: One of them, or some of it
acts.milestone: You can hear the difference between a thing and an amount of it.

acts.title: When the article disappears
acts.milestone: Two rules that both end in a bare de, and one that does not move at all.

acts.title: The other du, and the words banked
acts.milestone: You have separated two identical words, spelled them and said them out loud.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete.

recorded.desc: The ten amounts of the group drill, read in ONE TAKE by ONE voice at ONE speed. The learner is comparing four shapes of the same word, so a set split across takes has them comparing four performances instead. Keep du tight and rounded: it is /y/, not /u/ and not /ø/, and a relaxed reading of it lands on deux.

The two minimal pairs this lesson turns on, un against du and du against de, each pair recorded BACK TO BACK IN ONE TAKE by the same voice at the same speed, in the same way sons.07 pins rec-h-pairs and a1.11 pins rec-a1-11-pairs. Both pairs are one vowel and both carry the whole meaning. Then the four listening lines at natural pace and again at 0.65. The warning that matters: DO NOT OVER-ROUND du. Lengthened or relaxed it becomes deux, which is a real word a learner could plausibly have heard, and the exercise stops being about articles.

The four English-speaker traps, wrong form then right form, with a clear beat between them so the learner hears the difference rather than a correction. Je mange pain / Je mange du pain. Je voudrais un café / Je voudrais du café. Beaucoup du café / Beaucoup de café. Je ne mange pas du pain / Je ne mange pas de pain. Read the wrong version plainly, not comically: two of these four are things a French speaker says.

lessons.intro: Anyone can learn that du is masculine and de la is feminine; that takes five minutes and the noun decides it anyway. What stays hard is a line English never makes you draw. Un café and du café are both correct, they order different things, and nothing will correct you.

otherDu.body: Près du lit, le plat du jour, l apostrophe odeur du pain. None of these is about an amount of anything: they are de and le squeezed together, which French does automatically, and you have been reading them since your first lesson. Four out of five of the du in this corpus are this one. The test is whether you could put "some" in front of the English: some bread yes, some the bed no.
otherDu.title: The same three letters doing a different job

examples.note: Near the bed. There is no amount of bed involved.
The smell of the bread. The bread is a particular one, on a particular morning.

someOfIt.body: Use these when you mean some of a thing rather than a number of them. Du in front of most nouns, de la in front of the ones that take la, and de l apostrophe in front of a word starting with a vowel sound. English usually puts nothing here, or the word "some" when it wants to be careful, so there is nothing in your own language reminding you that French wants a word at all.
someOfIt.title: The word for an amount nobody has counted

examples.note: Bread, not a loaf. Nobody has weighed it.
Water, not a bottle. De l apostrophe because eau opens on a vowel sound.

deUnderNo.body: Je mange du pain becomes je ne mange pas de pain. You met this rule one lesson ago on un, une and des, and it is the same rule here with nothing added: say no and what was in front of the noun collapses to de. Before a vowel sound it shortens again, to d apostrophe. The one that does not move is le, la and les, which is how you can work out afterwards which word you had used.
deUnderNo.title: What is left once you say no

examples.note: Du went to de. Not pas du pain, and not pas le pain.
The sentence you need on your first day if you do not eat meat.

inGeneral.body: J'aime le café is I like coffee, all of it, for the rest of your life. That is a1.04's rule and it is here only so you can see it is not the answer to this lesson's question. Le names the whole category or the particular one you have both been talking about. Du names part of it, right now, on this table. Both look wrong to an English speaker and only one of them is what you meant.
inGeneral.title: The word for the whole of something

examples.note: Some of what is in the pot, now.
Buying cheese, so an amount of it, even though aimer is in the sentence.

oneOfThem.body: Use these when you mean one of something: one cup, one loaf, one apple. This is the half English gives you for free, because English has a and an and uses them in the same place. The trap is that it also works in front of the same nouns: un café and du café are both correct and they are two different orders.
oneOfThem.title: The word for a thing you can count

examples.note: One cup, on a saucer, at a counter.
One whole loaf, wrapped and paid for.

namedQuantity.body: Say how much and the article in front of the noun disappears. Beaucoup de café, un peu de sel, trop de sucre, and never beaucoup du café. Containers behave the same way, because a container is a quantity with a shape: un kilo de tomates, une bouteille d apostrophe eau, une tranche de fromage. This is completely regular and it is the opposite of what an English speaker expects, since English keeps "of the" in "a lot of the coffee".
namedQuantity.title: What is left once a quantity is named

examples.note: The same sentence as Je bois du café, with a quantity named.
A kilo is a quantity, so the noun goes in bare behind it.

lessons.title: Les articles partitifs

drills.coach: Read the English on the left. Say the French on the right, out loud, and do not let the word in front go missing.
drills.title: The word English leaves out

drills.q: You are telling somebody what you eat in the morning. Bread.
drills.why: French does not leave the slot empty after a verb. An amount of bread takes du.
opts: Je mange du pain le matin.
Je mange le pain le matin.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Read each line and ask one question: could you count what is being asked for? If not, it is du, de la or de l apostrophe.
drills.title: A thing, or some of a thing?

drills.q: You want cheese for the table. Not a whole cheese.
drills.why: Un fromage is one whole wheel and a stall will hand you one. Du fromage is an amount of it.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: The left is the sentence without a quantity. Say the right out loud, and notice what is no longer in it.
pairs: Je mets un peu de sel.
drills.title: Say how much, lose the word

drills.q: "A lot of coffee" in French is:
drills.why: Beaucoup already says how much, so nothing goes between it and the noun.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Say the negative out loud before you flip. Four of these collapse to de and one does not move at all.
pairs: Je ne mange pas de pain.
Je ne fais pas de soupe.
Je ne mange pas de légumes.
drills.title: Say no and watch it shrink

drills.q: Which sentence has a word in front of the noun that did NOT change?
drills.why: Le, la and les survive a negative untouched. Only du, de la, de l apostrophe and des collapse to de.
opts: Je ne mange pas de pain.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Put "some" in front of the English. Some bread works, so that one is an amount. Some the bed does not.
drills.title: An amount, or of the?

drills.q: Which one is NOT about an amount of something?
drills.why: À côté du salon is of the living room. There is no quantity of living room in it.
opts: Il ajoute du sel dans la soupe.
La cuisine est à côté du salon.
drills.title: One more time

contains: One of them against some of it

sections.title: One of them, some of it, all of it

rows.v: Je mange du pain, not Je mange pain. French does not leave that slot empty.
Un café is a cup. Du café is coffee. Both correct, and they order different things.
beaucoup de café, un peu de sel, trop de sucre. Never beaucoup du café.
un kilo de tomates, une tranche de fromage, une bouteille d’eau.
Je ne mange pas de pain. Du, de la, de l' and des all become de.
rows.say: Je ne mange pas de pain.

rows.v: Je n'aime pas le pain. Le, la and les do not move at all.

sections.title: The four places English points the wrong way

sections.body: Across the a1 corpus, roughly four rows in five holding du, de la or de l apostrophe are not about an amount at all. They are de and le squeezed together, and they turn up after a preposition (près du lit, à côté du salon), between two nouns (l odeur du pain, le plat du jour, la fin du repas), and in fixed compounds you already own (l emploi du temps). The test is one second long: put "some" in front of the English. Some bread works, so je mange du pain is this lesson. Some the bed does not, so près du lit is the other one. Nothing else in French depends on getting this right, but everything you READ does, because you will otherwise be looking for a quantity in four sentences out of five that do not have one.
sections.title: Telling the two du apart

lessons.reframe: Un is one of them. Du is some of it.

overview.introFr: Un café ou du café ? Les deux sont corrects, et ils ne commandent pas la même chose.

say.text: Watch this go wrong on a word you already know. Nothing here is mispronounced and nothing here is rude.

beats.text: Saturday morning in Lyon. You are cooking for two people tonight and you need bread for the table.
There is a queue behind you and the baker is already looking up. You know every word you need.

beats.prompt: One sentence, and the queue is waiting. Which one?

options.en: asking for a loaf
options.fr: Je voudrais un pain, s'il vous plaît.

options.en: asking for bread
options.fr: Je voudrais du pain, s'il vous plaît.

followUp.works: Yes. You want bread rather than a particular object, and du is how you say so.
followUp.breaks: Every word is correct. Watch what she reaches for.

beats.en: (I would like a loaf, please)
beats.fr: Je voudrais un pain, s'il vous plaît.

beats.en: A big one or a small one?
beats.stage: Her hand is already on a round loaf the size of a dinner plate.
beats.speaker: The baker

beats.body: A pain is a thing, sold by the piece, with a price of its own. Du pain is bread: an amount, cut to whatever you need. She was not confused for a second, and that is the problem.
beats.coach: Same shop, same noun, one syllable different. One of them is a thing and one of them is an amount.

right.en: bread, as much or as little as you need

wrong.en: one loaf, the round kind, wrapped and paid for

beats.heading: You ordered an object

beats.en: I would like some bread, please.
beats.fr: Je voudrais du pain, s'il vous plaît.
beats.speaker: Second try

beats.en: Half a baguette, will that do?
beats.stage: She has already left the round loaves alone.
beats.speaker: The baker

beats.text: She heard the difference before you finished the sentence, and served a different thing.

sections.title: The Loaf He Did Not Want

closing.text: Un is one of them. Du is some of it. She served the second one without being asked twice.

setting.place: A bakery on a corner, two streets from the market

sections.say: Un is one of them. Du is some of it. By the end of this lesson you will know which of the two a sentence wants, and the four places your English will hand you the wrong one.

goals.s: Order bread, coffee, water or cheese without accidentally ordering one whole object of it.
Hear the difference between a cup of coffee and coffee, and say which one you meant.
Name a quantity or a container and know that the word in front of the noun now goes.
Spot the du that is about an amount and the du that is nothing of the kind.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do

sections.say: You already own one of these four and nobody told you. Start there rather than with a table.
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.

cards.body: Last lesson des was the plural of un and une, and it is. It is also the plural of the three words on the next card, and it has been doing that job the whole time.
cards.head: You have been saying this
cards.label: Already yours

cards.body: Du in front of most nouns, de la in front of the ones that take la, and de l apostrophe when the next word starts with a vowel sound.
cards.head: One word, three shapes
cards.label: The other three

cards.sub: pain takes le, soupe takes la
cards.body: Which of the three you use is settled by the noun, and you settled that two lessons ago. Nothing new is being asked of you here, so it gets one screen and one drill.
cards.head: The noun decides, not you
cards.label: Revision, not teaching

cards.body: Un is one of them. Du is some of it. Every card after this one is that sentence in a different situation.
cards.head: What all four are for

sections.frSub: Du, de la, de l', des
sections.title: The Fourth One Is Yours

sections.say: Ten amounts, one per screen. The noun tells you which shape to use, so the only work is saying it.
sections.title: Say the Amount

sections.say: Un is one of them. Du is some of it. Both columns are correct French. Tap any row to hear the two of them back to back.

detail.say: Je prends un café. Je prends du café.
detail.body: Un café is one cup, on a saucer, at a counter. Du café is coffee: what is in the pot, what you want rather than tea, an amount nobody has measured. Order the first and one arrives.
detail.title: un café · du café

detail.say: Je voudrais un pain. Je voudrais du pain.
detail.body: Un pain is a loaf, the big round kind, sold by the piece. Du pain is bread, cut to whatever you need. This is the pair the bakery scene turns on and it is the one you will meet first.
detail.title: un pain · du pain

detail.say: Un fromage entier ? Non, du fromage.
detail.body: Un fromage is a whole cheese, the wheel on the board behind the counter. Du fromage is cheese, the thing you eat some of after a meal. Ask for the first at a market stall and you will be taken seriously.
detail.title: un fromage · du fromage

detail.say: Je prends une salade. Je fais de la salade.
detail.body: Une salade is a dish somebody brings you. De la salade is salad, the leaves, some of what is in the bowl. Salade takes la, so its amount form is de la rather than du. That is the only difference.
detail.title: une salade · de la salade

detail.say: J'entends un bruit. Il y a du bruit.
detail.body: Not food, and it is the same choice exactly. Un bruit is one noise, a single sound you heard once. Du bruit is noise, the kind the neighbours make. Nothing about this rule is about eating.
detail.title: un bruit · du bruit

sections.title: One Cup, or Coffee

sections.say: Un is one of them. Du is some of it. One noun in this passage arrives both ways in the same breath, and somebody says out loud what changed.
sections.text: It is Saturday morning and Claire is buying lunch for three people. The bakery smells of the ovens at the back, and there is a queue. « Bonjour madame. Je voudrais du pain, s'il vous plaît. » The baker reaches past the round loaves and picks up a half baguette instead. « Voilà. Et avec ça ? » Claire crosses the road to the cheese stall, where a man is already holding a knife. « Je voudrais du fromage. » He puts a whole wheel of comté on the board, the size of a car wheel, and waits. « Un fromage entier ? » Claire looks at it, and then says the sentence that fixes everything. « Non, pas un fromage. Du fromage. Une tranche, s'il vous plaît. » He cuts a slice and wraps it, and she remembers who she is cooking for tonight. « Il ne mange pas de fromage, lui. De la salade, alors. » The man laughs and reaches for the salad without putting the knife down. « Et de l'eau ? Il y a de l'eau à côté du pain. » Claire takes a bottle from the shelf beside the bread and pays for all of it. « Une bouteille d'eau. Merci beaucoup. »
sections.title: Saturday at the Market

glossary.note: Bread, cut to whatever she needs. Not a loaf, which would be un pain.
Cheese, an amount of it. The man hears something else, and that is the next line.
One cheese, the entire wheel. A real thing to order, and not what she meant.
Name the quantity and the article in front of the noun goes: une tranche de fromage.
Say no and du collapses to de. The same rule you met last lesson on un and des.
Salade takes la, so its amount form is de la. The noun decides, as always.
Eau opens on a vowel sound, so de la shortens to de l apostrophe.
This du is not about an amount of anything. It is de and le stuck together, meaning of the.
A container is a quantity with a shape, so it takes bare de, and d apostrophe before the vowel.

questions.a: He heard the question as being about one cheese rather than an amount of one, which is why she corrects it to du fromage in the next line.
questions.q: Claire asks for « du fromage » and the man puts a whole wheel on the board. What did he hear?

questions.a: Nothing about the cheese. Un fromage is one whole object you could carry out; du fromage is some of it, cut to size.
questions.q: What is different about « un fromage » and « du fromage »?

questions.a: « à côté du pain » means next to the bread. That du is de and le squeezed together, and it says where the water is rather than how much bread there is.
questions.q: The word « du » appears in the last exchange and it is not about an amount. Where, and what is it doing?

sections.say: Du against de, and du against deux. All three are one vowel and all three change what the sentence asks for.

lines.en: I drink a lot of coffee.

sections.title: Du, De, or Deux?

questions.q: In the first line, how much bread is being asked for?
questions.why: Du is the whole answer. It says the speaker wants bread without saying how much, and the baker decides the rest.
opts: All the bread in the shop

questions.q: What separates the third line from the fourth, at speed?
questions.why: Beaucoup already says how much, so French drops the word in front of the noun. Beaucoup du café is never said.
opts: The fourth names a quantity, so du goes

questions.q: Which pair is hardest to tell apart when somebody speaks quickly?
questions.why: Each pair differs by one rounded vowel and nothing else, so the ear has no consonant to hold on to. Slow the audio and all three separate cleanly.

cards.fr: un peu de · assez de · trop de
cards.body: Every quantity word behaves the same way. Un peu de sel, assez de pain, trop de sucre, moins de bruit. There are no exceptions to find.
cards.head: It is not just beaucoup

cards.body: De shortens in front of a vowel sound, exactly the way le and la do. Beaucoup d apostrophe eau, un peu d apostrophe huile.

cards.label: Before a vowel

cards.body: English says "a lot of the coffee" and keeps everything. French takes the article out the moment the quantity is named. Un is one of them. Du is some of it. Say how much, and neither one is needed.

rows.say: Je mange du pain. Je ne mange pas de pain.

detail.say: Je ne mange pas de pain.

rows.say: Je fais de la soupe. Je ne fais pas de soupe.

detail.say: Je ne fais pas de soupe.
detail.body: The la disappears with it. De does not agree with anything, which is one fewer thing to get right rather than one more.
detail.title: de la becomes de

rows.say: Je bois de l'eau. Je ne bois pas d'eau.

detail.body: De still meets a vowel sound, so it still shortens. That is why this one looks different: it is the same de, wearing the same shortening you already know.

rows.say: Je mange des légumes. Je ne mange pas de légumes.

detail.say: Je ne mange pas de légumes.
detail.body: This is the half you already met. Last lesson des was the plural of un and une and it collapsed to de under a negative. It does the same here for the same reason.
detail.title: des becomes de

rows.say: J'aime le pain. Je n'aime pas le pain.

detail.body: This is the half that makes the rule usable. If the word survives the negative it was le, la or les. If it collapsed to de, it was one of this lesson.

sections.say: Four sentences an English speaker produces in their first month. One per screen.
sections.title: Four Traps

errors.why: Your English has nothing in front of bread, so nothing reminds you that French wants a word there. A bare noun after a verb is not a thing French has, and this is the error that sounds most obviously wrong to a French ear.
errors.right: Saying « Je mange du pain » for "I eat bread".
errors.wrong: Saying « Je mange pain » for "I eat bread".

errors.why: Both are correct French, which is why nothing corrects you. Un asks for one countable thing and du asks for an amount, so this is the only trap here that gets you served the wrong item rather than a puzzled look.
errors.right: Saying « Je voudrais du café » when you meant coffee rather than one cup.
errors.wrong: Saying « Je voudrais un café » when you meant coffee rather than one cup.

errors.why: English keeps the whole phrase in "a lot of the coffee" and French does not. Once the quantity is named the article in front of the noun disappears, and this holds for every quantity word and every container.
errors.right: Saying « beaucoup de café » for "a lot of coffee".
errors.wrong: Saying « beaucoup du café » for "a lot of coffee".

errors.why: Du, de la and de l apostrophe all collapse to de under a negative, exactly as un, une and des did last lesson. Le, la and les do not move, which is how you can work out afterwards which word you had used.
errors.right: Saying « Je ne mange pas de pain » for "I do not eat bread".
errors.wrong: Saying « Je ne mange pas du pain » for "I do not eat bread".

sections.say: Most of the du you have read since your first lesson is not this word at all. Here is how to tell.

cards.sub: [preh dü LEE] · next to the bed

cards.body: Faire du sport, jouer de la guitare, entendre du bruit. Same word, same job, no food anywhere near it. Un is one of them. Du is some of it. This is a rule about French, not a rule about restaurants.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched a baker hand over the wrong thing, read a passage where one noun arrives both ways in the same breath, met the four shapes, learned what a quantity does to them, and separated the du that is about an amount from the du that is not. What is left is the part that tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.
sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Five rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round’s drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: The shapes, quickly.
rounds.label: The four shapes

questions.q: You are at a table and you want bread. There is none on the table yet.
questions.why: You want an amount of bread rather than one loaf or all the bread there is. Du is the word for an amount nobody has counted yet.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je mange pain. »
questions.why: English has nothing in front of bread so nothing reminds you. French does not leave that slot empty after a verb, and du is what goes in it.

questions.q: Soupe takes la. So an amount of it is:
questions.why: The noun decides the shape, and you settled that in the gender lesson. Soupe takes la, so its amount form keeps the la and adds de in front.

questions.q: Water starts with a vowel sound. Write "some water" in French.
questions.why: De la shortens in front of a vowel sound exactly the way la does on its own. That is one rule you already have rather than a new one.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: Du and deux are one rounded vowel apart and there is no consonant to hold on to. Slow it down and the tighter ü of du separates cleanly.

rounds.say: The choice the whole lesson is about.
rounds.label: One of them, or some of it

questions.q: You are standing at a counter and you want one cup of coffee to drink now.
questions.why: One cup is a thing you can count, and a thing you can count takes un. Du café would ask for coffee rather than a serving of it.

questions.q: Somebody is holding the pot and asking whether you want any. You do.
questions.why: They are offering an amount out of a pot rather than a fresh cup, so the answer is about how much and not how many. Un café orders a new one.

questions.q: You wanted cheese for the table, not one whole cheese. Fix this. « Je voudrais un fromage. »
questions.why: Un fromage is a whole wheel, a real thing a stall will hand you. Du fromage is an amount of it, which is what somebody buying lunch means.

questions.q: The waiter asks what you would like, and you want bread on the table. Complete: « Je voudrais ___ pain. »
questions.why: Bread on the table is an amount rather than a countable object, and pain takes le, so the amount form is du.

questions.q: What actually decides between un café and du café?
questions.why: Both are new to the listener, so newness cannot be it. What separates them is whether the thing is countable, which is the line English never makes you draw.
opts: Whether the listener has heard about it before
Whether you mean one thing you can count or an amount of something
Whether the sentence is a question

rounds.say: Where the article disappears.
rounds.label: Once a quantity is named

questions.q: Fix this. « Je bois beaucoup du café. »
questions.why: Beaucoup already says how much, so the word in front of the noun is not needed and French takes it out. Beaucoup du café is never said.

questions.q: A kilo is a quantity. So which is right?
questions.why: A container behaves exactly like beaucoup: it names the quantity, so bare de is all that is left between it and the noun.

questions.q: Fix this. « Une tranche du fromage, s’il vous plaît. »
questions.why: The slice is the quantity, so the du goes. One card earlier the same cheese was du fromage, and naming the slice is exactly what changed.
accept: Une tranche de fromage, s’il vous plaît.
Une tranche de fromage, s'il vous plaît.
questions.answer: Une tranche de fromage, s’il vous plaît.

questions.q: « Je bois de l’eau. » Now say you drink a lot of it. Complete: « Je bois beaucoup ___ eau. »
questions.why: The quantity takes the article out and leaves de, and de shortens in front of a vowel sound the same way le and la do.

questions.q: Fix this. « Elle met un peu du sel dans la soupe. »
questions.why: Un peu de is a quantity word like beaucoup de, so it behaves the same way. The un in front belongs to peu and changes nothing about the noun.
accept: Elle met un peu de sel dans la soupe.
questions.answer: Elle met un peu de sel dans la soupe.

rounds.say: The rule you already met, one noun-class further on.
rounds.label: Saying no

questions.q: Fix this. « Je ne mange pas du pain. »
questions.why: Under a negative du, de la and de l apostrophe all collapse to de, which is the same thing un, une and des did last lesson.
accept: Je ne mange pas de pain.
questions.answer: Je ne mange pas de pain.

questions.q: « Je bois de l’eau. » Now say you do not.
questions.why: The collapse to de happens first and the shortening in front of a vowel happens second, so what is left is d apostrophe rather than de l apostrophe.
opts: Je ne bois pas de l’eau.
Je ne bois pas de eau.

questions.q: Which sentence has a word in front of the noun that did NOT change under the negative?
questions.why: Le, la and les survive a negative untouched. That asymmetry is what lets you work out afterwards which kind of word you had used.
opts: Je ne mange pas de fromage.
Je ne bois pas de café.
Je ne veux pas de soupe.

questions.q: « Je mange du fromage. » Write it again, saying you do not.
questions.why: Du goes to de, not to pas du and not to pas le. The cheese was never a particular one, so there is nothing for le to point at.
accept: Je ne mange pas de fromage.
Je ne mange pas de fromage
questions.answer: Je ne mange pas de fromage.

questions.q: Say it out loud, to a waiter, before the cheese board arrives.
questions.why: Pas de runs together into one short block. A gap between them is what makes it sound like two separate words rather than one negative.
questions.target: Je ne mange pas de fromage.

rounds.say: Four in five of them are not this word.
rounds.label: Which du is it?

questions.q: Which of these du is about an amount of something?
questions.why: Only the third one would work with "some" in front of the English. The other three are of the: of the bed, of the day, of the bread.
opts: Le chargeur est près du lit.
Quel est le plat du jour ?
Le serveur apporte du pain frais.

questions.q: « à côté du salon » means "next to the living room". What is du doing there?
questions.why: French squeezes de and le into du automatically, and the result looks identical to the word this lesson teaches. Only the meaning tells them apart.
opts: Naming an amount of living room
Standing in for de and le together

questions.q: Somebody is offering you the pot and you want some. Fix this. « Je prends un café. »
questions.why: Un café orders a fresh cup, which is not what is being offered. When the coffee is already made and in front of you, what you want is an amount of it.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: All four are the same word agreeing with a different noun, so the ear has to catch the shape rather than the meaning. The vowel after de is what separates them.

questions.q: Fix this. « Il y a beaucoup du monde au marché. »
questions.why: The quantity is already named, so nothing goes between it and the noun. This one catches people because monde takes le and the du looks plausible.
accept: Il y a beaucoup de monde au marché.
questions.answer: Il y a beaucoup de monde au marché.

sections.say: Five things you did not have this morning.
sections.body: You can ask for an amount of something without accidentally buying one whole object of it, which is most of what this word is for. The last two points below are worth more to you than the shapes are: the shapes take five minutes and those two take a year, and you have just had them both named.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Un is one of them. Du is some of it.
Du, de la and de l apostrophe are one word agreeing with the noun. Des is the plural, and you already had it.
Name a quantity or a container and the article goes: beaucoup de café, un kilo de tomates.
Say no and it collapses to de, exactly as un, une and des did. Le, la and les do not move.
Four in five of the du you read is de and le stuck together. Try putting "some" in front of the English.

errorTriggers.description: Leaves the noun bare after a verb, because English puts nothing in front of it to translate.
Asks for one countable thing when they meant an amount, or the other way round. Both are correct French, so nothing corrects them.
Keeps du after a quantity word or a container: beaucoup du café, un kilo des tomates.
Keeps du, de la or de l apostrophe under a negative instead of collapsing all three to de.
Reads every du as an amount, including the four in five that are de and le squeezed together.

Elision of le and la to l apostrophe in front of a vowel sound
The indefinite article un, une and des, and its collapse to de under a negative
grammarIntroduced: The partitive article du, de la and de l', for an unspecified quantity of an uncountable noun
The countable/uncountable distinction as the choice between un and du on the same noun
Des as the partitive plural, extending the indefinite plural already taught in a1.11
Bare de after an expression of quantity or a container, and its elision to d apostrophe
The partitive reducing to de under negation, extending the same rule from the indefinite
The formal identity of the partitive du with the contracted preposition de + le, and how to tell them apart

lessons.intro: Every letter's real sound. Learn the French name and the in-word sound of all 26 letters, master the ones that trip up English speakers, and spell your own name and email aloud with total confidence.
lessons.title: L'alphabet français

overview.subFr: L'alphabet : le vrai son de chaque lettre
overview.introFr: Apprenez le nom et le vrai son des 26 lettres, maîtrisez celles qui piègent les anglophones, et épelez votre nom et votre email à voix haute avec une confiance totale.
overview.titleEn: The French Alphabet: Every Letter's Real Sound

sections.say: Here is a moment that catches almost every learner off guard. You are on the phone with a hotel in Lyon, and the receptionist asks for your email. You start spelling: P, A, U, L. And there is a long pause. She wrote down something completely different, because the letter you call AY is actually the French E, and the letter you call EE is the French I. The good news? This is a small, closed skill. Twenty six letters, they never change, and after this lesson you will own every one of them.
sections.body:
You are on the phone with a hotel in Lyon, and the receptionist asks for your email. You start reading it out: P, A, U, L. There is a long pause. She heard pay, ah, oo, ell, and wrote down something completely different, because in French the letter you call AY is actually E, and the letter you call EE is I. Two minutes later you still do not have your confirmation.

That exact moment happens to travellers every day: dictating an email, spelling a last name at a pharmacy, giving a booking reference. The good news: this is a small, closed skill. There are only 26 letters, they never change, and once you own them you can spell anything in French.
sections.title: Why this matters

sections.say: By the end of this lesson you will be able to name all twenty six letters the French way, keep a letter's name and its sound in separate boxes, survive the ambush letters, and spell your own name and email out loud, slowly and clearly, like a local.
sections.title: What you'll master
points: Say the French name of all 26 letters, the way a French person spells out loud.
Tell a letter's NAME (for spelling) from its SOUND (inside words), the mix-up beginners make most.
Handle the ambush letters: E, G, H, I, J, R, U, W, Y and the vowels.
Say double vé for W and i grec for Y like a local, instead of guessing.
Spell your own name out loud in French, slowly and clearly.
Dictate an email address in French, including the @, the dot, and the tricky letters.
Recognise the French alphabet song and why its ending sounds different.

sections.say: Here is the one idea that fixes half your mistakes. A letter has two separate jobs. Its name is what you say when you spell out loud. Its sound is the noise it makes inside a word. When you dictate your email, you use names. When you read a word aloud, you use sounds. Keep those two jobs in separate boxes in your head, and most of the confusion disappears.
sections.body:
A letter has two completely separate jobs, and beginners jam them together.

The NAME of a letter is what you say when you spell a word out loud, letter by letter. The SOUND is the noise it makes inside a word: the B in boat does not go bee, it goes a short buh.

French works the same way. When you dictate your email, you use names. When you read a French word aloud, you use sounds.

KEY RULE: Spelling out loud = letter NAMES. Reading a word = letter SOUNDS. Different tools for different jobs.
sections.title: The core concept: name versus sound

sections.say: A quick note on how sounds are written in this lesson. Every sound appears three ways: the precise phonetic symbol in slashes, a plain sounds-like hint, and a respelling in brackets with the stressed syllable in capitals. One special code to remember: z h means the soft buzzy sound in the middle of measure. Hold onto that, it is the key to the letters G and J.

rows.v: The precise symbols in slashes, like /a/. An anchor, not homework.

detail.body: The International Phonetic Alphabet gives every sound in every language its own exact symbol, so /a/ always means the same thing no matter what language you're reading it in. You never need to memorize the IPA to use this course: it's here as a precise anchor you can check against, not something to study on its own. Whenever the plain-English hint feels ambiguous, the IPA symbol next to it is the exact answer.
detail.title: IPA

rows.v: A plain English hint: ah as in father.

detail.body: The fastest way in: a short comparison to a sound you already make in English, like ah as in father. It gets you close enough to be understood on the first try. It is deliberately approximate, because French vowels and English vowels are never perfectly identical, which is exactly why every sound also gets the more precise IPA symbol and the respelling alongside it.
detail.title: Sounds like

rows.v: A respelling with the stressed syllable in CAPS: bonjour is [bon-ZHOOR].

detail.body: A respelling breaks a French word into rough English-readable chunks, with the syllable you stress hardest written in CAPS: bonjour becomes [bon-ZHOOR]. French stress is much flatter than English stress overall, but the last syllable of a phrase still lands a little heavier, and the capitalized chunk is your cue for where that is.
detail.title: [brackets]

rows.v: The soft buzz in the middle of measure or vision. The key to G and J.

detail.body: One special code worth memorizing on its own: zh is the soft, buzzy sound in the middle of the English words measure or vision: not a hard j, and not an h. It shows up constantly in French, and it is the exact sound both G (before E, I, Y) and J make. Say "mesure" slowly and feel where your tongue sits for that middle sound. That's zh.
detail.title: zh

sections.title: How sounds are written here

sections.say: This is the master grid, all twenty six letters. Tap any letter to open its card: you will hear its French name, see the sound it makes inside words, and get an example. Take your time here. And watch the AY family: B, C, D, G, P, T and V all rhyme, which is exactly why they cause email disasters on the phone.

sections.say: These are the traps, the letters that ambush English speakers. Spend most of your time here. Swipe through each card, listen, and say each French word out loud. The two biggest offenders: E, which is uh and never ee. And the great G J swap: G goes AY, J goes EE.
sections.hint: Swipe through each trap

cards.body: Its name is a soft uh: relaxed, half-open mouth. The English instinct is to call E ee, but that is the French letter I. Inside words French E is often so light it nearly vanishes. Burn it in: E is uh, I is ee.
cards.head: E is [uh], never ee
cards.label: THE TRAP · E

cards.body: In English, G is jee and J is jay. French flips it: G is [zhay], J is [zhee]. Both start with the soft zh of measure, with no hidden d at the front. Remember: G goes AY, J goes EE.
cards.head: The great swap
cards.label: THE TRAP · G and J

cards.body: The letter is named [ahsh], but inside words it makes no sound at all. Hôtel opens on the O. Heure, the hour, is [ur]. Never puff air for a French H.
cards.head: Always silent, every time
cards.label: THE TRAP · H

cards.body: Its name is [air], but the sound lives at the back of the throat, near where you gargle: a soft scrape, not the American tongue-curl. Try a gentle kh, as if lightly clearing your throat, then soften it. Feeling strange at first is completely normal.
cards.head: The throaty one
cards.label: THE TRAP · R

cards.body: English does not have it. The trick that works: say ee as in see, freeze your tongue exactly where it is, then push your lips into a tight kiss shape. Tongue says ee, lips say oo. That collision is U. It is never oo: tu is [tew], not too.
cards.head: The tight whistle vowel
cards.label: THE TRAP · U

cards.body: Worth stating because of the E and I swap: the letter I is named [ee] and usually sounds ee in words. Clean and flat, no glide.
cards.head: Just ee
cards.label: EASY WIN · I

cards.body: French borrowed W, so they literally call it double V: [DOO-bluh-vay]. Not double-you. In older borrowings it sounds like v, in newer English ones like w: le week-end.
cards.head: Double vé
cards.label: THE BORROWED ONE · W

cards.body: The name means Greek I, because the letter arrived from Greek. Say [ee-GREK]. In words it acts like a French I or a y glide.
cards.head: I grec
cards.label: THE GREEK ONE · Y

cards.body: The name is [zed], like British English, never American zee.
cards.head: Zède
cards.label: THE LAST ONE · Z

sections.title: The letters that ambush you

sections.say: English vowel letters are lazy and change constantly. French vowels are stable and clean. Tap any row to open that vowel's card and hear it. Your English autopilot will read A as ay, I as eye and E as ee. All three are wrong in French. Retrain them: A is ah, E is uh, I is ee.

detail.body: French A is an open, pure ah, as in father. Never the English ay. Ami, the friend, is [ah-MEE].
detail.title: A is [ah]

detail.body: A soft uh with a relaxed mouth, often nearly silent inside words. The English ee belongs to the letter I. Le is [luh].
detail.title: E is [uh]

detail.body: A clean, flat ee with no glide. English I is a diphthong, eye. French I never glides. Ici, here, is [ee-SEE].
detail.title: I is [ee]

detail.body: Similar to English, but tighter, with no glide at the end. Hôtel is [oh-TELL].
detail.title: O is [oh]

detail.body: No English twin. Say ee, freeze your tongue, round your lips as if to whistle. Tu is [tew], never too.
detail.title: U is [ew]

detail.body: Named Greek I after its origin. Nothing to do with why. In words it sounds ee or glides like y: yoga, [yo-GAH].
detail.title: Y is i grec

sections.say: This is the part that pays for the whole lesson. When French speakers spell something important on the phone, they do three things you should copy. One: they use the letter names, slowly. Two: they confirm blurry letters with a helper word, B comme Bernard, B as in Bernard. Three: for an email they name the symbols too. Let us build each piece.
steps: Use the letter NAMES, slowly. Paul becomes: [pay], [ah], [ew], [ell]. Names, not sounds.
Confirm blurry letters with a helper word, because B, C, D, G, P, T, V all rhyme on the phone. The formula is B comme Bernard: B as in Bernard. Any well-known first name works.
For an email, name the symbols too: arobase for @, point for the dot. The full list is two cards away.

sections.say: Good news: you already know the tune of the French alphabet song. It is Twinkle Twinkle Little Star, same as the English ABC song. Only the words change. Slow down at the unfamiliar ending: double vé, iks, i grec, zède. Singing it a few times is a genuinely good way to lock the order in.
sections.body:
Yes, there is a French alphabet song, and it uses the same tune as the English ABC song, which is the same tune as Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star. French children learn it exactly the way you did.

The difference is the names: a, bé, cé, dé, e, effe, gé, and so on. The ending feels different because W is double vé, Y is i grec and Z is zède, so the final stretch runs: double vé, iks, i grec, zède. It does not rhyme the way the English ending does.

Hum it a few times. The tune is muscle memory you already own; you are just swapping the words.

sections.say: Eight mistakes almost every English speaker makes, one per card. For each one you get the fix and the reason your mouth wants to make it. The reason matters: once you know why a mistake happens, you can catch yourself before it does.
sections.hint: One trap per card

cards.body: Why it happens: in English the letter E literally says ee, so your mouth defaults to it. Retrain: E is uh, I is ee.
cards.head: Calling E ee
cards.label: MISTAKE 1

cards.body: Why it happens: English I is a diphthong, eye. French vowels do not glide; I is a clean ee.
cards.head: Calling I eye
cards.label: MISTAKE 2

cards.body: Why it happens: English swaps them, G is jee and J is jay. French flips it back and softens both to the measure sound. Say: G goes AY, J goes EE.
cards.head: Saying G and J the English way
cards.label: MISTAKE 3

cards.body: Why it happens: English H is breathy and strong. French H makes no sound at all, so the word opens on the next letter.
cards.head: Puffing an h in hôtel
cards.label: MISTAKE 4

cards.body: Why it happens: oo is the closest English sound, so learners grab it. Say ee, then round your lips without moving your tongue.
cards.head: Saying French U like oo
cards.label: MISTAKE 5

cards.body: Why it happens: you are translating the English name. French names it after V, not U, because that is what it looks like.
cards.head: Calling W double-you
cards.label: MISTAKE 6

cards.body: Why it happens: the English name leaks through. French names it Greek I after its origin. Nothing to do with why.
cards.head: Calling Y why
cards.label: MISTAKE 7

cards.body: Why it happens: nobody teaches it, yet you need it for every email. Memorise it as its own vocabulary word.
cards.head: Forgetting the word for @
cards.label: MISTAKE 8

sections.title: Round-up
points: A letter has a NAME for spelling aloud and a SOUND inside words. Keep them separate.
The big swap: E is [uh], I is [ee]. Fixing this alone prevents most spelling errors.
G is [zhay], J is [zhee], both buzzing like measure.
H is always silent. U is a rounded ee, not oo. R lives in the back of the throat.
W is double vé, Y is i grec, Z is zède.
To dictate an email: letter names, helper words like B comme Bernard, arobase and point.
Rehearse your own name and email out loud. Ninety seconds now saves a frustrating phone call later.

segments.text: Bonjour !
Welcome to your very first Sons lesson. Today we take apart the French alphabet: all twenty six letters, their real names, and the sounds they make inside words.

Picture this: you are on the phone with a hotel in Lyon, spelling your email. You say the letters the English way, and the receptionist writes down something completely different. By the end of this lesson, that can never happen to you again.
One idea fixes half your mistakes: a letter has a NAME, for spelling out loud, and a SOUND, the noise it makes inside a word. They are different tools for different jobs.
Our focus today: the letter names, the traps, and spelling your own name and email aloud.
The biggest trap first. In French, the letter E is a soft uh, never ee. The letter that says ee is I. Listen: the word for I, the pronoun, is:
je
That soft ending is the French E. Now the great swap: G is zhay, J is zhee, both buzzing like the s in measure. Listen to the hard and soft G, cake then giraffe:
le gâteau, la girafe
And the silent ghost: H has a name, ahsh, but inside a word it makes no sound at all. The hotel:
l'hôtel
No puff of air. The word opens straight on the O.
Your turn. Repeat after me, slowly. First, the pronoun I:
je
Now thank you, with the French R colouring the first syllable:
merci
And the scariest-looking word that is secretly all your friends: today.
aujourd'hui
Now the payoff. Spell your own first name out loud, letter by letter, using the French names. Slowly. Remember: E is uh, I is ee.
Beautiful. Now say the French word for the at sign, the one you need for every email address:
Quick check. Which letter says ee when you spell out loud: E, or I?
And the French name for W?

Your cheat sheet: names for spelling, sounds for reading. E is uh, I is ee. G goes AY, J goes EE. H is silent. U is a rounded ee. W is double vé, Y is i grec, and the at sign is arobase. Spell your name and email out loud once before you travel, and you are ready.
Bravo, à bientôt !
