sections.say: Five things, and then the two lessons that pick this up.
sections.body: You can now put the right word in front of a verb, which is the half of a French sentence that has to be settled before the verb exists. The next unit is être and the one after it is avoir. Both of them are verb tables, and you are walking in with the left-hand column already learned and with six rows to fill rather than nine.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Nine pronouns. Six verb forms. il, elle and on share one; ils and elles share another.
on means we, out loud, and takes the form il takes. Never « On sommes ».
One man in a group of women, and the whole group is ils.
vous is the polite singular AND the plain plural, and the word will not tell you which.
il and ils are one sound, and so are elle and elles. The verb is what you listen for.

errorTriggers.description: Reaches for the wrong row of the table: il for a woman, tu for a group, nous where the room wants on.
Knows on means we and gives it the nous form, producing « On sommes ».
Reads every vous as the polite singular and answers for one person when a group was addressed.
Uses elles for a group that has a man in it, usually because the women are the majority.
Hears il/ils or elle/elles and guesses from the pronoun, which carries no information at all.
Reads « Il y a » or « Il pleut » as being about a man, and looks for one in the sentence before it.

recorded.desc: THE SIX FORMS AS ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE, IN PARADIGM ORDER, BY ONE VOICE AT ONE SPEED. This is the single most important instruction in this lesson. Six forms recorded in six sessions are six performances, and the learner is trying to hear a SET: any drift in pace, pitch or emphasis between them teaches a difference between the recordings rather than a difference in French. Read them at conversational pace with no pause for teaching between the rows, then the six full sentences in the same take. Do not stress the verb: these are the most frequent words in the language and they are never leaned on in speech.

Tu es ici pour la conférence ?
Il est ici pour la conférence.
Nous sommes ici pour la conférence.
Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?
Ils sont ici pour la conférence.

recorded.desc: vous êtes WITH ITS LIAISON INTACT, never as two words with a gap. The S of vous must arrive as a Z bound to the front of êtes so the pair is one phonetic word, [voo-ZET]. Do not articulate the two halves separately even for the slow take: the slow version must be the same join stretched, not the join taken apart, because a learner who hears it separated once will produce it separated forever. Do not sound the final S of êtes.
clipIds: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?

recorded.desc: ils sont AND ils ont RECORDED IN THE SAME TAKE, back to back, by one voice at one speed, so the contrast is real rather than an artefact of two sessions. ils sont opens on a clear S; ils ont carries a Z over from the silent S of ils. That single sound is the whole difference between this lesson and a1.07, so the two must be comparable against each other and not against a memory of a different recording. Do not sound the S of ils in either, and do not sound the T of sont.
clipIds: Ils sont ici pour la conférence.

recorded.desc: The c'est and il est pairs, each PAIR in one take back to back so the appearing and disappearing determiner is audible against itself: « C'est un médecin. » then « Il est médecin. », then « C'est le directeur. » then « Il est directeur. » Both halves must sound like ordinary speech; the difference being taught is a word, not a level of care. Run est straight into the following noun with no pause, because a gap there is exactly where a learner inserts the un.

The opening scene, French bubbles only, in the voice of one woman in her forties at an ordinary conference-lobby pace. The beat where she says it back (« Ah, il est médecin. Très bien. ») must be warm and passing rather than corrective: the whole point of the scene is that nobody tells the learner they were wrong, so any hint of emphasis on médecin would destroy it.
clipIds: Bonjour ! Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?
Ah, il est médecin. Très bien.

recorded.desc: The origin set. français and française must be recorded in ONE take back to back, because the whole teaching is that the e wakes the s and the two are audibly different; recorded apart, the learner hears two words rather than one contrast. Same for fatigué and fatiguée, where the point is the opposite: they must be INDISTINGUISHABLE, so do not let a second take drift them apart and do not lean on the ending of either.

lessons.intro: Six forms, no pattern behind them, and one of them in almost every sentence you will say. This is the verb that introduces you: who you are, what you do, where you are from and how you are, all on the same six words.

etre.body: To be, and the first verb worth memorising outright. Every regular verb hands you a stem and a set of endings, so parler gives parl- plus six endings and with it come hundreds of other verbs. être gives you nothing to build on: the six forms are six separate words. Learn them as six words and the cost is paid once.
etre.title: The verb with no stem

sixForms.body: Six forms for nine pronouns, because il, elle and on share one and ils and elles share another. That collapse is a1.05's and it holds for every verb in the language. What is particular to être is that the six cannot be derived from each other, so this is the one table you memorise rather than work out.
sixForms.title: suis, es, est, sommes, êtes, sont

noArticle.body: Nothing. Je suis professeur, elle est avocate, il est boulanger. English requires a word there and French forbids it, which makes this the one grammatical error a beginner produces out loud in the first minute of every introduction. vousLiaison.body: The one form in the six where the pronoun and the verb bind out loud. The silent s of vous wakes up in front of the vowel and the two words are said as one: voo-ZET, with no gap. Saying them separately is understood and marks you immediately, and it is the kind of error a learner cannot hear in their own mouth.

originShapes.body: Where you are from has two shapes and they behave differently. A nationality is an adjective and agrees with you: français for a man, française for a woman. de plus a place is a preposition and never moves at all, whoever is speaking. Both answer the same question and only one of them can be got wrong.

determinerTest.body: Look at what comes after the verb. If there is a little word in front of the noun, a un, une, le, la, mon or ma, the sentence takes c'est. If the noun stands bare, or if what follows is an adjective, it takes il est or elle est. A name is already as specified as a word can be, so it counts as having one: c'est Marc.

Sometimes it is audible instead: the e in grande wakes the d, and the one in française wakes the s.

sections.title: The full paradigm

sections.body: Four of the six end in something silent. The S of es and the T of est are both mute, which is why tu es and il est land on the same sound and only the pronoun separates them. The T of sont is mute and the vowel before it is nasal, so it is [SOHⁿ] and never [SONT]. The final S of vous is mute on its own and comes back as a Z in front of êtes, which is the one place in the paradigm where the pronoun and the verb are said as a single word. Only sommes ends on a consonant you really pronounce, and that is because the m is doubled in the spelling: a single m there would have made a nasal vowel instead.
sections.title: The letters you do not say

sections.body: avoir is the next unit and it breaks in exactly the same way: six forms, no stem to lean on, nothing derivable from anything. That is not a coincidence. être and avoir are the two most used verbs in French and they are the two most broken, because a form said a hundred times a day is never smoothed out by analogy the way a rare verb is. One pair is worth keeping apart from the start, because it belongs to both lessons at once: ils sont opens on a clear S, and ils ont has a Z carried over from the silent S of ils. Everything else in the language after these two has a stem and endings, so this is the last time you will be asked to learn a verb outright.

sections.title: c'est against il est, in full

sections.body: c'est points and il est describes. Everything in the table follows from that, but a learner in the middle of a sentence has no time to decide whether they are pointing or describing, so the mechanical version is the one to carry: look at the words after the verb and ask whether a little word sits in front of the noun. If it does, c'est. If the noun stands bare, or if what follows is an adjective, il est or elle est. A name counts as having one, because a name is already as specified as a word can be. The reason this is worth learning as a test rather than as a feeling is that it is the confusion that survives longest: learners who can hold a conversation still get it wrong, because at speed the meaning-based version is too slow to run and the mechanical one is not.

sections.setting: The coffee stand at the Lyon conference. Somebody you have not met turns towards you with a cup in each hand.

sections.say: Read it once for the shape. Every one of the six forms is in here. Tap any word you do not know.
sections.text: Nine in the morning at the badge table. Sylvie is already there. « Bonjour, vous êtes ici pour la conférence ? » « Oui. Je suis architecte, et je suis de Lyon. » A man arrives behind you and puts down two cups. « C'est mon collègue. Il est ingénieur. » Sylvie looks at the badges and then at the clock. « Ah, vous êtes les deux de Lyon. Elle est espagnole, elle. » She points at a woman by the door who is holding a folder. « Ce sont les organisateurs ? » « Non, ils sont en retard aussi. »
sections.title: Four People, One Badge Table

glossary.note: Bare after il est, like every job. C'est un ingénieur would need the un.
The adjective agreeing. A man would be espagnol, with no e and no L sound.
Plural and pointed at, so ce sont rather than c'est.
En retard is a state, not an adjective, so nothing agrees with anybody.
mon is the little word in front, which is what puts this sentence on c'est.

questions.a: mon is a little word in front of collègue, so that sentence takes c'est. Ingénieur stands bare, so that one takes il est. Same man, and the test is only about the words after the verb.
questions.q: The passage says « Il est ingénieur » and « C'est mon collègue » about the same man. Why do the two sentences take different forms?

questions.a: The verb still agrees. More than one person takes sont, so the plural of c'est is ce sont.
questions.q: « Ce sont les organisateurs ? » Why ce sont and not c'est?

questions.a: Espagnole is an adjective and takes an e because a woman is speaking. De Lyon is a preposition plus a place and never changes for anybody.
questions.q: Two people say where they are from and one of them agrees with the speaker. Which, and why?

sections.say: Rate each card objectively. Again, hard, or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.back: No pattern. Six forms. Every conversation. There is nothing to derive, so all six are learned outright.
cards.front: How many forms, and how much pattern behind them?

cards.say: Je suis ici pour la conférence.
cards.back: suis, es, est, sommes, êtes, sont.
Nothing at all. Je suis architecte, never je suis un architecte.
cards.front: What goes between être and a job?

cards.back: After c'est. C'est un médecin, and il est médecin.
cards.front: The one place the little word comes back

cards.back: c'est. A bare noun or an adjective means il est.
cards.front: A little word in front of the noun means…

cards.back: C'est Marc. A name is already specified, so it takes c'est.
Ce sont mes parents. The verb agrees even here.
cards.front: You are pointing at two people

cards.back: Je suis française. The e wakes the s and you can hear it.
cards.front: A woman saying she is French

cards.back: Je suis de Lyon. De never agrees with anyone.
cards.front: Anyone saying they are from Lyon

cards.say: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?
cards.back: as one word, voo-ZET. The silent S of vous wakes up in front of the vowel.
One is this verb and one is the next lesson. An S against a Z.
Je suis fatiguée. The extra e is real and it is silent.

sections.title: The Whole Verb, One Deck

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have met all six forms, sorted them by pronoun, heard the two that hide behind silent letters, said them out loud and spelled them from sound alone. You have used the verb for all four of the things it does. What is left is the part that says whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.
sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Five rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get a drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: Six rooms, six forms. No pattern will help you.
rounds.label: The six forms

questions.q: You are telling someone your job. Which form of être opens the sentence?
questions.why: je takes suis. It is the form you will say more than the other five together, because most of what you say is about yourself.

questions.q: Write the form of être that goes with nous.
questions.why: nous takes sommes, and the doubled m really is pronounced. Nothing in suis or es could have told you that.

questions.q: Three of you have just arrived and you want to say so the way it is actually said out loud. Which form?
questions.why: on means we and takes the form il takes, so it is est. The meaning pulls one way and the form goes the other.

questions.q: Fix this. You are speaking to one stranger, politely: « Vous es ici pour la conférence ? »
questions.why: vous takes êtes whether it is one person politely or a group. es belongs to tu and to nowhere else.
accept: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence
questions.answer: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?

questions.q: Fix this. You are speaking about yourself and a colleague: « Nous êtes en retard. »
questions.why: nous takes sommes. êtes is the vous form, and the two are neighbours in the table and nowhere else.

questions.q: Which of these is true of the six forms of être?
questions.why: No pattern. Six forms. Every conversation. There is nothing to derive, which is why the correct strategy here is memorising rather than pattern-hunting.
opts: They all share the stem êt-
Four of them are built from suis
They are six separate words with no shared stem

rounds.say: English wants a word here. French does not.
rounds.label: The gap after être

questions.q: You are an architect. Write the sentence.
questions.why: No un. English cannot say "I am architect" and French cannot say the other one, which is what makes this error automatic.

questions.q: Fix this. She works as a nurse: « Elle est une infirmière. »
questions.why: A job after être stands bare. Keeping the une would mean switching the front of the sentence to c'est une infirmière.

questions.q: Fix this. A man saying where he is from: « Je suis un français. »
questions.why: A nationality here is an adjective, and an adjective never took an article. It behaves exactly like a job.

questions.q: Which of these is written correctly?
questions.why: Small f and nothing in front. English capitalises the adjective and French keeps the capital for the noun, as in un Français.

questions.q: You are asking somebody politely whether they are an engineer. Which is right?
questions.why: êtes for vous, and no article in front of the job. Both halves of this lesson in one four-word question.

questions.q: What goes between a form of être and a job noun?
questions.why: Nothing. a1.11 gave you this as a fact about professions; it is really a fact about what follows être.

rounds.say: Two shapes, and only one of them agrees with you.
rounds.label: Where you are from

questions.q: A woman is saying she is French. Write the sentence.
questions.why: The adjective agrees, and here you can hear it: the e wakes the s, so française and français are genuinely different sounds.

questions.q: A woman is saying she is from Marseille. What changes compared to a man saying it?
questions.why: de plus a place is a preposition and never agrees with anybody. Only the adjective shape of origin moves.
opts: An e is added to Marseille

questions.q: Fix this. A group of Canadians, and there is a man among them: « Ils sont canadien. »
questions.why: The adjective takes the group with it, so it needs the plural s. The s is silent, so this one exists only on the page.

questions.q: Which pair sounds identical when said out loud?
questions.why: fatigué ends on a vowel, so adding the e changes nothing you can hear. The other three end on a consonant that the e wakes up.

questions.q: Tap the letter you do not say.
questions.why: The plural s is silent, which is why the agreement on a nationality is often invisible to the ear and only real in writing.

questions.q: How do you ask somebody where they are from?
questions.why: de plus où, elided to d'où. It is the one question that gets you either shape of answer.

rounds.say: One test, run on the words after the verb.
rounds.label: c'est or il est

questions.q: Fix this. He works as a doctor: « Il est un médecin. »
questions.why: il est takes the noun bare. The other repair is just as good: keep the un and it becomes c'est un médecin.

questions.q: You are pointing across the room at your sister. Which is right?
questions.why: ma is a little word in front of the noun, so the sentence takes c'est. Any of mon, ma, ton or votre does the same.

questions.q: Fix this. You are introducing a friend called Marc: « Il est Marc. »
questions.why: A name cannot be made more specific, so it behaves like a noun that already has its little word. Pointing at a person takes c'est.

questions.q: What decides between c'est and il est?
questions.why: A determiner in front of the noun takes c'est. A bare noun, or an adjective, takes il est. It is a question about the words, not about the meaning.
opts: Whether it is a person or a thing
Whether a little word sits in front of the noun

questions.q: Fix this. You are pointing at both your parents: « C'est mes parents. »
questions.why: The verb agrees even here. More than one person takes sont, and ce sont is the form almost everyone forgets exists.

questions.q: Somebody proposes meeting at eight. You want to say that is a good idea. Which is right?
questions.why: il est needs somebody or something to point back to. A verdict on a situation always takes c'est.

rounds.say: The letters you cannot hear are the ones doing the work.
rounds.label: By ear

questions.q: Listen. Which sentence is it?
questions.why: sont starts on an S. ils ont would give you a Z instead, and that single sound is the difference between this verb and the next lesson.

questions.q: Listen. Is this one person or a group?
questions.why: vous êtes is the same out loud either way. It is the polite singular and the plain plural at once, and only the room settles it.
opts: You cannot tell from the sound

audio.clip: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?

questions.q: Listen. How is it said?
questions.why: The silent S of vous wakes up as a Z in front of the vowel and the two words are said as one. A gap there is understood and marks you.
opts: With a pause between vous and êtes
With the S said as an S
With the final S of êtes sounded

questions.q: Say it out loud, the way you would answer at a badge table.
questions.ipa: /ʒə sɥi aʁ.ʃi.tɛkt e ʒə sɥi də ljɔ̃/
questions.why: Two uses in one breath and no article in either. Say it as two phrases, not seven separate words.
questions.target: Je suis architecte, et je suis de Lyon.

questions.q: Out loud, « tu es » and « il est » end on the same sound. Why?
questions.why: Two different forms with two different silent letters, landing on one sound. Only the pronoun in front separates them.
opts: The S of es and the T of est are both silent
Both end on a nasal vowel
The verb changes to match the pronoun

questions.q: Write what you would say to point at your colleague across the room.
questions.why: mon is the little word in front, so the sentence takes c'est. Il est mon collègue is the version to unlearn.

sections.say: Four things, and then the lesson that picks this up.
sections.body: You can now introduce yourself completely: who you are, what you do, where you are from and how you are, all on one verb. The next unit is avoir, and it is irregular in exactly the same way and for exactly the same reason. These two are the most broken verbs in French because they are the most used, and no other verb will ask this of you again. One thing to carry across: ils sont belongs to this lesson and ils ont belongs to that one, and a single sound separates them.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: No pattern. Six forms. Every conversation. suis, es, est, sommes, êtes, sont, and nothing derives from anything.
Nothing goes between être and a job. Je suis architecte, never je suis un architecte.
A little word in front of the noun takes c'est. A bare noun or an adjective takes il est.
A nationality agrees with you and de plus a town never does.

errorTriggers.description: Reaches for the wrong row of the table: êtes for nous, es for vous, sommes for on.
Puts un or une in front of a job or a nationality, because English requires one there.
Leaves a nationality unagreed, or tries to agree de plus a place with the speaker.
Uses il est where a determiner is present, or c'est where the noun is bare. The error that survives into B1.
Cannot separate es from est, or ils sont from ils ont, because the letters that differ are silent.

grammarAssumed: The nine subject pronouns, and the six verb forms they sit behind, introduced in a1.05
on takes third-person-singular agreement, introduced in a1.05
Gendered agreement on a bare adjective, introduced in a1.01 on enchanté and désolé
No article after être in front of a profession, introduced in a1.11
The indefinite and definite articles, introduced in a1.04 and a1.11
grammarIntroduced: The full present tense of être, as six forms with no derivable stem
être for identity, profession, origin and description
The determiner test: a little word in front of the noun takes c'est, a bare noun or an adjective takes il est
ce sont as the plural of c'est
Nationality adjectives, which agree, against de plus a place, which does not
The obligatory liaison in vous êtes

recorded.desc: THE THREE vous FORMS, IN ONE TAKE, AND THE THREE MUST SOUND EQUALLY ORDINARY: « Vous faites le lit. » then « Vous dites bonjour. » then « Vous lisez le menu. » This is the single most important instruction in this lesson. The whole screen is that two of these three walk away from an ending and the third does not, and the learner has to notice that from the SPELLING rather than from the reading. A reader who knows faites is the difficult one will lean on it, put a fraction of extra space in front of it, or brighten it; every one of those instincts has to be suppressed completely. If a listener can tell which of the three is the odd one out with their eyes shut, the recording has done the work the screen is asking the learner to do. Conversational pace, no teaching pause anywhere, and the three back to back.

THE SIX NUMBER LINES, IN THREE PAIRS, SINGULAR THEN PLURAL, EACH PAIR IN ONE TAKE: Il fait le lit / Ils font le lit, Il dit bonjour / Ils disent bonjour, Il lit le menu / Ils lisent le menu. Here the difference MUST be audible, which is the opposite instruction from the vous clip and is why they are separate recordings. Pair one is the big one: FEH against FOHⁿ is a completely different vowel and it goes into the nose, so do not soften it. Pairs two and three land a z at the very end of the verb and change nothing else at all, so the z must be clean and the vowel in front of it must not move. In every pair the PRONOUN must sound identical on both sides, because it is: il and ils are one sound. Any difference in the pronoun destroys the pair, because the learner will use it instead of the verb.

ALL THREE PARADIGMS, IN THE USUAL PRONOUN ORDER (je, tu, il, nous, vous, ils), one voice, one speed, faire then dire then lire, and the ten dictée sentences come out of this same take. Within each verb THE FIRST THREE MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM EACH OTHER: fais, fais and fait are one sound, dis, dis and dit are one sound, lis, lis and lit are one sound. Do not help by touching the final letter of any of them; the learner is being taught that the page is the only place those differences exist. nous faisons is the one to watch in the other direction: it is fuh-ZOHⁿ and not feh-ZOHⁿ, and a reader looking at the spelling will want to say the ai. The dictée sentences are the ones a learner replays four times while typing, so they need to be even in pace and completely flat in emphasis: any lean on an ending is a hint the screen is not supposed to give.

ONE EXPRESSION FROM EACH OF THE SIX GROUPS, read as a flat list at conversational pace, one voice: faire les courses, faire le lit, faire du sport, faire un voyage, il fait beau, faire la cuisine. The instruction is sameness. Every one of these begins with the same syllable and that repetition IS the teaching, so do not vary the intonation to keep the list interesting and do not put a break after faire in any of them: these are single lexical units to a French speaker and reading them as verb-plus-object teaches the learner to assemble what they should be storing whole. Keep roughly a second between them so a learner can repeat into the gap.

The three naming forms alone, read as a flat list at conversational pace, one voice: faire, dire, lire. The last two rhyme and the first does not, and that is a fact about them rather than something to perform. Keep roughly a second between them so a learner can repeat into the gap.

The ten do-and-make expressions, one take, flat: faire les courses, faire le ménage, faire la vaisselle, faire la lessive, faire ses devoirs, faire le lit, faire du bruit, faire un effort, faire des progrès, faire une erreur. Ten phrases beginning with the same word is monotonous to read and the monotony is the point, so resist varying it. No break after faire in any of them.

The eight go-and-take expressions, one take, flat: faire du sport, faire du vélo, faire du ski, faire de la natation, faire de la musique, faire une promenade, faire un voyage, faire les valises. The small word between faire and the noun (du, de la) must be unstressed and quick: a learner who hears it emphasised will think it is a choice they have to make, and this lesson deliberately does not teach that choice.

The seven expressions where English has a verb of its own, one take, flat: faire la cuisine, faire la queue, faire la fête, faire la sieste, faire attention, faire semblant, faire plaisir. faire semblant is two nasal vowels in a row and no n is released in either; do not let the second one become a consonant. faire attention runs the two words together across the vowel and should not be separated.

The five weather expressions, one take, flat, and read exactly as a1.10 reads them: il fait beau, il fait chaud, il fait froid, il fait frais, il fait mauvais. The learner has heard these before as single lumps and this lesson is taking them apart, so the reading must NOT change to help: no extra space after fait, no lift on the adjective. If they sound different here from the way they sound in a1.10, the learner will conclude that the two lessons are about two different things, which is the opposite of what this mission says.

The opening scene, French bubbles only. A flatmate at a kitchen table on a Sunday morning, entirely relaxed, holding a pen over a list. He is not testing anybody and he is not impatient: the whole scene turns on nobody minding, so any edge in « Alors, tu fais quoi ce matin ? » or any resignation in « D'accord. Je m'occupe du reste. » would destroy it. He asked an ordinary question, got nothing back, and moved on, and he is right to have done so.
clipIds: Alors, tu fais quoi ce matin ?

lessons.intro: Three verbs that will not come apart, and one of them turns up in 30 everyday expressions: the shopping, the cooking, the queue, the weather. The forms take ten minutes. The reach is the rest of the lesson.

nousOn.body: nous parlons is what you write. on parle is what you say. Both are correct and both mean we. on takes the same form as il, which on this verb means on fait and never on faisons. So the spoken we uses the same three letters as the weather does, and the only thing telling them apart is the word that comes next.
nousOn.title: The we you will actually hear

examples.note: The written we, with its own ending.
And the form on borrows.

theOnt.body: 4 verbs end ils on -ont, and you already had 3 of them. être at a1.06, avoir at a1.07, aller at a2.02, and now faire. That is the whole list: no other verb in the language ends its ils form that way, so once you have these four you never have to wonder again. It is a closed set and this is the lesson that closes it.
theOnt.title: sont, ont, vont, font

examples.note: The fourth and last one.
And the singular it belongs to, which sounds nothing like it.

theTes.body: 3 verbs in the language end vous on -tes. Every other verb you will ever meet ends it on -ez. You have had one of them since a1.06: vous êtes. These are the other two, and they are the single most-corrected forms at this level, because every regular pattern you own says the vous form ends in -ez and these two do not. Say faisez to a French person and you will be understood and you will also be heard.
theTes.title: vous faites, vous dites

examples.note: Not faisez.
Not disez, for the same reason.

theReach.body: French keeps faire where English reaches for a different verb every time. Do the shopping, make the bed, go swimming, take a trip, be sunny, cook, queue, pretend. Eight English verbs there and one French one, and the work that English gives to the verb is done in French by the noun after it. That is not a list of odd phrases: it is how the language divides up doing, and once you have seen it the thirty stop being thirty separate things to learn.
theReach.title: One verb, a dozen English ones

examples.note: English does. French does not.
And English has a whole verb here, cook.

theControl.body: lire keeps the endings you already have, and that is the whole reason it is here. vous lisez ends in -ez like every verb you have built since a2.01, and ils lisent ends in -ent like every plural you have ever written. Put it beside faites and font and you can see what those two are doing wrong. Without it, irregular reads as a warning about the whole language; with it, it is a short list you can finish.
theControl.title: lire, beside the other two

examples.note: The ordinary ending, in the cell where the other two break.
And the ordinary plural.

notTheNouns.body: The word after faire belongs to somebody else's lesson. What you are learning is the verb in front of it. The weather words belong to a1.10, and the shopping words to a2.26, and you do not need either of them to use what is here: take each expression as one piece, the way you take a single word, and the noun inside it will make sense later when somebody teaches it to you properly.
notTheNouns.title: Which half is this lesson

examples.note: One piece. You are not learning the word for dishes.
And one piece here too.

whatFollows.body: Two words, twice, and two sentences that have nothing to do with each other. Nothing in il fait tells you which one you are in: a word for how it is outside means the weather, a word for a thing means somebody is doing it, and there is no third option. So you do not read il fait and then work it out. You wait for the next word. You met this shape at a2.02 on a different pair of words, and it works the same way here.
whatFollows.title: Il fait beau. Il fait le lit.

examples.note: How it is outside. Nobody is doing it.
A thing. Somebody is.

saySomething.body: dire takes a thing: bonjour, the truth, no. Il dit bonjour. Elle dit non. That is all it does in this lesson, and it is most of what it does in a day. There is a second way of using it, for reporting what somebody else said, and it needs machinery you do not have yet; you will not be shown it here and you will not need it. Compare a2.13, which is the next lesson and is about three other verbs that will not come apart.
saySomething.title: dire, and one thing at a time

examples.note: A thing, straight after the verb.
And the plural, which is ordinary in shape.

nobodyDoingIt.body: a1.10 gave you this and gave it to you whole, as a phrase with nothing inside it. It is this verb. il fait is the same form as in Il fait le lit, and the difference is that here the il stands for no person at all: nobody is doing the weather. French needs a subject in every sentence, so it puts one there that means nothing. You now know the verb, which means you can hear what that sentence is made of.
nobodyDoingIt.title: il fait beau

examples.note: The one you already had.
And the same two words with a person behind them.

sections.body: Every reference sheet before this one in the level lists ENDINGS, because every pattern before this one had them: a2.01 holds the -er set in full, a2.10 the -ir set, a2.11 all three regular sets in one table, and a2.02 lists forms because its three verbs have none. This lesson's forms take ten minutes and they are in the second table above. The first table is the part you will actually come back for. French keeps faire where English reaches for a different verb every time. That is a fact about vocabulary rather than about grammar, and there is no rule anywhere that will produce those thirty phrases for you: they are learned as pieces, the way single words are. Read the left-hand column if you are in a hurry. Once you have noticed that English is the language changing verb, the French stops looking like a list of exceptions and starts looking like one habit.
sections.title: Why this sheet lists expressions and not endings

sections.body: Three things leave this lesson. The first is French keeps faire where English reaches for a different verb every time. Every time you catch yourself hunting for a French verb, try faire and a noun first; you will be right more often than not. The second is that two lists closed here, and the third table above holds both: no other verb in the language ends vous on -tes, and no other verb ends ils on -ont, so those are two questions you never have to ask again. The third is smaller and it will come back: what comes next decides. Il fait beau and Il fait le lit are the same two words doing completely different jobs, and only the word after them settles it. You met that shape at a2.02 on a different pair, and you will meet it again. a2.13 is next and it is three more verbs that will not come apart, so the ten minutes you spent on the forms here are about to pay for themselves.

detail.body: English says do the shopping, do the washing-up, do the laundry. French keeps one verb and lets the noun do the work. Here: faire les courses, faire le ménage, faire la vaisselle, faire la lessive, faire ses devoirs.
detail.title: 5 of them

detail.body: Make the bed, make a noise, make progress. English splits do and make between these two groups and French has never heard of that split. Here: faire le lit, faire du bruit, faire un effort, faire des progrès, faire une erreur.
detail.title: 5 of them

detail.body: Go swimming, play sport, play music. A small word arrives before the noun; take the whole phrase as it comes. Here: faire du sport, faire du vélo, faire du ski, faire de la natation, faire de la musique.
detail.title: 5 of them

detail.body: Take a trip, go for a walk, pack the bags. English reaches for take and French still has not changed verb. Here: faire une promenade, faire un voyage, faire les valises.

cells: il fait, and then how it is

detail.body: You met il fait beau long ago and it was one lump then. It is this verb, with nobody doing anything. Here: il fait beau, il fait chaud, il fait froid, il fait frais, il fait mauvais.
detail.title: 5 of them

cells: a verb of its very own

detail.body: Cook, queue, nap, pretend. English has a whole verb for each and French spends a noun. Nobody sees this group coming. Here: faire la cuisine, faire la queue, faire la fête, faire la sieste, faire attention, faire semblant, faire plaisir.

errors.why: Every pattern you own says the vous form ends in -ez, so the reflex is very strong and this is the form it breaks on. 3 verbs in the language end vous on -tes. Every other verb you will ever meet ends it on -ez.
errors.wrong: Saying « Vous faisez le lit ».

errors.why: The plural is not built off the singular and it is not built off the nous form either. 4 verbs end ils on -ont, and you already had 3 of them. That is the whole list and nothing else in the language joins it.
errors.wrong: Saying « Ils faisent » or « Ils fontent ».

errors.why: French keeps faire where English reaches for a different verb every time. There is no verb waiting for either of those, and the half-second you spend looking for one is the half-second the sentence dies in.
errors.right: Saying « faire la cuisine » and « faire la queue ».
errors.wrong: Looking for a French verb meaning to cook, or to queue.

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have three more verbs that will not come apart, and only three cells across all of them are actually strange. That was the short half. The long half is that one of those three verbs turns up everywhere: French keeps faire where English reaches for a different verb every time. You have also finished two lists that were open before you started, because the verbs that end vous on -tes and the ones that end ils on -ont are both closed sets and this lesson supplied the last of each. What is left is the part that says whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

questions.q: Vous ___ le lit. (faire)
questions.why: Not faisez. 3 verbs in the language end vous on -tes. Every other verb you will ever meet ends it on -ez.

questions.q: Vous ___ bonjour. (dire)
questions.why: The second of the two, and the -s of the stem is heard here as a t. Every other verb in the language except être ends this cell in -ez.

questions.q: Vous ___ le menu. (lire)
questions.why: lire keeps the endings you already have, and that is the whole reason it is here.

questions.q: Fix this. You and somebody else, making the bed: « Vous faisez le lit. »
questions.why: faisez is built off the nous stem and it is not a form. The real one is shorter than the one you expect.

questions.q: Which of these four is not a real form?
questions.why: faisez looks exactly right and is the reason this round exists. faites, font and faisons are the three you actually need.

questions.q: Tap the letters you do not say.
questions.why: The -ent is silent, exactly as it was on every regular verb. What you hear at the end is the s of the stem in front of it.

rounds.say: Each of these is a situation. Pick what somebody would actually say.
rounds.label: What faire covers

questions.q: The fridge is empty and the shops shut at six. What are you about to do?
questions.why: faire les courses is to do the grocery shopping. All four are the same verb and the noun is the whole of the difference.

questions.q: There is nothing clean left to wear. Which one?
questions.why: faire la lessive is to do the laundry. English says do the laundry, and French does not change the verb for it either.

questions.q: You are tired at three in the afternoon and there is an hour free. Which one?
questions.why: faire la sieste is to take a nap. English has a verb, to nap. French spends a noun instead.

questions.q: Somebody is trying to cross a busy road with a small child. What do you say to them?
questions.why: faire attention is to pay attention. It is the one everybody hears first and the one nobody guesses, because English uses a completely different verb.

questions.q: Fix this. Somebody is cooking dinner: « Il fait le ménage ce soir, il prépare le poulet. »
questions.why: faire le ménage is to do the housework and faire la cuisine is to cook. Same verb, and the noun decides completely.
accept: Il fait la cuisine ce soir, il prépare le poulet
questions.answer: Il fait la cuisine ce soir, il prépare le poulet.

questions.q: Il ___ la vaisselle. (faire)
questions.why: The -t is silent and this form sounds exactly like je fais and tu fais. Only the pronoun in front of it separates the three.

questions.q: Your friend has been going to the pool since January. What is she doing?

questions.q: The flight is at six tomorrow and the case is still empty. What is left tonight?
questions.why: faire les valises is to pack the bags. To pack is a whole English verb and French uses the word for the suitcases.

questions.q: A child is holding a book upside down and moving their lips. What are they doing?
questions.why: faire semblant is to pretend. There is no verb in the French phrase at all beyond faire, and semblant is a noun used for nothing else.

questions.q: Your French has got noticeably better since September. Type the expression for that, starting with faire.
questions.why: faire des progrès is to make progress. English makes progress and French does it, and neither language can be guessed from the other here.

questions.q: Fix this. Forty people are ahead of you at the window: « Je fais la fête. »
questions.why: faire la queue is to queue up / to wait in line and faire la fête is to party. One word apart and nothing else in the sentence moves.

questions.q: Which of these four is NOT one of the expressions in this lesson?

questions.q: Ils ___ bonjour. (dire)

sections.body: You can build three more verbs that will not come apart, and you found that only three cells across the eighteen are actually strange. Two lists closed while you did it: the verbs that end vous on -tes and the ones that end ils on -ont are both finished, and you will never have to wonder about either again. One verb, and 30 everyday things you could not say before. French keeps faire where English reaches for a different verb every time. And you know what the a1.10 weather phrases were made of all along, which is this verb with nobody behind it.

points: French keeps faire where English reaches for a different verb every time.
3 verbs in the language end vous on -tes. Every other verb you will ever meet ends it on -ez.

errorTriggers.description: Puts -ez on the two verbs that refuse it: faisez, disez. Every regular pattern the learner owns says vous ends in -ez, so the reflex is strong and this is where it breaks.
Goes looking for a French verb that does not exist, because English has one: a verb for cook, for queue, for pack. The sentence stops before the noun arrives.
Picks the wrong expression for the situation by translating the English noun rather than knowing the phrase: faire le ménage where the shopping was meant.
Runs the strangeness of faire and dire onto lire, or onto every verb in sight: lisez becomes lites, and irregular turns into a warning about the whole language.
Builds the ils form off some other form of the verb: faisent, fontent. The plural of faire shares no letters at all with its own singular.

recorded.desc: THE MOST IMPORTANT NOTE IN THIS LESSON. « sur » AND « sous » ARE ONE TAKE, one voice, one pace, adjacent, with no gap and no reset between them. This is the pair the learner's ear genuinely fails on and the pair the whole scene is built on. Recorded apart they become two performances and the learner compares the performances rather than the sounds. Read « Les clés sont sur le journal. » immediately followed by « Les clés sont sous le journal. », then « Il est sur le lit. » followed by « Il est sous le lit. » DO NOT LENGTHEN OR STRESS EITHER PREPOSITION. They are unstressed function words and the entire teaching point is that at ordinary speed they are hard to separate. A reader who helpfully clarifies them teaches the opposite of what the scene demonstrates. sur is /syʁ/, the tight ü with the tongue high and the lips rounded. sous is /su/, a plain oo with the lips pushed forward. Both short.
clipIds: Les clés sont sur le journal.
Les clés sont sous le journal.

recorded.desc: THE FIVE PREPOSITIONS RUN OVER ONE IDENTICAL PHRASE IN A SINGLE TAKE. « Le chat est sur la boîte, le chat est sous la boîte, le chat est dans la boîte, le chat est devant la boîte, le chat est derrière la boîte. » One breath group per sentence, one voice, one pace, read straight through as if reading a list. ONLY ONE WORD MOVES and that is the entire point of the hero screen: the learner has to hear that the frame is identical and the position word is the only variable. Do not vary the intonation between sentences and do not record these five separately. KEEP THE NASALS CLOSED. dans is /dɑ̃/ and devant is /də.vɑ̃/, and neither has an n sound behind the vowel at all. The app respells them DAHⁿ and duh-VAHⁿ deliberately, and both rows are repaired by this lesson from a shipped form that spelled a plain n.
clipIds: Le chat est sur la boîte.
Le chat est sous la boîte.
Le chat est dans la boîte.
Le chat est devant la boîte.
Le chat est derrière la boîte.

recorded.desc: EVERY COMPOUND PREPOSITION IS RECORDED AS A WHOLE PHRASE AND NEVER AS PARTS. « à côté de la boîte », « près de la boîte », « loin de la boîte », « en face de la boîte ». The rule this lesson teaches is that the de IS THERE, so a clip of « à côté » on its own teaches the exact error the lesson exists to prevent. Under no circumstances record the preposition without its de, and do not leave a pause before the de: it is unstressed and it belongs to the phrase in front of it, not to the noun behind. Record the contrast pair in ONE take: « Le chat est sur la boîte. » immediately followed by « Le chat est à côté de la boîte. » The frame is identical and the learner has to hear where the extra word sits. NEVER RECORD A PREPOSITION IN ISOLATION anywhere in this lesson. They are unstressed function words that only exist attached to a noun, and an isolated clip gives them a stress they never carry.
clipIds: Le chat est à côté de la boîte.
Le chat est près de la boîte.
Le chat est loin de la boîte.
Le chat est en face de la boîte.

recorded.desc: THE FOUR À ROWS IN ONE TAKE, THEN THE FOUR DE ROWS IN ONE TAKE. « Je suis au bureau. Je suis aux toilettes. Je suis à la maison. Je suis à l'école. » The learner has to hear that the first two are one word and the last two are two words, and that au and aux are the SAME SOUND. Say so by reading them identically: /o/ both times, with nothing on the x. The difference is written only, and a reader who sounds the x of aux invents a distinction French does not have. Then « à côté du lit, près des arbres, à côté de la porte, à côté de l'arbre », same instruction: du is /dy/ and des is /de/, and the last two keep de as its own unstressed word.

À AND A ADJACENT, IN ONE TAKE, AND STATED AS IDENTICAL. « il a » immediately followed by « à la maison », one voice, no gap. They ARE homophones and hearing them from one voice back to back is the only way to prove it to a learner who has been straining to hear a difference. DO NOT DIFFERENTIATE THEM IN ANY WAY. If the reader cannot resist marking the preposition, record the vowel once and use the same audio for both: that is a more truthful clip than a performed difference, and a learner who hears an invented distinction will spend a year listening for it. Then « il a un chat » followed by « il est à Paris », which is the pair that shows what actually separates them: a thing after a, a place after à. Same instruction again for « sur la table » and « je suis sûr », which are close enough that context does the work.

THE TWO DU, ADJACENT, IN ONE TAKE, READ IDENTICALLY. « à côté du lit » immediately followed by « je bois du café ». These are the same two letters doing two different jobs and they are pronounced exactly the same way, /dy/. The learner met the second one in the partitive lesson and this lesson names the first. Read them with no difference at all, because there is none: the separation is grammatical and contextual, never acoustic. Then « près des arbres » followed by « des amis », the same instruction for the des collision. Note that des arbres carries a liaison z onto the vowel and des amis does too, so both are /de.z/ and the parallel is exact.

THE SCENE'S SPOKEN LINES, AT ORDINARY CONVERSATIONAL SPEED. Camille is putting her coat on and half out of the room; she is not delivering a lesson. « Les clés sont sous le journal. » MUST BE READ CASUALLY AND UNSTRESSED, because the whole scene depends on the learner mishearing it. A clear, careful reading destroys the beat. Her later line « Sous ! Sous le journal. Soulève-le. » is the opposite: louder, clearer, slightly impatient, the way anybody repeats themselves. The contrast between the two readings IS the scene.

lessons.intro: Nine ways to say where something is, and one rule that splits them in two. Five are single words that sit straight against the noun. Four are phrases ending in de, and leaving that de out is the most common thing an English speaker gets wrong here.

surOrSous.body: These two are opposites and they sound close enough to lose in ordinary speech. Sur ends in the tight ü sound with the tongue high and the lips rounded, and sous is a plain oo with the lips pushed forward. Said slowly they are obviously different. Said at speed inside a sentence, with an unstressed function word carrying no weight of its own, they are the most confusable pair in this lesson. It matters because the two describe opposite places, so mishearing one sends you looking in exactly the wrong spot, and you will not doubt what you heard. Every other pair in the lesson sounds nothing alike.
surOrSous.title: The one pair the ear genuinely struggles with

examples.note: On top of the newspaper, where you would see them.
Underneath it, where you would not.

twoShapes.body: There are only two kinds here and you can tell them apart by eye. Some are a single word and they sit straight against the noun: sur la table, sous le lit, dans la boîte. Others are two or three words and the last one is always de: à côté de la table, près de la gare, en face de la banque. The de is not decoration and it is not optional. It is the last word of the preposition itself, in the same way that the of in "on top of" is part of the phrase and not something you could drop. Once you have noticed which shape you are holding, the rest of the sentence is the same either way.
twoShapes.term: one word, or a phrase ending in de
twoShapes.title: Every preposition of place is one shape or the other

examples.note: One word, straight onto the noun. Nothing between them.
The same cat and the same box, and this one needs the de.

theOtherDu.body: You have seen du before, and you were told then that most of the du in French is not about an amount of anything. This is that du. De and le will not sit side by side any more than à and le will, so à côté de le lit comes out as à côté du lit, and the du there means of the rather than some. The test you were given still works: try putting "some" in front of the English. Some bread makes sense, so je bois du café is the other one. Some the bed does not, so à côté du lit is this one. Des behaves the same way and collides with the des you use for several things, and the same test separates them.
theOtherDu.title: The partitive lesson named this one first

examples.note: de + le, with a place behind it rather than a quantity.
The same du in published French, meaning from the.

theDroppedDe.body: This is the most common thing an English speaker gets wrong in this part of French, and the reason it survives is that it works. Say « le café est à côté la banque » and every French speaker in the room understands you perfectly and carries on. Nothing breaks, nobody repeats it back, and you have no way of finding out. It simply marks you as a beginner for as long as you keep saying it. English is what causes it: "next to the bank" has nothing between "to" and "the", so there is no habit to carry over. The fix is to learn the phrase with the de already inside it, as one unit, so there is never a moment where you are deciding whether to add it.
theDroppedDe.title: À côté la banque is the error nobody corrects

examples.note: The de, in published French, exactly where it belongs.
A different phrase, the same de, doing the same job.

theAccentPair.body: À with the mark is the preposition and a without it is the verb: « il a » is he has, and you met that in the avoir lesson. They sound exactly the same, so nobody speaking French is ever choosing between them and nobody listening can tell them apart. This is a writing difference only. What separates them on the page is what comes next: a place or a thing after à, and something being owned after a. « Il a un chat » and « il est à Paris » can never be confused once you look past the single letter. The same is true of sur and sûr, where the mark is the difference between on and sure.
theAccentPair.title: One is a place, the other is has

examples.note: The preposition, with the mark, and a place behind it.
The same word before a vowel, and still no contraction.

theContraction.body: À and le do not appear side by side in French. Where you would expect « à le bureau » you get « au bureau », one word standing in for two, and where you would expect « à les enfants » you get « aux ». This is not something you choose to do and it is not a shortcut: the uncontracted version is simply not written or said. What matters as much as the rule is where it STOPS. À la does not change and à l' does not change, so « je suis à la maison » is exactly as it looks. Two of the four shapes contract and two do not, and a learner who over-applies this makes more errors than one who has never met it.
theContraction.title: Two words that will not sit next to each other

examples.note: à + le, and the two words are gone.
à + la, and nothing has happened at all.

sections.body: One word goes straight onto the noun. A phrase needs de first. Sur, sous, dans, devant and derrière are single words and they sit straight against the noun. À côté de, près de, loin de and en face de are phrases, and the de is the last word of the phrase rather than the first word of the thing. Leaving it out is understood perfectly and marks you as a beginner, which is why it survives so long: nobody will ever correct it for you.

sections.body: Entre needs two reference points rather than one: entre la banque et la poste. It goes straight onto the first noun, so it belongs with the five. Chez takes a person rather than a place and has no single English word: chez le médecin is at the doctor's, chez moi is at my place.

detail.body: Le chat est sur la boîte. Le chat est à côté de la boîte. Identical apart from the position, and the one on the right carries a de that cannot be left out.
detail.title: One word against three

rows.say: Le chat est sous la boîte. Le chat est près de la boîte.

detail.say: Le chat est sous la boîte. Le chat est près de la boîte.
detail.body: Le chat est sous la boîte. Le chat est près de la boîte. Sous is one of the five. Près de is one of the four, and its de is the last word of the position rather than the first word of the thing.
detail.title: Under it, against near it

rows.say: Le chat est devant la boîte. Le chat est en face de la boîte.

detail.say: Le chat est devant la boîte. Le chat est en face de la boîte.
detail.body: Le chat est devant la boîte. Le chat est en face de la boîte. Close in meaning and opposite in shape, which is the clearest evidence that you cannot work the shape out from the sense.
detail.title: The pair that means almost the same thing

rows.say: Le chat est derrière la boîte. Le chat est loin de la boîte.

detail.say: Le chat est derrière la boîte. Le chat est loin de la boîte.
detail.body: Le chat est derrière la boîte. Le chat est loin de la boîte. Four rows, eight positions, and the only thing you ever decide is which column a word lives in.
detail.title: And the last of each

sections.title: The Same Box, Both Ways

sections.say: This is a decision you will make every time you say where something is, so it is worth making it a few times on purpose.
sections.title: Which Column Does It Live In?

check.q: You want to say that the cat is on the box. How many words go between the position word and la boîte?
check.why: None. Sur is a single word and it sits directly against the noun. All five of these behave the same way, which is why they are worth learning as one group rather than five separate facts.

check.q: You want to say that the café is next to the bank. Which of these is French?
check.why: À côté de la banque. The de is the last word of the position and not an extra. Leaving it out is understood perfectly by everybody, which is exactly why nobody ever corrects it and why it can survive for years.
opts: Le café est à côté la banque
Le café est à côté de la banque
Le café est à côté à la banque
Le café est à côté banque

check.q: Which of these two is missing something?
check.why: Près la boîte is the broken one and needs de. Sur la boîte is complete as it stands. One word goes straight onto the noun. A phrase needs de first.
opts: Le chat est près la boîte
Le chat est sur la boîte
Both of them are missing a word

sections.say: Three errors, and the first is the one this whole lesson exists to prevent.
sections.title: Three Ways This Goes Wrong

errors.why: The de is missing. This is the single most common thing an English speaker gets wrong here, and it survives because it works: everybody understands you and nobody repeats it back. It marks you as a beginner for as long as you keep saying it.
errors.right: Le café est à côté de la banque.
errors.wrong: Le café est à côté la banque.

errors.why: The same error on a different phrase. Près, loin, à côté and en face all end in de, and the fix is to learn each one with the de already inside it so there is never a moment where you decide whether to add it.
errors.right: Nous habitons près de la gare.
errors.wrong: Nous habitons près la gare.

errors.why: The rule applied where it does not reach. Sur is one of the five that take nothing, and adding de to it is the error a learner makes in the week after this lesson rather than before it. Only the phrases take de.
errors.right: Le chat est sur la boîte.
errors.wrong: Le chat est sur de la boîte.

sections.say: One more word, and it behaves like none of the five.
sections.hint: Four cards, and one of them is about a missing mark.

cards.body: At, in, or to, depending on what follows. It is the word for being somewhere by name rather than being positioned relative to something, and it is the most common preposition in French.
cards.head: à
cards.label: the word

cards.fr: Je suis au bureau. · Je suis à la maison.
cards.body: None of the five did anything to the words around them. This one does. À plus le comes out as au, one word instead of two, and à plus la does not change at all. That is the next screen.
cards.head: It reacts to the word after it
cards.label: what makes it different

cards.fr: il a · il est à Paris
cards.sub: he has · he is in Paris
cards.body: You met a in the avoir lesson: il a is he has. The only difference on the page is the mark, and there is no difference at all out loud. Nobody speaking French is choosing between them, and this is a writing difference only.
cards.head: à and a are the same sound
cards.label: the one that is not it

cards.fr: il a un chat · il est à la maison
cards.sub: a thing being owned · a place
cards.body: A thing after a, a place after à. Once you look past the single letter the two can never be confused, and that is the only test you need. The same mark separates sur from sûr, which is on against sure.
cards.head: Look at what comes next
cards.label: how to tell them apart

sections.title: The Sixth Word

sections.say: Four rows. The two that do nothing are as important as the two that do.

detail.body: Je suis au bureau. I am at the office. À and le do not appear side by side in French. This is not a shortcut you may choose: the uncontracted version is simply not written or said.
detail.title: Two words become one

detail.body: Je suis aux toilettes. Out loud aux and au are the same sound. The difference is written and it follows the noun. Les enfants jouent aux cartes. shows the same word away from any place at all.
detail.title: The same thing in the plural

detail.body: Je suis à la maison. Both words stay exactly as they are. Mon frère travaille à la banque. is the same shape in published French. Reaching for a contraction here is the rule applied where it does not go.
detail.title: Nothing happens

detail.body: Je suis à l'école. I am at school. The l' is already the noun's own shortened article, and à leaves it alone. Two of these four rows change and two do not, which is the entire contraction.
detail.title: And nothing here either

sections.title: Two Change, Two Do Not

sections.say: Two groups and one control. The control is the one that catches over-application.
sections.title: Does It Contract?

check.q: You want to say: I am at the office. Le bureau is a le word. Which is French?
check.why: Au bureau. À and le will not stand next to each other, so the two collapse into au. À le bureau is not a thing you may say slowly and carefully instead; it does not exist.

items.en: to the, at the (before a le word)
to the, at the (before a plural word)

check.q: You want to say: I am at home. La maison is a la word. Which is French?
check.why: À la maison, with both words exactly as they were. Nothing contracts here, and reaching for a shortened form is this rule being applied where it does not reach.

items.en: to the, at the (before a la word)
to the, at the (before a vowel)

groups.label: These two stay as they are

check.q: Somebody has learned that à + le is au and now writes « je suis au école ». What went wrong?
check.why: À l'école. The rule was applied to a word it does not cover. Only le and les contract, and l' is neither: it is already a shortened article. This error is commoner after the lesson than before it.
opts: L'école takes à l', and nothing contracts
It should be à le école

sections.say: This is not new. The partitive lesson named it, and here is where it was going.
sections.hint: Four cards, and the first one is a reminder rather than a rule.

cards.body: When you learned du for some, you were told most du in French is not an amount at all, and you were shown près du lit. That was this. De and le collapse exactly as à and le do.
cards.head: The partitive lesson said this first
cards.label: what you already have

cards.fr: Le chat est à côté du lit.
cards.sub: The cat is next to the bed.
cards.body: À côté de, près de, loin de, en face de. The moment one meets a le word, the de and the le collapse into du. The same collapse you know, with a place behind it instead of a quantity.
cards.head: Every phrase in act two ends in de
cards.label: why it turns up here

cards.fr: Le chat est à côté du lit. · Il revient du travail à six heures.
cards.sub: next to the bed · back from work
cards.body: Some bread makes sense, so je bois du café is the other du. Some the bed does not, so à côté du lit is this one. That test came from the partitive lesson and it still separates them.
cards.head: Try putting some in front
cards.label: the test still works

cards.fr: Le chat est près des arbres.
cards.sub: [DAY] · The cat is near the trees.
cards.body: De plus les gives des, which is the same two letters as the des you use for several things. The same test separates these as well, and neither of them is a word you have to choose: both are collapses that happen on their own.
cards.head: Des collides too
cards.label: and the same for des

detail.title: And it collides with the other des

detail.say: Le chat est à côté de la porte.
detail.body: Le chat est à côté de la porte. The cat is next to the door. Le café est à côté de la banque. is the same shape in published French, and the de is plainly visible in it.
detail.title: Nothing happens

detail.say: Le chat est à côté de l'arbre.
detail.body: Le chat est à côté de l'arbre. The cat is next to the tree. La pharmacie est à côté de l'école. shows it in the wild. Two collapse and two do not, exactly as with à.
detail.title: And nothing here either

sections.title: The Same Four Rows Again

sections.say: Two pairs, both of them identical out loud, and both of them worth thirty seconds so you stop worrying about hearing them.
sections.hint: Three cards about a difference you can only see.

cards.body: One is the verb you met in the avoir lesson and one is the preposition from this one. They sound exactly the same and always will. There is nothing here for your ear to learn, because there is nothing in the sound to catch.
cards.head: à and a
cards.label: the pair

cards.fr: sur la table · je suis sûr
cards.sub: on the table · I am sure
cards.body: The same again with a different mark. On against sure, and out loud the difference is small enough that context does the work every time. Both of these are writing differences, and you will meet the second one properly much later.
cards.head: sur and sûr
cards.label: the other pair

cards.fr: il a un chat · il est à Paris
cards.body: Because these are identical in speech, no listening exercise can ever test them and none in this lesson does. What separates them is what follows: something owned after a, somewhere after à. That is a reading habit, and it is quick.
cards.head: You will never have to hear it
cards.label: what this means for you

sections.title: Sur, Or Sous?

questions.q: You hear « Les clés sont sous le journal. » Where do you put your hand?
questions.why: Underneath. Sous is under, and this is the sentence from the scene. The two words differ by one vowel and they send you to opposite places.

questions.q: You hear « Il est sur le lit. » Is the thing visible from the doorway?
questions.why: Yes. Sur puts it on top, in plain view. Sur has the tight ü sound with rounded lips; sous is a plain oo. Slowly they are obvious, and at speed they are the one pair worth practising.
opts: Yes, it is on top of the bed
No, it is under the bed
No, it is behind the bed

questions.q: Which of these two pairs actually needs your ear?
questions.why: Sur and sous. Devant and derrière sound nothing alike and never get confused. À and a are the same sound exactly, so no amount of listening will separate them and nothing in this lesson asks you to try.

sections.say: One short passage. Every position word in it is one you have met, and half of them take de.
sections.text: Voici mon appartement. La cuisine est à côté du salon. Le canapé est devant la fenêtre et la télévision est sur la petite table. Mon sac est sous le lit et les clés sont dans le sac. Le jardin est derrière la maison, et la boulangerie est en face de la gare, tout près de chez moi.
sections.title: The Flat

glossary.note: De and le collapsed into du, exactly as à and le collapse into au.
One word, straight onto the noun. No de.
The partner of sur, and the one pair here your ear has to work at.
A three-word phrase and the third word is de. It is never optional.
The same shape again. Près de chez moi is near my place.

questions.a: Next to the living room. The passage says à côté du salon, with de and le collapsed into du.

questions.a: In the bag, and the bag is under the bed. Dans le sac and sous le lit, two of the five that take nothing.
questions.q: Where are the keys?

questions.a: À côté du salon, en face de la gare and près de chez moi. The other five go straight onto the noun.

sections.say: Two words worth recognising now so they do not surprise you later. Neither is examined here.
sections.hint: Two cards. Neither is on the test.

cards.fr: Le magasin est entre la banque et la poste.

cards.body: Between, and the only position word here that cannot work with one reference point. You need both. It goes straight onto the first noun, so it belongs with the five.
cards.head: entre
cards.label: the one that needs two things

cards.fr: Mon école est entre la boulangerie et la pharmacie.
cards.sub: My school is between the bakery and the pharmacy.
cards.body: The same shape again, so the requirement reads as a rule rather than an accident. Entre always has an et behind it somewhere, naming the second thing.
cards.head: two things, every time
cards.label: a second pair

cards.fr: Je vais chez le médecin demain.
cards.sub: [SHAY] · I am going to the doctor's tomorrow.
cards.body: At somebody's place, and it takes a person rather than a building. There is no single English word for it and you will use it constantly.

cards.label: the one English has no word for

cards.fr: Nous restons chez nous ce week-end.
cards.sub: We are staying home this weekend.
cards.body: The same word with nobody named at all. Chez moi is my place, chez nous is ours, and the person is the destination rather than the address.

cards.label: chez without a building
