sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: The five, described in English so there is one answer.
rounds.label: Where is it

questions.q: The cat is inside the box, with the lid open. Which word?
questions.why: dans. Inside something is dans, and it is the reason the reference point in this lesson is a box: nothing is ever inside a chair. Sur would put the cat on the lid.

questions.q: The keys are underneath the newspaper, out of sight. Which word?
questions.why: sous. Underneath is sous, and this is the sentence the scene turned on. Sur would have you looking at the top of the paper, which is the ten minutes the scene spends.

questions.q: The garden is on the far side of the house, hidden from the street. Write the position word.
questions.why: derrière. Behind is derrière and devant is the near side. These two are opposites that sound nothing alike, so they are a reading and writing pair rather than an ear one.

questions.q: You want to say, in French: the cat is on the box. Write the whole sentence.
questions.why: Le chat est sur la boîte. Sur goes straight onto la boîte with nothing between them. Written as a whole sentence rather than a bare word, because a three-letter answer typed on its own is a coin toss rather than a test.
accept: Le chat est sur la boîte.
le chat est sur la boite
Le chat est sur la boite
questions.answer: Le chat est sur la boîte.

rounds.say: The de, and the four phrases that cannot do without it.
rounds.label: One word or a phrase

questions.q: Fill the gap: « Le café est à côté ___ la banque. »
questions.why: de. À côté is not a finished position word: the de is its last word. Leaving it out is understood perfectly by every French speaker, which is why nobody corrects it and why it survives for years.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Nous habitons près la gare. » Fix the sentence.
questions.why: près de la gare. Près is one of the four that end in de. This is the same error as the question before it arriving on a different phrase, and the two turn up together.
accept: Nous habitons près de la gare.
nous habitons pres de la gare
Nous habitons pres de la gare
questions.answer: Nous habitons près de la gare.

questions.q: Which of these position words does NOT need de after it?
questions.why: devant. It is one of the five single words that sit straight against the noun. The other three are phrases and every one of them ends in de, which is the only split this lesson asks you to keep.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Le chat est sur de la boîte. » Fix the sentence.
questions.why: Le chat est sur la boîte. This is the rule applied where it does not reach. Sur takes nothing at all, and adding de to it is the error people make in the week after this lesson rather than before it.
accept: Le chat est sur la boîte.
le chat est sur la boite
Le chat est sur la boite
questions.answer: Le chat est sur la boîte.

rounds.say: Two of the four shapes change. Two do not.
rounds.label: À and what follows it

questions.q: Fill the gap: « à + le = ___ »
questions.why: au. À and le do not stand side by side in French, so the two collapse into one word. This is not a shortcut you may decline: à le bureau does not exist.

questions.q: You want to say: I am at home. La maison is a la word. Which is French?
questions.why: Je suis à la maison. À plus la does not change at all, and both words stay exactly as they were. Half of this rule is knowing where it stops.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Je suis à le bureau. » Fix the sentence.
questions.why: Je suis au bureau. À and le collapse into au every time, with no exceptions and no slower careful version that keeps them apart.

questions.q: Somebody has learned that à + le is au and writes « je suis au école ». What went wrong?
questions.why: À l'école. The rule was applied to a word it does not cover: only le and les collapse, and l' is already a shortened article that à leaves alone. Over-applying this is more common after the lesson than before it.
opts: L'école takes à l', and that does not contract

rounds.say: The partitive lesson named this one. Here is where it was going.
rounds.label: The du you already met

questions.q: Fill the gap: « Le chat est à côté ___ lit. » Le lit is a le word.
questions.why: du. De and le collapse exactly as à and le do. This is the du the partitive lesson already named as the common one, arriving with a place behind it rather than a quantity.

questions.q: In « à côté du lit », what does du mean?
questions.why: Of the. The partitive lesson's test still separates them: some bread makes sense, so je bois du café is that one, and some the bed does not, so this is the other.
opts: To the, from à and le collapsing
It is a spelling of due
Of the, from de and le collapsing

questions.q: You want to say: the cat is near the trees. Les arbres is plural. Which is French?
questions.why: près des arbres. De and les collapse into des, which is the same two letters as the des you use for several things and a completely different job. Both collapses happen on their own rather than being chosen.
opts: Le chat est près de les arbres
Le chat est près du arbres
Le chat est près des arbres
Le chat est près les arbres

questions.q: Fill the gap: « La cuisine est à côté ___ la salle de bains. » La salle is a la word.
questions.why: de, unchanged. De plus la does not collapse, exactly as à plus la does not. The de is still compulsory; it simply stays as its own word.

rounds.say: Sur against sous, and nothing else, because nothing else in this lesson is hard to hear.
rounds.label: The one pair to hear

questions.q: Listen. Where are the keys?
questions.why: Underneath. Sous is a plain oo with the lips pushed forward; sur is the tight ü with the tongue high. This is the pair the scene was built on and the only one here worth practising.

audio.clip: Les clés sont sous le journal.

questions.q: Listen. Where is it?
questions.why: On the bed. Sur puts it on top and in plain view. Said at speed inside a sentence these two carry no stress of their own, which is what makes them close.

questions.q: Which pair sounds so similar that a French speaker could mishear it?
questions.why: sur and sous. Everything else in this lesson sounds nothing alike and never gets confused. Knowing which pair is genuinely hard means you can stop worrying about the ones that are not.

questions.q: Say it: the cat is under the box.
questions.why: Le chat est sous la boîte. Push your lips forward for sous and keep it short. This is the half of the pair that goes wrong when you are being understood rather than when you are listening.
accept: Le chat est sous la boîte.
le chat est sous la boite
questions.answer: Le chat est sous la boîte.
questions.target: Le chat est sous la boîte.

rounds.say: Everything at once, and one question about a mark you will never hear.
rounds.label: Say where things are

questions.q: Which of these means "he has a cat" rather than a place?
questions.why: Il a un chat, with no mark. A without the mark is the verb from the avoir lesson; à with it is the preposition. They sound identical, so this is a reading difference: a thing follows a, a place follows à.

questions.q: Describe the position: the pen is beside the notebook. Fill the gap: « Le stylo est ___ du cahier. »
questions.why: à côté. Beside is à côté de, and here the de has already collapsed with le into du, which is why the gap takes only the first two words. The phrase is never à côté on its own.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Le jardin est derrière de la maison. » Fix the sentence.
questions.why: derrière la maison. Derrière is one of the five and takes nothing after it. This is the over-applied de again, and it is the sign of a learner who has understood the rule and not yet found its edge.
accept: Le jardin est derrière la maison.
le jardin est derriere la maison
Le jardin est derriere la maison
questions.answer: Le jardin est derrière la maison.

questions.q: The bakery is across the road, facing the station. Which is French?
questions.why: En face de la gare. One word goes straight onto the noun. A phrase needs de first. En face is a phrase, so it takes the de, and this is the last of the four that behave that way.
opts: La boulangerie est en face la gare
La boulangerie est en face à la gare
La boulangerie est face de la gare
La boulangerie est en face de la gare

sections.say: Six points, and the second one is the one to carry out of here.
sections.body: Nine ways to say where something is, one rule that separates them, and a collapse that happens on its own whenever à or de meets a le word.
sections.title: What You Have
points: Five words go straight onto the noun: sur, sous, dans, devant, derrière. Nothing goes between them and the thing.
One word goes straight onto the noun. A phrase needs de first.
À côté de, près de, loin de and en face de all end in de, and leaving it out is understood perfectly, which is why nobody will ever correct it for you.
À plus le is au and à plus les is aux. À la and à l' do not change, and knowing where the rule stops matters as much as knowing it.
De plus le is du, which the partitive lesson already named, and de plus les is des. Both collide with words you know and the same test separates them.
Sur and sous are the only pair here your ear has to work at. Entre needs two things and chez needs a person, and you will meet both again.

errorTriggers.description: Reaches for the wrong one of the five: says sur for sous, or devant for derrière. The ordinary beginner error, and the only one in this lesson that produces a sentence with the wrong meaning rather than a wrong shape.
Drops the de from a compound preposition: à côté la banque, près la gare. The most common error in this area and the one nobody ever corrects, because the meaning survives intact.

Applies the contraction where it does not reach: au école, à l'la maison, or adds de to one of the five. The error of a learner who has understood the rule and not yet found its edge, and it appears AFTER the lesson rather than before it.

Merges the de + le du with the partitive du taught in a1.29, or the de + les des with the indefinite plural des from a1.11. Reads à côté du lit as some of the bed, or simply stops trusting either word.
Mishears sur as sous or the reverse, then searches confidently in the wrong place. Costs nothing in grammar and everything in the moment, which is why it is the scene rather than a trap card.

Believes à and a must be audibly different and concludes their listening is at fault, or writes one for the other. Costs confidence rather than accuracy, which is why it gets its own drill and no ear question anywhere in the lesson.

grammarAssumed: Noun gender, and that un and une follow it, introduced in a1.03
le, la, l' and les, and the elision of le and la in front of a vowel, introduced in a1.04
The plural of a noun, introduced in a1.03
The full present of être, which every production surface in this lesson is built on, introduced in a1.06
The full present of avoir, and the a in il a, introduced in a1.07
des as the plural of un and une, introduced in a1.11
du as an amount of something, and that most du in French is not that one, introduced in a1.29
The possessives mon, ma and mes, which appear in imported sentences, introduced in a1.17
grammarIntroduced: The prepositions of place sur, sous, dans, devant and derrière, introduced here for the first time
The preposition à as a locative, beyond its use in fixed expressions
The distinction between simple and compound prepositions of place
That a compound preposition of place terminates in de, which is obligatory
The contraction of à with the definite article: à + le = au, à + les = aux
That à + la and à + l' do not contract, which bounds the rule
The contraction of de with the definite article in a locative rather than a partitive context
The formal identity of the locative du with the partitive du of a1.29, and of the locative des with the indefinite des of a1.11
entre as requiring two reference points, and chez as taking an animate complement

acts.title: Two verbs, twelve cells
acts.milestone: You can build both verbs in all six persons, and every ending on them was already yours.

acts.title: What comes next decides

acts.title: The third verb, and the one that does not exist
acts.milestone: You can tell having learned from being allowed from having met, and you will not build the impossible sentence.

acts.title: Out loud

recorded.desc: THE TWELVE CELLS, TWO TAKES, ONE PER VERB, EACH VERB'S SIX IN ONE BREATH GROUP. Within the first three of EACH verb the verb itself must be acoustically identical: « Je sais nager. » « Tu sais nager. » « Il sait nager. » and then « Je connais Paris. » « Tu connais Paris. » « Il connaît Paris. » A reader who knows the third one is spelled differently will put a fraction of a t on it or brighten the vowel, and every one of those instincts destroys the screen that asks the learner to fail to hear a difference. If a listener with their eyes shut can say which of the three they just heard, the take is unusable. In the plural the opposite is required: the double s of connaissons, connaissez and connaissent must be clean and audible, because it is the only thing separating the plural from the singular by ear, and the v at the end of savent must not be swallowed. AND nager MUST SOUND IDENTICAL IN ALL SIX savoir LINES, and Paris in all six connaître lines. They are the control: the learner is being shown that only the middle of the sentence moves.

THE FOUR CARDS OF THE OWNS DECK AND THE FIVE SITUATION ROWS. « Je sais nager. » « Je connais Paris. » « Je sais que c'est loin. » « Je connais ce quartier. » then « Tu connais Marie ? » « Je sais où elle habite. » « Je peux nager. » THE READING MUST NOT MARK THE JOIN. There is a strong temptation to leave a teaching pause after the verb, because the word after the verb is the whole point of the screen, and that pause is exactly what must not be there. The learner has to hear these as ordinary sentences said at ordinary speed, because that is the speed at which they will have to make the choice. Conversational throughout, no emphasis on any verb, and no lift before the complement.

THE FOUR PLACE LINES, IN THIS ORDER, AS ONE TAKE: « Je connais ce quartier. » « Je sais où elle habite. » « Il connaît bien la ville. » « Vous savez où est la gare ? » This is the mission the lesson exists for and the recording carries half its weight. All four are about places and two take each verb, so the reader must give NO clue which is which. Same warmth, same pace, same weight on the verb in all four. If the two savoir lines are read as though they were the interesting ones, the learner hears which answer is being pointed at instead of working it out. The fourth line rises at the end because it is a question; the third does not.
clipIds: Vous savez où est la gare ?

recorded.desc: THE THREE-WAY TRAP, AS TWO PAIRS. « Je sais nager. » then « Je peux nager. » then « On peut nager ici. » then « Je sais nager, mais je ne peux pas aujourd'hui. » The first pair is a minimal pair and must be read as one: same speed, same pitch, same length, with ONLY the verb different. The learner is being shown that nothing else in the sentence moved, and any difference in delivery is the recording contradicting the screen. The fourth line is one sentence and not two; the mais is unstressed and there is no dramatic pause before it. It should sound like the ordinary, slightly regretful thing it is.
clipIds: Je sais nager, mais je ne peux pas aujourd'hui.

recorded.desc: THE SIX SINGULAR CELLS FOR THE LISTENING SCREEN, savoir's three then connaître's three, WITH AUDIO BEFORE TEXT. Same instruction as the grid take and it is worth repeating because it is counter-intuitive: within each group of three the verb must be indistinguishable, and the PRONOUN must be clear, unhurried and slightly forward, because it is the only information in the line. Between the two groups the difference should be obvious without being performed: one syllable against two, and completely different consonants.

THE SKILL SET. « nager », « cuisiner », « conduire » as single words, conversational and unstressed, then « Je sais nager. » « Tu sais cuisiner ? » « Elle sait conduire. » The three single words come from three different lessons and the learner should hear no family resemblance and no grouping: they are a bag of ordinary verbs, which is the point. The second of the three sentences is a question and rises; the other two do not.

THE FOUR KINDS OF THING: « Tu connais Marie ? » « Je connais Paris. » « Nous connaissons ce restaurant. » « Vous connaissez cette chanson ? » One take. The first and last rise, the middle two do not. The double s in the third and fourth must be audible, and Marie and Paris must be said the way somebody says a name they know, not the way somebody reads one off a card.

WRONG THEN RIGHT, AND THE WRONG ONE IS THE DIFFICULT INSTRUCTION. « Je connais où il habite. » is not French and has to be read as though it were: at ordinary speed, with no hesitation, no apology and no strangeness in the voice. It is what an English speaker actually produces, fluently and confidently, and if the reader signals that something is wrong the learner will conclude they would never say it. They would. Then « Je sais où il habite. » in exactly the same voice at exactly the same speed, so that the only audible difference is the verb.

THE FOUR PUBLISHED ROWS, READ AS WHAT THEY ARE: sentences written for other lessons that happen to prove this one. « Tout le monde connaît le nom du champion. » « Il connaît la vraie raison de son retard ce matin. » « Je ne sais pas si c'est l'heure. » « je ne sais pas. » Ordinary pace, no teaching emphasis anywhere, and in particular no weight on the verb. The whole value of the screen is that nobody was thinking about savoir and connaître when these were written.
clipIds: Tout le monde connaît le nom du champion.
Il connaît la vraie raison de son retard ce matin.
Je ne sais pas si c'est l'heure.

recorded.desc: TWO CLIPS. « reconnaître » alone, then « Je reconnais cette chanson. » Unremarkable and quick. This is a recognition card and nothing else, and a reader who gives it weight will make the learner think it is being taught.

THE STAIRWELL. The neighbour is friendly, slightly out of breath, holding shopping, and completely uninterested in teaching anybody French. « Tu connais la nouvelle voisine ? » is casual and quick, the way you ask somebody something on a landing. « Ah, parfait. Tu lui diras pour les poubelles, alors ? » is warm and already turning to go, and it must not sound like a trap closing: he is pleased, and he has misunderstood, and neither of those is audible. Nothing in this scene is unkind and nothing is slowed down. The whole cost of the exchange is invisible to both people in it.
clipIds: Ah, parfait. Tu lui diras pour les poubelles, alors ?

lessons.intro: English has one word for both of these and gives you no instinct at all, so a learner who guesses is wrong about half the time. The forms take a few minutes. The question that picks between them is the rest of the lesson, and you will run it in every sentence from here on.

nousOn.body: nous parlons is what you write. on parle is what you say.
nousOn.title: The we people actually say

examples.note: on takes the il form, so what follows it here is peut and nothing longer.

theChoice.body: English has one verb here and French has two, so nothing you already own tells you which to reach for. connaître stops at a thing. savoir keeps going. Ask one question before you pick: does my sentence stop here, or does it keep going? That is the whole lesson, and it is worth more than both sets of forms put together: those take a few minutes and the choice is the thing you will be making in every sentence for the rest of your life in French. A learner who guesses is wrong about half the time, and wrong in a way the other person hears immediately, because the two verbs do not mean nearly the same thing.
theChoice.title: One English verb, two French ones

examples.note: A verb follows, so the sentence keeps going.
A name follows, and the sentence stops there.

theChrome.body: The heading at the top of this screen is « Ce que vous savez faire », and it has been at the top of the last screen of every lesson you have finished. It is savoir followed by a verb: what you know how to do. Nobody explained it at the time because there was nothing yet to explain it with. Now there is, and you can read it. That is a small thing and it is the kind of small thing that turns a language from a subject into something you are inside of.
theChrome.title: You have read this at the end of every lesson

examples.note: The same shape, in the first sentence of the lesson.

theFamily.body: reconnaître [ruh-koh-NEHTR] means to recognise, and it takes every ending connaître takes: je reconnais, nous reconnaissons, ils reconnaissent. That is all you need from it here, and it is recognition rather than something to produce. What it can take AFTER it is a different question and a more interesting one, and it belongs to a2.15, which is the very next lesson. Do not assume it takes the same things after it, because it does not.
theFamily.title: The same endings, three letters longer

examples.note: The naming form. Recognition only.
Same endings. Do not read anything else into it yet.

thePlural.body: The three plural forms of connaître all take a double s: connaissons, connaissez, connaissent. It arrives with nous and it never leaves. savoir does the opposite and gets shorter: savons, savez, savent, and the last of those is four letters. The endings themselves are the ones you have had since a2.01 and none of them is new. What is new is which stem they land on.
thePlural.title: Where connaître grows

examples.note: The double s, and the ordinary -ons.
The -ent is silent, so what you hear is the double s.

savoirReach.body: savoir takes a verb, or a whole sentence. Je sais nager is a verb; je sais où elle habite is a whole sentence hanging off the first one. Both keep going, and that is what they have in common. The thing savoir does NOT take is a plain name on its own: if the only thing left to say is a name, you have reached for the wrong verb. English hides all of this because it says know for every one of them.
savoirReach.title: A verb, or a whole sentence

examples.note: A verb. I learned how.
A whole sentence, and it is about a place.
Another whole sentence, this time a fact.

theSingular.body: Je sais, tu sais, il sait. Two of those are spelled identically and the third differs by one silent letter, and all three are one sound in the mouth. connais, connais, connaît does exactly the same thing. a2.13 spent a whole screen proving it on vouloir, pouvoir and devoir, so this lesson is not going to prove it again: it is simply true of these two as well. In writing you must pick the right one; in speech there is nothing to pick, and the word in front is carrying all of it.
theSingular.term: why je, tu and il sound the same
theSingular.title: 3 persons, 2 spellings, one sound. a2.13 found the same thing on three other verbs.

examples.note: sais
sait, and not one sound different.

whatFollows.body: what comes next decides. a2.02 named that at seq 5, on one verb doing two jobs. This lesson is the same shape turned round: two verbs doing one job, and again it is the next word that picks. French does this often enough that it is worth learning the habit rather than the instance. The instinct to decide what a sentence means before it has finished is a hard one to switch off, and it is exactly the instinct that produces the wrong verb here.
whatFollows.title: You met this shape at a2.02

examples.note: Keeps going into a whole sentence. savoir.
Stops on a thing. connaître.

theThirdVerb.body: Je sais nager and je peux nager are both I can swim in English, and they are not the same claim. sais is about having learned: at some point somebody taught you and now you can do it. peux is about nothing standing in the way: the pool is open, the water is warm, nobody has stopped you. a2.13 built pouvoir in full and this lesson does not build it again; what it does is put the two side by side, because a learner who has these three straight has something most English speakers never fully sort out.
theThirdVerb.title: a2.13 gave you a verb that also becomes can

examples.note: Somebody taught me.
Nothing is stopping me. It says nothing about lessons.
Both at once, and they disagree.

theTwoFrames.body: a2.13 put eighteen sentences on one verb so that nothing at the back would move. Here the back of the sentence is the whole point, so the two sides cannot share one. Every sentence on the savoir side of the grid ends in nager and every sentence on the connaître side ends in Paris, and those two words are doing the teaching as much as the verbs are. Read across a line and the only differences are the verb and what kind of word is behind it. That is the shape you are being asked to notice, and it is the shape you will run in your head every time you build one of these.
theTwoFrames.term: why the two sides look different
theTwoFrames.title: One verb behind, one name behind

examples.note: nager is a verb.
Paris is a name.

theCircumflex.body: Only connaît carries it, and it appears on no other form of either verb. It changes nothing at all about how the word is said. Spelling reform allows the version without it and this course has never used one: every one of the 82 places an -aître word appears in this app spells it with the hat, so that is what you will read and that is what you should write. It is the kind of thing worth deciding once and never thinking about again.
theCircumflex.title: One form, one accent, no sound

examples.note: The only place it appears.
One person earlier, and it is gone.

theImpossible.body: « Je connais où il habite. » is what an English speaker builds by translating word for word, and it is the single commonest thing to get wrong here. connaître has to land on a thing. « où il habite » is a whole sentence, so it cannot. The right one is « Je sais où il habite. », and notice that nothing about the meaning changed: it was never a choice between two ways of saying it. Picking the right verb from a list is easy and producing this shape under pressure is not, which is why the exam makes you write it out rather than choose it.
theImpossible.title: connaître and a whole sentence

examples.note: The sentence keeps going, so savoir carries it.
The same shape in the form you will actually need.
The same shape again, with que run into the word after it.

connaitreReach.body: connaître takes a thing: a person, a place, a song, a street, and then the sentence is over. It never takes a whole sentence. That is not a tendency or a preference; there is no such sentence in French, and « Je connais où il habite. » is not a clumsy way of saying something, it is not a sentence at all. What connaître means underneath all of this is having been there or having met them: you have stood in the place, you have shaken the hand, you have heard the song.
connaitreReach.title: A thing, and then it stops

examples.note: A place you have stood in.
A person you have met.
A song you have heard.

sheets.title: Two verbs, and the question that picks between them
contains: Both verbs, every person, side by side
The third verb, and what it is not

sections.title: What may come next, and what it means

sections.body: The obvious version of this table would put people and places on one side and facts and skills on the other, and it is what the most-quoted rule about these two verbs says. It is also what one sentence already published in this app says, in French. It breaks in a week, and the sentence that breaks it is « Je sais où elle habite. ». That is a place, and it takes savoir, and a learner running the meaning rule reaches for the wrong verb on one of the most useful sentences in the language. The version in the first table above cannot break that way, because it does not ask you what the sentence is about. connaître stops at a thing. savoir keeps going. Ask one question before you pick: does my sentence stop here, or does it keep going? One caution: a sentence can put its thing in front of the verb rather than behind it, and later lessons will show you how. When that happens the thing is still there, which is the part that matters.
sections.title: Why this sheet does not sort them by meaning

sections.body: Three things leave this lesson. The first is the question: connaître stops at a thing. savoir keeps going. It is a syntax rule rather than a meaning rule, and that is why it holds. The second is that English gives you one word, can, for two completely different claims, having been taught and having nothing in your way, and French keeps them apart with savoir and a2.13's verb. Learners who never sort that out say the wrong one for years and are understood every time, which is why nobody corrects it. The third is small and it will come back: what comes next decides. You met that shape at a2.02 on one verb doing two jobs, and this lesson is the same shape turned round. a2.15 is next and it takes up the family reconnaître belongs to, which is worth waiting for: verbs in a family share their endings, and they do not always share anything else.
sections.title: What carries forward

errors.why: connaître has to land on a thing. « où il habite » is a whole sentence, so it cannot. Word for word out of English it looks right, and there is no version of French in which it works. Not building it under pressure is the skill.
errors.right: Saying « Je sais où il habite. ».
errors.wrong: Saying « Je connais où il habite. ».

errors.why: Nothing is ungrammatical about the first one, which is exactly why it costs you something. You will be understood to have said you have heard of her, and nobody will correct you.

errors.wrong: Answering « Tu connais la nouvelle voisine ? » with a form of savoir.

errors.why: English gives you can for both, so the reflex is strong. je peux nager says the water is there. It says nothing at all about whether you would float.
errors.wrong: Reaching for the a2.13 verb when you mean you were taught.

errors.why: The double s arrives with nous and stays for all three plural forms. It is audible, so if you can say it you can hear which one you meant to write.
errors.wrong: Writing connaissons or connaissez with one s.

sections.body: You have two verbs where English gave you one word, and every ending on both of them is one you already write. That was the short half. The long half is the question you now run before you open your mouth: connaître stops at a thing. savoir keeps going. You have used it on a place that takes savoir and on a place that takes connaître, which is the pair no semantic rule survives. What is left is the part that says whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.
sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get a drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: The situation is in the question. Read it, decide, then answer.
rounds.label: Which of the two

questions.q: You met Marie at a party last year. Which verb?
questions.why: A person, and the sentence stops on her. connaître. « Je sais Marie. » is not a sentence in French.
opts: It depends how well you know her

questions.q: Somebody taught you to swim when you were six. Which verb?
questions.why: savoir. A verb follows and the sentence keeps going. connaître stops at a thing. savoir keeps going.

questions.q: Je ___ nager. (you were taught, years ago)
questions.why: Having learned is savoir, every time. The other verb would say the pool is open.

questions.q: Tu ___ Paris ? (have you been there)
questions.why: A name follows and it is the last thing in the sentence, so connaître.

questions.q: Which of these four is not a French sentence?
questions.why: connaître has to land on a thing. « où il habite » is a whole sentence, so it cannot. The other three are all correct and two of them are about the same kind of thing.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je connais où il habite. »
questions.why: connaître has to land on a thing. « où il habite » is a whole sentence, so it cannot. Nothing about what you wanted to say changes; only the verb does.

rounds.say: Both verbs, in writing. The double s is the only thing here that is not already yours.
rounds.label: The twelve cells

questions.q: Nous ___ Paris. (connaître)
questions.why: The double s arrives with nous and the ending is the ordinary -ons from a2.01.

questions.q: Ils ___ nager. (savoir)
questions.why: savoir gets shorter in the plural where connaître grows. The -ent is silent, as it has been since a2.01.

questions.q: Vous ___ cette chanson ? (connaître)
questions.why: Double s, then the ordinary -ez. Two s and not one, and you can hear the difference when you say it.

questions.q: Which of these is spelled correctly?
questions.why: The accent goes on the i of connaît and the ending is -t. No other form of either verb carries it, and every one of the 82 places this word appears in the app spells it that way.

questions.q: Fix this. « Nous connaisons ce restaurant. »
questions.why: Two s. It arrives with nous and it stays for vous and ils as well.

questions.q: Nous ___ nager. (savoir)
questions.why: The stem goes to sav- and takes the -ons. Nothing about this form is irregular.

rounds.say: Every one of these turns on the word directly after the verb. Nothing else.
rounds.label: What comes next

questions.q: Je ___ où elle habite. (which verb)
questions.why: It is about a place and it takes savoir, because a whole sentence follows. What comes next decides, and not what it is about.

questions.q: Which of these can follow connaître?
questions.why: Only the third is a thing. The other three are whole sentences and connaître cannot carry one.

questions.q: Vous ___ où est la gare ? (which verb)
questions.why: A whole sentence follows, so savoir. This is the version of the question you will actually ask a stranger.

questions.q: Fix this. « Nous connaissons que le train est en retard. »
questions.why: A whole sentence follows que, so it cannot be connaître. Same mistake as the first round, in the plural and with a fact instead of a place.
accept: Nous savons que le train est en retard
questions.answer: Nous savons que le train est en retard.

questions.q: Il ___ bien la ville. (which verb)
questions.why: The sentence lands on la ville and stops. bien slides in before the thing and changes nothing about the shape.

questions.q: Which pair is about the same neighbourhood and still needs two different verbs?
questions.why: The second. One stops on the neighbourhood and the other keeps going into where the station is, and that is what picks the verb.
opts: Je connais Paris / Tu connais Paris
Je connais ce quartier / Vous savez où est la gare ?
Je sais nager / Tu sais nager
Tu connais Marie ? / Tu connais la nouvelle voisine ?

rounds.say: a2.13's verb is back, and English turns it into the same word as one of yours.
rounds.label: And the third verb

questions.q: You learned to drive ten years ago and your car is in the garage today. Which is true?
questions.why: You were taught, so sais. Nothing about the lesson has changed; what has changed is whether anything is in the way today.
opts: Je sais conduire, mais je ne peux pas.
Je peux conduire, mais je ne sais pas.
Je sais conduire et je peux conduire.

questions.q: Je ___ nager. (there is a lifeguard and the pool is open)
questions.why: Nothing is stopping you, which is a2.13's verb. It says nothing about whether anybody taught you.

questions.q: On ___ nager ici. (swimming is allowed)
questions.why: Allowed, so it is the a2.13 verb, and on takes the il form rather than one of its own.

questions.q: Listen. Which one did you hear?
questions.why: SEH against PUH. These two are easy to separate by ear, which is not true of any two persons of the same verb.

questions.q: Which of these three verbs can be followed by a bare name like Marie?
questions.why: Only connaître. The other two both want something that keeps going, which is why neither can take a person on its own.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je peux nager depuis l'âge de six ans. »
questions.why: Since the age of six is about having learned, so it is savoir. The other verb would say nothing has been in your way for twenty years, which is not what anybody means.
accept: Je sais nager depuis l'âge de six ans
questions.answer: Je sais nager depuis l'âge de six ans.

rounds.say: Three persons of each verb are one sound. The pronoun is doing all the work.
rounds.label: Saying it

questions.q: In « Je sais nager », « Tu sais nager » and « Il sait nager », what separates the three?
questions.why: 3 persons, 2 spellings, one sound. a2.13 found the same thing on three other verbs.
opts: The word in front of it

questions.q: Which two words in this lesson are spelled differently and said identically?
questions.why: sais and sait, and connais and connaît do the same thing. Two spellings, one sound, and the ear will not save you.

questions.q: Say it: I know how to swim.
questions.why: Three words. Do not swallow the je, because it is the only thing telling anybody which person you mean.

questions.q: Tap the letters you do NOT say.
questions.why: The -ent, exactly as it has been silent on every verb since a2.01. What you do hear is the v in front of it, arriving at the end of the verb.

questions.q: And here?
questions.why: The same silent -ent. What you hear at the end of this one is the double s, and that is the only thing separating it from the singular by ear.

questions.q: Ils ___ Paris. (connaître)
questions.why: Double s, silent -ent. What you hear at the end of the verb is the s, and that is the only thing separating it from the singular by ear.

rounds.say: The last round is the stairwell. Nothing here is a trick and all of it is the choice.
rounds.label: Out in the world

questions.q: Somebody asks « Tu connais la nouvelle voisine ? » and you have never met her. What do you say?
questions.why: They asked whether you have met her, so the answer uses their verb. The other three all answer a question about information, and the last two are how the conversation in the scene went wrong.
opts: Non, je ne connais pas encore la voisine
Oui, je sais qu'elle habite ici

questions.q: Tu ___ ce restaurant ? (have you eaten there)
questions.why: A place you have been inside. The sentence stops on it, so connaître.

questions.q: Je ne ___ pas. (you have no idea, and it is the commonest sentence in the lesson)
questions.why: savoir, and this one has nothing after it at all. It is worth learning whole, because you will say it more often than any other sentence here.

questions.q: Which of these two would you say to somebody who just asked where you learned French?
questions.why: You were taught, so savoir and a verb behind it. The first says you are acquainted with the language, which is a thing a linguist says about a language they study.

questions.q: Fix this. « Tu sais mon frère ? »
questions.why: A person on his own after the verb, so the sentence stops there and it has to be connaître.

questions.q: What does « Ce que vous savez faire » at the top of the next screen mean?
questions.why: savoir followed by a verb: what you know how to do. It has been at the top of the last screen of every lesson you have finished, and this is the first one where you could read it.
opts: The things you are acquainted with
What you know how to do

sections.say: Four things, and then read the two words at the top of this screen again.
sections.body: You have two verbs where English gave you one, and one question that picks between them: connaître stops at a thing. savoir keeps going. You used it on a place that takes savoir and a place that takes connaître, which is the pair that no rule about meaning survives. You know that the third verb from a2.13 turns into the same English word and means something else again, and that « Je connais où il habite. » is not clumsy French but no French at all. And the heading at the top of this screen, « Ce que vous savez faire », has been there at the end of every lesson you have finished. It is savoir with a verb behind it: what you know how to do. Nobody explained it before because there was nothing to explain it with. a2.15 is next, and it takes the family this lesson only pointed at.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: connaître stops at a thing. savoir keeps going.
Ask one question before you pick: does my sentence stop here, or does it keep going?
Je connais où il habite. is not a sentence. Je sais où il habite. is.
3 persons, 2 spellings, one sound. a2.13 found the same thing on three other verbs.

errorTriggers.description: Picks by what the sentence is about rather than by what follows the verb: connaître for anything involving a person or a place, savoir for anything involving a fact. It works most of the time and fails on exactly the sentences a learner needs.

Builds « Je connais où il habite. » by translating word for word out of English. It is not a clumsy sentence, it is not a sentence, and no amount of choosing the right verb from a list stops a learner producing it under pressure.
Writes connaisons, connaisez or connaisent with one s. The double s arrives with nous and stays for all three plural forms, and it is audible, so the mistake is written rather than spoken.
Uses the a2.13 verb where the sentence is about having been taught. English gives can for both, so the reflex is strong and the resulting sentence is grammatical and says something else.
Drops or slurs the pronoun on the singular forms, where three persons are one sound and the pronoun is carrying all of the information. Nothing in the verb recovers it.
Answers a connaître question with savoir or the reverse. Both sentences are correct, neither is corrected, and the conversation continues on a false footing until somebody acts on what they heard.

grammarAssumed: The six subject pronouns and the nine they cover, introduced in a1.05
on takes third-person-singular agreement, introduced in a1.05
nous as the written first-person plural against on as the spoken one, introduced in a2.01
The present tense of regular -er, -ir and -re verbs, introduced in a2.01, a2.10 and a2.11
The silent -e, -es and -ent endings, introduced in a2.01
The present tense of vouloir, pouvoir and devoir, introduced in a2.13
The modal-plus-infinitive construction, introduced in a2.13
That three singular persons of an irregular verb are commonly one sound, introduced in a2.13
One form doing two jobs, distinguished by what follows it, named in a2.02
Yes/no questions formed by intonation alone, introduced in a1.19
ne ... pas wrapping the conjugated verb, introduced in a1.18
The definite and demonstrative determiners inside the objects of these sentences, introduced in a1.04
grammarIntroduced: The present tense of savoir and connaître, as two stems per verb
The double-s plural stem of connaître, against the shortening plural stem of savoir
The circumflex on the third-person singular connaît, as the only diacritic in either paradigm
The complement distinction between savoir and connaître: savoir takes an infinitive or a subordinate clause, connaître takes a direct object noun phrase and nothing else
That the distinction is syntactic rather than semantic, so a locative complement takes savoir when it is clausal and connaître when it is nominal
The lexical contrast between savoir plus infinitive (acquired ability) and pouvoir plus infinitive (permission or possibility), both of which English renders with can
reconnaître as sharing connaître's inflection, for recognition only, with its complement behaviour deferred to a2.15

acts.milestone: You have watched one verb decide whether a sentence existed at all.

acts.title: The forms, and the join
acts.milestone: You have all six, and you can hear the z that separates two verbs.

acts.title: French has it, English is it
acts.milestone: Twelve separate things turned out to be one thing, and three turned out not to be.

acts.title: Where English points the wrong way
acts.milestone: You can read a page of this verb without looking for possessions that are not there.

recorded.desc: THE SIX FORMS AS ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE, IN PARADIGM ORDER, BY ONE VOICE AT ONE SPEED. Six forms recorded in six sessions are six performances, and the learner is trying to hear a SET: any drift in pace, pitch or emphasis between them teaches a difference between the recordings rather than a difference in French. Read the bare forms first, then the six full sentences in the same take. THE FOUR LIAISONS ARE THE POINT AND THEY ARE NOT OPTIONAL: nous avons, vous avez and ils ont are each ONE phonetic word with a z in the middle, and the slow take must be that join stretched rather than the join taken apart. A learner who hears them separated once will produce them separated forever. Do not sound the s of as, the t of ont, or the final s of ils.
clipIds: Tu as un cadeau pour Léa ?
Il a un cadeau pour Léa.
Nous avons un cadeau pour Léa.
Vous avez un cadeau pour Léa ?
Ils ont un cadeau pour Léa.

recorded.desc: The two minimal pairs this lesson turns on, EACH PAIR RECORDED BACK TO BACK IN ONE TAKE by the same voice at the same speed, in the way sons.07 pins rec-h-pairs and a1.11 pins rec-a1-11-pairs. ils ont against ils sont is a liaison z against an s and it is the same take or it is nothing: recorded apart, the learner compares two performances instead of two verbs. il a against ils ont is a liaison that exists against one that does not, and the temptation is to lean on the ils to make it clearer. DO NOT. The whole difficulty is that nobody leans on it in speech. Then the four listening lines at natural pace and again at 0.65.
clipIds: Il a un cadeau pour Léa.
Ils ont un cadeau pour Léa.

recorded.desc: The scene break and the swap deck. « Je suis vingt ans. » must be read PLAINLY and at ordinary pace, not comically and not hesitantly: the entire teaching of the scene is that it sounds like a normal sentence right up until it stops, and any performance signalling that it is wrong destroys that. Then « J'ai vingt ans. » in the same take at the same pace, so the only audible difference is the verb. Run the verb straight into the number with no pause, because a gap there is exactly where a learner inserts être.

The eleven expressions as ONE TAKE in the order the drill shows them, one voice, one speed, no teaching pause between them. The learner is being shown that eleven separate things are one thing, and eleven separately recorded clips would teach eleven separate things. Keep the nasals closed: faim ends on a nasal vowel with NO m sound, raison ends on a nasal vowel with NO n sound, and honte likewise. Those three are the ones a reader will over-articulate.

The four English-speaker traps, wrong form then right form, with a clear beat between them so the learner hears the difference rather than a correction. Je suis vingt ans / J'ai vingt ans. Je suis faim / J'ai faim. Je suis chaud / J'ai chaud. Je n'ai pas de faim / Je n'ai pas faim. Read every wrong version plainly rather than comically: two of these four are real French sentences that mean something else, and a performance that marks them as errors removes the reason they are dangerous.

The opening scene, French bubbles only, in the voice of one woman in her seventies at an ordinary kitchen-table pace. The beat where she asks again (« Pardon ? Vous avez quel âge ? ») must be patient and unbothered rather than corrective or impatient: the whole point of the scene is that she is not correcting anybody, she simply did not receive a sentence, so any edge on it turns the moment into a telling-off and the teaching is lost.
clipIds: Ah, vingt ans. Vous avez faim ?

lessons.intro: Six forms, no pattern behind them, and a verb that spends most of its time not meaning have. This is how you say your age, how you say you are hungry, cold, right or afraid, and how you read the sentences where it has stopped meaning have at all.

ageRule.body: An age in French is a number of years that belong to you, so it takes avoir and the word ans is never left off. You already own every number you need for this: they were the whole of three earlier lessons, and nothing about counting changes here. What changes is the frame the number sits in, and there is exactly one of them. Ask it with quel âge and answer it with a form of avoir plus a number plus ans.
ageRule.title: Years are something you have

examples.note: The number is the part you already had.
The question that gets you the answer, in the tu form.

sixForms.body: Nine pronouns sit behind six forms, which is the arithmetic you were given two lessons ago and which holds here unchanged. What is new is that four of the six start on a vowel, so the pronoun in front binds to them: nous avons is said as one word with a Z in the middle, and so are vous avez, ils ont and elles ont. That join is not optional and it is the thing that separates ils ont from ils sont.
sixForms.term: ai, as, a, avons, avez, ont
sixForms.title: Six forms, and three of them join up out loud

examples.note: noo-za-VOHⁿ, one word out loud.
eel-ZOHⁿ. The S of ils wakes up, exactly as it did in vous êtes.

haveNotBe.body: English puts "am" in front of hungry, cold, afraid, right and twenty. French puts "have" in front of all five, and the word after it is a thing rather than a description: hunger, cold, fear, reason, years. So the sentence is not built the way yours is, and translating it word by word gives you something that is not French at all. This is the single most audible beginner error there is, because it lands in the first sentence anyone says about themselves.
haveNotBe.title: The swap English makes you get wrong

examples.note: Hunger, had. Not hungry, been.
Twenty years, had. Je suis vingt ans is not a sentence.

pastAmbush.body: Nearly a quarter of the sentences in this course that open on a form of avoir are not about having anything. J ai perdu mes clés is I lost my keys, not I have lost-keys. When the word after the form of avoir is another verb, the pair is a past tense and the have has gone. You are not learning that tense yet. What you need now is to recognise it on sight, so that a sentence you meet in the wild does not get read as a possession that is not there.
pastAmbush.term: j'ai in front of a verb
pastAmbush.title: When have stops meaning have

examples.note: Lost, in the past. There is no having in this sentence.
A real possession, for comparison. One noun after the form, no second verb.

withComplement.body: Eleven of these expressions are a straight swap of have for be. These three are not: they land on need, want and hurt rather than on be, and all three carry a little word after them that has to come too. Besoin and envie take de, which shortens to d apostrophe in front of a vowel. Mal takes à, and then the à joins whatever article the body part wants: au dos, à la tête, aux dents. Learn them as a group of three and the other eleven stay simple.
withComplement.term: besoin de, envie de, mal à
withComplement.title: The three that behave differently

examples.note: need, and the de that has to come with it.
hurt, and the à that merged with le to make au.

noArticleUnderNo.body: Say no to a thing you could count and the word in front of it collapses to de: j ai une voiture becomes je n ai pas de voiture. Say no to one of these expressions and nothing collapses, because there was never an article there to lose: j ai faim becomes je n ai pas faim. Both halves are on the same screen for a reason. Which one you get tells you which kind of sentence you were in, and it is the whole of what the negation unit will ask you to do.
noArticleUnderNo.term: pas de, and pas on its own
noArticleUnderNo.title: Two ways a negative can land

examples.note: une became de. The rule you met on un, une and des.
Nothing to collapse, so nothing collapsed. Never pas de faim.

lessons.title: Le verbe avoir

drills.coach: The pronoun is on the left. Say the form out loud before you turn the card, and join it up where it joins.
drills.title: Pronoun in, form out

drills.q: You and one colleague have an appointment. Which form?
drills.why: nous takes avons. avez belongs to vous, and the two are the pair most often swapped because both bind to their pronoun.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Read the English on the left. Say the French on the right out loud, and notice which verb you reached for first.
drills.title: Have it, do not be it

drills.q: You have not eaten since breakfast. What do you say?
drills.why: Faim is hunger, a thing, so it is had rather than been. The English am in front of hungry is what makes the wrong one feel right.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Every line here is a real age sentence. Say each one out loud and listen for the two things that are never missing: the verb, and the word ans.
drills.title: A number of years, held

drills.q: She is forty. Which is right?
drills.why: The verb is avoir and the word ans is never dropped. The third option gives a number with nothing to count, which is not an age in French.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Three buckets and eleven of the fourteen belong in the last one. Put each line where the word after the expression tells you it goes.
drills.title: What comes after it?

drills.q: You need a pen. Which is right?
drills.why: Besoin always carries de, and de shortens in front of a vowel sound. Mal is the one that takes à, and the other eleven take nothing at all.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Read each one and ask who is warm. If it is somebody, the verb is avoir. If it is the day, the verb is neither of the two you have learned.
drills.title: The person, or the room?

drills.q: The weather is warm today. Which is right?
drills.why: The weather takes neither of this lesson's verbs. Il a chaud would say that a particular man is too warm, which is a sentence about a person.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Say the negative out loud before you flip. Half of these leave a de behind and half of them leave nothing.
drills.title: What does the no leave behind?

drills.q: Which one is right for "I am not hungry"?
drills.why: Faim never had an article, so the negative had nothing to collapse to de. The de only appears where a un, une or des had to be removed.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Read the word straight after the form of avoir. A noun means somebody has something. Another verb means a past tense, and nothing is owned.
drills.title: Having, or something else?

drills.q: Which one is NOT about having something?
drills.why: Perdu is a verb and it sits directly after the form of avoir, so the pair is a past tense. Nothing is being owned in that sentence.
opts: J'ai perdu mes clés ce matin.
drills.title: One more time

sections.title: The full paradigm

sections.body: Four of the six start on a vowel, and every one of them pulls the silent consonant in front of it back to life. Nous ends in a silent s and avons starts on an a, so the s returns as a z and the two words are said as one: noo-za-VOHⁿ. The same happens with vous avez, ils ont and elles ont. Je is the fifth case and it behaves differently: rather than binding, it disappears, because ai starts on a vowel and je loses its e and is written j apostrophe. Only tu as and il a stand apart with nothing joining them, and those two happen to be the pair that sound identical, since the s of as is silent. So the six forms produce five distinct sounds, and the pronoun is what tells you which of the two identical ones you are hearing. That is why French never drops a subject pronoun the way English drops one in a list.
sections.title: The four that join up

sections.body: These are the two most used verbs in French and they are the two most broken, for the same reason: a form said a hundred times a day is never smoothed out by analogy the way a rare verb is. You have now learned both outright and no other verb will ask this of you again. One pair is worth keeping apart from the start because it belongs to both lessons at once: ils sont opens on a clear s and means they are, while ils ont carries a z over from the silent s of ils and means they have. Slowed down they are obvious. At conversational speed the z against the s is the only thing separating them, and there is no other clue in the sentence, because both are followed by whatever comes next with no pause. The written forms are further apart than the spoken ones, so reading them will not train your ear. That is what the listening mission is for.
sections.title: Against être, which you already have

sheets.title: The fourteen, and the two rules around them

rows.v: J'ai vingt ans, never Je suis vingt ans. And ans is never left off.
J'ai faim, J'ai froid, J'ai peur. Eleven of them, all the same swap.
Il fait chaud for the room. J'ai chaud for the person.
besoin de, envie de, mal à. The other eleven carry nothing.
Je n'ai pas de voiture. The une collapsed to de.
Je n'ai pas faim. Nothing collapsed, because nothing was there.

sections.title: The four places English points the wrong way

sections.body: Across the a1 corpus, 119 of the 522 rows that open on a form of avoir are not about having anything, which is 23 out of every hundred. J ai perdu mes clés is I lost my keys. Elle a pris le bus is she took the bus. Nous avons réservé une table is we booked a table, and the table belongs to a restaurant. In every one of them the form of avoir is doing a job you have not been taught yet, and the word straight after it is what gives it away: one noun means somebody has something, another verb means a past tense. The reason this matters now rather than later is that you will read four or five times as much French as you produce for the next year, and a learner who meets j ai only as I have will read almost a quarter of what they meet as a possession that is not there. You are not being asked to use this. You are being asked to see it and move on.
sections.title: The sentences where it stops meaning have

lessons.reframe: French has it. English is it.

overview.introFr: Six formes, et un verbe qui passe le plus clair de son temps à ne pas vouloir dire avoir.

say.text: One question, twice, and nothing you said was mispronounced. Watch which word was missing.

beats.text: A flat in Nantes on a Saturday evening. It is your friend Léa's birthday and you have met nobody here before.
Her grandmother has taken the chair beside you and turned it to face you properly. She is going to ask you something.

beats.en: How old are you?
beats.speaker: Léa's grandmother

beats.prompt: You are twenty. What goes back?

options.en: the one English hands you
the one with a different verb in it

followUp.works: Yes, and the verb is the whole of it. Watch what the other one does to the room.
followUp.breaks: Every word in that is a real word. Watch what happens next anyway.

beats.en: (I am twenty years)
Sorry? How old are you?
beats.stage: She says it again, slower, and glances at Léa while she waits.
beats.speaker: Léa's grandmother

beats.body: She heard "I am twenty years" and waited for the rest of it. There was nothing to guess at, so she asked again instead of correcting you. That is why this error survives: it never gets fixed for you.
beats.coach: One verb, and it is the same swap on eleven other sentences you will need this week.

right.en: I have twenty years, which is how French says it

wrong.en: I am twenty years, and then it stops

beats.heading: She did not hear a mistake

beats.en: I am twenty.
beats.speaker: Second try

beats.en: Ah, twenty. Are you hungry?

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do

sections.say: You have met this arithmetic before and you have already filled it in once. This is the second time.
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.

cards.body: You counted the nine and were shown the six slots they sit in, and nothing filled them. il, elle and on share one; ils and elles share another. That has not changed and it is not re-taught here.
cards.head: Nine pronouns. Six verb forms.
cards.label: Two lessons ago

cards.body: être took the first of those two sets. You learned its six outright because nothing could be derived from anything, and that is the deal for exactly two verbs in the language.
cards.head: One set filled
cards.label: Last lesson

cards.body: avoir is the other one. Six forms, no stem, and after this every verb you meet has a pattern behind it. Ten minutes of memorising and the closed set is closed.
cards.head: The second, and the last
cards.label: This one

cards.body: The forms are the easy half and they are on one screen. French has it. English is it. That is the half that will still be catching you in a year, so it gets five missions and the forms get three.
cards.head: Not the six
cards.label: What is actually hard

sections.title: The Second Set Of Six

sections.say: Six rows for nine pronouns, exactly as last time. Tap any row to hear the whole sentence.

detail.body: Je never survives in front of this one. Ai starts on a vowel, so je loses its e and the two are written as one word. You have made that drop since your first lesson on le and la, and here it is compulsory.
detail.title: j'ai

rows.say: Tu as un cadeau pour Léa ?

detail.body: Two letters and the s is silent, so out loud this is the same sound as the il form. Only the pronoun in front separates them, which is why the pronoun is never dropped.
detail.title: tu as

rows.say: Il a un cadeau pour Léa.

detail.body: One letter, and it takes no accent: à with an accent is a different word meaning to or at. Three pronouns share this form, and on means we and still takes it, which is the mismatch a1.05 spent a mission on.
detail.title: The row that does the work

rows.say: Nous avons un cadeau pour Léa.

detail.body: The first of the four that bind. Avons starts on a vowel, so the silent s of nous wakes up as a z and the two words are said as one. Never noo, then a-VOHⁿ.
detail.title: nous avons

rows.say: Vous avez un cadeau pour Léa ?

detail.body: The same join you learned on vous êtes, on a different verb. If you can already say that one you can say this one, and the two are the most common openings to a question you will hear in a shop.
detail.title: vous avez

rows.say: Ils ont un cadeau pour Léa.

detail.body: A nasal vowel, a silent t, and a z carried over from the silent s of ils. Hold this one carefully: ils sont is a different verb and one consonant is the whole difference between them.
detail.title: ils ont

cards.label: 1 of 6

cards.label: 2 of 6

cards.body: He has. One letter, no accent.
cards.label: 3 of 6

cards.body: We have. Joined by a z.

sections.say: Read the pronoun, say the form, then check. Nothing derives from anything, which is the point.
sections.title: Pronoun, Then Form

check.q: Which of these is the form that follows on?
check.why: on means we and takes the form il takes, so it is a. That collapse was a1.05's and it holds for every verb in the language.

check.q: You hear a z between the pronoun and the verb. How many of the six do that?
check.why: Four: nous avons, vous avez, ils ont and elles ont. Every form starting on a vowel pulls the silent consonant in front of it back to life.

sections.say: Two pairs, and each of them is one consonant. Slow the audio down before you answer.

lines.en: They have white sheets of paper.
He has a present for Léa.
lines.fr: Il a un cadeau pour Léa.

lines.en: They have a present for Léa.
lines.fr: Ils ont un cadeau pour Léa.

sections.title: Two Verbs, One Consonant

questions.q: What separates ils ont from ils sont, out loud?
questions.why: Both end on the same nasal vowel with a silent t. The s of ils comes back as a z in front of ont, and sont brings its own s. That is the whole of it.

questions.q: Lines three and four differ by more than the verb. What else moved?
questions.why: il became ils, and that is the only clue you get in writing, because the s of ils is silent. In speech the z is what tells you.
opts: The pronoun, from one person to several

questions.q: Which pair is harder to separate at speed?
questions.why: The first pair differs by a liaison that either exists or does not; the second by which consonant that liaison produces. Slowed down both separate cleanly.

sections.say: Read this one properly. It is the reason twelve separate things in this lesson are one thing.
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.

cards.body: French has it. English is it. Your English puts am in front of hungry. French puts have in front of hunger, and the second word is a thing rather than a description.
cards.head: Six words for twelve rules
cards.label: The line

cards.body: Nothing about the French here is irregular. English is the odd one: it uses be for states that most languages treat as things you carry. Translate word by word and you get something that is not a sentence.
cards.head: The trouble is on your side
cards.label: It is about English

cards.body: Before you say any of these, put the English into the shape French wants: I have hunger, I have twenty years, he has fear. If that reads as odd English, it is right French.
cards.head: Say the English literally
cards.label: Test it on yourself

cards.body: Eleven of the fourteen expressions in this lesson work this way and so does every age anybody will ever tell you. Three of the fourteen do not, and they get their own screen so you know which three.
cards.head: Eleven, plus your age
cards.label: How far it goes

sections.title: The Swap

sections.say: French has it. English is it. You already own every number in this table. What is new is the frame around it, and there is one.

detail.body: The number came from the counting lessons and nothing about it changes here. What changes is that French counts years as something you hold, so the verb is avoir and the word ans is never dropped. Twenty on its own is not an age.
detail.title: Twenty years, had

detail.body: This sentence was written for the numbers lesson, where sixty was the thing being taught. You already read it once and never asked why the verb was there. It is the same rule and it holds for every person.
detail.title: The same on somebody else

detail.body: Quel âge as-tu to somebody you would call tu, and quel âge avez-vous to anybody else. The register split is a1.01's and nothing here changes it. Answer either one the same way.
detail.title: The question, both ways

rows.say: Elle a six ans et demi.
cells: Elle a six ans et demi.
She is six and a half

detail.body: Et demi after ans, and it is the sentence every parent of a small child says. Nothing about the rule moves for it. This one was already in the corpus and no course teaches it.
detail.title: The half year, free

rows.say: Le chien de mon grand-père a treize ans.
cells: Le chien de mon grand-père a treize ans.

detail.say: Mon voisin a soixante-dix-sept ans mais il court encore.
detail.body: A dog, a building, a bottle of wine. If it has an age, it has years, and the verb does not change because the thing is not a person. This is where a learner stops expecting avoir and reaches for être again.
detail.title: Anything with an age

sections.title: How Old Are You

sections.say: Eleven screens. Every one of them is the same swap, so there is one thing to remember and eleven places to use it.
sections.title: The Eleven

sections.say: One question, and the difference between the two wrong answers is the whole of the next mission.
sections.title: Cold, Or A Cold Room?

check.q: You are cold. What do you say?
check.why: Cold is something you have here. Je suis froid describes your personality rather than your temperature, and il fait froid is about the room.

sections.say: Three of the fourteen do not follow the line above. Knowing which three is worth more than knowing the eleven.
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.

cards.fr: besoin de · envie de · mal à
cards.body: The eleven all turn English am into French have. These three turn into need, want and hurt instead, so there is no be to swap out and nothing to translate literally.
cards.head: These land somewhere else
cards.label: Not a swap

cards.body: Besoin and envie both carry de, and it shortens to d apostrophe in front of a vowel sound. Leave the de out and the sentence stops: j ai besoin eau is not French.
cards.head: Two of them take de
cards.label: de, twice

cards.body: Mal takes à, and the à then merges with whatever the body part wants: au dos, à la tête, aux dents. This is the commonest of the fourteen in real speech by a distance.
cards.head: The third takes à
cards.label: à, once

cards.body: A learner told there are fourteen expressions memorises fourteen. A learner told there are eleven of one kind and three of another has a shape, and a shape survives a week off.
cards.head: Three, not fourteen
cards.label: Why it is worth naming

sections.title: The Three That Differ

sections.say: One question. The little word after the expression is what the answer turns on.
sections.title: Which Kind Is It?

check.q: You want to say you need a pen. Which is right?
check.why: Besoin always carries de, and de shortens in front of the vowel of un. The verb is avoir, so the third option is wrong twice over.

sections.say: French has it. English is it. And when it is the weather rather than you, French uses neither of them.

detail.say: Elle a chaud dans la salle d'attente.
detail.body: The first says you are too warm. The second says the weather is. They are not interchangeable and swapping them produces two different mistakes: il a chaud about the weather, and je suis chaud about yourself, which means something else entirely.
detail.title: J'ai chaud · il fait chaud

rows.say: Tu as froid ? Il fait froid ?

detail.say: Il a froid dans le bureau.
detail.body: Tu as froid asks about the person in front of you. Il fait froid asks about outside. Get the pair right on chaud and froid comes with it, because the split is identical and there is nothing extra to learn.
detail.title: The same pair, on cold

detail.body: Je suis chaud is real French and it is not about temperature at all: in everyday speech it means you are keen or up for something. Said in a warm room it will be understood as an answer to a question nobody asked.
detail.title: The one to avoid

sections.frSub: J'ai chaud ou il fait chaud
sections.title: Hot Rooms And Hot People

sections.say: Nearly a quarter of the sentences you will meet with this verb are not about having anything. Here is how to see it coming.
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.

cards.fr: J'ai perdu mes clés ce matin.
cards.sub: I lost my keys this morning
cards.body: There is no having in that sentence. J ai is there, and what follows it is another verb, and the pair of them together is a past tense you have not met yet.
cards.head: Not a possession
cards.label: Almost a quarter

cards.fr: Elle a pris le bus ce matin.
cards.sub: She took the bus this morning
cards.body: One noun after the form means having. Another verb after the form means the past. That is the whole check and it takes a second.
cards.head: Look at the next word
cards.label: The test

cards.fr: Nous avons réservé une table pour six personnes.
cards.sub: We reserved a table for six
cards.body: There is a table in it, so it looks like a possession. Read the word straight after avons: it is a verb, so this is the past and nobody currently owns a table.
cards.head: A noun turns up anyway
cards.label: The one that fools people

cards.fr: Ils ont pris le premier bus du matin.
cards.body: You are not learning this tense yet. What you need today is to stop reading it as possession, so that a page of French stops looking like a list of things people own.
cards.head: Recognise, do not use
cards.label: What to do now

sections.title: When Have Stops Meaning

sections.say: The same negative on two sentences, and it leaves a different thing behind each time.

rows.say: J'ai une voiture. Je n'ai pas de voiture.

detail.body: Une collapses to de under the negative, which is the rule you met on un, une and des one lesson ago. Not pas une voiture and not pas la voiture. Nothing new is being asked of you here.
detail.title: A thing you could count

rows.say: J'ai faim. Je n'ai pas faim.

detail.body: Faim never had a word in front of it, so there was nothing for the negative to collapse. It is pas faim and never pas de faim. This is the half nobody teaches, and it catches the learner who took the first half seriously.
detail.title: An expression, with no article

rows.say: Je n'ai pas de voiture. Je n'ai pas faim.

detail.body: This works backwards too. If the de turned up, you were talking about a countable thing. If it did not, you were using one of the fourteen. That is the ground the negation unit builds on, and you have it before you get there.
detail.title: What the answer tells you

sections.title: Saying No, Two Ways

sections.say: French has it. English is it. Four sentences an English speaker produces in their first month, one per screen.
sections.title: Four Traps

errors.why: This one costs the most, because it lands in the first sentence you say about yourself and it is not a near miss. Je suis vingt ans says "I am twenty years" and stops, so a listener has nothing to repair and asks again instead.
errors.right: Saying « J'ai vingt ans » for "I am twenty".
errors.wrong: Saying « Je suis vingt ans » for "I am twenty".

errors.why: The same swap on a different noun, and the same shape of failure. Faim is hunger, a thing, so French puts have in front of it. This holds for eleven of the fourteen expressions in this lesson and there is nothing to memorise beyond that.
errors.right: Saying « J'ai faim » for "I am hungry".
errors.wrong: Saying « Je suis faim » for "I am hungry".

errors.why: Wrong twice. Warmth is had here, and je suis chaud is a real sentence meaning you are keen or up for something, so it is understood as an answer to a question nobody asked. Il fait chaud is the version for the weather.
errors.right: Saying « J'ai chaud » when the room is warm.
errors.wrong: Saying « Je suis chaud » when the room is warm.

errors.why: A rule applied one noun too far. De turns up under a negative only where an article had to be removed, and faim never had one. Je n ai pas de voiture is right for that same reason: it had a une in it.
errors.right: Saying « Je n'ai pas faim » for "I am not hungry".
errors.wrong: Saying « Je n'ai pas de faim » for "I am not hungry".

sections.say: Six sentences in this passage use the verb and not one of them means have. Tap any underlined word.
sections.text: It is Sunday and Claire is at her grandmother's table for the first time. Her grandmother pours the wine and looks at her over the top of her glasses. « Vous avez quel âge ? » Claire has practised this one on the train, twice, out of the window. « J'ai vingt ans. » Her grandmother nods and passes the bread without saying anything else about it. « Et vous avez faim ? » Claire has not eaten since seven in the morning. « Oui, j'ai très faim. » Her cousin leans across the table and says the sentence Claire has been dreading all week. « Moi, j'ai mal à la tête. Je n'ai pas faim. » Nobody offers him anything, and nobody asks him to explain himself. Her grandmother turns back and points at the window with the knife she is holding. « Tu as chaud ? Il fait chaud aujourd'hui. » Claire looks at those two questions and works out that only one of them was about her. « Non, ça va. Mais j'ai soif. »
sections.title: Sunday At Her Grandmother's

glossary.note: The polite form of the question. Quel âge as-tu to somebody you would call tu.
Twenty years, had. Je suis vingt ans is not a sentence, and it is the error this lesson opens on.
The same verb again, on a different noun. Hunger is a thing you have.
Très goes in front of the noun rather than in front of a description, because faim is a noun.
One of the three that take a little word after them. Mal takes à, and à plus la is à la.
No de anywhere, because faim never had an article for the negative to remove.
About the person. This is the question she is really asking.
About the weather, and a different verb entirely. The two sit in the same breath here on purpose.
Thirst, had. The eleventh of the eleven, and the last one in the passage.

questions.a: The first is about Claire and uses avoir. The second is about the weather and uses a different verb, faire, so only the first one needs an answer about how she feels.
questions.q: Claire's grandmother asks two questions in one breath near the end. What is the difference between them?

questions.a: Because faim never had an article in front of it, so the negative had nothing to collapse. If he had said he did not have a car, the une would have become de.
questions.q: The cousin says two things and both use the same verb. Why is there no « de » in the second one?

questions.a: None of them. Every use of avoir here is an age, a state or a pain, which is the whole point: the verb is called "to have" and most of what a beginner does with it is something else.
questions.q: Count the sentences in the passage where this verb means have. What did you find?

sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.back: J'ai vingt ans. French has it. English is it.
cards.front: Somebody asks how old you are. You are twenty.

cards.back: J'ai faim. Hunger is a thing you have, not a way you are.
cards.front: You have not eaten since seven this morning.

cards.back: J'ai chaud. Il fait chaud would be about the room instead.
cards.front: The room is too warm for you personally.

cards.back: Tu as raison. Never tu es raison.
cards.front: Your friend has just proved they were correct.

cards.back: J'ai besoin d'un stylo. Besoin always carries de.
cards.front: You want to say you need a pen.

cards.back: J'ai mal à la tête. Mal takes à, and à plus la is à la.
nous avons, said as one word with a z in the middle.
cards.front: The nous form, with its join.

cards.back: ils ont. With an s instead of the z it would be ils sont.
cards.front: You hear a z, then a nasal vowel. Which verb?

cards.back: Je n'ai pas de voiture. Une collapsed to de.
cards.front: « J'ai une voiture. » Now say you do not.

cards.back: Je n'ai pas faim. Nothing collapsed, because nothing was there.
cards.front: « J'ai faim. » Now say you do not.

cards.back: No. A second verb follows the form, so it is a past tense and nothing is owned.
cards.front: « J'ai perdu mes clés. » Is that a possession?

cards.back: Quel âge avez-vous ? With somebody you call tu it is quel âge as-tu.
