sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched an evening cool by one degree because a question was asked too carefully, and nothing in that sentence was wrong. Since then you have taken one question apart into three shapes that mean exactly the same thing, found that the difference between a statement and a question can be nothing but the direction of your voice, learned a block you can bolt onto anything without moving a word, and closed a list of twelve swapped-round forms including two with a letter in the middle that means nothing at all. You also have a word for yes that only works when somebody has put a not in the question. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.
sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: The situation is in every question. The label is in none of them.
rounds.label: Who is it for

questions.q: You are writing to a landlord you have never met, asking whether the flat is still free. Which shape fits best?
questions.why: Swap the words round. Writing to a stranger is where the careful shape belongs, and a letter has no voice for a rising contour to live in. Est-ce que would also be correct here and read a shade plainer.
opts: Swap the words round: Est-elle libre ?
Let your voice rise: Elle est libre ?
Say it twice to be safe

questions.q: You are cooking with a close friend and want to ask if they are hungry. Which of these would sound oddly formal?
questions.why: As-tu faim ? is correct French and it is the one that lands as careful. That is the whole of the opening scene: nothing was wrong, and the room noticed anyway. The other two are both comfortable with a friend.
opts: None of them, they are identical in feel

questions.q: A shop assistant asks a customer whether they have a smaller size. Which shape are they most likely to use, and why?
questions.why: Swapped round. « Avez-vous la taille en dessous ? » is a published sentence doing exactly this: a stranger being served, by somebody whose job is to be careful. The corpus agrees: this shape is five times commoner in formal settings than casual ones.
opts: Voice only, because shops are informal
Swapped round, because they are being professionally careful with a stranger
Est-ce que, because shops require it
Any of them, the situation does not matter

questions.q: Ask a friend, out loud, whether they are ready. Use the shape that suits a friend.
questions.why: Tu es prêt ? with your voice rising at the end. No words moved and nothing was added. Half the mark here is the contour: said flat, this is a statement and it will be heard as one.

rounds.say: Four listens. This is the one method that exists only as a sound.
rounds.label: What your ear does

questions.q: Listen. Is this a statement or a question?
questions.why: A question, and the voice rising on the last syllable is the only thing that says so. The words are identical to the statement « Tu es prêt. » This is the one contrast in A1 that nothing but your ear can settle.

questions.q: Listen. Which shape is this?
questions.why: The est-ce que block. It runs together into something like ess-kuh and nobody leans on it, which is why it can be easy to miss at speed: the sentence you are meant to hear starts after it.

questions.q: Listen. Is this asking about a man or a woman?
questions.why: A woman: est-ce qu'elle. This is the one genuine ear question in the lesson, because ess-KEEL and ess-KEL sit very close together at speed. Everything else here you can see on the page.

questions.q: Listen. Which shape is this?
questions.why: Swapped round: Es-tu. The verb came first. Out loud the two words run together as one, which is what the hyphen is showing you on the page, and it is why the hyphen is not optional.

rounds.say: The one that always works, and the one place it changes shape.
rounds.label: The safe block

questions.q: Turn « Tu es prêt. » into a question using est-ce que. Write the whole thing.
questions.why: Est-ce que tu es prêt ? The statement went in untouched: same words, same order, three more on the front. Nothing inside a sentence ever moves for this method, which is exactly why it is the safe one.

questions.q: You want to ask whether he is ready. Which is correct?
questions.why: Est-ce qu'il. The e of que is cut in front of a vowel and an apostrophe stands where it was. You have watched French refuse to let two vowels meet three times before this: l'amie, mon amie and n'ai.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Est-ce que elle est prête ? ». Fix it.
questions.why: Est-ce qu'elle. A vowel follows, so the e goes and an apostrophe replaces it. The rule is about the sound rather than the spelling: anything starting with a vowel sound does this, and nothing starting with a consonant does.

questions.q: What changes inside the sentence when you put est-ce que on the front of it?
questions.why: Nothing at all. Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices. That is precisely why: there is no form to remember, no hyphen to place and no letter to insert, so it cannot go wrong under pressure the way the other two can.
opts: The verb moves to the front

rounds.say: Twelve forms, one hyphen, and a letter that means nothing.
rounds.label: Swapping them round

questions.q: You want to ask, carefully, whether he is hungry. Which is correct?
questions.why: A-t-il faim ? A ends in a vowel and il begins with one, so a t goes between them. It means nothing and exists only to stop the two vowels colliding. This is one of two places in twelve forms where anything is inserted.

questions.q: You want to ask a group, carefully, whether they are ready. Write the two words that start the question.
questions.why: Êtes-vous. The verb comes first and the pronoun second. Note that what you typed cannot show whether you used the hyphen, because the checker ignores punctuation: on paper it is compulsory, and « Etes vous » is a typo rather than a question.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Est-t-il prêt ? ». Fix it.
questions.why: Est-il, with no extra t. Est already ends in one, so there is nothing to keep apart. The insertion only happens when the verb ends in a vowel, which is why a-t-il needs it and est-il does not.

questions.q: Why can you learn all of these as a list rather than working them out?
questions.why: Because you can conjugate two verbs so far. Six persons times two verbs is twelve, which is a list you finish rather than a pattern you extend. When a third verb arrives the same swap works on it in the same way.
opts: Because French only has twelve verbs
Because you can conjugate two verbs so far, so there are twelve forms
Because the swapped forms are irregular
Because only être can be swapped

rounds.say: Three ways to ask, and you use exactly one of them.
rounds.label: One method at a time

questions.q: Which of these is correct French?
questions.why: Est-ce que tu es prêt ? The block already made it a question, so swapping the words as well asks twice. This is the commonest thing that goes wrong once all three methods are available, and the fix is to pick one and stop.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Est-ce que as-tu faim ? ». Fix it.
questions.why: Either « Est-ce que tu as faim ? » or « As-tu faim ? », and both are accepted here. What you cannot do is use both methods in one question. Est-ce que wants an ordinary statement behind it, with the words in their normal order.

questions.q: You want to ask whether you yourself are hungry, out loud, without sounding strange. Write the question.
questions.why: Est-ce que j'ai faim ? The swapped-round je form is ai-je, and nobody says it: it appears in none of the twenty-seven thousand sentences this app holds. When the swap produces a form real speakers avoid, est-ce que covers it.

questions.q: Which one of the three is correct in every situation there is?
questions.why: Est-ce que. Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices. The other two are both correct French and both say something about how close you are, so either can be the wrong temperature. Est-ce que says nothing, which makes it safe.

rounds.say: Four answers, and one of them only exists because of a not.
rounds.label: Answering

questions.q: Somebody asks you « Tu n'es pas prêt ? » and you are, in fact, ready. What do you say?
questions.why: Si, je suis prêt. The question has a not in it and you are disagreeing with the not, which is the one job si does. Answering oui there would sound like you were agreeing that you were not ready.

questions.q: Somebody asks you « Tu es prêt ? » with no not in it, and you are ready. What do you say?
questions.why: Oui. Si only turns up when there is a negative to push back against, so using it on an ordinary question is as odd as using oui on a negative one. No not in the question means no si in the answer.

questions.q: Answer « Tu as faim ? » in the affirmative, saying more than one word. Write it.
questions.why: Oui, j'ai faim. The word on its own would have been a complete answer, and adding the reason is friendlier. Note j'ai rather than je ai, for the same reason est-ce qu'il is not est-ce que il.

questions.q: Say the answer you would give if you genuinely did not know yet.
questions.why: Peut-être. It works as a whole reply on its own, exactly like oui and non, and it is the answer people give most often in real conversation. Two words joined by a hyphen, said as one.

sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can ask any yes-or-no question three ways, choose between them by looking at who is in front of you rather than at the sentence, produce all twelve swapped-round forms including the two with an inserted letter, and answer with oui, non, peut-être or si. The habit underneath all of it is worth keeping: when you are unsure, the safe form exists and costs you nothing. The next unit is about asking for information rather than for a yes or a no, and it is built directly on the block you have just learned, so nothing here is going to be replaced.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices. The safe one is a real thing and it is worth having.
A statement and a question can be four identical words, separated by your voice going up.
Est-ce que never moves anything inside the sentence. That is the whole reason it is safe.
The swapped-round forms are a closed list of twelve, and nobody says ai-je.
Si is the answer to a question with a not in it, and it has no other job.

errorTriggers.description: Picks a question shape without reference to who is listening: uses the swapped-round form with a close friend, or the voice-only form in a letter. Produces perfectly correct French that lands at the wrong temperature, and nobody ever corrects it.

Says a voice-only question with a flat contour, so it lands as a statement and is answered as one. The one failure mode the first method has, and the learner can eventually hear it, which is why it is a drill rather than a scene.

Writes « Est-ce que il » without cutting the e. The fourth appearance of one anti-hiatus rule, and the first three were all repaired differently, so the learner has three precedents and no reason to prefer this one.
Drops the compulsory hyphen in « Es tu », or gets the inserted t wrong in either direction: « A-il faim ? » with none, « Est-t-il ? » with one it does not need.

Asks the question twice in one sentence: « Est-ce que es-tu prêt ? ». The commonest thing that goes wrong once all three methods are on the table, and unlike the register error it produces something that is not French.
Answers a negative question with oui, which reads as agreeing with the negative rather than contradicting it. Also the reverse: reaching for si on an ordinary question that has no not in it.

grammarAssumed: The nine subject pronouns, introduced in a1.05
The full present of être, introduced in a1.06, which asked nine questions with the voice alone and named none of them as a method
The full present of avoir, introduced in a1.07, including avoir faim
ne… pas around a finite verb, and the elision of ne, introduced in a1.18
non as a whole answer rather than a piece of a sentence, introduced in a1.18
The rising contour on a final syllable, and that up is a question and down is a statement, introduced in sons.08
Elision as a repair for two vowels meeting, introduced in sons.07
Liaison, and that a silent final consonant attaches to a following vowel, introduced in sons.10
tu against vous as a choice about the listener, introduced in a1.05 and used throughout
grammarIntroduced: The three yes-no interrogative strategies, and the register that selects between them
Rising intonation named as an interrogative strategy for the first time, having been used since a1.01
The est-ce que periphrasis, and that it leaves constituent order untouched
The elision of est-ce que to est-ce qu' before a vowel or mute h
Subject-clitic inversion, restricted to être and avoir as a closed twelve-form paradigm
The obligatory hyphen in an inverted verb-clitic group
Epenthetic -t- between a vowel-final verb and a vowel-initial third-person clitic
That ai-je and suis-je are avoided in real usage and are not taught as production
si as the positive reply to a negative question, against oui after a positive one
n'est-ce pas and non as tag questions, for recognition only

lessons.intro: In French, a whole word can turn on a single vowel that English does not even have. This is the deep dive into the core French vowel sounds: why French vowels stay pure instead of sliding like English ones, and how to finally make the hardest two, the U and the two EU sounds.
lessons.title: Les voyelles, en profondeur

overview.introFr: En français, un mot entier peut basculer sur une seule voyelle que l'anglais ne possède même pas. Plongez dans les voyelles orales : pourquoi elles restent pures, et comment enfin réussir les deux plus difficiles.
overview.titleEn: French Vowels in Depth: Pure Sounds, No Gliding

say.text: Listen to what almost went wrong on an ordinary café morning.

beats.text: You are ordering breakfast. Everything you are about to say, you already know how to say. One vowel is going to decide how much butter arrives.

beats.en: Good morning! What would you like?
beats.speaker: Serveur

beats.prompt: You want a little butter with your bread. How do you say « un peu de beurre » ?

options.en: a little butter, the EU held flat and rounded
letting the EU slide toward an O

followUp.works: That is it. Now see how little has to slip for the other one to come out.
followUp.breaks: That is the slide, and the waiter has no way to know you did not mean it.

beats.body: EU and O are one small move apart. Let the EU relax backward and you have not made an accent mistake, you have ordered something else. The waiter hears a word that exists and serves it.
beats.coach: Keep the lips rounded and the tongue forward. The moment it drifts back, you are asking for a tub.
beats.heading: One vowel, a whole tub of butter.

beats.en: A whole tub of butter? Are you sure? A tub is a lot!
beats.fr: Un pot de beurre ? Vous êtes sûr ? Un pot, c’est beaucoup !
beats.stage: He pauses, already reaching for the tub.
beats.speaker: Serveur

beats.text: The waiter comes back with an entire tub of butter, not the small pat that was expected.
Nobody misheard you. French vowels carry meaning on their own, and this lesson is about holding each one still enough that the word you meant is the word that lands.

closing.text: « Un peu de beurre » and « un pot de beurre » are one vowel apart, and they produce completely different amounts of butter.

setting.place: A café counter

sections.say: Here's what this lesson will get you doing by voice.

goals.s: Produce French A [a] without the English glide toward 'ah-uh'.
Tell closed é, open è, and schwa [ə] apart, both by ear and by mouth position.
goals.t: É, È, and schwa, told apart

goals.s: Hold I [i] as a pure, unmoving sound, crisper and further forward than the English 'ee'.
Identify which spellings give a closed O [o] and which give an open O [ɔ], then pronounce both correctly.
goals.t: Closed or open O, predicted in advance

goals.s: Produce U [y] inside real words, not just as an isolated letter name.
Nail closed EU [ø] and open EU [œ], the one vowel pair with no English equivalent.
Tell U [y] and OU [u] apart by ear, the most common vowel mix-up for English speakers.
Read an unfamiliar French sentence aloud and correctly predict every vowel sound from the spelling alone.
goals.t: Read a vowel right the first time

sections.title: What You'll Be Able to Do

sections.hint: Six anchors before we dive into the detail

cards.body: French vowels are pure and unmoving. Each one keeps a single mouth position from start to finish, with no glide, unlike English, where many vowels drift toward a second sound.
cards.head: Pure, held vowels

cards.body: Front versus back: where the tongue sits in the mouth. Spread versus rounded: whether the lips stretch wide or close into a small circle. These two axes map out the entire French vowel system.
cards.head: Two axes that organize everything

cards.body: A [a] and I [i] already exist, almost identically, in English. A great place to start, as long as you keep them pure and don't let them glide.
cards.head: A and I: the two easy vowels

cards.body: O changes sound depending on what follows it. Closed at the end of a word or before a silent letter (mot, beau), open before a pronounced consonant (porte, bonne).
cards.head: O: closed or open

cards.body: An unaccented E is a quiet schwa (le), an é is closed (été), an è or ê is open (mère). Three sounds, three possible meanings.
cards.head: E: three sounds in one letter

cards.body: U [y] and EU [ø] / [œ] have no equivalent in English. Once you've mastered them, they're what really makes a French accent land.
cards.head: U and EU: the two 100% French sounds

sections.title: The Basic Idea
The Eleven Oral Vowel Sounds, One by One

sounds.memo: Closed at the end of a word, or before a silent letter. ô, au, and eau are always closed, no exceptions at this level.
Open when a consonant is actually pronounced right after it, in the same syllable.
No English equivalent. Say 'ee', keep your tongue still, then round your lips forward as if about to whistle.
sounds.sound: no English equivalent, rounded lips with a forward tongue

sounds.memo: Say the closed é of 'été', then round your lips without moving your tongue.
Say the open è of 'mère', then round your lips without moving your tongue.

The syllable is open, or ends in a silent letter
The word contains the letter U
It only depends on regional accent

say.text: This is the one that changes words on you. Slow down and feel where your tongue sits.

cards.tip: Feel where your tongue goes: keep it all the way forward, as if saying 'ee', then round only your lips. If your tongue pulls back, you get 'tout', not 'tu'.
Put a finger on your chin: for U, the jaw barely moves. Keep your tongue pressed behind your lower teeth, not back in your throat.
The sound stays short and tense at the front of the mouth, never relaxed toward the back like 'sous'.
Aim for 'i' with rounded lips. If you feel your whole mouth pull back, you've slipped into 'vous' by mistake.

sounds.sub: The sound with no English equivalent, and trap number one
sounds.label: U [y]
steps: Say 'ee' [i], feel your tongue high and forward, lips spread.
Hold the 'ee', don't let your tongue move.
Slowly round your lips into an 'oo' shape, as if about to whistle.
The sound that comes out is [y], French U. Repeat: tu, la rue, la lune, le mur.

sounds.sub: The second 100% French sound, in two versions
sounds.label: EU fermé et EU ouvert
steps: Say the English word 'her', but drop the R entirely, you're left with a neutral central vowel.
Without moving your tongue, purse your lips forward into a small circle, like you're about to blow out a candle.
For the closed version [ø] (word-final): keep the circle tight, sound short and bright.
For the open version [œ] (before a consonant): relax the circle slightly, let your jaw drop a touch more.

errors.why: English vowels default to diphthongs, so the mouth glides automatically if you're not paying attention.
errors.right: Hold each French vowel flat and still, one mouth position from start to finish
errors.wrong: Gliding pure vowels like English does (é becomes 'ay-ee', o becomes 'oh-oo')

errors.why: English has no rounded front vowel, so the brain substitutes the closest sound it already knows: [u].
errors.right: [y] = tongue forward like for 'ee', lips rounded like for 'oo', both at the same time
errors.wrong: Pronouncing U [y] like the English 'oo' (tu becomes 'too')

errors.why: This is the most common vowel mistake among English speakers, because both sounds sound like a generic 'oo' to an untrained ear.
errors.right: Feel your tongue's position: forward for U, back for OU
errors.wrong: Confusing U [y] and OU [u] in real words (vu and vous, su and sous)

errors.why: English O varies with accent and rhythm, but it never carries meaning the way [o] and [ɔ] do in French.
errors.right: Closed at the end of a word or before a silent letter, open before a pronounced consonant
errors.wrong: Treating closed O and open O as one single sound (beau and bonne)

lessons.intro: Four sounds with no English equivalent. The air escapes through the nose, and the n or m is never pronounced as a consonant. Master these and an entire layer of French grammar, including gender, becomes audible for the first time.
lessons.title: Les voyelles nasales

goals.s: Produce [ɑ̃] without ever sounding the N.
Produce [ɔ̃] and tell it apart from [ɑ̃] by ear.
Produce [ɛ̃] and tell it apart from the other three nasals.
Produce [œ̃] and recognize its merger with [ɛ̃] in casual speech.
Apply it: a vowel plus N or M at the end of a syllable nasalizes, and the N or M stays silent.
Apply it: a doubled N or M, or an N or M followed by a vowel, blocks nasalization, both sounds are heard.
Tell masculine from feminine by nasal versus oral quality alone, as in bon and bonne.
Predict whether liaison keeps a nasal, as in un homme, or denasalizes it, as in bon ami.

sections.hint: Six cards, then you'll hear all four nasals in action.

cards.body: A nasal vowel is one pure sound, not a vowel plus a consonant. The rule: a vowel followed by N or M at the end of a syllable nasalizes, and that N or M stays silent. bon becomes bɔ̃, temps becomes tɑ̃.
cards.head: The basic idea and the golden rule

cards.body: Nasalization is blocked in two cases: a doubled N or M, or an N or M followed by a vowel. bonne stays bɔn, ami stays ami. In both, the consonant is fully pronounced.
cards.head: The anti-rule

cards.body: The open nasal. Spelled an, am, en, or em.
cards.head: [ɑ̃] as in temps

cards.body: The rounded nasal. Spelled on or om.
cards.head: [ɔ̃] as in bon

cards.body: The front nasal. Spelled in, im, ain, aim, ein, eim, yn, or ym.
cards.head: [ɛ̃] as in pain

cards.body: The rarest nasal. Spelled un or um. Often merges with pain's sound in casual speech.
cards.head: [œ̃] as in un

sections.frSub: Le labo du voile du palais
sections.title: The soft palate lab

sounds.sub: Lower your soft palate while keeping your mouth in the vowel position, no consonant at all
sounds.label: How to nasalize: the soft palate technique
steps: Say 'ah' [a] normally, and notice your soft palate is raised, sealing off your nose.
Now hum 'mmm' and notice the opposite: your palate is fully lowered, all air through the nose, mouth closed.
Say 'ah' again, and this time, lower your soft palate exactly as you did for 'mmm', but keep your mouth open in the 'ah' position instead of closing it.
Air should now be escaping through both your nose and your open mouth at once. That is a nasal vowel.

sounds.sub: Check what follows: a vowel or a doubled N or M blocks the nasal
sounds.label: The anti-rule in motion
steps: As you approach a nasal word, glance ahead at the very next sound.
Consonant or silence follows: keep the nasal, say the word as spelled and nasalized.
A vowel follows, and the word is an article or number (un, mon, ton, son, bien, combien...): keep the nasal AND link the consonant forward.
A vowel follows, and the word is a fronted adjective like bon: switch to the oral, N-pronounced form, exactly as the feminine would sound.

errors.why: English always sounds its written consonants, but French nasal spelling is a signal, not a sound to produce.
errors.right: The vowel alone carries the nasality, the consonant is silent.
errors.wrong: Pronouncing the N or M inside a nasal vowel, so temps comes out sounding like tahnps.

errors.why: Learners over-apply the golden rule once they've learned it, forgetting the exceptions exist for a reason.
errors.right: N or M plus a vowel, or a doubled N or M, means oral: pronounce the consonant fully.
errors.wrong: Nasalizing words where the anti-rule blocks it, so ami sounds like ahn-mee, or bonne sounds like bohn.

errors.why: Both get flattened into one vague awn sound by an untrained English ear.
errors.right: [ɑ̃] is neutral-lipped, [ɔ̃] is rounded: genuinely different vowels, different words.
errors.wrong: Confusing [ɑ̃] and [ɔ̃], so that sans and son sound the same.

errors.why: English readers default to sounding out each letter individually.
errors.right: Both are single, fixed spellings for one nasal sound, [ɛ̃].
errors.wrong: Reading ain or ein as two separate vowel sounds.

errors.why: This exception applies to some of the most frequent words in the language, bien, rien, combien.
errors.right: en after i or y is pulled to [ɛ̃]: bien is [bjɛ̃], not [bjɑ̃].
errors.wrong: Assuming en is always [ɑ̃], even after i or y, so bien comes out sounding like byahn.

errors.why: This is genuine grammar hiding inside pronunciation, not a random performance detail.
errors.right: Articles and numbers usually keep the nasal and link, as in un homme, while a small set of pre-posed adjectives denasalize, as in bon ami.
errors.wrong: Treating every nasal-plus-vowel-initial-word boundary the same way.

errors.why: Treating a live sound change as either wrong or the only correct form both cause confusion. It's genuinely a spectrum across speakers and regions.
errors.right: Learn the distinct [œ̃] first, and recognize that many speakers merge it into [ɛ̃] in casual speech. Both are fine to understand and produce.
errors.wrong: Assuming [œ̃] must always sound identical to [ɛ̃], or always keeping them artificially separate even in casual contexts.

errors.why: Written French marks gender with extra letters, spoken French frequently marks it with nasality alone.
errors.right: Give the nasal or oral contrast the same care you'd give any other grammar rule, it changes meaning, not just accent.
errors.wrong: Forgetting that nasal versus oral is often the only spoken signal of grammatical gender, as in américain versus américaine.

sections.body: You just mastered the one feature of French that English has no equivalent for at all: four pure vowel sounds carried entirely through the nose. That skill alone unlocks an entire hidden layer of French grammar you could not hear before.
sections.title: The nasals are yours
points: You can produce all four nasal vowel qualities: [ɑ̃] in temps, [ɔ̃] in bon, [ɛ̃] in pain, and [œ̃] in un.
You apply the golden rule automatically: a vowel plus N or M at the end of a syllable nasalizes, and the N or M disappears.
You catch the anti-rule every time: a doubled N or M, or an N or M followed by a vowel, keeps both sounds oral.
You hear grammatical gender that used to be invisible, in pairs like bon and bonne, un and une, américain and américaine.
You predict liaison correctly, keeping the nasal in un homme and denasalizing bon ami.
This closes out the Sons unit. Your next stop is A1.

recorded.desc: THE MOST IMPORTANT CLIP IN THE LESSON. ONE SENTENCE ASKED WITH ALL SEVEN WORDS, IN ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, read straight down the list with no gap and no reset between rows. « Où est-ce que tu pars ? Quand est-ce que tu pars ? Pourquoi est-ce que tu pars ? Comment est-ce que tu pars ? Avec qui est-ce que tu pars ? Combien de temps est-ce que tu pars ? À quelle heure est-ce que tu pars ? » THE LAST FOUR WORDS MUST BE ACOUSTICALLY IDENTICAL IN ALL SEVEN. That sameness IS the lesson. A reader who records these seven separately will vary the pace and the intonation of the tail, and the learner will hear that variation as something the question word did. It did not. Read the seven as one list at one pace with one contour. EST-CE QUE IS UNSTRESSED THROUGHOUT and runs together as a single block, ess-kuh. Do not give it three separate words and do not put a beat before it. The stress in every one of these seven sentences falls on PARS and nowhere else.
clipIds: Avec qui est-ce que tu pars ?
Combien de temps est-ce que tu pars ?
À quelle heure est-ce que tu pars ?

recorded.desc: THE SCENE'S CHOICE, AND THE TWO LINES MUST BE IDENTICAL FROM THE SECOND WORD ON. « Où est-ce que le train part ? » immediately followed by « Quand est-ce que le train part ? », ONE TAKE, one voice. The only difference the learner may hear is the first word. DO NOT MAKE THE WRONG ONE SOUND WRONG. It is correct French and it gets a correct answer, and the whole scene depends on it sounding completely ordinary. Any hesitation or emphasis on the first line turns a slip nobody catches into a mistake somebody signalled, which is the opposite of what happened.
clipIds: Où est-ce que le train part ?
Quand est-ce que le train part ?

recorded.desc: ALL FOUR FORMS OF QUEL IN A SINGLE TAKE, CONSECUTIVELY, PRECISELY SO THE LEARNER HEARS THAT NOTHING CHANGES. « quel, quelle, quels, quelles », one after another, one voice, one pace, no gap. RECORDED APART, A SPEAKER WILL DRIFT AND INVENT A DIFFERENCE THAT DOES NOT EXIST, and a learner who hears an invented difference will spend a year listening for it. If a reader cannot resist marking the feminine or the plural, RECORD quel ONCE AND USE IT FOR ALL FOUR: that is a more truthful clip than a performed difference. Then, in the same take, the four sentences: « Quel train est là ? Quelle valise est là ? Quels trains sont là ? Quelles valises sont là ? » The first word of all four is the same word and must be read as the same word. The s of quels, valises and trains is SILENT in every one of these four lines. Do not sound any of them.

« où » AND « ou » IN ONE TAKE, ADJACENT, AND THEY MUST BE THE SAME SOUND, because that is exactly what they are. Same reason and same risk as the quel group: two separate recordings are two performances, and a reader who knows one of them is a question word will lift it. Do not. If in doubt, record ou once and use it for both. Then in the same take: « Où est le train ? » and « Le train ou le bus ? », so the learner hears the same sound doing two different jobs in one situation. Read both plainly. The teaching is that the ear cannot help and only the position can, and a performed difference teaches the opposite of it.

« qui » AND « que » ADJACENT, ONE TAKE, and this is the one pair in the lesson that IS a real minimal pair. Read them at ordinary speed with no exaggeration: qui has a clear ee and que has the ordinary unstressed vowel. Do not lengthen either. The difference is genuinely there and does not need help. Also in this take, and separately from the pair: « quand » and « comment » adjacent, at CONVERSATIONAL SPEED rather than slowly. Both end in the same nasal and at speed they are closer than a learner expects, which is the point of the clip. A carefully slowed reading makes them trivially distinguishable and teaches nothing.

NEVER RECORD « est-ce que » IN ISOLATION. It is an unstressed block that only exists in front of a sentence, and a clip of it alone would give it a stress pattern it never has in speech. If a request for one arrives, it is a mistake in the request. What IS recorded here is the frame IN PLACE: « Est-ce que tu es prêt ? » with nothing in front of it, then « Où est-ce que tu habites ? » and « Est-ce que le train part à midi ? ». In all three the frame runs together as one unstressed block, ess-kuh, and the stress falls at the end of the sentence. The two blocks built on it, « qu'est-ce que » and « qu'est-ce qui », ARE recorded on their own, because unlike the bare frame they are things a learner says as a unit. Read them adjacently so the learner hears that only the last syllable separates them.
clipIds: Est-ce que le train part à midi ?

recorded.desc: The five that stand alone, each on a published sentence: « Où est la gare ? Quand commence le cours ? Comment vas-tu ? Pourquoi est-ce que tu es en retard ? Qui es-tu ? » One take, one voice, ordinary pace. KEEP EVERY NASAL CLOSED AND UNRELEASED. quand, comment and combien are nasal vowels with NO n sound behind them at all, and the app respells them KAHⁿ, koh-MAHⁿ and kohⁿ-BYAⁿ deliberately. The shipped cards used to close all three with a plain n and this lesson repairs them, so a recording that sounds the n would put the error back where the transcription no longer has it. The d of quand and the t of comment are silent.
clipIds: Pourquoi est-ce que tu es en retard ?

recorded.desc: « Combien de valises as-tu ? » and « Combien d'amis as-tu ? » ADJACENT, ONE TAKE, because the only difference between them is what happens to de and the learner has to hear that de is still there in both. In the second one the d attaches to the front of amis and comes out as one word, da-mee. Do not read it as combien, pause, d'amis. BOTH NASALS IN COMBIEN ARE OPEN VOWELS WITH NO N BEHIND THEM. This is the word whose shipped respelling closed both of them with a plain n, and it is the worst row this lesson repairs. Also in this take: « Combien de temps dure le film ? », where de is in front of a consonant again.
clipIds: Combien de temps dure le film ?

recorded.desc: One question in three positions, ONE TAKE, adjacent: « Qu'est-ce que tu fais ? », « Tu fais quoi ? », « Que fais-tu ? ». The learner has to hear that these are the same question, so read all three at the same pace and with the same weight. Do NOT read the third one more formally than the others: register is a1.19's lesson and this one does not teach it, and a performed formality would teach it by accident. The subject and object pair, in the same take: « Qu'est-ce qui est dans le sac ? » and « Qu'est-ce que tu as dans le sac ? ». Everything from dans onwards is identical and must sound identical.
clipIds: Qu'est-ce qui est dans le sac ?
Qu'est-ce que tu as dans le sac ?

recorded.desc: The five written traps, wrong version then right version, with a clear beat between them. Read EVERY wrong version plainly and at ordinary pace rather than comically. THREE OF THE FIVE ARE ACOUSTICALLY IDENTICAL TO THEIR CORRECT VERSIONS and that is the point of recording them at all: « Ou est le train ? » against « Où est le train ? » is one sound twice, and « Quel heure est-il ? » against « Quelle heure est-il ? » is one sound twice. Record them as such. A reader who marks the wrong one destroys the lesson those two traps exist to teach. « Combien enfants avez-vous ? » against « Combien d'enfants avez-vous ? » DOES differ audibly. So does « Tu fais que ? » against « Tu fais quoi ? », and the first of those genuinely sounds wrong, which is correct: it is the one trap in the group a French ear rejects immediately.

The opening scene, French bubbles only. The man at the information desk is in his fifties, has answered four hundred questions today and is STILL GENUINELY PLEASANT. His line « Voie 7. Tout droit, puis à gauche. » MUST BE HELPFUL AND COMPLETELY UNSUSPICIOUS. He has not noticed anything, because there is nothing to notice: the question he was asked was a good question and he answered it correctly. ANY HINT OF A QUESTION IN HIS VOICE TURNS THE SCENE INTO A CORRECTION and loses the whole point, which is that the error is invisible from both sides and costs a train anyway.
clipIds: Voie 7. Tout droit, puis à gauche.

lessons.intro: Seven words that decide which answer you get, and one frame that carries all of them. This is how to ask where, when, who, why, how and how many, put quel in front of a thing, and tell the two differences your ear can never reach.

deAfterCombien.body: Combien on its own asks how much something costs or weighs. The moment you name the thing you are counting, de arrives between them: combien de valises, combien de temps. And when the thing starts with a vowel, de loses its own vowel and becomes d apostrophe, which is the fifth time you have watched French refuse to let two vowels meet. Le became l apostrophe, ma became mon, ne became n apostrophe, and est-ce que becomes est-ce qu. One pressure, five rules, and now you only have to remember the pressure.
deAfterCombien.title: And de gets cut in front of a vowel

examples.note: A consonant follows, so de keeps its vowel.
A vowel follows, so de loses it. The same repair as l'ami.

quelTakesANoun.body: Six of these words stand on their own and never change. Quel does neither. It has to have a thing straight behind it, and it takes the shape of that thing exactly the way a colour does: quel train, quelle valise, quels trains, quelles valises. You have done this three times already, with colours, with the six adjectives that come first, and with where a describing word sits. This is the fourth, and it is the easiest of the four, because all four shapes are pronounced identically.
quelTakesANoun.title: The one that is not a question word like the others

examples.note: A train is the un kind, so quel.
A valise is the une kind, so quelle. Out loud these two are the same word.

firstWordCarries.body: Where, when, why and how are four completely different questions in English and four completely different answers in French, and the sentences that ask them can be identical from the second word on. That is not a trick of this lesson, it is how the language is built: the word at the front says what you want and the rest of the sentence says what you are asking about. So you are not learning seven ways to build a question. You are learning seven words that all drop into one.
firstWordCarries.term: the first word carries the question
firstWordCarries.title: Everything after it can stay the same

examples.note: Where. The last four words of this are the same as the next one.
When. One word changed and the whole question did.

onlyThePageKnows.body: Two things in this lesson are invisible to listening and both of them matter. Ou and ou with an accent are one sound: one means or and the other means where, and only the mark tells you which. And the four shapes of quel are one sound as well, all four of them, so the ending you write is never the ending you say. This is the same idea the colours lesson called endings you write and never say, arriving somewhere it changes the meaning rather than just the spelling. If you find yourself listening harder, stop. There is nothing in the recording to find.
onlyThePageKnows.term: differences you read and never hear
onlyThePageKnows.title: Your ear is not the problem here

examples.note: Where, with the accent on it.
Or, without one. Same sound, and the accent is the whole difference.

frameYouAlreadyHave.body: You met est-ce que asking yes and no questions, and you already know the two things that matter about it: it goes on the front of an ordinary sentence and moves nothing inside it, and it shortens to est-ce qu before a vowel. Nothing about it changes here. All that happens is that a word goes in front of it, and the answer stops being yes or no. A question word on its own is not a question: ou is just the word for where until something carries it.
frameYouAlreadyHave.title: The block from the last lesson, doing more work

examples.note: The frame with nothing in front of it, which is a yes or no question.
The same frame carrying a question word, published long before this lesson.

lessons.title: Les mots interrogatifs

drills.coach: Every one of these has the same frame in it. What separates the two piles is whether anything is standing in front of that frame, and that is the whole difference between a yes and a fact.
drills.title: What is missing?

drills.q: You want to ask where somebody lives. What goes between où and « tu habites »?
drills.why: est-ce que. Without it you have a question word standing in front of a statement, which is not yet a question.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Read the answer and ask yourself what kind of thing came back. A place, a person, a time, a reason, a number. Each one could only have come from one of the seven words, and that is how you check a question after you have asked it.
drills.title: Which question produced this?
buckets: a time, a reason or a number

drills.q: Somebody answers « C'est derrière la gare. » Which word did you ask with?
drills.why: où. A place came back, so a place was asked for. That is the only check available, and it happens after the answer rather than before.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Say all six out loud first. The first word is identical in every one of them, so listening will not sort this. Look at the noun instead and ask which kind it is, exactly as you did with le and la.
drills.title: Which shape?

drills.q: You want to ask which suitcase, and la valise is the une kind. Which shape?
drills.why: quelle. The une kind, one of them, so an e that you write and never say.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: These all ask the same thing. What separates the piles is where the word for what has ended up, and the spelling follows from that: que and its block at the front, quoi at the end. It is one word in two places.
drills.title: Where does the word sit?

drills.q: Which of these is French?
drills.why: Tu fais quoi ? Que cannot sit at the end of a sentence. When the word for what lands there, it is spelled quoi.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Every one of these has de in it, which is the first thing worth noticing: combien never appears without it in front of a thing. What decides the apostrophe is only ever the first letter of the noun behind it.
drills.title: de, or d apostrophe?

drills.q: You want to ask how many children somebody has. Which two words go first?
drills.why: combien d'enfants. De arrives because a thing is being counted, and it loses its vowel because enfants starts with one.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Play every one of these and you will hear the same sound in all five, because that is what they are. Sort them by where the word sits instead: opening a question, or standing between two things you are choosing from.
drills.title: Which one is on the page?

drills.q: Which of these asks where the station is?
drills.why: Où est la gare ? with the accent. Without it the word means or, and nothing in the sound will ever tell you which one was meant.
drills.title: One more time

sheets.title: The seven words, and the frame

rows: a way, or what something is like
sections.title: What each word asks for

sections.body: Your word, then est-ce que. That always works. Est-ce que is three small words that never change and never move. Put your question word in front of them, then say a sentence you already know, and you have asked. Où est-ce que tu pars, quand est-ce que tu pars, pourquoi est-ce que tu pars: the last four words are identical every time and only the first one decides what comes back. Two of the seven need one adjustment and both are worth knowing before you meet them somewhere else. Que does not stand in front of the frame, it joins it, and the two run together into qu'est-ce que: qu'est-ce que tu fais. And quel cannot stand on its own at all, so what goes in front of the frame is quel plus its thing, which is why the question about the time is à quelle heure est-ce que tu pars rather than quel on its own. Neither of those is a different rule. Both are the same slot with something bigger in it. There are two other ways of asking a question in French, one of them without any frame at all and one with the verb moved in front of the person, and they arrive in their own lesson. This one works everywhere in the meantime and nothing about it has to be unlearned.
sections.title: The frame, and the two adjustments

sections.body: Two things in this lesson are invisible to listening, and knowing which is which stops you listening for something that was never recorded. Où and ou are ONE SOUND. One means where and one means or, and both published cards carry the same transcription, so no recording could separate them. What tells you which was meant is where the word sits: où opens a question, ou stands between two things somebody is choosing from. The four shapes of quel are the same situation. Quel, quelle, quels and quelles are all pronounced identically, because the e and the s on the end are written and never said, so the agreement is entirely a decision you make with your eyes on the noun. That is the same idea the colours lesson called endings you write and never say, arriving on a word where it opens the question rather than describing something. The one pair in this lesson your ear genuinely can do is qui against que: qui has a clear ee sound and que has the small unstressed vowel French uses everywhere. That one is worth practising. The other two are worth knowing about so that you stop trying.
sections.title: What you read and never hear

sections.body: Combien on its own asks how much something costs, weighs or takes: combien ça coûte, combien de temps. The moment you name the thing you are counting, de arrives between the two: combien de valises, combien de frères, combien de personnes. There are no exceptions to this and leaving it out is the single most common thing an English speaker does with the word. It survives because nothing punishes it: combien valises is understood perfectly by everybody and simply marks a beginner, so no conversation you have will ever give you a reason to fix it. When the thing starts with a vowel, de loses its own vowel and an apostrophe takes the place: combien d'amis, combien d'enfants, combien d'heures. That is not a new rule either. It is the fifth time you have watched French refuse to let two vowel sounds run into each other, after le becoming l apostrophe, ma becoming mon in front of a vowel, ne becoming n apostrophe, and est-ce que becoming est-ce qu. One pressure, five rules, and now there is only the pressure to remember.
sections.title: combien, and the de that comes with it

cards.sub: Are you ready? · the frame with nothing added

sections.title: One Frame, And You Already Have It

sections.say: Your word, then est-ce que. That always works. Read down the right-hand column. It never changes. Tap any row to hear the whole question.

detail.body: Où est-ce que tu pars ? Where are you going? The word for where, and everything after it is a sentence you already had. Nothing but the word itself goes in front.
detail.title: où: Where are you going

detail.body: Quand est-ce que tu pars ? When are you leaving? One word changed from the sentence above and the answer changed completely. Nothing but the word itself goes in front.

detail.body: Pourquoi est-ce que tu pars ? Why are you leaving? The only one of the seven whose answer has a grammar of its own: parce que. Nothing but the word itself goes in front.
detail.title: pourquoi: Why are you leaving

detail.body: Comment est-ce que tu pars ? How are you travelling? The word the unit description leaves out, and one you have been saying since the first lesson. Nothing but the word itself goes in front.
detail.title: comment: How are you travelling

rows.say: Avec qui est-ce que tu pars ?

detail.say: Avec qui est-ce que tu pars ?

rows.say: Combien de temps est-ce que tu pars ?

sections.title: Seven Questions, One Sentence

sections.say: Five words with no endings, no agreement and no second form. Two missions and they are yours.
sections.hint: Five cards, one per word, and none of them has a second shape.

cards.body: The accent is not decoration. Without it the same three letters are the word for or, and the two sound identical. That is act two of this lesson and it is coming.
cards.head: où
cards.label: where

cards.body: The d on the end is silent and the vowel is nasal, so this is one sound rather than two. It is the word the man at the station was never asked.

cards.label: when

cards.body: You have been saying this since the very first lesson, inside a greeting nobody took apart. Here it is as a word you can use anywhere. The t on the end is silent.
cards.head: comment
cards.label: how

cards.fr: Pourquoi est-ce que tu es en retard ?
cards.body: The only one of the seven whose answer has a word of its own. Ask with pourquoi and you get parce que back, which is act five.
cards.head: pourquoi
cards.label: why

cards.sub: [KEE] · Who are you? · Who do you live with?
cards.body: When the person is the one doing something, qui goes straight in front. When they are not, a small word goes in front of it: avec qui, à qui, pour qui.
cards.head: qui
cards.label: who

cards.sub: What is your name? · one form each, always
cards.body: Your word, then est-ce que. That always works. No endings, no agreement, nothing to check before you say them. The word that does have a second shape is the next act, and it is only one word out of seven.

sections.title: Five That Never Change

sections.say: Four decisions. Each one is about which fact you want rather than about how to build the sentence.
sections.title: Which Word Gets The Answer?

check.q: You are at a station and you want the departure time. Which word goes in front?
check.why: quand. This is the exact decision from the opening scene and it is worth making twice on purpose. Où is a real question and gets a real answer, which is why nothing about saying it feels wrong.

check.q: You are lost and you want to know where the station is. Which word?
check.why: où, with the accent. Without it the word means or, and the two are one sound, so nothing you can hear will ever tell you which one somebody said.

check.q: Somebody is late and you want to know the reason. Which word?

items.fr: Pourquoi est-ce que tu es en retard ?

detail.say: Où est le train ? Le train ou le bus ?

sections.title: One Sound, Two Words

sections.say: Six of the seven stand alone. This one has to lean on something, and it takes that thing's shape.

cards.body: Où on its own is a question. Quel on its own is not. It has to have a thing straight behind it, and once it does, it copies that thing.

cards.body: The e and the s are written and never said. This is the same idea the colours lesson called endings you write and never say, arriving on a word where it opens the question.

sections.say: Look at the thing behind it, not at the question. That is the only thing that decides.

sections.say: Three sentences, one meaning. The word for what is in a different place in each of them.
sections.hint: Four cards on the word that moves.

cards.body: The block you already have, with the word for what bolted onto the front of it. Que joined the frame rather than standing in front, and the two ran together. This is the form to reach for.

cards.body: Same question, and the word has moved to the end and changed shape. Que never sits at the end of a sentence; quoi is what it becomes when it does.

cards.label: at the end

cards.body: The third place, with the verb pulled in front of the person. You will read this far more often than you say it, and it means exactly what the other two mean.
cards.head: que
cards.label: in front of the verb

cards.fr: Qu'est-ce que tu fais dans la vie ?

cards.head: The meaning never moved
cards.label: what changes and what does not

sections.title: One Word, Three Places

sections.say: Three rows, one question. Tap each and listen to how little the meaning moves.

detail.body: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ? What are you doing? Que and the frame ran together. There is always a person or a thing between this block and the verb.

detail.body: Tu fais quoi ? What are you doing? The same question with the word at the end. Que cannot sit there, so it becomes quoi. Also c'est quoi ?

detail.body: que fais-tu ? what are you doing? The verb has come in front of the person. Que fais-tu le matin ? is the same shape in a published sentence.

sections.title: Where The Word Sits

sections.say: Three cards to recognise rather than to produce. You will hear this constantly and it is not tested.

cards.body: The thing you are asking about is the one doing something, and nothing comes between the block and the verb. That is the whole test.
cards.head: qu'est-ce qui
cards.label: the thing is doing it

cards.head: qu'est-ce que
cards.label: somebody is doing it to the thing

cards.sub: What is happening here? · nothing between the block and the verb
cards.body: One of the most common questions in spoken French, and it is the qui shape because the thing is the one happening. Recognise it and move on. Nothing here is on the exam.

sections.title: One More, To Recognise

sections.say: Three pairs. One of them your ear can do and two of them nobody's can, and saying so is the point.

lines.en: this pair is real: one is a clear ee sound and the other is not
these two are one sound, and only the accent on the page separates them

sections.title: What Your Ear Can Do

questions.q: qui and que. How much of the difference can you hear?
questions.why: All of it. Qui has a clear ee and que has the small unstressed vowel French uses everywhere. This is the one pair in the lesson worth practising, and it is a real difference in the signal.
opts: all of it: the vowels are completely different
only if the speaker slows down

questions.q: où and ou, said out loud. What separates them?
questions.why: Nothing at all. Both published cards carry the same transcription and they are one sound. The accent is on the page and nowhere else, so a recording of one is a recording of the other.

questions.q: quel, quelle, quels and quelles. How many sounds is that?
questions.why: One, said four times. The e and the s are written and never pronounced. If you find yourself listening harder to catch the plural, stop: it is not in the recording and no practice will put it there.
opts: three, because two are the same

sections.say: One word, and a small one that comes with it as soon as you name what you are counting.
sections.hint: Four cards, and the idea in the last one is not new.

cards.sub: [kohⁿ-BYAⁿ duh] · How many suitcases do you have?
cards.body: Name the thing you are counting and de arrives between them. Every time, with no exceptions, and leaving it out is the single most common thing an English speaker does with this word.
cards.head: combien de
cards.label: with a thing

cards.sub: [kohⁿ-BYAⁿ d] · How many friends do you have?
cards.body: The thing starts with a vowel, so de loses its own and an apostrophe takes the place. Only the first letter of the noun changed between this card and the one before it.
cards.head: combien d'
cards.label: in front of a vowel

cards.sub: How many children do you have? · one pressure, five rules
cards.body: Le became l apostrophe. Ma became mon. Ne became n apostrophe. Est-ce que becomes est-ce qu. French will not let two vowel sounds meet, and this is the same refusal again.
cards.head: You have watched this four times already
cards.label: the fifth time

cards.fr: Combien de frères et sœurs as-tu ? · Combien de temps dure le film ?
cards.sub: a consonant both times, so de keeps its vowel
cards.body: Your word, then est-ce que. That always works. Those two and the children one differ in exactly one thing: what letter the noun starts with. Nothing else in any of them chose between de and d apostrophe.
cards.head: The corpus does both
cards.label: in the wild

sections.say: You get the answer and you work out the question. Only one of the seven words could have produced each of these.
sections.title: Work Backwards From The Answer

check.q: Somebody answers you: it is behind the station. Which word did you ask with?
check.why: où. A place came back, so a place was asked for. This is the only kind of question in the lesson you can check after the fact, and it is why asking the wrong word is so hard to notice.

groups.label: A person, a place, a time

check.q: The answer starts parce que. Which word did you ask with?
check.why: pourquoi. Parce que means because and it answers nothing else. This is the only one of the seven whose answer announces which question it came from before it says anything.

items.en: It is because it is raining.

check.q: Somebody answers you: there are three of us. Which word did you ask with?
check.why: combien. A number came back. If you had named the thing you were counting, de would have come with it: combien de personnes, and never combien personnes.

check.q: You asked where the train leaves from and you wanted the time. What was the cost?
check.why: A true answer you did not need. Nobody was wrong and nothing sounded odd, which is exactly why this error survives: there is no feedback anywhere in the exchange to tell you it happened.
opts: He corrected you and you learned something
He did not understand and you asked again
He gave you a true answer to a question you did not need
Nothing, because both questions mean the same

sections.say: Your word, then est-ce que. That always works. Five things an English speaker writes in their first month, one per screen.
sections.title: Five Traps

errors.why: The highest-value one in the lesson, because it is the only error here that nobody will ever point out. Both sentences are correct French and both get a helpful answer. Only one of them is the answer you needed.
errors.right: Asking « Quand est-ce que le train part ? »
errors.wrong: Asking « Où est-ce que le train part ? » when you want the time.

errors.why: Combien brings de with it the moment you name the thing being counted. Leaving it out is understood and simply marks a beginner, which is why it survives so long: nothing about it stops the conversation.
errors.wrong: Writing « Combien enfants avez-vous ? » with no de.

errors.why: Heure is the une kind, so quel takes an e. You cannot hear the difference and you never will, so this is a decision made with your eyes on the noun rather than your ear on the sentence.
errors.wrong: Writing « Quel heure est-il ? » with no agreement.

errors.why: Without the accent the word means or, and out loud the two are identical. This is the one error in the lesson that changes what you said rather than how well you said it, and no recording can catch it.
errors.wrong: Writing « Ou est le train ? » with no accent.

errors.why: Que never sits at the end of a sentence. When the word for what lands there it becomes quoi, which is the same word standing somewhere else rather than a different one to learn.
errors.wrong: Saying « Tu fais que ? » with que at the end.

sections.say: Four questions asked at one desk in five minutes, and each one gets a completely different answer.
sections.text: The queue at the information desk moves slowly and you can hear every question in it, which is the cheapest French lesson in the building. The woman in front of you wants a departure time and she asks for it directly. « Quand est-ce que le train part ? » She gets a time, writes it on her hand and leaves, which is what happens when the word at the front matches the fact you wanted. The man behind her wants the platform and asks a question that differs from hers by exactly one word. « Où est-ce que le train part ? » He gets a platform number, and neither he nor the man behind the desk has any reason to think anything unusual has happened. A third person is travelling with luggage and needs to know about a charge. « Combien de valises est-ce que je peux prendre ? » The de is doing quiet work in that sentence and taking it out would not stop anybody understanding her, which is exactly why it is so easy to leave out for a year. The last one in the queue points at the board, where two trains are listed for the same city four minutes apart, and asks the question this lesson has been building towards. « Quel train est à l'heure ? »
sections.title: The Information Desk

glossary.note: The word for when, with the borrowed frame behind it. Everything after this is a sentence she already knew.
One word different from hers, and the answer that comes back is a place rather than a time.
Combien brings de with it as soon as the thing being counted is named. Every time, with no exceptions.
Le train, so the un kind, so quel with nothing on the end. Out loud all four shapes of this word are identical.

questions.a: Because the word at the front is what chose which fact came back. Everything after it was the same in both sentences, so the whole difference in meaning was carried by a single word, and neither the questioner nor the man answering had any way of noticing if it was the wrong one.
questions.q: The first two people in the queue asked sentences that differ by one word. Why did they get such different answers?

questions.a: She would have been understood perfectly and nobody would have corrected her. That is what makes it worth naming: combien de is not needed for comprehension, so nothing in the conversation will ever teach it to you. It has to be learned deliberately or not at all.
questions.q: What would have happened if the third person had left out the de?

questions.a: The train. Le train is the un kind, so quel takes nothing on the end. It has nothing to do with the question or with who is asking, and it cannot be heard: quel and quelle are one sound, so this is a decision made by looking at the noun.
questions.q: The last question uses quel rather than quelle. What decided that?

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched a train leave without somebody who asked a perfectly good question and got a perfectly good answer. Since then you have taken a frame that never changes and put seven different words in front of it, met the one word here that has to lean on a thing and copy its shape, and found two distinctions that live entirely on the page and are invisible to listening. Along the way you have worked backwards from an answer to the question that produced it, which is the only thing in this lesson that tests what the words mean rather than what they look like. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.
sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: The move, five times.
rounds.label: One slot, seven words

questions.q: You know the sentence « tu pars ». You want to ask when. What goes between the word and the sentence?
questions.why: est-ce que. Your word, then est-ce que. That always works. It never changes and it takes all seven words, which is why this lesson can teach seven words instead of seven grammars.

questions.q: You want to know what time the train leaves. Complete it: « ... le train part ? »
questions.why: Quand est-ce que. The word for when, then the frame, and the sentence behind it does not move. Asking where instead gets a platform number, which is the whole opening scene.

questions.q: In « Pourquoi est-ce que tu pars ? » and « Comment est-ce que tu pars ? », how much of the two sentences is identical?
questions.why: Everything except the first word. That is the point of the whole lesson: the word at the front carries the entire question and the rest of the sentence does not move when it changes.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Où tu pars ? » meaning to ask where you are going. Fix it.
questions.why: Où est-ce que tu pars ? The word was right and the frame was missing, so what was there was a question word standing in front of a statement rather than a question.

questions.q: You want to ask who somebody is travelling with. Say the whole question.
questions.why: Avec qui est-ce que tu pars ? Qui takes a small word in front of it when the person is not the one doing something, and the whole thing still goes in the same slot.
accept: Avec qui est-ce que tu pars ?
avec qui est-ce que tu pars
questions.answer: Avec qui est-ce que tu pars ?
questions.target: Avec qui est-ce que tu pars ?

rounds.say: The answer comes first. You work out the question.
rounds.label: Which fact do you want

questions.q: Somebody answers you « Parce qu'il pleut. » Which word did you ask with?
questions.why: pourquoi. Parce que means because and answers nothing else, so this is the one question in the seven whose answer tells you which word produced it before it says anything.

questions.q: Somebody answers you « C'est à huit heures. » Which word did you ask with?
questions.why: quand. A time came back, so a time was asked for. Working backwards like this is the only way to check a question word after the fact, and it is what the man at the station could not do for you.

questions.q: You want to ask how somebody is, the way the very first lesson taught you. Complete it: « ... ça va ? »
questions.why: comment. The word for how, and the unit description for this lesson leaves it out. It is taught here anyway, because you have been saying it inside that greeting since the first lesson.

questions.q: Listen. Which word is it?
questions.why: qui. This is the one pair in the lesson your ear can genuinely do: qui has a clear ee and que has the small unstressed vowel. The accent on où and the endings on quel are not in the signal at all.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Comment est-ce que le train part ? » wanting the departure time. Fix it.
questions.why: Quand. Comment asks how it travels and would get a true answer about the train rather than about the time. Nothing in the frame was wrong; only the word at the front was.
accept: Quand est-ce que le train part ?
quand est-ce que le train part
Quand est-ce que le train part
questions.answer: Quand est-ce que le train part ?

rounds.say: Look at the thing behind it. Your ear will not help.
rounds.label: The one that agrees

questions.q: You want to ask which suitcase, and la valise is the une kind. Which shape?
questions.why: quelle. The une kind and one of them, so an e on the end. All four of those options are the same sound, so this question can only be answered by looking at the valise.

questions.q: You want to ask which trains, meaning several, and le train is the un kind. Write the two words.
questions.why: quels trains. The un kind and more than one, so the s and nothing else. Writing is the only way this can be tested: out loud it is identical to quel train, quelle valise and quelles valises.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Quel heure est-il ? » Fix it.
questions.why: Quelle heure est-il ? Heure is the une kind. The time lesson gave you this sentence as one lump you did not take apart, and this is the e that was inside it all along.

questions.q: Why can you not check quel against quelle by listening to a recording?
questions.why: Because the endings are silent. All four shapes are one sound, so no recording can separate them and no amount of listening practice will produce the ability. This is a decision you make with your eyes.
opts: Because the two words mean different things
Because both endings are written and never pronounced
Because only native speakers make the difference

rounds.say: One word, and where it sits changes how it is spelled.
rounds.label: que and quoi

questions.q: You want to ask what somebody is doing. Complete it: « ... tu fais ? »
questions.why: Qu'est-ce que. Que did not stand in front of the frame, it joined it, and the two ran together into one block. This is the form the corpus uses far more often than either of the others.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Tu fais que ? » Fix it.
questions.why: Tu fais quoi ? Que never sits at the end of a sentence. When the word for what lands there it becomes quoi, which is the same word standing somewhere else rather than a second one to learn.

questions.q: In « Qu'est-ce qui se passe ici ? » what decided the qui rather than que at the end of the block?
questions.why: The thing is the one doing something, and nothing comes between the block and the verb. When a person sits in between, the block ends with que instead. Recognise this and move on: it is not drilled here.
opts: The thing being asked about is the one doing something
The question is about a person
There is no verb in the sentence

questions.q: Listen. Which word is it?
questions.why: que. The vowel is the small unstressed one rather than the clear ee of qui. These two are a genuine pair for the ear, unlike où against ou or the four shapes of quel.

rounds.say: Name the thing you are counting and something arrives with it.
rounds.label: combien, and the word it brings

questions.q: You want to ask how many suitcases somebody has. Write the first two words.
questions.why: combien de. Name the thing being counted and de arrives, every time and with no exceptions. Leaving it out is understood perfectly, which is exactly why nobody will ever correct it for you.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Combien enfants avez-vous ? » Fix it.
questions.why: Combien d'enfants. Two things at once: de was missing, and enfants starts with a vowel so de loses its own vowel. That is the same refusal to let two vowels meet that turned le into l apostrophe.

questions.q: Why is it « combien de valises » but « combien d'amis »?
questions.why: Because amis starts with a vowel. That is the only difference between the two, and it is the fifth time you have watched French refuse to let two vowel sounds run into each other.
opts: Because amis starts with a vowel
Because valise is the une kind
Because amis is a person and valise is a thing

questions.q: Somebody answers you « Nous sommes trois. » Which word did you ask with?
questions.why: combien. A number came back. If you had named what you were counting, de would have come with it, so the question would have been combien de personnes rather than combien personnes.

rounds.say: Two differences you can never hear, and one mark that changes the word.
rounds.label: What only the page knows

questions.q: Which of these asks where the train is?
questions.why: Où est le train ? with the accent. Without it the word means or. Out loud the two are identical, so this is the one thing in the lesson that can only ever be settled in writing.

questions.q: Somebody says « Le train ou le bus ? » out loud. How do you know which word they used?
questions.why: From where it sits. The two are one sound, so listening will not do it. Où opens a question and ou sits between two things you are choosing from, and that position is the only clue there is.
opts: By the vowel, which is longer in one of them
By the sound, if you listen carefully
From where it sits in the sentence

questions.q: You want to ask which suitcases, meaning several of them. Say it.
questions.why: Quelles valises sont là ? Both endings on quelles are silent, so what you say here is identical to quel, quelle and quels. The spelling is a decision you make before you open your mouth.

questions.q: Which two things in this lesson are invisible to listening?
questions.why: The accent and the endings. Both live entirely on the page. Everything else in this lesson is audible, including qui against que, which is a real pair worth practising.
opts: The accent on où, and the endings on quel
The frame, and the word at the front
que and quoi, and qui and que

sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the rest of A1.
sections.body: You can ask any question you can think of, by putting one of seven words in front of a frame that never changes and a sentence you already knew. You can pick the word by deciding which fact you want rather than by remembering a list. You can use quel in all four shapes by looking at the thing behind it, and you know that its endings and the accent on où live entirely on the page. What carries forward is smaller than it looks: one slot, and the habit of deciding what you want to know before you decide how to say it. There are two other ways of asking a question in French and they arrive in their own lesson. Nothing you have learned here has to be unlearned when they do.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Your word, then est-ce que. That always works. The word says which fact, and the frame carries it.
Five of the seven never change. quel agrees with its thing and combien brings de.
où against ou, and all four shapes of quel, are differences you read and never hear.
pourquoi is the only one whose answer has a word of its own: parce que.

errorTriggers.description: Puts the question word in front of a statement with nothing between them: « Où tu pars ? ». The word is right, the sentence is right, and there is no question in it.

Builds the question perfectly and reaches for the nearest word they are sure of, getting a correct sentence and a true answer to something they did not ask. The scene error, and the only one here nobody will ever point out.
Writes quel in front of a une word or a plural: « Quel heure », « Quel valises ». Invisible to the ear in both directions, so no amount of listening or speaking practice touches it.
Puts que where quoi belongs or the reverse: « Tu fais que ? », « Quoi est-ce que tu fais ? ». One word, and where it sits decides how it is spelled.
Writes « Combien enfants ? » with no de. Understood perfectly every time, which is why it survives for a year: nothing in any conversation gives the learner a reason to fix it.
Writes « Ou est le train ? » without the accent, which turns the word for where into the word for or. The only error in the lesson that changes what was said rather than how well.

est-ce que, that it goes on the front of a statement and moves nothing inside it, and that it elides to est-ce qu before a vowel, introduced in a1.19
That est-ce que is correct in every register, which is a1.19's reframe and is not restated here
Comment ça va and Comment vous appelez-vous as fixed greetings, shipped in a1.01 and taken apart here
Quelle heure est-il and Quel temps fait-il as unanalysed blocks, shipped in a1.12 and a1.10 and taken apart here
grammarIntroduced: The interrogative words qui, que, quoi, où, quand, comment, pourquoi and combien
comment specifically, which the unit canDo omits and which is taught here deliberately
NOT the est-ce que frame, which a1.19 introduced and this lesson only reuses
That a question word occupies a fixed pre-frame slot and that the clause behind it is invariant
The interrogative adjective quel in all four forms, agreeing with its head noun in gender and number
That the four forms of quel are homophonous, so the agreement is orthographic only
que against quoi as one lexeme in complementary distribution by position
qu'est-ce qui against qu'est-ce que as subject and object, for RECOGNITION ONLY and produced nowhere
combien de, and the elision of de to d' before a vowel, as a fifth instance of anti-hiatus
The minimal pair où against ou, distinguished by the grave accent and homophonous in speech
parce que as the answer form selected by pourquoi

acts.title: Four spellings, one sound

recorded.desc: THE FOUR SILENT FORMS, IN ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE, BY ONE VOICE AT ONE SPEED, AND THEY MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM EACH OTHER. This is the single most important instruction in this lesson and it is the opposite of the usual note. Do not help. Do not differentiate them. Do not lean on the ending of ils parlent to make it clearer than il parle, and do not add the faintest vowel after a silent -e. If a listener can tell any of these four apart from the audio alone, the recording has taught the opposite of what the lesson teaches. Read them at conversational pace with no pause for teaching between them. Four recordings made in four sessions are four performances and the drift between them will be heard as French; one take is the only way this works.

All six forms as one continuous take, in paradigm order, by one voice at one speed, then the six full sentences in the same take. The two audible endings must sound ORDINARY rather than emphasised: -ons is a nasal vowel with no N on the end of it, and -ez is AY, identical to the naming form parler. Do not stress the verb anywhere. These are the most frequent words in the language and they are never leaned on in speech, and the whole trap this lesson drills is an English speaker putting weight where French puts none.

The homophone pairs, EACH PAIR IN ONE TAKE BACK TO BACK, so the identity is real rather than an artefact of two sessions: « Il parle français. » then « Ils parlent français. », then « Elle travaille ici. » then « Elles travaillent ici. » The point of every pair is that the two halves are the same, so any difference in pace, pitch or emphasis between them is a defect. The third pair is different and must be recorded differently: « Tu cherches la gare. » against « Il cherche la gare. » are NOT identical, because tü and eel are audibly different, and that pair is what proves the pronoun is doing the work. Keep the verbs identical and let the pronouns differ naturally.

The stress trap, WRONG THEN RIGHT in one take. The wrong version is an English speaker leaning on the ending: ils par-LENT with a real second syllable, tu cher-CHES with an audible s, elle travaille with a small uh after it. The right version is flat, one syllable for the verb, weight at the end of the phrase and nothing on the word. Both halves must be spoken by the same voice at the same pace, because the difference being taught is where the weight sits and not how careful the speaker is. Do not caricature the wrong one; it should sound like a competent learner, which is what makes it worth correcting.

The thirty naming forms, read as a flat list at conversational pace, one voice. Every one of them ends in the same AY sound and that sameness is the teaching: the learner should come away hearing -er as one ending rather than thirty word-endings. Do not vary the intonation to keep the list interesting. Keep roughly a second between them so a learner can repeat into the gap.

The opening scene, French bubbles only, one woman in her thirties at an ordinary reception-desk pace. The beat where she moves on (« Bon. Je vous mets au mardi, alors. ») must be brisk and unbothered rather than pointed: the whole scene turns on nobody minding, so any hint of impatience or of correction would destroy it. There is a four-second wait written into the stage direction before that line and it should be audible as a pause, not filled.
