lessons.intro: Nine in ten French verbs work exactly like this one, so learning the pattern once gives you thousands of them. Six endings, four of which make no sound at all, which is why the little word in front of the verb is doing more work than you think.

stem.body: parler gives parl-. regarder gives regard-. chercher gives cherch-. It does not move, whoever is speaking, so once you have it you have all six forms of that verb and you never have to learn them separately. This is why a regular verb is worked out rather than memorised, and why etre and avoir were the exception rather than the rule.
stem.title: What is left when -er comes off

nousOn.body: nous parlons is what you write. on parle is what you say. Both are correct and both mean we. on takes the same form as il, so it costs you no new ending at all: on parle, on regarde, on cherche. Every table in this level prints nous, and almost every conversation you hear will use on. Writing nous is never wrong; it just sits a register above where the conversation is.
nousOn.title: One meaning, two registers

audibleTwo.body: These two are syllables of their own, so they arrive at the ear as clearly as anything else in the sentence. -ons is a nasal vowel, OHⁿ, with no N sound at the end of it. -ez is AY, which means vous parlez and the naming form parler are said exactly the same way. Those two are the whole of what your ear gets from an -er verb.
audibleTwo.title: -ons and -ez

flatEnding.body: English puts weight on the end of a verb: he WALKS, they WALKED. French has nothing there to weigh, because in four of the six forms there is no sound at the end at all. Leaning on the ending is the single most recognisable thing an English speaker does to a French verb, and it is a habit rather than a gap in knowledge. The weight goes at the end of the phrase, not the end of the word.
flatEnding.title: Nothing to lean on

examples.note: Said flat, and the last thing you hear is parl.

infinitive.body: parler, regarder, chanter. This is the form a verb is listed under and it is not a form anybody uses in a sentence. Its last two letters are the instruction: cut them off and what is left is the part that never changes. Thirty of the verbs in this lesson end this way, and so do roughly nine in ten French verbs.

silentEnding.body: -e, -es and -ent are all silent. il parle and ils parlent are six letters apart on the page and identical in the air. French writes distinctions it does not say, and this is the first place you meet that: the spelling is doing work for the reader that the sound is not doing for the listener. Nothing is dropped or slurred. The letters were never pronounced.
silentEnding.title: Letters that are written and not said

sections.body: Four of the six endings are silent, and they are silent completely: nothing is slurred or dropped, and the letters were never pronounced in the first place. The -e of je parle and il parle makes no sound. The -es of tu parles makes no sound, and the s there is the same silent s you already write on tu es. The -ent of ils parlent makes no sound either, and it is the longest ending in the set and the emptiest one, which is why it is the ending learners most want to pronounce and the one that marks a sentence as read rather than spoken. So je parle, tu parles, il parle and ils parlent are four spellings and one sound, and out loud only the pronoun in front separates them. That is the reason French keeps its subject pronouns everywhere English could drop them: the verb is not carrying the person, so something has to. Only two endings survive the trip to somebody else's ear. The -ons of nous parlons is a nasal vowel with no N sound at the end of it, and the -ez of vous parlez is AY, which is exactly how the naming form parler is said, so vous parlez and parler are one sound and two jobs.
sections.title: The letters you do not say

sections.body: These six endings do not change again. The next unit keeps every one of them and moves a single letter in the stem in front of them, for a reason you can predict from the spelling, so nothing you have learned here is spent. The -IR and -RE units after it swap the endings for two other short sets and leave the method exactly as it is: find the stem, add the person. The unit on the past tense will take the naming form you started from, change its last two letters, and produce something that sounds identical to what you started with, which is a problem it will hand you fully formed rather than one you have to see coming. And the two later units on agreement rest on one thing you already have: French writes distinctions it does not say. You met that here, on four endings that exist entirely for the reader.
sections.title: What carries forward

sections.body: Every verb here has a stem that does not move. Take the last two letters off and what is left is the same for all six persons and stays the same however the verb is used, so one pattern gives you thirty verbs and about a hundred and eighty forms. That is not true of every verb ending in -er. A small group changes one letter in the stem, and they are deliberately not on this list even though several of them are more common than some that are: manger, commencer, acheter, appeler, préférer, payer, essayer and jeter all keep these endings exactly and move something in front of them. They are the next unit and they will make more sense once this one is automatic. One verb ending in -er belongs to neither group. aller looks exactly like the thirty and behaves like nothing in this lesson, and it has a unit of its own. If you try the machine on it you will produce something that no French speaker says, so it is worth knowing by name from the start rather than discovering it at speed.

questions.a: Vous cherchez and vous travaillez, both -ez, plus nous restons with -ons. The -e and -ent endings on parle, habitent and parlent give the ear nothing, so the pronoun is the only evidence in those three.
questions.q: Two sentences in this passage use an ending you could hear, and three use one you could not. Which two are audible?

questions.a: Only the ils in front of it, and the two other people waiting behind you. There is no sound anywhere in the sentence that settles it.
questions.q: « Ils parlent bien » and « Il parle bien » would sound identical. What decides which one is written here?

questions.a: nous commençons. on is what gets said and nous is what gets written, and on takes the same form as il, so the ending she used is the silent one.
questions.q: Nadia says « on commence à sept heures ». What would she have written instead?

sections.say: Rate each card objectively. Again, hard, or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.back: Four of the six forms sound the same, so the pronoun carries the person. Two of six, and the pronoun covers the rest.
cards.front: How many of the six can the ear name?

cards.back: Cut the last two letters off the naming form, then put the person on what is left.
cards.front: How do you build any -er verb?

cards.back: -ons and -ez. OHⁿ and AY, each a syllable of its own.
-e, -es, -e, -ent. One sound between all four of them.
The il form, every time. on regarde, never on regardons.
-es. Silent, and the one most often left off in writing.
cards.front: The ending only tu ever takes

cards.back: parler, the naming form. Only the vous in front separates them.
Stem bavard-, tu ending -es. The machine works on anything regular.
cards.front: A verb you were never taught: tu bavardes

cards.back: aller. It is its own unit further along the trail.
cards.front: The one -er verb this does not work on

sections.title: The Whole System, One Deck

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have taken the naming form apart, put six endings on it, heard which two of them survive the trip to somebody else's ear, and written the four that do not. You have used the pattern on a verb this lesson never showed you. What is left is the part that says whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.
sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Five rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get a drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: Two letters off, one person on.
rounds.label: Building the form

questions.q: What is the stem of regarder?
questions.why: The last two letters come off and nothing else moves. regard- takes all six endings without changing.

questions.q: Write the form that goes with je, for the verb habiter.
questions.why: Stem habit-, je ending -e. The e is silent, so nothing about the sound would have told you it was there.

questions.q: Fix this. Somebody asking about your week: « Je travailler lundi. »
questions.why: The naming form cannot stand in a sentence. English lets a bare verb do this and French has no bare form at all, which is why the reflex is so strong.

questions.q: You have never met the verb bavarder, meaning to chat. Write the nous form.
questions.why: Stem bavard-, nous ending -ons. You were not taught this verb, and that is what regular means.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a regular -er verb?
questions.why: aller ends in -er and behaves like nothing in this lesson. It is the one real trap in the ending and it has a unit of its own.

questions.q: How many endings does a regular -er verb have in the present?
questions.why: Six endings for nine pronouns, because il, elle and on share one and ils and elles share another. That collapse is a1.05's and it holds for every verb.

rounds.say: The sound will not help you here. Read the pronoun.
rounds.label: The four you cannot hear

questions.q: Ils ___ français. (parler)
questions.why: ils takes -ent, four letters and no sound. Out loud this is identical to il parle, so only the ils decides it.

questions.q: Tu ___ la gare. (chercher)
questions.why: tu always takes the s and you will never hear it. It is the ending most often left off in writing for exactly that reason.

questions.q: Fix this. One woman, at work: « Elle travaillent ici. »
questions.why: elle is one person and takes -e. Both spellings are said the same way, which is why this survives being read back aloud.

questions.q: Which ending belongs to tu, and to nothing else in the six?
questions.why: -es is tu's alone. -e is shared by je and il, and -ent belongs to ils and elles.

questions.q: Tap the letters you do not say.
questions.why: The whole ending. It is the longest of the six and the emptiest, and treating it as a syllable is the most audible mistake in this lesson.

questions.q: Fix this. You, about yourself: « Je parles français. »
questions.why: The s belongs to tu. Nothing you can hear will ever catch this one, so it has to be caught by the pronoun on the page.

rounds.say: Two of these the sound settles. One of them it does not, and saying so is the right answer.
rounds.label: By ear

questions.q: Listen. Which is on the page?
questions.why: Both, and no recording could separate them. This is the whole lesson in one question: the sound does not decide, and the pronoun on the page does.
opts: Both are said exactly like this

questions.q: Listen. Who is speaking?
questions.why: -ons carries its own syllable, so here the verb really does tell you. That is true of exactly two of the six endings.

questions.q: Which two endings could you identify with your eyes shut?
questions.why: Those two are syllables of their own. The other four give the ear nothing at all, which is why the pronoun is what you hold on to.

questions.q: You hear « voo tra-va-YAY ». Which two things could that be?
questions.why: -ez and -er are the same sound, so the vous in front is the only thing separating the sentence form from the dictionary one.
opts: vous travaillez or the naming form travailler

questions.q: Somebody says a verb with no pronoun in front of it and the ending is silent. How many people could be doing it?
questions.why: je, tu, il and ils all land on the same sound. Without the pronoun there is nothing left to go on, which is why French never drops it.
opts: One or several, the sound does not say

questions.q: Write what a whole team of women working here would be, in full.
questions.why: Said out loud this is identical to Elle travaille ici. Four letters of difference exist only for the reader.

rounds.say: One meaning, two registers, and two different endings.
rounds.label: nous or on

questions.q: Which form does on take?
questions.why: on takes the il form, so it is on regarde and never on regardons. That is what makes it cost you no new ending.

questions.q: Fix this. Somebody saying what the two of you are watching: « On regardons la télé. »
questions.why: on means we and takes the il ending. The meaning pulls one way and the form goes the other, which is the whole difficulty of it.

questions.q: Nous ___ à la maison. (rester)
questions.why: nous takes -ons. This is one of the two endings you would have heard, so getting it wrong in writing means you were reading rather than listening.

questions.q: You are writing an email to a class about what your group does. Which is right?
questions.why: Writing takes nous, and nous takes -ons. The first option is not wrong French; it is just the spoken register in a written place.

questions.q: You are saying the same thing out loud to a friend. Which would you actually say?
questions.why: Speech takes on, and on takes the il form. Both of the first two are correct French and only one of them is what a room sounds like.

questions.q: Vous ___ la gare. (chercher)
questions.why: vous takes -ez, said AY. It is the second of the two audible endings, and it sounds exactly like the naming form.

rounds.say: Flat, and stopping where the stem stops.
rounds.label: Out loud

questions.q: How is « ils parlent » said?
questions.why: One syllable for the verb, and the card ends where the stem ends. Sounding the -ent turns one syllable into two and is heard immediately.

questions.q: Say it out loud, the way you would answer at the desk.
questions.why: One movement, no weight on the verb. The four letters you added to travaill- do not exist for the person listening.

questions.q: Where does the weight land in a French phrase?
questions.why: At the end of the phrase, not the end of the word. English leans on the end of a verb and French has nothing there to lean on.
opts: On the last syllable of the phrase

questions.q: Fix this. A group at a party: « Elles dansent bien », said as elles dahⁿ-SENT bien.
questions.why: dansent is one syllable. The -ent adds four letters to the page and nothing to the air.

questions.q: Which pair is said exactly the same way?
questions.why: Both land on parl and stop. Only the pronoun in front separates them, which is true of four of the six forms.

questions.q: Write the sentence you would say about a friend who works here.
questions.why: One person takes -e, silent. If you wrote the plural, the sound would have been no help either way and the pronoun was the only clue.

sections.say: Four things, and then the lesson that picks this up.
sections.body: You can build the present tense of any regular -er verb, including ones nobody has shown you, and that is most of the verbs in the language. You know which two of the six endings survive the trip to somebody else's ear and which four do not, which is why French keeps its subject pronouns when English could drop them. The next unit takes the same six endings and moves one letter in the stem in front of them, for a reason you will be able to predict. Nothing about the endings changes again.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Four of the six forms sound the same, so the pronoun carries the person.
Cut the last two letters off the naming form, then put the person on what is left.
-ons and -ez are the two you hear. -e, -es, -e, -ent give the ear nothing.
Write the nous form and say the on one. on takes the il ending, so it costs you nothing new.

errorTriggers.description: Reaches for the naming form under pressure, or cuts the wrong amount off it: je travailler, je travail.
Writes the wrong silent ending, because no sound distinguishes them: je parles, ils parle, elle travaillent.
Tries to name the person from the verb, which for four of the six forms is not information the sound carries.
Puts the nous ending on on, or writes on where a written register wants nous.
Leans on the ending out loud, sounding -ent or adding a vowel after a silent -e. A habit, not a knowledge gap.

on takes third-person-singular agreement, introduced in a1.05
The tu against vous register split, introduced in a1.05
The present tense of être, introduced in a1.06
The present tense of avoir, introduced in a1.07
The definite and indefinite articles, introduced in a1.04 and a1.11
grammarIntroduced: The present tense of regular -er verbs, as a stem plus six endings
The infinitive as the form a verb is listed under and never used in
That -e, -es and -ent are silent and -ons and -ez are not
That the subject pronoun carries the person where the ending cannot
nous as the written first-person plural against on as the spoken one

acts.title: What these three do not cover

recorded.desc: THE NINE SINGULAR CELLS, IN THREE GROUPS OF THREE, AND WITHIN EACH GROUP THE THREE MUST BE ACOUSTICALLY IDENTICAL ON THE VERB: « Je veux payer. » « Tu veux payer. » « Il veut payer. » then the same for peux/peux/peut and dois/dois/doit. This is the single most important instruction in this lesson and it is the opposite of what a reader will want to do. The whole screen is that these three cells CANNOT be told apart by ear, and the learner has to discover that by failing to hear a difference. A reader who knows the third one is spelled differently will put a fraction of a t on it, or brighten the vowel, or leave a hair more space before it. Every one of those instincts destroys the mission. If a listener with their eyes shut can say which of the three they just heard, the take is unusable. The PRONOUN must carry all the difference, and it must be clear and unhurried, because it is the only information in the line. Conversational pace, no teaching pause anywhere.

THE EIGHTEEN CELLS AS ONE FRAME, READ IN GRID ORDER, EACH VERB'S SIX IN ONE TAKE. Here the plural MUST be audible, which is the opposite instruction from the singular clip and is why they are separate recordings. veulent, peuvent and doivent each land a consonant at the very end of the verb, VUHL, PUHV, DWAHV, and that consonant is the only thing separating them from the singular, so it must be clean and unswallowed. The nous and vous rows add a syllable and go into the nose at nous; do not soften the nasal. AND payer MUST SOUND EXACTLY THE SAME IN ALL EIGHTEEN LINES. It is the control: the learner is being shown that the back of the sentence does not move, and any variation in stress, length or vowel on payer is the recording quietly contradicting the lesson. Read it as if it were one word you happened to say eighteen times.

THE FOUR REGISTER LINES, IN TWO PAIRS, BLUNT THEN POLITE: « Je veux payer. » / « Je voudrais payer. » then « Je veux un café, s'il vous plaît. » / « Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît. » THE DIFFICULTY IS THAT THE DIFFERENCE MUST NOT BE PERFORMED. The blunt version is not rude, not aggressive and not clipped; it is exactly how a small child asks for something, and an adult saying it sounds like one. If the reader makes it sound hostile, the learner concludes it is a rudeness they would never commit, and the lesson fails. Read both halves of each pair in the same warm, ordinary voice at the same pace, and let the VERB do all the work. The please on the third line must be perfectly sincere and must not save it.
clipIds: Je veux un café, s'il vous plaît.
Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.

recorded.desc: THE GENERALISATION MISSION. « arroser » alone, then « Je peux arroser le jardin. » then « Tu dois arroser le jardin. » The single word first, slowly and clearly, because this is the only time the learner will hear it before being asked to use it. Three syllables,, ah-roh-ZAY, stress on the last. Then the two sentences at completely ordinary pace, with NO emphasis on arroser at all. That is the point: it must sound like the least remarkable word in the sentence, because the claim is that an unknown verb behaves exactly like a known one. A reader who leans on it is telling the learner it is special, and it is precisely not.

THE THREE NAMING FORMS AND THE TEN BORROWED VERBS, each as a single word, conversational and unstressed. vouloir, pouvoir and devoir first: all three end in the same -oir and the reader must not differentiate them beyond what the spelling requires. Then payer, commander, attendre, choisir, boire, acheter, aider, chercher, conduire, arriver. These ten come from ten different lessons and the learner should hear no family resemblance and no grouping. They are a bag of ordinary verbs,, which is the whole reason they are in this lesson.

THE BAKERY. The boulangère is friendly, busy and completely uninterested in teaching anybody French, because she is closing in ten minutes. « Bonjour, je vous écoute. » is warm and quick. « Voilà. Et avec ceci ? » is already moving on to the next customer; the learner has to feel that the moment passed rather than that they were judged. Nothing in this scene is unkind and nothing is slowed down for them. The failure is entirely one of speed.

lessons.intro: Three verbs that will not come apart, and what they buy is every other verb in the language: put any one of them in front and the next verb never changes. The forms take ten minutes. What you can say afterwards is the rest of the lesson.

nousOn.body: nous parlons is what you write. on parle is what you say.
nousOn.title: The we people actually say

examples.note: on peut takes this form, never on pouvons.

theOwing.body: what comes next decides. a2.02 named that shape and this is another one of it. Put a verb after dois and it means have to. Put a thing after it and it means owe. Tu me dois de l'argent is not about obligation in general; it is about ten euros. You will not need to produce this for a while, and you should recognise it, because the two sentences look identical until the word after the verb.
theOwing.term: devoir with no verb after it
theOwing.title: The same word, owing money

examples.note: A verb follows. Obligation.
A thing follows. Money.

theReach.body: One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does. That is the whole of it, and it is worth more than any list of verbs. Once you can say je veux, je peux and je dois, you can put ANY verb after them in the shape it has in the dictionary, including verbs nobody has taught you and verbs you met once on a sign. Six lessons have been building toward a point where changing the verb stops being necessary, and this is that point.
theReach.title: Three verbs, every other verb behind them

examples.note: One verb changed. payer did not.
And nobody taught you this second one.

theStems.body: Each of these verbs has a short stem for je, tu and il, a longer one for nous and vous, and a third for ils. The third is not a new thing to learn: take the short stem and add the last letter of the long one. veu + l = veul · peu + v = peuv · doi + v = doiv Three verbs, one recipe, no exceptions. If you can see that, you never have to memorise the ils row again.
theStems.title: Two stems, and the third one you can work out

examples.note: veu plus the l from voulons.
peu plus the v from pouvons.
doi plus the v from devons. Same recipe, third time.

thePolite.body: voudrais is not a present tense and it is not a version of veux you can build. It is one fixed form, and voudrions is the only other one worth carrying at this stage. Its proper name and its whole family come much later; for now, learn these two the way you learned bonjour. The reason to bother is not grammar: je veux un café is a demand and voudrais un café is a request, and the person behind the counter hears the difference immediately.
thePolite.title: A form to learn whole

examples.note: Correct, and blunt.
The same sentence, and now you will be served.

theSenses.body: English splits this across three words and French does not. may is asking whether you are allowed; might is saying a thing could happen; can is saying somebody is able. All three are pouvoir, and no French speaker feels a difference between them. This matters at the moment you want to ask for something: if you believe pouvoir means only being able, you will look for another verb to ask permission with, and there is not one.
theSenses.title: One French verb, three English ones

examples.note: may, asking whether you are allowed
might, saying a thing could happen
can, saying somebody is able

theUnseen.body: arroser means to water, and this lesson has not taught it, will not drill it, and does not expect you to keep it. It is here to prove something: you did not need the lesson. Put it after je peux or tu dois in the shape it has above, and the sentence is correct. That is true of every verb in the dictionary, which is roughly eleven thousand of them, and it is what these three verbs bought you.
theUnseen.title: The point of the whole lesson

examples.note: A verb you met thirty seconds ago.
And behind a different first verb, unchanged.

theRegister.body: Bonjour is the price of entry. That was a1.01, and it also put voudrais in your mouth in the very first lesson without saying what it was. This is where that is paid off. The difference between the blunt form and the polite one is not correctness, because both are correct French. It is whether the interaction goes well, and in a shop, a station or a doorway that is the only thing being measured.
theRegister.title: a1.01 already gave you this

examples.note: Correct French, and it lands as a demand.
The sentence a1.01 handed you before you could build it.

theSingular.body: Je veux, tu veux, il veut. Two of those are spelled identically and the third differs by one silent letter, and all three are one sound in the mouth. The same is true of peux, peux, peut and of dois, dois, doit. Nothing separates them when spoken except the word in front, which is why the pronoun is never optional here. In writing you must pick the right one; in speech there is nothing to pick.
theSingular.term: why je, tu and il sound the same
theSingular.title: 3 persons, 2 spellings, one sound.

examples.note: veux
veut, and not one sound different.

whatFollows.body: what comes next decides You met that shape at a2.02, and this lesson holds the cleanest example of it in the level. dois with a verb after it means having to. dois with a thing after it means owing money. Same verb, same person, nothing to tell them apart until the next word arrives. It is worth knowing that French does this at all, because you will meet it again and the instinct to decide what a word means before the sentence has finished is a hard one to switch off.
whatFollows.title: One form, two sentences

examples.note: A verb follows. Obligation.
A thing follows. Ten euros.

theNewLetter.body: 4 of the 6 endings are ones you already have. One letter here is new. That letter is the -x on veux and peux. It is silent, exactly as the -s has been silent on every verb since a2.01, so it changes nothing you say and one thing you write. dois takes an ordinary -s instead, which is the singular you already met on the -RE verbs in a2.11.
theNewLetter.title: veux and peux, and nothing else in the language you have met

examples.note: A -x, and you hear nothing.
A plain -s here. Same silence.

theImpersonal.body: This one has no person at all. Il faut réserver does not say who has to book; it says booking is what is required. French reaches for it constantly, far more often than for any single form of the three verbs in this lesson, and you will hear it long before you need to produce it. Two words, one shape, no changes. Recognise it and move on: it is not part of what you are building here.
theImpersonal.title: Nobody is doing it

examples.note: Nobody named, and everybody knows who is meant.
The same two words, doing the same job.

theSecondVerb.body: payer, commander, attendre, choisir, boire, acheter, aider, chercher, conduire, arriver. Every one of those came from another lesson, and every one arrives here in exactly the shape the dictionary gives it. It does not matter whether it is an -ER verb, an -IR verb or an -RE verb; after one of these three, nothing happens to it at all. That is not a simplification for beginners. That is the rule, and it does not change later.
theSecondVerb.title: The second verb in every sentence here belongs to somebody else. What you are learning is the first one.

examples.note: attendre is an -RE verb from a2.11, and it does not move.
choisir is an -IR verb from a2.10, and it does not move either.

lessons.title: Irréguliers 3 : vouloir, pouvoir, devoir

drills.coach: A front on the left. Say the whole sentence before you turn the card, and do not let the second verb take anything.
drills.title: What goes on the back

drills.q: Nous devons ___. (attendre)
drills.why: Not attendons. One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: A verb on the left. Say the plural before you turn the card, and build it from the short stem rather than the long one.
drills.title: Where the plural comes from

drills.q: Ils ___ payer. (vouloir)
drills.why: veu plus the l from voul. The long stem alone does not produce it.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Play each one and look at the spelling rather than listening for it. All of these endings are silent, so the ear cannot help you here.
drills.title: Which ones take the new letter

drills.q: Je ___ payer. (pouvoir)
drills.why: The new letter, and it is silent. devoir is the one that takes a plain -s instead.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Every one of these is correct French. Sort them by who you would say them to, not by whether they are right.
drills.title: Who are you talking to?

drills.q: A waiter you have never met is waiting. Which one?
drills.why: The please on the end of the first one does not rescue it. The verb has already decided how it lands.
opts: Je veux un café, s'il vous plaît.
Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: A French sentence on the left. Say which English word it needs before you turn the card. All three are the same French verb.
pairs: may, asking whether you are allowed
might, saying a thing could happen
drills.title: Which English word

drills.q: You want to ask whether you are allowed to take a photo. Which verb?
drills.why: pouvoir, the same verb as being able. French does not split permission off into its own word.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Look at the word straight after the verb every time. That is the only thing deciding which bucket a sentence goes in.
drills.title: What comes after the verb

drills.q: « Tu me dois de l'argent. » What is it about?
drills.why: what comes next decides A thing after dois rather than a verb, and the sentence is about ten euros.
drills.title: One more time

The recipe, and where each row comes from

Verbs you can put behind any of the eighteen

sections.body: Every reference sheet before this one in the level lists ENDINGS, because every pattern before it had them: a2.01 holds the -er set in full, a2.10 the -ir set, a2.11 all three regular sets at once, and a2.02 lists forms because its verbs have none. This lesson has eighteen forms, and only one of them is worth memorising as a shape, the plural, and even that one is produced by a rule. veu + l = veul · peu + v = peuv · doi + v = doiv Read the third table if you want to know why an ending looks familiar; read the second one if you have forgotten a plural. The first table is the one to photograph, because it is the only place in the course where three verbs sit on a single sentence and the difference between them is two letters wide. 3 persons, 2 spellings, one sound.
sections.title: Why this sheet gives you a recipe and not a list

sections.body: Three things leave this lesson. The first is the big one: One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does. Any verb at all goes behind these three in the shape a dictionary gives it, including verbs nobody has taught you, and nothing later in the course takes that back. The fourth table above is a starting set and it is not a limit. The second is that voudrais and voudrions are fixed forms worth carrying whole, and that the choice between them and veux is about how an exchange lands rather than about being correct, which is the same thing a1.01 was telling you with Bonjour is the price of entry. The third is smaller and it will come back: what comes next decides. dois followed by a verb and dois followed by a thing are two unrelated sentences, and you met that shape at a2.02 on a different pair. a2.14 is next and it brings pouvoir back to stand against a verb that also becomes can in English, so the eighteen cells you have just built are about to be worth more than they were.
sections.title: What carries forward

lessons.reframe: One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does.

overview.introFr: Trois verbes irréguliers, et tous les autres verbes derrière eux.

say.text: Nobody is impatient here. Watch what happens when you have the verb and nothing to put in front of it.

beats.text: A bakery in Nantes on a Saturday, ten minutes before it shuts. Four people behind you. There are two kinds of loaf on the shelf and you want the round one.

beats.en: Hello, what can I get you?
beats.speaker: La boulangère

beats.en: Bread... choose?
beats.stage: You know the word for the loaf and you know the word for choosing. What you cannot do is put yourself in front of either of them.

beats.prompt: Her hand is already moving. What goes out?

options.en: two words in front, and it is a request
pointing, and hoping

followUp.works: She turns the tray towards you and waits. Nothing about that was difficult.
followUp.breaks: She takes the nearest one, wraps it, and is already looking past you at the next person.

beats.en: There you are. Anything else?

sections.title: Four Ways This Comes Apart

errors.why: Six lessons of building endings makes this reflex very strong, and this is the one place it must be switched off. One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does.
errors.right: Saying « Je veux payer. » and « Nous pouvons payer. ».
errors.wrong: Saying « Je veux paye » or « Je peux payons ».

errors.why: Both are correct and only one of them is a request. Adding please to the first does not fix it, because the verb has already set the tone.
errors.right: Saying « Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît. ».
errors.wrong: Saying « Je veux un café » to somebody you have never met.

errors.why: The plural stem is the short one plus a letter from the long one. veu + l = veul · peu + v = peuv · doi + v = doiv Building it off the nous form instead is the commonest written slip here.
errors.wrong: Writing « ils voulent » or « ils peuvent » with the wrong stem.

errors.why: English splits this across can, may and am able to. French does not split it at all, and the second you spend looking for the right one is the second the sentence dies in.
errors.wrong: Looking for another verb when you want to ask permission.

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have three more verbs that will not come apart, and a recipe that builds the hardest row of all three of them. That was the short half. The long half is what they let you do: One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does. You proved it on a verb this course has never taught you, thirty seconds after meeting it. What is left is the part that says whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.
sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get a drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: Type the whole answer. In every one of these the second verb is already in the shape it needs.
rounds.label: The verb that never moves

questions.q: Je ___ payer. (vouloir)
questions.why: The -x is silent and it is the only new letter in the lesson.

questions.q: Nous devons ___. (attendre)
questions.why: Not attendons. One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does. The nous has already been dealt with by devons.

questions.q: Ils peuvent ___. (choisir)
questions.why: Not choisissent. An -IR verb behaves here exactly as an -ER verb does, which is not at all.

questions.q: Fix this. « Nous voulons payons. »
questions.why: The ending went on twice. Six lessons trained that reflex and this is the one place it is wrong.

questions.q: You have never met the verb « ranger ». « Je dois ranger la cuisine. » What can you tell?
questions.why: A front, then a verb in its dictionary shape, like every sentence in this lesson. One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does. You will not know what ranger means and you will know what kind of sentence you are in.
opts: It is a form you have not learned
It is somebody having to do something, and ranger says what

questions.q: Which of these four is wrong?
questions.why: The third. Everything else on this screen leaves the second verb alone.

questions.q: Tu ___ arroser le jardin. (devoir)
questions.why: A plain -s on this verb rather than the new letter. And arroser did not move, because it never does.

questions.q: Vous ___ commander ? (vouloir)
questions.why: The ordinary -ez from a2.01, on the long stem. Nothing about the vous form here is strange.

rounds.say: The plural of all three is built the same way. If you can do one, you can do the other two.
rounds.label: The eighteen cells

questions.q: Ils ___ payer. (vouloir)
questions.why: veu plus the l from voul. Not voulent, which builds it off the wrong stem.

questions.q: Ils ___ payer. (pouvoir)
questions.why: peu plus the v from pouv. Same recipe, second verb.

questions.q: Ils ___ payer. (devoir)
questions.why: doi plus the v from dev. Third verb, and it did not break.

questions.q: Fix this. « Ils voulent payer. »
questions.why: The plural is built off the short stem, not the long one. voulent takes the nous stem and there is no such form.

questions.q: Nous ___ payer. (pouvoir)
questions.why: The long stem and the ordinary -ons. This is the row that supplies the letter the plural needs.

questions.q: Which pair shares a stem?
questions.why: nous and vous share the long stem. The plural is the odd one: it borrows from both.

questions.q: Il ___ payer. (devoir)
questions.why: A -t, and it sounds exactly like dois. In writing you have to pick; in speech there is nothing to pick.

rounds.say: One letter in eighteen cells is new. This round is about which cells get it.
rounds.label: The one new letter

questions.q: Which two verbs take -x on je and tu?
questions.why: vouloir and pouvoir. devoir takes the ordinary -s you already write.

questions.q: Tu ___ payer. (pouvoir)
questions.why: Not peus. The letter is silent, so nothing about saying it changes, and everything about writing it does.

questions.q: Je ___ payer. (devoir)
questions.why: A plain -s. This is the singular you already met on the -RE verbs in a2.11, arriving on a verb that is not one.

questions.q: What does the -x sound like?
questions.why: Nothing, exactly as the -s has been silent since a2.01.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je peus payer. »
questions.why: peus is not a form. Two of these three verbs take the new letter and this is one of them.

questions.q: How many of the six endings in this lesson were already yours?
questions.why: 4 of the 6 endings are ones you already have. One letter here is new.

questions.q: Vous ___ payer. (devoir)
questions.why: The ordinary -ez. This is also the sentence a waiter says to you at the end of a meal.

rounds.say: Every question here has a situation in it, because politeness has no answer without one.
rounds.label: Asking, not demanding

questions.q: You are ordering from a waiter you have never met. Which one?
questions.why: The second is correct French and lands as a demand, and the please on the end does not rescue it. The verb has already set the tone.
opts: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
Je veux un café, s'il vous plaît.

questions.q: Your close friend asks what you want to drink. Which one is fine?
questions.why: With a friend, veux is completely normal. The polite form is for people who are serving you or who you do not know, not for everybody all the time.
opts: Only the polite form is ever acceptable

questions.q: Je ___ payer, s'il vous plaît. (the polite form)
questions.why: A fixed form, learned whole. It is not built from veux and you cannot make it from anything in this lesson.

questions.q: Can you build voudrais from the forms in this lesson?
questions.why: No. It belongs to a family this course has not reached, and two forms of it is all you are carrying for now.
opts: Yes, by adding -rais to the stem

questions.q: You want to ask whether you are allowed to sit down. Which verb?
questions.why: pouvoir. French does not have a separate verb for permission, and looking for one is the hesitation the sentence dies in.

questions.q: Fix this, said to a stranger behind a counter. « Je veux payer. »
questions.why: Nothing about the first is incorrect. One word changes it from a demand into a request, and everything after it holds still.

questions.q: Nous ___ payer, s'il vous plaît. (the polite form, two of you)
questions.why: The only other one worth carrying. Two fixed forms, and nothing else from that family until much later.

questions.q: a1.01 already put one of these in your mouth. Which?
questions.why: Bonjour is the price of entry. The polite form arrived in the very first lesson as a whole phrase, with no way to explain it yet.
opts: Je veux un café, s'il vous plaît.
Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.

rounds.say: English splits this three ways. Each question is one of the three.
rounds.label: One verb, three English words

questions.q: « Je peux commander ? » Which English word is pouvoir doing here?
questions.why: may, asking whether you are allowed. All three are the same French verb and no speaker feels a difference.

questions.q: « Il peut arriver demain. » Which English word is pouvoir doing here?
questions.why: might, saying a thing could happen. All three are the same French verb and no speaker feels a difference.

questions.q: « Elle peut conduire. » Which English word is pouvoir doing here?
questions.why: can, saying somebody is able. All three are the same French verb and no speaker feels a difference.

questions.q: Which of the three senses needs a different French verb?
questions.why: None. That is the point of the mission: one verb covers all three, and English is the language doing the splitting.

questions.q: Je ___ commander ? (pouvoir)
questions.why: Asking to be allowed, and the rising voice makes it a question exactly as it did in a1.19.

questions.q: Elle ___ conduire. (pouvoir)
questions.why: Being able, and it sounds identical to peux. Only the word in front separates them.

questions.q: You are told « Il peut arriver demain ». What does it mean?
questions.why: Nobody is able to do anything here. It says the thing could happen, and English reaches for might.
opts: He is able to arrive tomorrow

questions.q: Vous ___ m'aider ? (pouvoir)
questions.why: This is the form you will use most, because it is how you ask a stranger for anything at all.

rounds.say: Two things this lesson only asks you to recognise, and one it hands to the next one.
rounds.label: The edges

questions.q: « Tu me dois de l'argent. » What is this about?
questions.why: what comes next decides A verb after dois means having to; a thing after it means owing.

questions.q: Which of these is about obligation rather than money?
questions.why: The second. Same verb, same person, and only the word after it decides which sentence you are in.

questions.q: « Il faut réserver. » Who has to book?
questions.why: Nobody is named. It says booking is what is required, and it is the commonest way French says this.

questions.q: What happens to the verb after « il faut »?
questions.why: Nothing. It is the same shape as everything else in this lesson, on a front with no person in it.
opts: Nothing, as after the other three

questions.q: Ils ___ arroser le jardin. (devoir)
questions.why: The hardest cell of the three, on a verb nobody taught you. Both halves came from somewhere other than a list.

questions.q: Fix this. « Vous devez attendez. »
questions.why: The ending is on twice. One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does.

questions.q: Which of these does this lesson NOT teach you to do?
questions.why: That is a different verb and it is the whole payload of a2.14, which is the next lesson on this trail.
opts: Say you have learned how to do something

sections.say: Four things, and the second one is bigger than the whole rest of the lesson.
sections.body: You can build three more verbs that will not come apart, and you found a recipe that produces the hardest row of all three of them from the two rows above it. 4 of the 6 endings are ones you already have. One letter here is new. That was the short half. One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does. You proved that on a verb this course has never taught you and never will, thirty seconds after meeting it, and it works the same way on every other verb in the language. You also know which sentence gets you served and which one gets you a baguette you did not ask for. a2.14 is next, and it brings one of these three back to stand against a verb you have not met.
sections.frSub: Ce que vous pouvez faire maintenant
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does.
veu + l = veul · peu + v = peuv · doi + v = doiv
3 persons, 2 spellings, one sound.
voudrais rather than veux, and the difference is whether the exchange goes well.

errorTriggers.description: Puts an ending on the second verb: Nous voulons payons, Vous devez attendez. Six lessons of building endings have made this reflex automatic, and this lesson is the first place it is wrong.
Builds the plural off the long stem rather than the short one: voulent, pouvent, devent. The plural borrows from both stems and neither one alone produces it.
Writes veus and peus, or puts the new letter on devoir: doix. Two of the three take it and the third does not, and all of it is silent so the ear gives no help.
Uses veux with somebody serving them, and adds please to fix it. Both sentences are correct French and only one of them is a request; the please does not change what the verb already said.
Believes pouvoir means only being able, and goes looking for another verb to ask permission with. There is not one, and the hesitation is where the sentence dies.
Reads dois plus a thing as an obligation, or expects il faut to have a person in it. Both are recognition failures rather than production ones, and both are common in real reading.

recorded.desc: THE SEVEN DAYS AS ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE, IN WEEK ORDER STARTING ON MONDAY, BY ONE VOICE AT ONE SPEED. Seven days recorded in seven sessions are seven performances, and the learner is memorising a SEQUENCE: any drift in pace, pitch or emphasis between them teaches a difference between the recordings rather than a difference in French. Read the seven straight through with an even beat, the way somebody counts, then again slowly in the same take. EVERY ONE TAKES THE STRESS ON ITS LAST SYLLABLE and none of them is stressed on the first, which is the single most common thing an English speaker does to these words. Keep the nasals closed: lundi opens on one with NO n sound, vendredi carries one with NO n sound, and dimanche carries one in the middle with NO n sound. Those three are the ones a reader over-articulates.

The contrast this lesson exists for. EACH PAIR IS ONE TAKE: « le lundi » immediately followed by « lundi » by the same voice at the same pace, so the ONLY difference the learner hears is the article. Recorded apart, they compare two performances instead of two meanings, and the whole teaching is lost. Do not lean on the le to make it clearer: it is an unstressed syllable in ordinary speech and a learner who hears it emphasised will never recognise it at conversational speed. All seven pairs, in week order, then the four sentence pairs (« Je suis libre le samedi » / « Je suis libre samedi », and the same for the other three). SEPARATELY, and this is the other half of this recording: mardi and jeudi ADJACENTLY IN THE SAME TAKE, because they are the pair that genuinely collides at speed, and the m against the zh is the whole of the difference. Do not slow that pair down on the natural-pace take.

The frame words, one take, one voice: la semaine, le week-end, le jour, hier, demain, le calendrier, tous les jours. le week-end is borrowed from English and must be read as FRENCH, with the stress on the second half and no English diphthong on the week: a reader who says it the English way teaches the learner to code-switch mid-sentence. Keep the nasal in calendrier closed.

The four English-speaker traps, wrong version then right version, with a clear beat between them so the learner hears a difference rather than a correction. Read EVERY wrong version plainly and at ordinary pace rather than comically: three of the four are real French sentences that mean something else, and a performance that marks them as errors removes the reason they are dangerous. « Je suis libre samedi » is not a mistake at all out of context, which is the point of the first one. « On se voit sur samedi » is the only one that is not a sentence, and it still gets read straight.

The opening scene, French bubbles only, in the voice of a woman in her twenties reading messages at an ordinary texting pace rather than a teaching pace. The beat where she gives up (« Ah, d'accord. Bon, une autre fois alors. ») must be light and unbothered rather than hurt or pointed: the whole point of the scene is that nobody is upset and nobody is corrected, the plan simply does not happen. Any edge on that line turns it into a telling-off and the teaching is lost.
clipIds: Ah, d'accord. Bon, une autre fois alors.

lessons.intro: Seven short words, and one that decides whether you meant one day or every one of them. This is how you name the days, say what your week looks like, and make a plan for a particular Saturday without accidentally describing your year.

oneDay.body: A day with nothing in front of it is one particular day, and which one is decided by the conversation you are already in. Said on a Wednesday, samedi is this coming Saturday. Said about the past, it is the one just gone. Nothing marks it and nothing needs to, because there is only ever one Saturday close enough to mean. Prochain and dernier are there when you want to be certain: samedi prochain, samedi dernier.
oneDay.title: The bare day, which is one day

examples.note: This Saturday. An answer to an invitation.
Prochain, when being certain is worth two extra syllables.

everyWeek.body: Put le in front of a day and you have stopped talking about one day and started talking about all of them. Le lundi is every Monday, as a rule, the way your week is arranged. This is the same le you met in front of a general noun a few lessons ago: j'aime le café is coffee in general rather than one cup, and le lundi is Mondays in general rather than one Monday. It is one idea you already have, pointed at a day.
everyWeek.term: le, in front of a day
everyWeek.title: The article that means every week

examples.note: Every Monday. It is what your timetable says.
Every Saturday. A fact about your week, not a plan.

lowercase.body: English capitalises the days and French does not. A day name is an ordinary noun here and takes a capital only where any word would: at the start of a sentence. This is inaudible, which is why it survives for years in the writing of people who speak well. It is worth fixing now rather than later, because every message you send is written and the habit is easier to break in the first week than in the fifth year.
lowercase.title: Days are lowercase in French

examples.note: A capital, and only because it opens the sentence.
Two days mid-sentence, and both are lowercase.

noPreposition.body: English needs a preposition in front of a day and French does not. On Monday is lundi, and there is nothing in front of it. Neither sur lundi nor a bare à lundi is a way of saying when something happens: sur means physically on top of, and à lundi is a way of saying goodbye until Monday. The urge to put a small word there is strong and it is the one error in this lesson that produces something a listener cannot repair, because the sentence stops making sense rather than shifting meaning.
noPreposition.title: French does not need on

examples.note: On Monday, and nothing in front of it.
Two bare days in one sentence, neither with a preposition.

weekStartsMonday.body: A printed French calendar starts its week on Monday and ends it on Sunday, so the two days at the right-hand edge are the weekend. Lundi is le premier jour de la semaine and nobody says so out loud because nobody needs to. It matters the first time you read a timetable, a shop notice or a diary and count the columns from the wrong end, and it is why le week-end sits where it does rather than wrapping around.
weekStartsMonday.title: What a French calendar looks like

examples.note: Next week, which starts on a Monday and not on a Sunday.
Every day, which is the whole row rather than one column of it.

lessons.title: Les jours de la semaine

drills.coach: The English is on the left. Say the French out loud before you turn the card, and keep the stress on the last syllable.
drills.title: English in, French out

drills.q: Which day comes straight after mercredi?
drills.why: jeudi. mardi is the day before mercredi, and the two that sound alike sit on either side of it, which is what makes this order worth saying out loud rather than reading.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Read the word straight in front of the day. If there is a le, it is every week. If there is nothing, it is one day, and the conversation has already decided which.
drills.title: One day, or all of them?

drills.q: You have a class every Monday. Which is right?
drills.why: Le lundi, singular, with the article. A bare day is one Monday and the plural is Mondays as a set, so only the middle one says every week.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Read the habit on the left. Say the version on the right, which is about one day, and notice that the only thing you did was delete a word.
pairs: Le magasin est fermé le mardi.
Le musée est gratuit le dimanche.
drills.title: Take it away again

drills.q: A friend asks if you are free this Saturday. What is a yes?
drills.why: She asked about one Saturday. The other two describe your usual week, which is true and is not an acceptance, so she has no way of knowing whether you are coming.
opts: Je suis libre tous les samedis.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Two shapes mean every week: le plus a singular day, and tous les plus a plural one. Everything else is one day. Sort on that and nothing here is ambiguous.
drills.title: Where the plural belongs

drills.q: Which of these does NOT mean every Saturday?
drills.why: Les samedis is Saturdays as a set of days, which is real French and is not how you say every Saturday. The article does that job on its own, in the singular.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Read the English on the left. Say the French on the right, and count how many words are in front of the day. The answer is always zero or one.
drills.title: Nothing in front of it

drills.q: Which one means "we are meeting on Saturday"?
drills.why: Nothing in front of the day. Sur is physically on top of something, and à samedi means see you Saturday, which is a goodbye rather than a statement about when.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Every line here is correct French, which is the point: look at where each capital falls. A day only ever gets one because it opened the sentence, never because it is a day.
drills.title: Small letters

drills.q: Which is written the way French writes it?
drills.why: The day takes a small letter and the sentence takes a capital. The third option gets the day right and drops the capital that any first word would have.
drills.title: One more time

sheets.title: The week, in full

rows.v: The week, running lundi to dimanche. Feminine.
Borrowed from English, hyphenated, masculine, and at the END of the row.
The day, as a unit. Masculine.
Yesterday and tomorrow. Neither takes an article or a preposition.
The calendar, which starts its week on Monday here.
Every day. The plural is correct here, after tous les.

sections.body: Five of the seven carry a planet and they are the same five planets behind the English names, which is why this is worth thirty seconds rather than a mission. Lundi is the moon, as Monday is. Mardi is Mars, where English took the Norse god Tiw instead. Mercredi is Mercury, where English took Woden. Jeudi is Jupiter, and English took Thor, so Thursday and jeudi are the same god arriving by two different roads. Vendredi is Venus, and English took Frigg, and both are the goddess of love. That leaves the two at the end of the row, which are not planets at all: samedi comes from the Sabbath and dimanche from dies dominica, the Lord's day. English kept the sun in Sunday and French did not. The reason this sticks is that it is checkable. You can hold the French list against the English one and watch five of them line up, and a fact you verified yourself is a different kind of memory from a fact you were handed.
sections.title: Five planets and two days off

sheets.title: Every week, or one day
contains: Both halves on all seven days
The four errors, and which are audible

rows.v: Je suis libre samedi for every Saturday. Audible, and it costs you a plan.
Je suis libre le samedi for this Saturday. Audible, and it reads as a polite no.
sur lundi, en lundi. Audible, and the sentence stops making sense.
les lundis for le lundi. Audible only in writing, since both sound the same.
Je viens Lundi. Inaudible, so nothing ever corrects it.

rows.k: The one plural that is right
rows.v: tous les samedis. Every Saturday, said as strongly as it can be said.

sections.title: The four errors, and which you can hear

sections.body: English and French both mark the difference between one Monday and every Monday, and they mark it in different places with different machinery, which is the whole reason this is hard. English uses a plural on the noun: on Monday against on Mondays. French uses a singular article in front of it: lundi against le lundi. So the English signal is at the end of the word and the French signal is a separate word in front of it, and the French form is singular exactly where the English one is plural. A learner translating word by word from English arrives at les lundis, which is a real phrase meaning Mondays as a set of days, so nothing about it looks wrong and no listener repairs it. That is why this error survives years of otherwise good French. The fix is not to translate the mechanism but to replace it: decide first whether you mean every week or one day, then put le in front or leave it off. The article is the same one you learned in front of a general noun, and it is doing the same job it does there. J'aime le café is coffee in general rather than one cup. Le lundi is Mondays in general rather than one Monday. It is one idea pointed at two different kinds of word, not two rules to keep apart.

detail.body: English needs on and French needs nothing. Sur is physically on top of something, and à lundi is how you say goodbye until Monday. Neither says when. This is the one error here that leaves a listener with nothing to repair.

errors.why: This one costs the most, because it lands while somebody is making a plan with you. A bare day is one day, so you have answered about this week when you meant your whole year, or the other way round.

errors.why: English needs on and French needs nothing at all. Sur means physically on top of, so this asks to meet standing on a Saturday and there is nothing for a listener to repair. À lundi is real, and it means see you Monday.

errors.why: Days are ordinary nouns in French and take a capital only at the start of a sentence. Nobody will hear this and everybody will read it, which is why it survives for years in the writing of people who speak the language well.

errors.why: The English plural, moved across. Les lundis is real French meaning Mondays as a set, so nothing marks it wrong and it never gets corrected. The habitual form is singular. Tous les lundis is where the plural belongs.

sections.say: Every day in this passage is lowercase and half of them carry an article. Tap any underlined phrase.
sections.text: There is a printed card taped inside the window of the bakery on the corner, and under it somebody has stuck a second one, handwritten. The printed one has been there for years. « Le magasin est fermé le mardi. » The handwritten one went up this morning, in biro, slightly crooked. « Le magasin est fermé mardi. » Read quickly they are the same sentence and one word apart, and the difference between them is a week of your shopping. The printed card is about every Tuesday, for ever, which is when this baker takes his day off. The handwritten one is about one Tuesday, the one coming, because something is happening that week. Underneath both, in the same biro, he has added the part that matters to his regulars. « On se voit mercredi. » Nobody needs telling which Wednesday.
sections.title: The Note On The Door

glossary.note: Every Tuesday, for ever. The article is the whole difference, and this is what a printed sign means.
One Tuesday, the one coming. This is what the handwritten one means.
Masculine, so le rather than la. Nothing to do with the day rule.
Read this as a whole phrase. The verb behind it is not one you have been given yet.
Lowercase, and with nothing in front of it. Both are the French default, and a bare day is the nearest one.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched a plan quietly fail over one word, learned the seven names in the order a French calendar prints them, and found out that the difference between every Monday and one Monday is an article your last-but-four lesson already taught you. You have seen both halves of that rule side by side on one screen, met the two written habits English hands you and French does not want, and read a shop door where one word was a week of your shopping. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.
sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: The names, quickly.
rounds.label: The seven names

questions.q: A French calendar has seven columns. Which day is in the first one?
questions.why: lundi. The French week runs Monday to Sunday, so the weekend is the last two columns rather than one at each end. Counting from the wrong end puts every appointment one place out.

questions.q: Write the day that comes between mardi and jeudi.
questions.why: mercredi, from Mercury. It is the longest of the seven and sits in the middle of the week, which is the pair of facts that makes it easy to place.

questions.q: Listen. Which day is it?
questions.why: jeudi. It and mardi are two syllables ending in the same DEE, and the opening consonant is the whole difference. At speed that is what sends somebody to a meeting two days early.

questions.q: Five of the seven are named after planets. Which one is not?
questions.why: samedi, from the Sabbath, and dimanche from the Lord's day. The other five are the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter and Venus, and they are the same five planets behind the English names.

rounds.say: The article, and what it does.
rounds.label: Every week

questions.q: Your timetable puts a class on every Monday. How do you say it?
questions.why: Le makes it every week. A bare day is one day, so the first option describes a single Monday. The article is the only thing in the sentence saying how often.

questions.q: You mean every Saturday. Fix this. « Je suis libre samedi. »
questions.why: Without the article this is about one Saturday, which is an answer to an invitation rather than a fact about your week. Adding le turns one Saturday into all of them.

questions.q: Which lesson taught you this same le already?
questions.why: The definite articles taught le in front of a general noun, where English uses none at all: j'aime le café is coffee in general. A day works the same way, so this is one idea rather than two.

questions.q: You are closed every Tuesday. Write the two words for "on Tuesdays".
questions.why: le mardi. Singular, with the article, and that is what goes on a printed sign because it is true for ever rather than for one week.

rounds.say: The bare day, and which one it is.
rounds.label: One day

questions.q: Somebody asks if you are free on Saturday. You are, this week. What answers them?
questions.why: She asked about one Saturday, so answer about one Saturday. The other three all describe your usual week, which is true and is not a yes, and that is how a plan quietly fails.
opts: Je suis libre tous les samedis.

questions.q: One Thursday, the one coming. Write the French for "on Thursday".
questions.why: jeudi, on its own. No article, because it is one day, and no preposition, because French does not use one. Two things to leave out and nothing to add.

questions.q: The museum is free this Sunday only, because of an event. Fix this. « Le musée est gratuit le dimanche. »
questions.why: With the article this says every Sunday, which is a standing arrangement rather than a one-off. Take it away and you have one Sunday, the nearest one.

questions.q: Say it out loud: you are free this coming Saturday.
questions.why: No article and no preposition. The mic is listening for what is NOT in front of the day, which is the hardest thing to hear yourself leave out.

rounds.say: The English plural, and where it does belong.
rounds.label: Singular, not plural

questions.q: You are writing your timetable out for a friend. Which form means "every Monday"?
questions.why: le lundi, singular. English marks this with a plural S and French marks it with a singular article, so there is nothing to carry across and the English instinct gives you the wrong one every time.

questions.q: Fix this. « J'ai cours les lundis. »
questions.why: Les lundis is real French and means Mondays as a set of days, so nothing marks it as an error and nobody corrects it. The form that means every week is singular.

questions.q: Fix this. « Elle est à Paris les jeudis. »
questions.why: The same swap on a different day, and the same reason: the habitual form is le plus a singular day. It holds for all seven with no exceptions.
accept: Elle est à Paris le jeudi.
elle est a paris le jeudi
questions.answer: Elle est à Paris le jeudi.

questions.q: Where does a plural day belong?
questions.why: tous les samedis, every Saturday, said as strongly as it can be said. That is the one frame where the day goes plural, and it is a reinforcement of the rule rather than an exception to it.

rounds.say: The word English makes you add.
rounds.label: No word for on

questions.q: How do you say "on Monday" in French?
questions.why: lundi, with nothing in front of it. Sur is physically on top of, and à lundi is how you say goodbye until Monday rather than a way of saying when something happens.

questions.q: Fix this. « On se voit sur samedi. »
questions.why: Sur asks to meet standing on top of a Saturday, so there is nothing for a listener to repair and they ask again instead. This is the one error here that stops the sentence making sense rather than shifting its meaning.

questions.q: Fix this. « Nous avons une réunion à vendredi. »
questions.why: The day needs nothing in front of it. À vendredi is a real phrase and it means see you Friday, so putting it here says goodbye in the middle of a sentence about a meeting.

questions.q: French does put one word in front of a day. Which, and what for?
questions.why: Le makes it every week. It is an article rather than a preposition, and it changes the meaning rather than just being grammar. That is why leaving it out is not a small error.
opts: le, and it means every week
en, and it marks the future

rounds.say: What only shows in writing.
rounds.label: On the page

questions.q: You are writing a message. Which is spelled correctly?
questions.why: Days are ordinary nouns in French, so lundi takes a small letter mid-sentence. Je keeps its capital because it opens the sentence, which is the only reason any word gets one here.

questions.q: Prochain never takes an article. Fix this. « Je suis libre le dimanche prochain. »
questions.why: Prochain already picks out one Sunday, so the article has nothing left to do and would contradict it. This is the over-correction that arrives once the every-week rule has landed.

questions.q: A printed sign reads « Fermé le mardi ». A handwritten one reads « Fermé mardi ». Which comes down next week?
questions.why: The handwritten one is about a single Tuesday, so it says nothing once that Tuesday has passed. The printed one describes a habit and stays up for years.

questions.q: Write the French for "the week".
questions.why: la semaine, feminine. It runs lundi to dimanche here, which is a different seven days from the one an English calendar draws even though both have seven.

sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can name all seven days in the order a French calendar prints them, say what you do every week, and make a plan for one particular day without accidentally describing your year. The second and third of those are the same rule read in two directions, and it is one you already had before this lesson started: it is the le from the definite articles, pointed at a day. Months are next, and they inherit every habit on this list.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Le makes it every week. Take it away and you are talking about one day instead.
No word for on. Lundi, never sur lundi, and à lundi is a goodbye.
Lowercase, always, except where any word would take a capital.
The habitual form is singular: le lundi. Les lundis is Mondays as a set.

errorTriggers.description: Reaches for the wrong day, most often mardi for jeudi: two syllables, the same ending, and one consonant apart.
Says a bare day when they mean every week. The error the reframe exists to kill, and the one the opening scene turns on.
Says le plus a day when they mean one particular day. The over-correction that arrives once the first half of the rule has landed.
Writes les lundis for every Monday, carrying the English plural across. Real French, wrong meaning, and nothing corrects it.
Puts sur, à or en in front of a day, because English needs on. The one error here that stops a sentence making sense.
Writes Lundi mid-sentence. Inaudible, so nobody corrects it, and it survives for years in the writing of people who speak well.

recorded.desc: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT NOTE IN THIS LESSON. « la chambre », « les pièces » and « la salle » ARE ONE TAKE, one voice, one pace, read straight through with no gap and no reset. The claim the whole lesson rests on is that these are three different rooms rather than three ways of saying one word, and three separate recordings are three performances: a reader who records them in separate sessions will give one of them more weight and the learner will hear that weight as a difference in importance rather than in meaning. KEEP THE NASAL IN « chambre » CLOSED. It is /ʃɑ̃bʁ/ with a nasal vowel and NO n sound behind it: the app respells it lah SHAHⁿBR deliberately, and a reader who lets an n out of it teaches a sound that is not in the word. Then, in the same take, the two whole sentences: « Notre appartement a trois pièces. » and « Il y a cinq pièces dans la maison. »
clipIds: Il y a cinq pièces dans la maison.

recorded.desc: « la salle de bain » AND « les toilettes » ADJACENT IN ONE TAKE, one voice. This is the pair the opening scene turns on and the learner has to hear them as two rooms rather than as two registers of one. Read both plainly and at the same pace: any hint that the second is more colloquial or more delicate than the first invents a difference the language does not have. Both are the ordinary words. GIVE « les toilettes » ITS PLURAL FULLY. The s is silent but the les is not, and a reader who lets it slide toward « la toilette » is recording the error the lesson is about. Then, in the same take: « Où est la salle de bain ? » and « Où sont les toilettes ? », so the learner hears the verb move with the plural.
clipIds: Où est la salle de bain ?

recorded.desc: « le sol » AND « le seau » ADJACENT, ONE TAKE, AND THIS IS THE ONLY GENUINE EAR CONTRAST IN THE LESSON. The two differ in the vowel and in whether the syllable closes, and a gap of even a few seconds between the two recordings lets the reader reset their vowel. Read them back to back, at the same pitch, with the same little word in front of both. ALSO IN THIS TAKE: « la poêle », which is /pwal/. THIS IS NOT A TYPO AND MUST NOT BE "CORRECTED" LATER. The oê spelling predicts the sound so badly that the whole reason the word is in this lesson is that a learner has to be told. Anybody reading it as a spelling pronunciation is recording the trap rather than the word. NEVER RECORD « salle » IN ISOLATION. There is no clip anywhere in this lesson of salle on its own, deliberately: it does not occur alone in a home and a clip of it teaches a word the learner will never need by itself. If a request for one arrives, it is a mistake in the request.

THE TWELVE ROOMS, EACH READ WITH ITS LITTLE WORD ATTACHED AND NEVER WITHOUT IT. Read as ONE LIST in one take at an even pace, because the learner is being asked to store the little word as part of the room and a pause between the two teaches the opposite. EVERY NASAL CLOSED, and there are five of them in this list: la maison, le salon, le jardin, le balcon and la salle à manger. All five are respelled with a superscript in the app and all five were shipped wrong until this build. A reader who lets an n out of any of them undoes the repair. Then the four published sentences: « Il y a un canapé dans le salon. », « Nous avons deux chambres et une salle de bains. », « La salle de bain est au bout du couloir. », « Le salon a deux fenêtres et une porte. »
clipIds: Il y a un canapé dans le salon.
Nous avons deux chambres et une salle de bains.
La salle de bain est au bout du couloir.
Le salon a deux fenêtres et une porte.

recorded.desc: The furniture, read GROUPED BY ROOM rather than as one alphabetical run, with a clear beat between groups. The whole organising idea of act three is that these come in room-sized sets, and a flat list of eleven read at one pace destroys it. Living room, then bedroom, then the soft things, then the things that hold things. Then the three published sentences in the same take: « Il y a un grand lit dans la chambre. », « Le chat dort sur le grand lit blanc. », « Les rideaux sont bleus dans le salon. »
clipIds: Il y a un grand lit dans la chambre.
Le chat dort sur le grand lit blanc.
Les rideaux sont bleus dans le salon.

recorded.desc: THE THREE COMPOUNDS FIRST, TOGETHER, AS A GROUP: « le lave-vaisselle », « le sèche-linge », « le micro-ondes ». Then a beat. Then the two that are not compounds: « la machine à laver », « la cuisinière ». The grouping IS the teaching, and reading all five as one list makes the rule invisible. EACH COMPOUND READ AS ONE WORD, not as two words with a hyphen between them. lave-vaisselle is one unit and the whole point is that the unit is what carries the gender; a reader who pauses at the hyphen is arguing with the lesson. « le sèche-linge » ENDS IN A NASAL, respelled luh sehsh-LAⁿZH, and it was one of the rows this build repaired. Keep it closed. Then « Le frigo est vide. »

The four published sentences act four is built on, read PLAINLY and at ordinary conversational pace: « Le lit est près de la fenêtre. », « La cuisine est à côté du salon. », « La salle de bain est au bout du couloir. », « Il y a une table dans le salon. » DO NOT STRESS THE SMALL WORDS. près de, à côté du, au bout du and dans belong to the previous unit and are deliberately not taught here, so a reader who leans on them turns act four into a preposition lesson, which is exactly what this lesson is forbidden from being. The NOUNS carry the weight in every one of these.

recorded.desc: The five written traps, wrong version then right version, with a clear beat between them. Read EVERY wrong version PLAINLY and at ordinary pace rather than comically, because a learner saying them does not hesitate either. « Où est la salle de bain ? » is a perfectly ordinary French sentence and sounds like one, which is the entire point: nothing about it signals an error, which is why it survives and why it costs. « la toilette » in the singular should be read with no special emphasis on the missing s, because the learner cannot hear it and pretending otherwise teaches a signal that is not there.

The opening scene, French bubbles only. Claire is hosting a dinner, in her thirties, warm and slightly busy. HER OFFER OF A TOWEL MUST BE COMPLETELY UNREMARKABLE AND GENUINELY HELPFUL. She has not noticed an error and she is not making a point: she heard a request for the room with the bath in it and answered it, and offering a towel is simply what you do for somebody who wants to wash. Any hint of amusement or correction in her voice turns the scene into a telling-off and loses the whole point, which is that nothing visibly went wrong. Marc's single line at the end is a different speaker and should be flatter and quicker: it is the version where nothing happens, and it should sound like nothing happening.

lessons.intro: English says room and lets the sentence sort out which one. French makes you choose first, and there are three words to choose between. This is how to pick the right one, name every room in a home, and name what is in each of them.

twoRooms.body: In most French homes the bath is in one room and the toilet is in another, and the two have separate names because they are separate places. La salle de bain has the bath, the shower and the basin in it. Les toilettes has the toilet. Asking for the first when you want the second is understood perfectly and sends you to the wrong door, and the person helping you will assume you meant what you said. Note the s on the end of toilettes as well: this one is always plural and there is no singular of it, which is unlike every other room in the lesson.

twoRooms.title: Where the towel comes from
