sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have put the article where English gave you nothing, worked the three questions in order, and found the one letter that behaves two ways. What is left is the part that tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Four rounds. Most of these ask you to write the answer rather than pick it, because picking was never the hard part.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: The half of this lesson that is not about which article. It is about whether there is one.
rounds.label: The missing word

questions.q: Write in French: I like coffee.
questions.why: When English says nothing, French says le. Coffee in general still takes le, and without it this is not a sentence.

questions.q: Fix this: « Nous aimons français. »
questions.why: A language is a general idea, so French keeps the article. English drops it, which is why the gap is invisible.

questions.q: Cats love sleeping in the sun. What does the French sentence start with?
questions.why: Cats as a species is the general case. French marks that by keeping a word where English removes one.

questions.q: Write in French: I am learning French.
questions.why: School subjects, languages, sports and instruments all take the article, and English gives none of them one.

questions.q: Fix this: « Elle aime musique. »
questions.why: Music is feminine, so la, but the reason a word is needed at all has nothing to do with gender.

questions.q: English says "Sport makes children stronger". How many articles does the French have?
questions.why: Le sport and les enfants. Both nouns are general, and English happens to mark neither of them.

rounds.say: The third question, and the only one of the three that needs the gender.
rounds.label: Le or la

questions.q: Maison is feminine. Write "the house".
questions.why: Feminine, singular, and it starts on a consonant sound, so you reach the third question and answer it with la.

questions.q: You need the gender of a noun in order to choose:
questions.why: Les and l apostrophe both settle it without asking. Only the third branch needs the gender.

questions.q: Livre is masculine. Write "the book".
questions.why: Masculine, singular, consonant sound. The one branch of the three where what a1.03 taught you is doing the work.

questions.q: Fix this: « le maison »
questions.why: Nothing in the word maison says it is feminine. That is why the article is stored with it.

questions.q: Lune is feminine and soleil is masculine. Write "the sun and the moon".
questions.why: Two everyday things with opposite genders and no reason behind either. This pair is worth storing as one card.

rounds.say: Two branches, and neither of them asks you a thing about the noun's gender.
rounds.label: When gender stops counting

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: The Z at the join gives it away. It appears only when the noun starts on a vowel sound.

questions.q: Toilettes is feminine and plural. Write "the toilet".
questions.why: Plural, so the first question already answered it and the gender was never consulted.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: Livres starts on a consonant, so the two words stay apart and there is no Z. Le livre would be one word shorter.

questions.q: École is feminine. Which is right?
questions.why: A vowel sound follows, so la shortens and the gender goes invisible before you needed it.

questions.q: Eau is feminine. Write "the water".
questions.why: La cannot sit in front of a vowel sound, so it shortens. There is no French that says la eau.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: One word, not two. Heure starts on a vowel sound despite the h, so the article shortens and joins onto it.

rounds.say: A closed list, not a rule. The article is the only place the difference is ever visible.
rounds.label: The two kinds of h

questions.q: Write "the owl". Hibou is masculine.
questions.why: This h behaves like a consonant, so le stays whole. Nothing on the page distinguishes it from the other kind.

questions.q: Both hôtel and hibou start with h. Why does only one take l apostrophe?
questions.why: The split is a leftover of where the words came from. It is two lists, and gender is not in it.
opts: There is no rule; the two are separate lists

questions.q: Fix this: « le heure »
questions.why: Heure behaves like a vowel, so the article shortens. Store the pair together and you never have to work it out.

questions.q: Write "the green beans".
questions.why: It is plural, so the first question settles it and the h never gets a chance to matter.

questions.q: Say it out loud: I like coffee.
questions.why: When English says nothing, French says le. If you said three words, the missing one is this lesson.

sections.say: Six things, and one that a later lesson finishes for you.
sections.body: You can pick the right article for any noun you know, in three questions, and two of those three never ask you about gender. More usefully, you can hear the place where English gave you nothing and French wants a word, which is the error that marks a beginner more reliably than any accent does.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: When English says nothing, French says le. Say it to yourself before a general noun and you will stop losing the sentence.
Plural takes les, whatever the gender. A vowel sound takes l apostrophe, whatever the gender.
Only le and la need the gender, which makes it one branch of three rather than the whole decision.
Every French h is silent, and only the article ever tells you which kind you are holding.
Store the noun with its article, the way a1.03 asked. This lesson is where that habit gets paid.
The Z you heard in les amis is a system of its own, and the sons track has a whole lesson on it.
du, au and aux are these same articles wearing a disguise. a1.29 takes them apart.

segments.text: I am Camille. Today is the four little words in front of French nouns, and the reason you keep leaving them out.
J'aime le café.
Four words. In English that sentence has three, and the one you do not have is the one we are here for.
English gives you three ways to introduce a noun. The coffee. A coffee. And plain coffee, meaning coffee in general.
French has the first two and not the third. When English says nothing, French says le. That is the whole lesson.
Les chats adorent dormir au soleil.
Cats, meaning cats everywhere. English marks that by taking a word away and French marks it by keeping one.
Now which one. Three questions, and you stop at the first yes. Is it plural?
Les parents. Les toilettes.
One of those is masculine and one is feminine and you could not tell, because les never asks.
Second question. Does the noun start on a vowel sound?
L'eau. L'école. L'appartement.
Again the gender is hidden, and again you did not need it. Only if both answers were no do you reach the third question.
Le fromage. La maison.
One letter behaves two ways, and the article is the only place you will ever see it. Listen.
L'heure. Le hibou.
Both spelled with an h, both silent, and only one of them lets the article shorten. There is no rule. Store the pair.
Your turn, with nothing in front of you. Say that you like coffee.
Now the green beans. Careful, this one answers two questions at once.
And the school. It is feminine, and I want to know whether that changed anything.
One question. I will say a sentence and you tell me what English would have left out.
Nous aimons le français.
Le. In English you would have said we like French, with nothing in front of it, and that gap is the one thing no course points at.
Three things to keep. When English says nothing, French says le.
Plural takes les and a vowel sound takes l apostrophe, and neither of them asks about gender. Only le and la do.
And the h words are two lists, not a rule. Store the article with the noun and you never have to choose.
À bientôt.

errorTriggers.description: Leaves a general noun bare, the way English does: J'aime café, Les chats becomes Chats, Le français becomes Français.
Reaches the third question and answers it with the wrong gender: le maison, la livre.
Keeps le or la where the noun is plural or starts on a vowel sound: le eau, la école, le parents.
Guesses at an h word rather than recognising which list it is on: l'hibou, le heure.

grammarAssumed: Every noun carries a gender, and it is stored with the noun rather than derived from it
The indefinite articles un and une, as the form gender is stored in
grammarIntroduced: The definite articles le, la, l apostrophe and les, and the order of the three questions that choose between them
The definite article in front of a general noun, where English uses no article at all
Nouns beginning with h splitting into two groups, distinguishable only by the article they take

recorded.desc: THE EIGHTEEN CELLS, THREE TAKES, ONE PER VERB, EACH VERB'S SIX IN ONE BREATH GROUP. Within the first three of EACH verb the verb must be acoustically identical: « Je prends la clé. » « Tu prends la clé. » « Il prend la clé. » A reader who knows the third is spelled differently will shorten the vowel or put a fraction of a d on it, and either instinct destroys the screen that asks the learner to fail to hear a difference. If a listener with their eyes shut can say which of the three they just heard, the take is unusable. In the plural the opposite is required and it is the whole lesson: the n at the end of « Ils prennent » must be clean, audible and unhurried, and it must be plainly a different sound from the nasal vowel that ends « Il prend ». Same for the t of « Ils mettent » and « Ils battent ». AND la clé MUST SOUND IDENTICAL IN ALL TWELVE prendre AND mettre LINES. It is the control: the learner is being shown that only the middle of the sentence moves.

THE PAIR THE LESSON TURNS ON, AS ONE TAKE, IN THIS ORDER: « Nous prenons la clé. » then « Ils prennent la clé. » then « Nous mettons la clé. » then « Ils mettent la clé. » The first two are a minimal pair in the strict sense and must be read as one: same speed, same pitch, same length, and the ONLY difference audible anywhere in the line is where the verb finishes. Read them as two separate sentences and the learner hears two performances instead of one contrast. The second pair is the control and must sound duller than the first: nothing surprising is happening in it and the reading should not pretend otherwise.

THE FAMILY, AS THREE ROWS OF THREE. « je prends · j'apprends · je comprends », then the nous row, then the ils row, and each row is ONE breath group with the smallest possible gap between the three verbs. This is the take that does the teaching on the identity screen: the learner has to hear that the end of all three words is the same sound, arriving three times. Any pause between them lets the ear treat them as three separate words rather than one word wearing three fronts. Do not stress the fronts. They are the part that does not matter.

THE mettre COMPOUNDS, AND ONE PAIR MATTERS MORE THAN THE REST. « Je mets la clé. » then « Je remets la clé. » must be one take, same speed, same everything, so that the two syllables of difference are the only thing in the line that moved. The learner is being shown that a compound is its base verb with something on the front, and this is the only place in the lesson where the two sentences are otherwise identical word for word.

THE SMALL ONE. « battre », « combattre », then « Je bats Paul. » « Il bat Paul. » « Nous battons Paul. » « Ils battent Paul. » Brisk and unremarkable, and that is a direction rather than an accident: battre gets two missions in this lesson because it earns two, and a reading that gives it the weight of the other two would be arguing with the design. The t at the end of « Ils battent » is the one thing that has to be clean, because it is the audible plural.

THE SIX LINES FOR THE LISTENING SCREEN, WITH AUDIO BEFORE TEXT, IN SINGULAR-PLURAL PAIRS: prendre, then mettre, then battre. Each pair is one take. The instruction is the opposite of the grid take and it is worth stating plainly: here the difference must be as clear as the language allows, because the learner is being asked to hear it. Land on the final consonant of each plural. Do not add one to the singular.

THE BOUNDARY. « il vend » then « il prend », then « vendre » then « prendre », then « Nous prenons la clé. » The first pair is the point: the two singular forms rhyme exactly, which is why the mistake is so easy to make, and the reading must let them rhyme rather than helping the learner tell them apart. The difference does not arrive until the plural, and the last clip is where it arrives.

THE THREE FAMILY LISTS, READ AS LISTS: « apprendre, comprendre, surprendre », « permettre, promettre, remettre », « combattre, débattre, abattre ». Even pace, even weight, no rising list intonation that would make the last item sound like a conclusion. Nine words in three groups, and the value of the take is that all nine sound like ordinary vocabulary rather than like a rule being announced.

THE FOUR PUBLISHED ROWS, READ AS WHAT THEY ARE: sentences written for other lessons that happen to prove this one. Ordinary pace, no teaching emphasis anywhere, and in particular no weight on the verb. The whole value of the screen is that nobody was thinking about prendre or mettre when these were written.
clipIds: J'apprends le français depuis le printemps.
Elle met sa veste et ferme la porte.
Tu mets du beurre sur tout, toujours.

recorded.desc: THE LAST MISSION BEFORE THE EXAM, AND IT IS TWO WORDS. « reprendre » and « admettre », each said once, plainly, with no example sentence and no conjugated form after them. That restraint is the mission: the learner is about to be asked to build four forms of these two and nothing in the audio may give one away. Do not read them slowly, do not separate the front from the rest, and do not follow either with a pause that invites the learner to expect more.

THE BREAK CARD. « je prends » then « j'apprends », as one take, back to back, with the smallest gap the recording allows. They must sound like the same word twice with something added at the front the second time, because that is what they are. Any pause, any change of pitch, any extra weight on the ap and the learner hears two words instead of one.

THE CLIMBING GYM. She is friendly, slightly out of breath, unhurried and completely uninterested in teaching anybody French. « Tu apprends le français ici ? » is casual and quick, the way you ask somebody something while pulling a shoe off. The English line afterwards is the important one and it must not sound like a defeat or a rebuke: she switches language without thinking about it, cheerfully, because it is the shortest route to a conversation. That is exactly what makes it expensive, and nothing in the delivery should point at it.

lessons.intro: Three verbs go in and a dozen come out. Each of these is the head of a family, and every verb in the family takes its endings exactly, without a single new form to learn. The last screen before the exam hands you a verb this lesson never shows you and asks for it anyway.

nousOn.body: nous parlons is what you write. on parle is what you say.
nousOn.title: The we people actually say

examples.note: on takes the il form, so on prend is this row with one word changed and no new spelling to learn.

theEar.body: The singular ends on a nasal vowel and the plural ends on an n, and those are two completely different sounds. That makes this one of the few plurals in French you can hear without being told. a2.10 had the same gift on a different verb, where the plural grew a whole syllable in the middle. mettre and battre give you the same thing with a t: met has nothing at the end and mettent finishes on a hard consonant. Three verbs, three audible plurals, and it is the only place in this lesson the ear is on your side.
theEar.title: prend against prennent

examples.note: Ends on the nasal vowel.
Ends on an n, and nothing else about the line moved.

theFrame.body: Every prendre sentence and every mettre sentence on these screens ends in la clé. That is deliberate and it is doing as much teaching as the verbs are: if the back of the sentence never moves, everything you notice is happening to the verb. Read down a column and the only thing changing is the middle. battre cannot join in, because you do not beat a key, and it takes Paul instead. That is the one place the pattern breaks and it breaks for a reason you can see.
theFrame.title: Why every sentence ends the same way

examples.note: Take it.
Put it down. Same four words behind the verb.
And the one that cannot use them.

notVendre.body: a2.11 named these three and would not build them, because the model it taught you would have produced a form nobody says. This is the lesson it was waiting for. prendre ends in -re and it is not one of those verbs. Run the regular pattern on it and the plural comes out with a d in it, which is a sound no French speaker makes in this word. Look at prenons beside the regular plural and the difference is a whole letter that has left the building. This is the second time you have been shown a verb that looks like a group it is not in, and it will not be the last.
notVendre.title: What a2.11 would not do

examples.note: The d is gone.
And here it is replaced by a second n.

theFamily.body: Three verbs to learn, and 12 you can build. Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. A verb with something stuck on the front of it takes every ending the verb underneath it takes, without exception and without a single new form to learn. apprendre, comprendre, surprendre all run on prendre; permettre, promettre, remettre all run on mettre. That is the largest return on memorisation anywhere in this level, and it is the reason the last four lessons were worth the time.
theFamily.title: One verb, and the ones that come with it

examples.note: The head verb, in the plural.
A compound, and the verb behind it has not moved.
The question at the start of the lesson, and the verb in it is one of these.

theIdioms.body: prendre turns up in a great many set phrases where it has stopped meaning take at all, and English does not use take in any of them. Those belong to two later units and they are the whole opening of both: a2.27 for the ones about getting somewhere and a2.07 for the ones about ordering something. Nothing in this lesson teaches them, on purpose. What this lesson gives you is the six forms, which is what you will need on the day either of those arrives.
theIdioms.title: Where the fixed expressions are taught

examples.note: The plain meaning, which is the one being built here.

theControl.body: mettre and battre change once and stop. prendre changes twice. Both of them lose a t in the singular and get it back for the whole plural: mets, then mettons, mettez, mettent, and not one of those three is different from the others. That is worth noticing because it is what prendre does NOT do, and reading the two side by side is the fastest way to see what makes prendre the difficult one.
theControl.title: mettre and battre change once

examples.note: One t.
Two, and they stay for all three.
battre does the same thing on the same cell.

threeStems.body: prend- pren- prenn- for prendre. met- mett- for mettre and bat- batt- for battre. prendre keeps 3 stems where the other two keep 2. In the singular the d is written and never said, so prends, prends and prend are one sound. For nous and vous the d goes and an ordinary ending arrives. For ils a second n turns up. Three shapes in six cells is more than any verb you have met so far, and it is the only genuinely hard thing here.
threeStems.title: Where prendre keeps changing

examples.note: The d is there and you do not say it.
The d has gone and there is one n.
And now there are two.

battreSmall.body: It is here because it finishes the set and because combattre is worth recognising, and it is not here in the same quantity as the other two. There is no sentence anywhere in this course that puts battre into one of its six forms, and there are two hundred and thirty-four holding a form of prendre. Learn its shape from mettre, which it copies exactly, keep combattre for recognition, and spend the time you saved on the first two. A course that gave all three equal weight would be teaching you that frequency does not matter.
battreSmall.title: battre is not the same size as the other two

examples.note: The naming form, and it did not exist until this lesson.
Two t in the plural, exactly like mettre.

theDoubling.body: One n for nous, two for ils. a2.09 doubled the l of appeler in the cells where the ending went silent. prennent doubles its n for the same reason: the -ent makes no sound, so the stem has to end in one. a2.09 said it first, about a different verb: The spelling changes so the sound does not. When the ending makes no sound, the stem is the last thing anybody hears, so there has to be something left in it to hear. prenons does not need a second n because the -ons is doing the sounding. prennent does, because the -ent is doing nothing at all. Two lessons, one reason, and it is the same reason both times.
theDoubling.title: Why prennent has two

examples.note: The ending sounds, so one n is enough.
The ending is silent, so the n has to carry the end of the word.

coverTheFront.body: Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. A verb you have never seen? Take the front off it, and what is left is one you built ten minutes ago. It is a thing you do with your eye rather than a rule you recall, which is why it survives being needed halfway through a sentence. Somebody says remettre and you have never seen it: put a thumb over the re, read mettre, and every one of its six forms is already yours. Put the re back on the front and you are finished. Nothing else in this lesson is worth as much as that.
coverTheFront.title: What to do when a new one arrives

examples.note: The verb underneath.
And the same verb with a front on it.
The answer the scene wanted, built out of a verb you already had.

theParticiples.body: These three have past forms that nothing about the present tells you, and they are among the most useful in the language. They are not in this lesson and that is deliberate rather than an omission: a2.20 is built around them and it comes after the two lessons that give you the tense they live in. What you have here is the present, in all six persons, for three families of verbs. That is enough to be going on with.
theParticiples.title: a2.20 takes that

examples.note: The present, which is what this lesson is.

theCompoundMeaning.body: re- usually means again or back, so remettre is to put back. com- and ap- and sur- do other things and none of it is predictable, so what a verb MEANS is a vocabulary question and you look it up. The endings are not a vocabulary question. They are settled the moment you can see which verb is underneath, and they are settled for every verb in the family that exists, including the ones nobody has taught you.
theCompoundMeaning.title: The front changes the meaning, not the endings

examples.note: com- plus prendre, and it means to understand.
sur- plus prendre, and it means to surprise.
com- plus battre, and it means to fight.

sections.title: The stems, and how many each verb has

sections.body: a2.09 doubled the l of appeler in the cells where the ending went silent. prennent doubles its n for the same reason: the -ent makes no sound, so the stem has to end in one. That is not a rule about this verb, it is a rule about French, and a2.09 stated it seven lessons ago in a lesson that had nothing to do with these three: The spelling changes so the sound does not. A silent ending leaves the stem holding the end of the word on its own, and a stem in that position has to end in something you can hear. prenons does not need it because the -ons is sounded. prennent does, because the -ent is not. Once you have seen it here you will recognise it everywhere, which is worth more than the cell itself.
sections.title: Why the second n is there

sections.body: Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. It is a syntax move rather than a memory one, and it holds for every compound of these three that exists, including the ones this course has not written a card for. Three verbs to learn, and 12 you can build. Two things are deliberately not in this lesson and both of them are worth waiting for. The past forms of these three do not follow from anything in the present and they are the centre of a2.20. And prendre turns up in a great many fixed expressions where it stops meaning take entirely; those open a2.07 and a2.27, and what you have built here is exactly what both of them assume you arrive with.
sections.title: What carries forward

overview.introFr: Trois verbes à apprendre, et une douzaine qui viennent avec.

say.text: Nobody in this scene is impatient and nobody is corrected. Watch what four seconds of hunting for a verb actually costs.

beats.text: A climbing gym in Grenoble on a Wednesday evening. You are sitting on a mat pulling your shoes off, and the person next to you starts talking.

beats.en: Are you learning French here?
beats.speaker: La grimpeuse

beats.en: Yes... uh...
beats.stage: You have said « je prends » a hundred times this week. The word she used is that verb with two letters on the front of it, and you are searching for it as though you had never met it.

beats.prompt: Four seconds have gone. She is still waiting. What comes out?

options.en: the same verb she used, given back
and the conversation changes language

followUp.works: She nods and asks how long you have been at it, in French, and you are still in the conversation.
followUp.breaks: She switches to English without thinking about it and stays there. Everything after this is a chat about climbing shoes in your own language.

beats.en: Ah, you live here? How long have you been in Grenoble?
beats.fr: Ah, you live here? How long have you been in Grenoble?
beats.stage: Nobody was unkind and nobody corrected anything. She simply took the shortest route to being understood, and the shortest route was not French.
beats.speaker: La grimpeuse

beats.body: You did not need a new verb. You needed the one you already had, with two letters in front of it and nothing else changed at all.
beats.coach: Cover the front and look again.
beats.heading: Same verb

beats.text: This is the last of the five irregular lessons and it is the one that pays for the other four. Three verbs go in and a dozen come out, and the proof is a verb nobody in this lesson is going to show you.

closing.text: Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. A verb you have never seen? Take the front off it, and what is left is one you built ten minutes ago.

detail.body: apprendre [a-PRAHⁿDR] is to learn, and prendre is what is left when you cover the first two letters. Every one of its six forms is one you have already written. Ils apprennent le français.

sections.title: Prend Or Prennent

questions.q: Il prend la clé against Ils prennent la clé. What is the difference you can hear?
questions.why: The end of the verb. One finishes inside the nose and the other finishes on a consonant, and those are two completely different sounds.
opts: The first ends on a nasal vowel and the second on an n

questions.q: And Il met la clé against Ils mettent la clé?
questions.why: A t arrives. The one you have been writing since nous is the one you now hear, because the -ent behind it makes no sound to cover it.

questions.q: a2.10 gave you a plural you could hear as well. What is going on in all of these?
questions.why: A sound arrives at the end of the verb. a2.10 did it with a whole syllable in the middle and these three do it with one consonant, and both are rarer in French than you would like.
opts: The plural adds a sound the singular did not have
The pronoun is doing the work

questions.q: Which pairs in this lesson can the ear NOT separate?
questions.why: The three singular persons of every verb here are one sound. That is why the word in front is never optional, and it is the fourth lesson in a row to say so.

sections.title: Four Ways It Breaks

errors.why: The regular group keeps its d in every person and this verb does not have one past the singular. a2.11 named these three and would not build them for exactly this reason.
errors.wrong: Building ils prendent from the pattern a2.11 taught.

errors.why: The -ent makes no sound, so the stem has to end in something. You can hear which one you meant: with one n the word would finish on a vowel, and it does not.
errors.wrong: Writing prennent with one n.

errors.why: The other way round, and just as common. The -ons is doing the sounding here, so the stem has nothing to prove and stays short.
errors.wrong: Writing prenons with two.

errors.why: mettre and battre change once and stop. prendre changes twice. Only one verb in this lesson has a third shape, and spreading its habit onto the other two costs you the thing that made them easy.
errors.right: Keeping mett- for all three plural persons.
errors.wrong: Giving mettons and mettent different stems, the way prendre does.

The past of all three, which nothing about the present tells you.

sections.title: The Whole Thing

sections.say: One screen, and then one last thing to build before the exam.
sections.body: You have three verbs, all six persons of each, and one doubled letter in one cell. That was the short half. The long half is what you do with a verb nobody has taught you, and the next screen is going to hand you two of those and ask for the forms. It is the only screen in this lesson that matters, and if you can do it then everything in the three families is yours, including the parts of them nobody has written a card for yet. Each round of the exam is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Two verbs. Neither of them appears anywhere else in this lesson and you are not going to be shown their forms. Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left.
sections.title: One You Have Not Met

check.q: reprendre means to take back, to start again. Which is the nous form?
check.why: Cover the re and you are looking at prendre, whose nous form loses the d and keeps one n. Two of the wrong answers give it a second n and the third leaves the d in.

groups.label: reprendre, and nothing else on this card

check.q: And the ils form of reprendre?
check.why: Two n, because the -ent is silent and the stem has to end in something. It is the same cell that moved on prendre and on both of its compounds.

check.q: admettre means to admit. Which is the ils form?
check.why: Two t and a silent -ent, which is what mettre does and what permettre and promettre do. Nothing about ad- changes any of it.

check.q: You have now built four forms of two verbs. How many of those forms were on a card in this lesson?
check.why: None. A verb you have never seen? Take the front off it, and what is left is one you built ten minutes ago. That is what three verbs are actually worth, and it is why the last five lessons were not a list.

sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get a drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: Six on the shapes themselves. Every question fixes the person for you.
rounds.label: The three of them

questions.q: Nous ___ la clé. (prendre)
questions.why: The d goes and one n is enough, because the -ons is doing the sounding.

questions.q: Il ___ la clé. (mettre)
questions.why: One t in the singular. The second one arrives with nous and not before.

questions.q: Nous ___ Paul. (battre)
questions.why: Two t and the ordinary -ons, which is exactly what mettre does in this cell.

questions.q: Which of these four is spelled correctly?
questions.why: Two n and no d. The first is what the regular pattern gives you and it is the form a2.11 refused to put in front of anybody.

questions.q: How many different stems does prendre use across its six forms?
questions.why: prend- pren- prenn- for prendre. met- mett- for mettre and bat- batt- for battre.

questions.q: Fix this. « Nous mettons la clé. » in the ils form.
questions.why: Same stem, different ending. mettre settles into two t and stays there for the whole plural.

rounds.say: This is the round the lesson is really about. a2.09 taught the reason seven lessons ago.
rounds.label: One n or two

questions.q: Ils ___ la clé. (prendre)
questions.why: a2.09 doubled the l of appeler in the cells where the ending went silent. prennent doubles its n for the same reason: the -ent makes no sound, so the stem has to end in one.

questions.q: Which one has the doubled letter?
questions.why: Only the last one, and only because its ending makes no sound. Every other cell has something audible after the stem.

questions.q: Fix this. « Nous prennons la clé. »
questions.why: One n. The -ons is sounded, so nothing has to be doubled to hold the end of the word up.

questions.q: Ils ___ le français. (apprendre)
questions.why: Two n, because the verb underneath has two n in this cell. The front of the word changes nothing at all.

questions.q: Why does prennent double its n and prenons not?
questions.why: a2.09 doubled the l of appeler in the cells where the ending went silent. prennent doubles its n for the same reason: the -ent makes no sound, so the stem has to end in one.
opts: It is an exception with no reason
One ending is silent and the other is not

questions.q: Nous ___ la question. (comprendre)
questions.why: One n, no d, and four letters at the front that have no say in any of it.

rounds.say: Cover the front of each one before you answer.
rounds.label: Which family

questions.q: Which of these follows mettre?
questions.why: promettre. Cover the pro and mettre is what is left. The second and fourth run on prendre and the third is a regular verb with no front on it at all.

questions.q: And which of these follows prendre?
questions.why: surprendre. The last one ends the same way and is a regular verb, which is the distinction this whole round turns on.

questions.q: Ils ___ le feu. (combattre)
questions.why: Two t and a silent -ent, because battre does that and combattre is battre with three letters on the front.

questions.q: Je ___ la clé. (remettre)
questions.why: One t, because mettre has one t here. The re- means back and it does nothing to the ending.

questions.q: A verb ends in -re. What tells you whether it is regular?
questions.why: Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. vendre has no front on it, so there is nothing to cover and nothing underneath; that is how you tell it apart from the four verbs above it.
opts: The ending is enough on its own
Whether there is a familiar verb left when you cover the front

questions.q: Fix this. « Ils comprendent la question. »
questions.why: No d, two n. This is the regular pattern applied to a verb that is not in the regular group, one front along.

rounds.say: Two verbs you have not been taught. You have everything you need for both of them.
rounds.label: One you have not met

questions.q: reprendre means to take back, to start again. Nous ___ la clé.
questions.why: Cover the re and prendre is what is left, and its nous form drops the d and keeps one n. You have never seen this word written down.

questions.q: And the plural. Ils ___ la clé. (reprendre)
questions.why: Two n, for the same reason ils prennent has two: the -ent makes no sound and something has to hold the end of the word up.

questions.q: admettre means to admit. Nous ___ notre erreur.
questions.why: Two t and the ordinary -ons. mettre is underneath it and mettre has settled into its plural stem by this cell.

questions.q: And Ils ___ leur erreur. (admettre)
questions.why: Two t and a silent -ent. Four forms of two verbs, and not one of them was on a card anywhere in this lesson.

questions.q: How did you build those four?
questions.why: Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. It works on every verb in all three families, including the ones nobody has taught you and the ones nobody has written a card for.
opts: By covering the front and using the verb underneath

questions.q: Fix this. « Nous reprendons la clé. »
questions.why: The d does not survive into the plural on any verb in this family, and a front on the word does not bring it back.

rounds.say: The plural is audible on all three of these, which is rarer in French than you would like.
rounds.label: Saying it

questions.q: Listen. Which one did you hear?
questions.why: The verb ends on an n, so it is the plural. The pronoun would not have told you: il and ils are one sound.

questions.q: And this one?
questions.why: No t at the end, so it is the singular. The plural would have finished on a hard consonant you could not miss.

questions.q: Tap the letters you do NOT say.
questions.why: The d. It is written in all three singular persons and said in none of them, and it disappears from the spelling the moment the plural arrives.

questions.q: And here?
questions.why: The -ent, silent as it has been on every verb since a2.01. What you do hear is the t in front of it.

questions.q: Say it: they take the key.
questions.why: Finish the verb on the n. If it comes out through the nose you have said the singular, and nothing else in the sentence will correct it.

questions.q: Which three words in this lesson are said identically?
questions.why: Two spellings across three persons and one sound for all of them. mets, mets, met does the same thing, and so does bats, bats, bat.

rounds.say: The last round is the gym. Nothing here is a trick.
rounds.label: Out in the world

questions.q: Somebody asks « Tu apprends le français ici ? » What do you say?
questions.why: The verb she used, given back with the person changed. The second uses the wrong verb, the third drops the s, and the fourth is how the scene at the start went wrong.
opts: Oui, je prends le français ici.

questions.q: Vous ___ la clé à la fin ? (remettre)
questions.why: Two t and the ordinary -ez. It is mettez with two letters in front and nothing else moved.

questions.q: Ils ___ la question. (comprendre)
questions.why: Two n. It is the cell that moves on prendre, and every compound of prendre moves in the same place.

questions.q: Which sentence would a French speaker actually say for we are taking the key?
questions.why: Both of the first two are correct and the second is what people say. nous parlons is what you write. on parle is what you say. on takes the il form, so it costs no new spelling at all.

questions.q: Fix this. « Vous mettes la clé ici. »
questions.why: The vous ending is -ez on every verb in this lesson and on every verb since a2.01. Nothing about these three is irregular in that cell.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT taught in this lesson?
questions.why: The past. a2.20 is built around the past forms of these three and it arrives after the two lessons that give you the tense they live in.
opts: The present of prendre in all six persons

sections.say: Four things, and the last of them is where the rest of prendre lives.
sections.body: Three verbs, eighteen cells, and one doubled letter in one of them. Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. You used that on two verbs nobody showed you and it worked, which means it will work on every other verb in these three families, including the ones no lesson in this course has got to yet. a2.11 named these three and would not build them; that is finished now, and the irregular block is finished with it. Two things are deliberately not here. The past of all three belongs to a2.20, and prendre in its fixed expressions belongs to a2.07 and a2.27, which open on them. What you have is the present, in six persons, for the 12 verbs this lesson names and for every other one in the three families.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left.
Three verbs to learn, and 12 you can build.

One n for nous, two for ils. a2.09 doubled the l of appeler in the cells where the ending went silent. prennent doubles its n for the same reason: the -ent makes no sound, so the stem has to end in one.
mettre and battre change once and stop. prendre changes twice.

errorTriggers.description: Runs the regular -re pattern on prendre and produces a plural with a d in it. It is the error a2.11 predicted and refused to print, and it is what a learner reaches for when the naming form is the only thing they have looked at.

Writes ils prenent with one n, or nous prennons with two. The doubling belongs to exactly one cell and it is the cell whose ending makes no sound, which is a2.09 principle arriving on a verb nobody expected it on.

Meets a compound and treats it as a verb they have never seen, stopping the sentence to look for a form they already own. It is the scene at the top of this lesson and it costs a conversation rather than a mark.

Covers the front of a compound, builds the verb underneath correctly, and then forgets to put the front back on: nous prenons where the sentence wanted nous reprenons. The half of the move that gets dropped is the half nobody drills.

Hears the plural and writes the singular, because il and ils are one sound and the only thing separating the two sentences is the end of the verb. It is the one place in this lesson where the ear can settle it, and a learner who is not listening for it will not hear it.
Spreads prendre habit of changing stem twice onto mettre and battre, which change once. It is the cost of teaching the hard one first, and it turns two easy verbs into two more hard ones.

grammarAssumed: The six subject pronouns and the nine they cover, introduced in a1.05
on takes third-person-singular agreement, introduced in a1.05
nous as the written first-person plural against on as the spoken one, introduced in a2.01
The present tense of regular -er verbs and the silent -e, -es and -ent endings, introduced in a2.01
Stem changes that preserve a sound, and the doubled consonant that writes an open vowel before a silent ending, introduced in a2.09
The present tense of regular -ir and -re verbs, introduced in a2.10 and a2.11
That a2.11 explicitly excluded prendre, mettre and battre from the regular -re class and deferred them here
That three singular persons of an irregular verb are commonly one sound, introduced in a2.13
Audible plural marking on a verb stem, introduced in a2.10
The definite and demonstrative determiners inside the objects of these sentences, introduced in a1.04
grammarIntroduced: The present tense of prendre, with three stems: prend- in the singular, pren- for the first and second person plural, and prenn- in the third person plural
The present tense of mettre and battre, with two stems each: a single-consonant singular and a geminate plural
That the geminate in prennent is orthographic support for the stem-final consonant where the inflectional ending is silent, which is the mechanism a2.09 introduced for appeler and jeter

Prefixed derivatives as inheriting the base verb inflection without exception: apprendre, comprendre, surprendre on prendre; permettre, promettre, remettre on mettre; combattre, débattre, abattre on battre
That the derivation is productive, so an unseen prefixed verb is inflectable from its base without further instruction
The formal contrast between prendre and the regular -re class taught in a2.11, which shares an infinitive ending and no stem behaviour

acts.title: What you like

recorded.desc: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT NOTE IN THIS LESSON. « J'aime le café. » AND « Je bois du café. » ARE ONE TAKE, one voice, one pace, read straight through with no gap and no reset. Then, in the SAME take, « Je n'aime pas le café. » and « Je ne mange pas de pain. » The claim the whole lesson rests on is that these are one decision made two ways, and two separate recordings are two performances: a reader who records the liking column in its own session will lean on the le, and the learner will hear that lean as a difference in emphasis rather than as a difference in meaning. NEITHER LITTLE WORD IS STRESSED. Both le and du are unstressed and run straight into the noun. A reader who separates them is teaching the learner to stop on the word this lesson needs them to say without thinking.
clipIds: Je ne mange pas de pain.

recorded.desc: THE SIX ELIDED WORDS IN ONE TAKE, ADJACENT, ONE VOICE: l'eau, l'huile, l'orange, l'oignon, l'ail, l'œuf. The teaching point is that the elided article sounds IDENTICAL regardless of which kind the word is, and that only holds if one voice says all six in one pass. Recorded apart, the learner compares six performances and may hear a difference that is not in the language.

EVERY NASAL CLOSED, NO N SOUND BEHIND IT. le pain is /pɛ̃/ and the app respells it luh PAⁿ deliberately; a reader who lets an n out of it is teaching the error the transcription repairs. The same applies to le croissant, le jambon (TWO nasals), le poisson, le citron, le raisin, le melon, l'oignon, le champignon (TWO), le vin, la confiture, la viande, l'orange and un sandwich. AND THE OPPOSITE, WHICH MATTERS AS MUCH: la crème, la banane, la farine and la pomme have REAL m and n sounds and must NOT be nasalised. Their transcriptions carry no superscript on purpose.

The sixty food cards, read one per clip, at an even pace with no list intonation. A reader who performs these as a shopping list will drop the pitch on every word after the first, and each card is heard on its own rather than in sequence. le bœuf is ONE syllable in the noun, /bœf/, and must not be stretched into two.

lessons.intro: Sixty words you will use every day, each one stored with the little word it arrives with. Then the choice nobody teaches: what you like is all of it, and what you are eating is some of it, and the verb in front decides which one you need.

aPartOfIt.body: Eating and drinking are different. You are not consuming bread as an idea, you are having some, so the word in front changes to the one you already know: je mange du pain, je bois de l'eau, je prends de la soupe. This is not a new rule and there is nothing to learn here that you have not already been taught. The only new thing is that it is a CHOICE, and that the verb in front is what makes it. Same noun, different verb, different little word.
aPartOfIt.title: What you are eating is some of it

examples.note: The same coffee, now a quantity of it.
And in a negative it collapses to de, which aimer never does.

noSingular.body: A few foods are plural in French and have no everyday singular. You would not order une pâte or une frite any more than you would ask for a spaghetti in English. They take les, they take des when you are having some, and the words behind them agree. There are only a handful and you have met most of them already, so this is a thing to recognise rather than a thing to study.
noSingular.term: words that only come in plural
noSingular.title: les pâtes, les frites, les céréales

examples.note: les pâtes, plural in French and singular in English.
les frites, the same shape.

wholeThing.body: When you say you like something, you are not talking about the piece in front of you. You are talking about bread, everywhere, as an idea. French marks that with the ordinary little word: j'aime le pain, j'adore le fromage, je déteste le poisson. This catches almost everybody, because the lesson just before this one spent its whole length teaching you that uncounted food takes du, and that rule is right and does not reach this far. After aimer, adorer, détester and préférer, it is le, la or les, every time, with no exceptions to remember.
wholeThing.title: What you like is all of it, always

examples.note: Coffee as a whole idea, not a cup of it.
And it survives a negative: still le, not de.

articleIsPartOfIt.body: Food words in French are almost never said bare. It is le pain, la pomme, l'eau, and the little word in front is not decoration. You met this habit with noun gender and again with countries, and it arrives here on the words you will use most often. Nothing about a tomato tells you it is the la kind and nothing about bread tells you it is the le kind. The corpus stores every one of these sixty words with its article for exactly this reason, and the card you are shown is the whole word.
articleIsPartOfIt.term: the article is part of the word
articleIsPartOfIt.title: Store le pain, never pain

examples.note: le pain, stored the way it is used.
la pomme, and the article is the only difference between them.

theApostropheHides.body: In front of a vowel the little word shrinks to l', and once it has shrunk you cannot see which kind the word is. L'eau is the la kind. L'oignon is the le kind. L'huile is the la kind and l'ail is the le kind, and nothing on the card or in the sound tells you which is which. These are the words you will still be getting wrong in a month, so they are worth learning as a small list rather than meeting one at a time. When you learn one, learn what it turns into when something follows it.
theApostropheHides.term: l' hides which kind it is
theApostropheHides.title: l'eau and l'oignon look identical and are not

examples.note: l'eau is the la kind, and you cannot hear it.
l'oignon is the le kind, and you cannot hear that either.

lessons.title: La nourriture

drills.coach: None of these can be worked out. Two things from the same fridge take different articles, and two red things from the same shelf do too. The article is a fact about the word rather than about the food.
drills.title: Which little word came with it?

drills.q: You meet a new food word. What goes into your head with it?
drills.why: Its article, because every choice this lesson asks you to make needs it and none of them can be made without it.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Six words, three of each, and the card looks identical for all six. This is a short list and it is worth learning as a list, because you will not be able to reason your way to any of them.
drills.title: The article is hiding

drills.q: l'huile and l'ail. Which is the la kind?
drills.why: l'huile is the la kind and l'ail is the le kind. Nothing in the spelling or the sound separates them, which is why the six are learned together.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Sort by the verb rather than by the food. Aimer, adorer, détester and préférer point at the whole category. Manger, boire and prendre point at an amount. Nothing about the food itself decides.
drills.title: Liking is about all of it
buckets: takes du, de la or des

drills.q: You want to say you love cheese.
drills.why: J'adore le fromage. Cheese as a whole category. Du answers how much, and loving something has no how much in it.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: The same test in the other direction. If you could put a quantity on it, you are in the amount column. If you are naming the thing as an idea, you are not.
drills.title: Eating is about some of it

drills.q: You are eating some chicken right now.
drills.why: Je mange du poulet. The first is grammatical and means the chicken, a specific one you have both already talked about.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Only the amount column collapses. The category column never had an amount word in it, so a negative has nothing to act on and the le, la or les stays exactly where it was.
drills.title: Which one moves?

drills.q: You do not like coffee.
drills.why: Je n'aime pas le café. There is no amount word in the sentence, so the negative has nothing to collapse and the le is untouched.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Three of these live in the plural and have no everyday singular, the way a spaghetti is not a thing in English. The rest behave normally.
drills.title: No singular anybody uses

drills.q: You want some chips.
drills.why: Je voudrais des frites. Plural, and an amount of them, so des. One chip is not what anybody is asking for.
drills.title: One more time

sheets.title: Both columns, and all sixty words
contains: The six that hide their article

sections.title: The verb chooses, not the food

sections.body: The choice is made by the verb and never by the food. Aimer, adorer, détester and préférer all point at a thing as a category, so they take the ordinary little word: j'aime le pain, je déteste le poisson, je préfère les légumes. Manger, boire and prendre point at an amount of something, so they take the words the partitive lesson gave you: je mange du pain, je bois de l'eau, je prends de la soupe. The same food appears in both columns with a different word in front of it, and nothing about the food has changed. The negative is where this gets tested, because only one of the two columns moves. After a negative, du, de la and des all collapse to a bare de: je ne mange pas de pain. The other column has no amount word in it at all, so there is nothing for the negative to act on and it stays exactly as it was: je n'aime pas le pain, with the le untouched. Getting that asymmetry the wrong way round is the commonest mistake once the two columns themselves are secure.
sections.title: What each column is doing, and the negative

sections.body: In front of a vowel the little word shrinks to l', and once it has shrunk the card cannot tell you which kind the word is and neither can the sound. There are six of them in this lesson and they split three and three. The la kind: l'eau, l'huile, l'orange. The le kind: l'oignon, l'ail, l'œuf. There is no pattern connecting the members of either group and there is nothing to work out, so these six are worth learning as a short list rather than one at a time as they turn up. The moment it matters is the moment something has to follow: de l'eau against du poisson, or an adjective that has to agree behind them.
sections.title: The six that hide which kind they are

say.text: Every word correct, one word wrong, and the evening switches language. Watch which word.

beats.text: Salomé has been invited to dinner at a colleague's flat. She has been learning French for four months and she has been looking forward to this all week.
Her host is cooking and wants to get it right, so he asks the ordinary question a host asks.

beats.en: What do you like?
beats.speaker: Malik

beats.text: She knows this one. She finished the partitive lesson two days ago and she knows exactly which word goes in front of food you have not counted.

beats.en: I like some chicken.
beats.stage: Every word is a real word.

beats.prompt: One word is wrong. Which sentence should it have been?

options.en: I like some chicken.
I like chicken.

followUp.works: Chicken as a whole idea rather than a portion of it. After aimer it is always le, la or les, and that is the whole lesson.
followUp.breaks: That is the sentence the evening turned on. Du is right for what you are eating and wrong for what you like, and the rule behind it was taught to you two lessons ago.

beats.body: Nothing was misheard and nothing was corrected. He heard somebody still assembling sentences, switched to English to make it easier for her, and the evening she had been looking forward to happened in English.
beats.coach: She had a rule, the rule was correct, and it does not reach this far. That is the only thing between these two lines.
beats.heading: He understood her perfectly

beats.text: Sixty food words is the easy half of this lesson. Choosing between those two little words is the half that decides which language the evening happens in.

goals.s: Each one stored with its article, because the article is the half you cannot work out later.
J'aime le pain. The whole category, and the ordinary little word in front of it.
Je mange du pain. Some of it, using the word the last lesson gave you.
One of the two changes when you say no and the other does not, which is where this gets tested.

sections.say: Four cards before the shelves, because this habit is what the shelves are for.
sections.hint: Four cards before any food list.

cards.body: The noun gender lesson asked you to store the article rather than the noun. The countries lesson asked again. Food is where you will use it most often, because these are the words that come up every single day.
cards.head: You have been asked for this twice already
cards.label: what you already do

cards.body: Milk is the le kind and cream is the la kind. Same shelf, both white, both poured into coffee, and nothing about either predicts its article. This is not a rule with exceptions. There is no rule underneath it.
cards.head: Two things from the same fridge
cards.label: nothing in the word tells you

cards.body: Familiar objects are exactly where people stop storing the article, because the word feels like something they already own in English. La tomate and le citron. Knowing what the thing is has never once helped.
cards.head: You know what a tomato is
cards.label: the guess feels safe here

cards.fr: J'aime le café. · Je bois du café.

sections.say: Four lines off a note, and both columns are in it.
sections.text: Somebody has left a note on the fridge for the person cooking tonight, and between four short lines it uses both halves of this lesson. « J'aime le café. » That is the first line, and it is about coffee in general rather than any particular cup. Underneath, a note about what is actually in the kitchen right now. « Nous mangeons du pain avec du beurre. » Two foods, two small words, and both of them are amounts rather than categories. The third line is the one worth reading twice, because it is a negative and only one of its two halves behaves the way you would expect. « Je ne mange pas de pain. » And the last line answers a question the cook had asked earlier about what to buy. « Est-ce que tu préfères le thé ou le café ? »
sections.title: A Note On The Fridge

glossary.note: Coffee as a whole category, so the ordinary little word. This is the half the scene got wrong.
An amount of bread rather than bread as an idea, which is the partitive lesson unchanged.
The amount word collapses to de after a negative. Aimer never had one, so it has nothing to collapse.
Both categories, both with the ordinary word, inside a question.

questions.a: The verb in front. Liking something points at the whole category and takes le, la or les. Eating or drinking something points at an amount and takes du, de la or des. Nothing about the coffee or the bread came into it.
questions.q: The first line says le and the second says du. What decided between them?

questions.a: Because the amount word collapses to de after a negative, so du pain becomes de pain. That is the partitive rule and it is correct. What it does not do is reach the other column: a negative sentence about liking something keeps its le untouched.
questions.q: The third line is a negative. Why is it worth reading twice?

questions.a: No. It is still about tea and coffee as categories, so it still takes the ordinary little word. The choice is made by the verb, not by whether the sentence is a question, a statement or a negative.
questions.q: The last line is a question rather than a statement. Does that change anything?

errors.why: The commonest error in this lesson by a distance, and it comes from applying the partitive rule correctly in a place it does not reach. Liking has no amount in it.
errors.wrong: J'aime du pain.

errors.why: This is a real sentence and it means something else: the bread, a specific one you have both already talked about. If you mean some bread, it is du.
errors.wrong: Je mange le pain.

errors.why: The collapse to de belongs to the amount words. Aimer never had one, so there is nothing there to collapse and the le stays exactly where it was.
errors.wrong: Je n'aime pas de café.

errors.why: Pâtes lives in the plural in French and has no everyday singular, the way a spaghetti is not a thing in English. Frites and céréales behave the same way.
errors.wrong: Je voudrais une pâte.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched an evening move quietly into English over one small word, and nothing that was said in it was hard. Since then you have stored a set of everyday foods the way they are actually used, met the six whose article vanishes into an apostrophe, and learned to choose between two columns you already owned separately. What is left tells you whether the choice is automatic yet. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and missing too many in a round gets you that round's drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the penalty.
sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: The fact everything else needs.
rounds.label: The article

questions.q: Which of these is the way to store a food word?
questions.why: le pain. The article is part of the word and it is the half you cannot recover later. Aimer takes the whole thing. Manger takes a part of it.

questions.q: Write the word for cheese, with its article.
questions.why: le fromage. Written whole rather than as a bare article, because a two-letter answer typed on its own is a coin toss rather than a test.

questions.q: le lait and la crème sit on the same shelf. What decides which article each takes?
questions.why: Nothing you can see or hear. There is no rule underneath this and no pattern to find. The two words are stored with their articles or they are guessed at.
opts: Nothing you can see or hear

questions.q: Write the word for grapes, with its article.
questions.why: le raisin. Grapes are singular in French for the fruit as a whole, and it is the le kind while la banane and la cerise beside it on the same shelf are not.

rounds.say: Six words, and the card tells you nothing.
rounds.label: The ones that hide it

questions.q: l'eau. Which kind is it?
questions.why: The la kind. You cannot see it and you cannot hear it, which is exactly why these six are worth learning as a short list rather than one at a time.

questions.q: l'oignon. Which kind is it?
questions.why: The le kind, and it looks identical to l'eau on the card. Three of the six are the le kind and three are the la kind.

questions.q: Listen. Which kind is this one?
questions.why: l'huile is the la kind. The sound gives you nothing at all here, which is the point of the whole group.

questions.q: Why do these six words need learning differently from the other fifty-four?
questions.why: The article has shrunk to an apostrophe, so the one fact you need is not on the card and is not in the sound either. Every other food word shows you its article every time you look at it.
opts: Their article is not visible on the card

rounds.say: The half the lesson before this one set you up to get wrong.
rounds.label: What you like

questions.q: You are telling somebody that you like bread, in general.
questions.why: J'aime le pain. Bread as a whole category, so the ordinary little word. The first option is the sentence the opening scene turned on.

questions.q: Correct this sentence: J'adore du chocolat.
questions.why: Adorer behaves exactly like aimer: it points at the whole category, so le. Du answers how much, and loving something has no how much in it.

questions.q: Which of these four verbs does NOT take le, la or les with a food?
questions.why: boire. It points at an amount you are drinking, so it takes du, de la or des. The other three all point at the whole category.

questions.q: Write: I like fish.
questions.why: J'aime le poisson. Fish as a category. Note that the spelling check ignores the apostrophe, so what is being tested here is the le.

questions.q: The last lesson taught you that uncounted food takes du. Why does that not apply after aimer?
questions.why: Because there is no amount involved. Du answers the question how much, and liking something is not a quantity of it. The partitive rule is correct and this is simply not a place it reaches.
opts: Because liking has no amount in it
Because aimer is an irregular verb
Because du is only for drinks

rounds.say: The column you already owned, now that it is a choice.
rounds.label: What you are having

questions.q: You are at a table and you are eating some bread.
questions.why: Je mange du pain. An amount of bread. The first option is a real sentence meaning the bread, a specific one you have both already mentioned.

questions.q: Write: I am drinking some water.
questions.why: Je bois de l'eau. Eau is the la kind and starts with a vowel, so de la shortens to de l'. That shortening is the partitive lesson's and has not changed.

questions.q: Correct this sentence: Je mange le fromage tous les jours.
questions.why: Du, because you are eating an amount of cheese rather than one specific cheese you have both been discussing. With le it is grammatical and means something else.
accept: Je mange du fromage tous les jours.
je mange du fromage tous les jours
questions.answer: Je mange du fromage tous les jours.

questions.q: Which sentence means you are having some chicken right now?
questions.why: Je mange du poulet. The first is about liking chicken in general, the second is about one specific chicken you have both already mentioned, and the third is not a sentence.

questions.q: Say it out loud: you are drinking some coffee.
questions.why: Je bois du café. Du is unstressed and runs straight into the noun. It is never a word you stop on.

rounds.say: Both columns in one round, including the negative.
rounds.label: Choosing between them

questions.q: Same food, two sentences. Which pair is right?
questions.why: Liking points at the whole category and drinking points at an amount, so le on the left and du on the right. Nothing about the coffee changed between the two.
opts: J'aime du café. / Je bois le café.
J'aime le café. / Je bois du café.
J'aime le café. / Je bois le café.
J'aime du café. / Je bois du café.

questions.q: You do not like cheese. Write it.
questions.why: The le survives the negative untouched. There is no amount word in the sentence, so there is nothing to collapse to de.

questions.q: Correct this sentence: Je ne mange pas du poisson.
questions.why: Du collapses to de after a negative, which the partitive lesson taught. This is the column where that happens.
accept: Je ne mange pas de poisson.
je ne mange pas de poisson
questions.answer: Je ne mange pas de poisson.

questions.q: Write: I do not eat cheese.
questions.why: Je ne mange pas de fromage. Du collapses to de after the negative. Compare the sentence two questions ago, where the liking column kept its le untouched.
accept: Je ne mange pas de fromage.
je ne mange pas de fromage
questions.answer: Je ne mange pas de fromage.

questions.q: Listen, and say which column this sentence is in.
questions.why: It is a liking sentence, and you can tell from the le surviving the negative. An eating sentence would have collapsed to de.

rounds.say: The word list, and the three that behave differently.
rounds.label: The sixty

questions.q: Which of these would a French speaker never say?
questions.why: Une pâte. Pâtes lives in the plural with no everyday singular, the way a spaghetti is not a thing in English. Frites and céréales are the same.

questions.q: Correct this: Je voudrais une frite.
questions.why: Frites is plural, and you are asking for an amount of them, so des. One chip is not what anybody is ordering.

questions.q: Write the word for water, with its article.
questions.why: l'eau. The article shrank to l', which is why this word has to be learned along with the fact that it is the la kind.

questions.q: Say it out loud: you like bread.
questions.why: The pattern is J'aime le, and the little word runs straight into the noun without a stop. Say the whole thing as one run rather than three words.

sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can name sixty everyday foods with the article each one is stored with, say what you like and what you are having and keep the two apart, handle the six words whose article has vanished into an apostrophe, and get the negative right in both columns when only one of them changes. The thing worth keeping underneath all of it is that the choice is made by the verb rather than by the food. Nothing about bread decides whether it is le pain or du pain, and once that is automatic you stop translating the sentence and start saying it.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Aimer takes the whole thing. Manger takes a part of it. The verb decides, and the food never does.
aimer, adorer, détester and préférer take le, la or les. manger, boire and prendre take du, de la or des.
In a negative the amount word collapses to de, and the other column does not move at all.
Six food words hide their article in an apostrophe, and pâtes, frites and céréales have no singular.

errorTriggers.description: Stored the food without its article, so the fact every later choice needs is simply not available. The error that happens weeks before any of the others, and the one familiar objects invite most.
Cannot recover the gender of l'eau, l'huile, l'oignon, l'ail, l'œuf or l'orange, because the article vanished into an apostrophe and the sound carries nothing either.

Says « j'aime du pain », applying a1.29's partitive rule to a verb it does not reach. THE CENTRAL ERROR OF THIS LESSON, and it is created by the lesson immediately upstream rather than by carelessness.
Over-corrects after learning the rule above and says « je mange le pain » when meaning some bread. Grammatical, and a different sentence: it names a specific loaf both speakers already know about.
Collapses the wrong column in a negative: « je n'aime pas de café » (there was no amount word to collapse) or « je ne mange pas du pain » (there was one and it did not collapse).
Invents a singular for pâtes, frites or céréales, or treats the les on them as a definite article and reaches for a singular partitive.

grammarAssumed: Noun gender, and that the article in front of a noun is the choice that gender makes, introduced in a1.03
le, la, l' and les, and the elision of le and la in front of a vowel, introduced in a1.04
un, une and des, and the difference between first mention and second, introduced in a1.11
du, de la and des for an uncounted amount, and their collapse to de after a negative, introduced in a1.29
ne ... pas around the verb, introduced in a1.18
The full present of avoir, which j'ai faim and j'ai soif are built on, introduced in a1.07
est-ce que as the safe question frame, introduced in a1.19
grammarIntroduced: That aimer, adorer, détester and préférer take the definite article with a food, because they name a category rather than a quantity
That manger, boire and prendre take the partitive with a food, which is a1.29's rule applied rather than a new one
That the negative collapse to de reaches the partitive column and not the definite one
Sixty food nouns as a set, each stored with its article
That an elided l' conceals gender, and which six food nouns it conceals it on
Plural-only food nouns, and that they have no singular in ordinary use
