sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched a sale nearly fall through over one silent letter, learned twelve colours attached to things you can already name, and met the idea that a describing word changes shape to match what it describes, which nothing before this lesson has asked of you. You have seen one colour take four shapes and another take none, found out that most of those shapes sound identical and that no amount of listening will separate them, and worked out why two of the twelve refuse to move at all. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.
sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: The names, quickly.
rounds.label: The twelve names

questions.q: Listen. Which colour is it?
questions.why: jaune. It is the one colour in this lesson whose n is a real consonant you pronounce rather than a nasal ending, so it sounds closer to the English word zone than to anything nasal.

questions.q: Which of these is the word for white?
questions.why: blanc. Its final c is silent and the vowel is nasal, so it sounds like blahn with no n you actually say. Bleu is blue and beige is beige, and both start the same way, which is what makes this cluster worth a second look.

questions.q: Write the French word for red.
questions.why: rouge. It is one of the four colours that already end in an e, so the feminine asks nothing of it and only a plural s is ever added to it.

questions.q: Which colour is named after something you can eat?
questions.why: orange, and marron is the other one. Both were things before they were colours, which is exactly why neither of them ever takes an ending.

rounds.say: The thing decides the shape.
rounds.label: Making it match

questions.q: Une jupe is feminine. You want to say the skirt is green. What do you write?
questions.why: Une jupe verte. The colour takes an e because the skirt is the une kind, and it sits after the thing rather than in front of it the way English would put it.

questions.q: Fix this. « Les voitures sont noir. »
questions.why: Several feminine things, so the colour takes an e and an s. Neither of them is audible, which is why this sentence sounds completely correct as it stands and is still wrong on the page.

questions.q: Mes vestes are feminine and plural, and the colour is bleu. Write the colour.
questions.why: bleues. The e is for the jackets being the une kind and the s is for there being more than one, in that order. All four shapes of bleu sound identical, so this had to be worked out rather than heard.

questions.q: What decides which ending a colour takes?
questions.why: The thing being described. Nothing about the colour has any say in it, which is why the same colour appears in four different shapes across four sentences that are otherwise identical.
opts: Where the colour sits in the sentence
Whether you can hear the ending

rounds.say: Four of the twelve do something extra.
rounds.label: The feminines that change more

questions.q: La porte is feminine and the colour is blanc. Write the colour.
questions.why: blanche. It is the only colour here whose feminine changes the consonant rather than adding to it, and unlike most feminines you can hear this one clearly. blance is not a word.

questions.q: Write the feminine of violet.
questions.why: violette, with two t letters. The silent t of violet wakes up and the spelling doubles it, so violete would be both misspelled and mispronounced.

questions.q: Fix this. « Sa chemise est gris. »
questions.why: grise. A shirt is the une kind, so the colour takes an e, and here the e wakes the sleeping s into a z sound. This is one of the few agreement errors you can actually hear.

questions.q: Which of these feminines does NOT change the sound of the word?
questions.why: noire. It sounds exactly like noir. The other three all wake a letter that was silent: verte says its t, grise says its s as a z, and blanche turns its c into a ch.

rounds.say: Half of this lesson is invisible to your ear.
rounds.label: What you cannot hear

questions.q: Listen to these two: « bleu » then « bleue ». What is the difference?
questions.why: They are identical. Bleu ends in a vowel sound already, so the feminine e adds nothing your ear can pick up. If you thought you heard a difference, that is the spelling you were expecting rather than the sound.
opts: The second one ends in a soft sound
There is no difference, they sound identical

questions.q: How many of the four shapes of vert can you tell apart by ear?
questions.why: Two. Vert and verts are one sound, verte and vertes are another, and the plural s is never pronounced on any of them. So your ear separates the masculine from the feminine and can do nothing at all about the number.

questions.q: Mes sacs are masculine and plural, and the colour is vert. Write the colour.
questions.why: verts. It sounds exactly like vert, because the plural s on a colour is never pronounced, so the only reason to write it is that there is more than one bag.

questions.q: You are listening carefully and still cannot hear whether somebody said bleue or bleues. What does that mean?
questions.why: The information is genuinely not there. A native speaker cannot hear it either, and works the ending out from the thing being described exactly as you have to. Slowing the audio down will never help with this one.
opts: The information is not in the sound at all
The speaker was not articulating clearly
You need to slow the recording down further

rounds.say: The half of the lesson people remember wrongly.
rounds.label: The two that never change

questions.q: You are writing an ad for brown shoes. What goes in it?
questions.why: marron, with nothing added. Colours agree. Things that became colours do not. It is a chestnut being used as a colour, and the s on the first option is the single most noticeable written error in this lesson.

questions.q: Fix this. « Les rideaux sont oranges. »
questions.why: orange, unchanged. The fruit takes an s when you are counting fruit, but the colour is the fruit being borrowed and there is nothing to count, so it stays exactly as it is.

questions.q: Why does « des oranges » take an s while « des fleurs orange » does not?
questions.why: The first counts fruit, so it behaves like any other thing you can count. The second uses the fruit as a colour, and the flowers are what is plural rather than the oranges, so there is nothing for the s to attach to.
opts: The first is a thing being counted, the second is a colour
The first is feminine and the second is masculine
The second is an exception with no reason behind it
The second is plural and the first is singular

questions.q: La table is feminine and the colour is marron. Write the colour.
questions.why: marron, unchanged. A feminine thing in front of it makes no difference at all, and marronne is not a word. This is the same answer you would give for a masculine thing, a plural, or anything else.

rounds.say: The last round, and you already know the answer to all of it.
rounds.label: Colours made of two words

questions.q: Fix this. « Les murs sont verts pommes. »
questions.why: Neither half takes an ending. Once a colour is built from two words it has become a description of a thing rather than a plain colour, so the same rule that stops marron moving stops this one too.

questions.q: Say this out loud: the shoes are brown.
questions.why: Nothing in the sound tells anybody whether you wrote the s or not, which is exactly why this is the error that survives. Saying it correctly and writing it correctly are two separate skills here.

questions.q: Write the French for dark green eyes. The word for eyes is yeux.
questions.why: Neither half changes. Adding the endings looks like being careful, and it is the same instinct that puts an s on marron: a rule applied in the one place it does not reach.

questions.q: What do marron, orange and vert pomme have in common?
questions.why: Colours agree. Things that became colours do not. A nut, a fruit and a description of an apple. None of the three is a plain colour word, so the endings never reach them. One idea, not three things to memorise.
opts: They are all shades of brown
They are all borrowed from other languages
They are all irregular and must be memorised separately
None of them is a plain colour word, so none of them changes

sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can name twelve colours, make them match the thing they describe, tell which endings you will ever hear, and leave the two that were something else alone. The second of those is the first time in this course that a describing word has changed shape, and it is not the last: the same mechanism is waiting for you on every adjective you meet from here. Basic adjectives are next, and everything in this lesson transfers to them unchanged.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Colours agree. Things that became colours do not. A nut and a fruit keep the shape they had.
The thing being described decides the ending, never the colour itself.
The plural s is never pronounced, and on bleu and noir the feminine e is not either.
The colour comes after the thing, and colours made of two words never move at all.

errorTriggers.description: Reaches for the wrong colour name, most often inside the blanc / bleu / beige cluster or between violet and rose.
Leaves the colour in its plain form on a feminine or plural thing. The default error, and the one every learner starts with because English never asks for this.
Regularises a feminine that changes more than its ending: writes blance for blanche, or violete for violette.
Believes the silent endings should be audible and concludes their listening is at fault. Costs confidence rather than accuracy, which is why it gets its own drill.
Puts an ending on marron or orange. The highest-value error in the lesson: inaudible, so nobody corrects it, and it is the first thing a French reader sees.
Agrees one or both halves of a two-word colour: writes des yeux verts foncés. The same instinct as the s on marron, arriving one step later.

grammarAssumed: Noun gender, and that un and une follow it, introduced in a1.03
le, la, l' and les, introduced in a1.04
The plural of a noun, introduced in a1.03
The full present of être, introduced in a1.06
The full present of avoir, introduced in a1.07
mon, ma and mes, introduced in a1.05
That a final consonant is usually silent, and that a following e wakes it, introduced in sons.06
The nasal vowels and the fact that a following vowel blocks them, introduced in sons.03
grammarIntroduced: Adjective agreement, introduced here for the first time in the course, through colour
The feminine -e on an adjective, and the four colours where it is audible
The plural -s on an adjective, which is never pronounced
The combined feminine plural -es
Irregular feminine formation: blanc to blanche, violet to violette
Invariable colour adjectives derived from nouns: marron and orange
Invariable compound colour adjectives: vert pomme, vert foncé, bleu clair
The postposition of colour adjectives, stated as a fact and not as a system

recorded.desc: The frame, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE: "Mon dos fait mal." immediately followed by "J'ai mal au dos." The learner must hear these AS A CONTRAST. Recorded apart they become two performances and the learner compares delivery instead of grammar, which loses the whole scene.

The four shapes, ONE TAKE, in this order and adjacent: "à la tête", "au dos", "aux dents", "à l'oreille". This is the only genuinely audible distinction in the lesson and the whole listening mission rests on the four being separable by ear in a single voice.

The fourteen parts, each with its article, read at an even pace. NEVER record a part without its article: the article is what the rest of the lesson runs on and a bare noun teaches the wrong storage. "les yeux" is [lay ZYUH], WITH the liaison, which is the decision this lesson took against fr.a1.mots-essentiels.002 and must not be silently normalised back.
The describing frame: "J'ai les yeux bleus." and "Elle a les cheveux longs." Adjacent in one take so the shared shape is audible across two different people.

ADJACENT IN THE SAME TAKE, and this constraint cannot be recovered later: "les yeux bleus" then "les yeux marron". The teaching is that the second adds nothing where the first added an s, and the learner needs both side by side to trust that the sound is identical.

lessons.intro: You already know the words for the body. What stops the sentence working is the shape around them, and it is one shape that covers both saying what hurts and describing how someone looks.

notYours.body: You learned mon, ma and mes recently and they are right almost everywhere. This is the place they stop. A body part inside these sentences takes le, la or les, because the person is already carried by the verb and saying it twice is what marks the sentence as foreign.
notYours.title: Where the possessive stops

examples.note: Not « ma tête fait mal ». The person is in j'ai.
Not « mes yeux sont bleus ». The person is in j'ai.

theFrame.body: French puts the person in the verb and leaves the body part with its ordinary little word. You say the equivalent of "I have pain at the head" rather than "my head hurts". Nothing about it is optional: this is simply how the sentence is built.
theFrame.title: How French says something hurts

examples.note: The person is in j'ai. The head keeps la.
Same shape, different person, and le dos becomes au dos.

leftAlone.body: You met this in the colours lesson: a colour that started life as something else keeps its own shape. Marron is a chestnut. Châtain clair is two words. Neither ever takes an ending, and the eyes and the hair are where you will meet both.
leftAlone.title: The colours that refuse the s

examples.note: marron, with nothing added, after a plural les yeux.
Two words, and neither half changes.

bothPlural.body: Hair is one thing in English and many in French, and so is the pair of eyes. Both take les, and any colour or shape word after them takes an s to match. You cannot hear that s, which is exactly what a1.13 warned you about.
bothPlural.title: Two words that are always plural

examples.note: bleus, with an s you never pronounce.
longs, same silent s.

describing.body: The same move again. Where English says his eyes are blue, French says he has the blue eyes. The person is in the verb, and the eyes and the hair keep les.
describing.title: Describing someone, the French way

examples.note: J'ai, then les yeux. Never « mes yeux sont ».
Elle a, then les cheveux.

theFourShapes.body: You already have these from the prepositions lesson. À plus le becomes au and à plus les becomes aux, while à la and à l' are left alone. The body part decides which one you get, and you never choose it freely.
theFourShapes.term: à la, au, aux, à l'
theFourShapes.title: The four shapes of the little word

examples.note: le dos, so au dos.
les dents, so aux dents.
l'oreille, so à l'oreille, with no change at all.

drills.q: Which one is the la kind?
drills.why: la main. There is nothing about a hand that explains it, which is why it is stored rather than worked out.

drills.coach: À plus le is au and à plus les is aux. À la and à l' are left alone.

drills.q: Complete: J'ai mal ___ pied.

drills.coach: The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les. Read each one and find the sentence that put the person in the wrong place.

drills.q: Which one is what people actually say?
drills.why: J'ai mal à la tête. The person is in j'ai and the head keeps la.

drills.coach: Every sentence in this lesson is an avoir sentence. Être is what English makes you expect.

drills.q: She has blue eyes. Which verb do you need?
drills.why: avoir. Elle a les yeux bleus, not elle est.
drills.title: One check

drills.coach: Les yeux and les cheveux are plural, so whatever follows takes an s you will never hear.

drills.q: Which is right?
drills.why: les cheveux longs. Both words are plural and neither plural is audible.
drills.title: One check

drills.coach: A nut and a two word description. Neither is a plain colour word, so nothing attaches to either.

drills.q: Brown eyes. Which one?
drills.why: les yeux marron, with nothing added, whatever the noun in front of it is doing.

sections.body: The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les. avoir + mal + à + the body part, and the body part keeps whichever little word it always had. Change the person and only the verb moves: j'ai mal, tu as mal, il a mal, elle a mal, nous avons mal.

cards.body: English puts the person on the noun, in my, and the hurting in the verb. French puts the person in the verb, in j'ai, and leaves the head with its ordinary la. Same meaning, opposite build.
cards.head: Where does the person go?

cards.body: The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les. Change the person and only the verb moves.
cards.head: avoir + mal + à + the body part

cards.body: Mal sits bare in this frame. Le mal exists and means something else entirely, so adding a little word in front of it changes the sentence into philosophy.

detail.body: À la stays exactly as it is. This is the easy one and it is half the body.

detail.body: The one people expect to contract and it does not. À l' behaves like à la, not like au.

questions.q: In the first line, which shape did you hear?

questions.q: Which of the three lines had two syllables between mal and the body part?
questions.why: The second. À la is two, au and aux are one each, so the la kind is audibly longer.

cards.body: English hangs the person on the noun and puts the colour in the verb. French puts the person in j'ai and leaves the eyes with les. You have seen this exact swap already.
cards.head: Where does the person go?
cards.label: The same idea, built two ways

cards.body: The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les. Nothing here is new except the words on the end.
cards.head: avoir + les + the feature + the word for it
cards.label: Any person, any feature

cards.body: Hair is one thing in English and many in French, so the word after it takes a plural ending you will never hear.
cards.head: les cheveux, always
cards.label: And hair is plural

sections.title: The Same Move Again

sections.say: You did the colours already. Both of these words are plural, so every colour takes the s.

detail.body: Bleu becomes bleus because les yeux is plural. It sounds exactly the same, which is why this is a writing decision rather than a listening one.
detail.title: The s you cannot hear

detail.body: Vert becomes verts. The t was already silent and the s changes nothing about the sound.
detail.title: Same again

detail.body: Blond becomes blonds for the same reason. Les cheveux is plural whether you think of hair as one thing or not.
detail.title: And on the hair

sections.title: Colours On The Eyes And The Hair

sections.say: You met this rule with clothes. Here is where it actually costs you something.
sections.hint: Three cards, and this is the one people get wrong for years.

cards.body: Les yeux is plural and marron takes nothing anyway, because marron is a chestnut being borrowed as a colour and the chestnut keeps its own shape.
cards.head: marron never changes
cards.label: Brown eyes, and the ending that must not be there

cards.fr: Elle a les cheveux châtain clair.
cards.body: Once a colour is built from two words it has stopped being a plain colour, so the endings never reach it. Same idea, not a second rule.
cards.head: châtain clair never changes
cards.label: Two words, so neither half moves

cards.fr: les yeux marron · les cheveux châtain clair
cards.body: A nut and a two word description. Neither is a plain colour word, so nothing attaches to either.
cards.head: Borrowed things keep their shape
cards.label: Why this is one idea and not three

cards.body: Blond, fair. Takes a plural s after les cheveux, like any ordinary colour.

cards.body: Curly. Also takes the plural s, and also silent.
cards.label: Newly written for this lesson

cards.body: The beard. Il a une barbe, with the un kind, because a beard is a thing you have rather than a feature everyone has.

errors.why: The s looks like being careful and it is the single most noticeable written error in this lesson. Marron is a nut and nothing attaches to it.
errors.wrong: Il a les yeux marrons.

errors.why: Les cheveux is plural, so long takes the s. You cannot hear it, which is exactly why it has to be worked out rather than listened for.
errors.wrong: Elle a les cheveux long.

errors.why: The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les. It is understood, and it is the phrasebook sentence rather than the one anybody says.
errors.wrong: Ses yeux sont bleus.

sections.text: Il est neuf heures et la salle d'attente est pleine. Un homme attend près de la porte. Il a les cheveux blonds et il a les yeux marron. Il a mal au dos depuis trois jours. À côté de lui, une femme lit son téléphone. Elle a les cheveux longs et châtain clair, et elle porte des lunettes. Son fils a mal aux dents et il ne veut pas parler. Le médecin ouvre la porte et regarde sa liste. « Monsieur Barré ? » L'homme se lève lentement, parce que son dos ne va toujours pas bien.

sections.title: Before The Exam

sections.say: One number matters here and it is the last one.

sections.say: Six rounds. A round you fail gives you its drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: The words, quickly.
rounds.label: The parts

questions.q: Listen. Which part of the body is it?
questions.why: la jambe, the leg. It is one of the la kind, which is worth storing now because it decides whether you say à la or au later.

questions.q: Which of these is the word for the back?
questions.why: le dos, with a silent s. It is the word from the pharmacy scene and the one this lesson opened on.

questions.q: Write the French for the tooth, with its little word.
questions.why: la dent. It is the la kind, and in practice you will nearly always want it plural, as les dents.

questions.q: Which one of these is always plural in French?
questions.why: les cheveux. Hair is one thing in English and many in French, and les yeux behaves the same way.

rounds.say: The body part decides the shape.
rounds.label: Where it hurts

questions.q: Your back hurts. Complete: J'ai mal ___ dos.
questions.why: au. Le dos is the le kind, and à plus le is written au every time. À le dos is never written down.

questions.q: Your ear hurts. Write the whole sentence.
questions.why: à l'oreille, unchanged. This is the one people expect to contract, and it behaves like à la rather than like au.

questions.q: Fix this. « J'ai mal à les dents. »
questions.why: aux dents. À plus les is aux, the same contraction you already use for going places. À les is never written.

questions.q: Which of these body parts does NOT change the little word after à?
questions.why: la tête. À la is left alone, and so is à l'. Only le and les ever contract.

rounds.say: The half of this lesson that contradicts the last one.
rounds.label: Where mon and ma stop

questions.q: Fix this. « Mon dos fait mal. »
questions.why: Every word in the original is correct and the shape is English. The person belongs in the verb, and the back keeps its ordinary little word.

questions.q: Why is « Ma tête fait mal » not what people say?
questions.why: The person goes in the verb. Ma tête is perfectly good French in other sentences; it is this frame that will not take it.
opts: The person is already in the verb, so saying it twice marks the sentence
Because tête is feminine and ma is wrong for it
Because fait is the wrong verb for a head
Because the sentence is too short to be polite

questions.q: Which verb does this frame always use?
questions.why: avoir. J'ai mal, il a mal, elle a mal. Être is what English makes you expect and it is not used here at all.

questions.q: Your head hurts. Write the whole sentence.
questions.why: J'ai mal à la tête. The la kind, so nothing contracts, and the person never appears on the noun.

rounds.say: The same move, on a face.
rounds.label: Describing someone

questions.q: You want to say she has green eyes. What do you write?
questions.why: Elle a les yeux verts. The person is in a, and the eyes keep les. The first option is understood and is the phrasebook sentence rather than the one anybody says.

questions.q: He has blond hair. Write the whole sentence.
questions.why: Il a les cheveux blonds, with the s on blonds because les cheveux is plural. You will never hear that s.

questions.q: Fix this. « Mes yeux sont bleus. »
questions.why: The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les. Describing and hurting are the same sentence with different words on the end.

questions.q: Listen. What colour are the eyes?
questions.why: marron, brown. Nothing in the sound tells you whether an s was written, which is what makes the next round a writing problem rather than a listening one.

rounds.say: Both of these words are plural, always.
rounds.label: The s you cannot hear

questions.q: Les cheveux and the word long. Write the colour word as it should appear.
questions.why: longs, with an s, because les cheveux is plural. It sounds exactly like long and the only reason to write it is the noun in front.

questions.q: How many of these are spelled correctly? « les yeux bleus », « les cheveux blonds », « les yeux vert »
questions.why: Two. The third needs verts, because les yeux is plural like everything else here. Nothing about the sound would have told you.

questions.q: Why does the colour take an s after les yeux?
questions.why: The noun is plural, so the word describing it matches. It is the rule you already met with colours, applied to a word that happens to always be plural.
opts: Because eye colours are always plural in French
Because les yeux is plural, so the word describing it matches
Because the colour comes after the noun
Because you can hear the s in careful speech

questions.q: She has curly hair. Write the word for curly as it should appear.
questions.why: frisés. Same silent s as blonds and longs, for the same reason, on a word that did not exist in this corpus until this lesson.

rounds.say: The last round, and you already know why.
rounds.label: The two that refuse

questions.q: Fix this. « Il a les yeux marrons. »
questions.why: marron, with nothing added. The s is the most noticeable written error in this lesson and it looks exactly like being careful.

questions.q: Why does marron refuse the s when bleu takes it?
questions.why: It is a chestnut being used as a colour. You met this with clothes already, and it is one idea rather than a list of exceptions.
opts: Because marron is longer than bleu
Because marron is irregular and has to be memorised on its own
Because brown is not a real colour in French
Because marron is a nut being borrowed as a colour, and it keeps its own shape

questions.q: Say this out loud: he has brown eyes.
questions.why: Nothing in the sound tells anybody whether you wrote the s, which is exactly why that error survives. Saying it and writing it are two separate skills here.

questions.q: What do marron and châtain clair have in common?
questions.why: Neither is a plain colour word. A nut and a two word description, so the endings never reach either of them. One idea, not two things to memorise.
opts: Both are shades of brown, so both are irregular
Neither is a plain colour word, so neither ever changes
Both are only used for hair
Both take an s only after les cheveux

sections.say: One sentence, two jobs.
sections.body: You can name fourteen parts of the body, say which one hurts, and describe what somebody looks like. All three run on the same sentence. The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: J'ai mal au dos, and the person never appears on the noun
Au and aux contract, à la and à l' do not
Les yeux and les cheveux are plural, so the colour takes a silent s
Marron and châtain clair take nothing at all

errorTriggers.description: Names the wrong body part, or the right one with the wrong little word.
Writes à le or à les instead of au or aux.
Uses mon, ma, mes or ses on the body part instead of the definite article.
Builds the frame with être or faire instead of avoir.
Leaves the colour singular after les yeux or les cheveux.
Adds an ending to marron or to châtain clair.

grammarAssumed: Noun gender, and that the little word in front follows it, introduced in a1.03
le, la, l' and les, introduced in a1.04
The full present of avoir, introduced in a1.07
Adjective agreement, the silent plural -s, and the invariable colours marron and orange, introduced in a1.13
The possessive adjectives mon, ma, mes and their determiner slot, introduced in a1.17
The contraction of à with the definite article: à + le = au, à + les = aux, and that à la and à l' do not contract, introduced in a1.21
grammarIntroduced: The avoir mal à frame: an inalienable body part taking a definite article where English takes a possessive
The same frame for physical description: avoir + definite article + feature + adjective
That the possessive is excluded from both frames, which bounds the rule a1.17 introduced
Plural agreement on les yeux and les cheveux, both of which are plural-only nouns
Invariable colour adjectives applied to a person: marron and the compound châtain clair

drills.coach: Arriving and leaving take different words, and bonsoir and bonne soirée are the pair that get swapped. One is hello, the other is goodbye.
drills.title: Which one, and when

drills.q: You are leaving a dinner at eleven at night. Which?
drills.why: Bonne soirée. Bonsoir is for arriving and bonne nuit says you are going to bed.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Two rules and both are about what follows. et on the six that end in one, and the s only when nothing comes after.
drills.title: The shapes that trip

drills.q: Which is 81?
drills.why: quatre-vingt-un. The s goes the moment anything follows, and 81 never takes et.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Three articles and they are not interchangeable. Ask what the verb points at: one of them, an amount, or the whole category.
pairs: coffee as a thing you like
pas le café, in J'aime pas le café
drills.title: One of them, some of it, all of it

drills.q: Which means: I eat bread
drills.why: du pain, an amount. le pain would be the whole loaf on the table.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: English is it, French has it, and the list of states is short enough to learn whole. The one exception is a job, which takes être and no article.
drills.title: Has, not is

drills.q: Which means: I am thirty
drills.why: J'ai trente ans. French has its age, and ans is never dropped.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: The little word is the whole meaning. le makes it a habit, en names a month, and a point on the clock takes nothing at all.
pairs: in the morning, as a habit
drills.title: Once, or every week

drills.q: You are free every Saturday. Which?
drills.why: le samedi. Without the le you have offered exactly one Saturday.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Three frames and one adjective. The weather makes, a person has, a thing is. pleut and neige are already whole and take no il fait.
drills.title: Makes, has, is

drills.q: It is cold outside. Which?
drills.why: Il fait froid. Il a froid is a person, and il est froid is an object.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Most adjectives agree and you can usually hear it. marron and orange never move, because both were things before they were colours.
drills.title: What moves, and what never does

drills.q: Which is right for brown shoes?
drills.why: marron never agrees. Des marrons would be a bag of chestnuts.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Ten words go in front and everything else goes behind. When in doubt, put it after: the group behind is the whole rest of the language.
drills.title: In front, or behind

drills.q: Which is right?
drills.why: A colour goes behind the noun. English puts it first and French does not.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: The possessive agrees with the thing owned. Whether the owner is a man or a woman never enters into it, which is the opposite of English.
drills.title: What is owned, not who owns it

drills.q: Her father. Which?
drills.why: son père. père is masculine, so son, whoever the owner is.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was. After avoir, un and du become de. After être, nothing moves, and le never moves at all.
drills.title: What collapses, and what does not

drills.q: Turn « J'ai une voiture » negative.
drills.why: After avoir, une collapses to de.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Three methods and you use one at a time. Est-ce que is the one that is never wrong, spoken or written.
pairs: a has no t of its own
drills.title: Pick one method

drills.q: Which is wrong?
drills.why: The last one stacks two methods and asks the question twice.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: A one-word preposition goes straight onto the noun. A phrase needs de first, and then de and à contract with le and les.
drills.title: One word, or a phrase

drills.q: Which is right?
drills.why: à côté DE. A multi-word preposition always needs its de.
drills.title: One more time

rounds.label: Lesson 1 · Greetings

questions.q: You walk into a bakery at ten in the morning. What comes out of your mouth first?
questions.why: Bonjour is the price of entry. Salut is for people you tutoie, bonne journée is said leaving, and allô exists only on the phone. Lesson 1.

questions.q: Write the French a man says for: Pleased to meet you
questions.why: Enchanté, with a second e as enchantée if you are a woman. Lesson 1.

questions.q: A learner leaves a dinner party at eleven at night and says « Bonne nuit ». Fix it.
questions.why: Bonne nuit is for sleep, and it tells the room you are going to bed. Leaving after dark takes bonne soirée. Lesson 1.

questions.q: Listen. Which form did you hear?
questions.why: Te against vous is one syllable and it is the whole difference between them. Lesson 1.

questions.q: Which is the everyday answer to merci?
questions.why: De rien is the everyday one. Je vous en prie is its formal twin, bienvenue is welcome to a place, and pardon is an apology. Lesson 1.

rounds.say: One to twenty. The endings move, and that is the lesson.
rounds.label: Lesson 2 · Numbers 1 to 20

questions.q: Write the French for: sixteen
questions.why: seize. There is nothing of six in it, which is exactly why it gets heard as six. Lesson 2.

questions.q: Listen. Which number is it?
questions.why: quinze ends on a z and cinq ends on a k. They share a vowel, so the ending is the only thing separating five from fifteen. Lesson 2.

questions.q: A learner asks for « un baguette » at the counter. Fix it.
questions.why: un is the only number with a gender, and baguette is feminine. Lesson 2.

questions.q: How is « dix » said in « dix minutes »?
questions.why: Alone it is DEES, before a consonant the s vanishes, before a vowel it is a z. minutes starts with a consonant. Lesson 2.
opts: DEE, with no s at all

questions.q: Say it: three
questions.why: trois. Saying a number is a different test from recognising one, and it is the half most learners skip. Lesson 2.

rounds.say: Twenty-one to a hundred. Learn the shape, not the sum.
rounds.label: Lesson 3 · Numbers 21 to 100

questions.q: Write the French for: 71
questions.why: soixante et onze. The et rule covers 21, 31, 41, 51, 61 and 71 only, and those six take no hyphens. Lesson 3.

questions.q: Which is 92?
questions.why: quatre-vingt-douze. The s comes off quatre-vingts the moment anything follows it, and nonante is Belgian and Swiss rather than France French. Lesson 3.

questions.q: A learner writes eighty-one as « quatre-vingts-un ». Fix it.
questions.why: quatre-vingt-un. quatre-vingts keeps its s only when nothing follows. Lesson 3.

questions.q: Listen. Which number is it?
questions.why: soixante-seize is 76, sixty and sixteen. The trap is hearing the seize as six. Lesson 3.

questions.q: Which of these takes NO et and NO s?
questions.why: quatre-vingt-onze. 91 never takes et, and the s is gone because onze follows. 71 takes et, 80 alone keeps its s, and 21 takes et. Lesson 3.

rounds.say: cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun.
rounds.label: Lesson 4 · Large numbers

questions.q: Write the French for: 200
questions.why: deux cents. cent is multiplied and nothing follows it, so it takes the s. Lesson 4.

questions.q: Which is 330?
questions.why: trois cent trente. cent is multiplied, but trente follows it, so the s comes straight off. Lesson 4.

questions.q: A learner writes two thousand as « deux milles ». Fix it.
questions.why: deux mille. mille never takes an s in any position. The s was carried over from cents, where it is real. Lesson 4.

questions.q: A learner says « huit millions visiteurs ». What is missing?
questions.why: huit millions de visiteurs. million is a noun, so it reaches its noun through de, and the s on millions is unconditional. Lesson 4.

questions.q: A French price tag reads 124,80 €. How much is it?
questions.why: The comma is the decimal point in French and the space is the thousands separator, so 124,80 € is a hundred and twenty-four euros eighty. Lesson 4.

rounds.say: Gender. Learn the article, not the noun.
rounds.label: Lesson 5 · Noun gender

questions.q: A noun ends in -tion. Which article does it almost certainly take?
questions.why: une. Thirty-six -tion nouns in the corpus and every one of them is feminine: la direction, la natation, la destination. Lesson 5.

questions.q: Write the article that goes with: bureau
questions.why: le bureau. The -eau ending is masculine ninety-two percent of the time, and l'eau and la peau are the two that break it. Lesson 5.

questions.q: A learner reasons: « livre ends in e, so it is feminine ». What is wrong?
questions.why: A final e is worth a lean and nothing more. le livre is the book and la livre is the pound in weight, so the same spelling runs both ways. Lesson 5.
opts: A final e is a lean, not a rule, and le livre is masculine
livre is feminine, the learner is right
Only nouns ending in -e take une

questions.q: A learner learns the word « armoire » from a card, with no article. Fix the habit.
questions.why: une armoire. Storing the bare noun stores half the word, and the half you dropped is the half you need to speak. Lesson 5.

questions.q: Which of these endings takes une?
questions.why: -ure is feminine: la confiture, la peinture, la ceinture. The other three are masculine endings. Lesson 5.

rounds.say: le, la, l and les. When English says nothing, French says le.
rounds.label: Lesson 6 · The definite articles

questions.q: Complete: « J'aime ___ café. » (I like coffee, as a thing in general)
questions.why: J'aime le café. English drops the article on a whole category and French never does. Lesson 6.

questions.q: Write the definite article for: eau
questions.why: l'eau. Both le and la elide to l' before a vowel sound, which is why the apostrophe hides the gender. Lesson 6.

questions.q: Which of these takes le rather than l'?
questions.why: le hibou. Its h is aspirated so it behaves like a consonant, along with le hamster, le homard and le héros. The other three have an h muet. Lesson 6.

questions.q: A learner writes « les ami ». Fix it.
questions.why: les amis. les is the plural article, so the noun has to be plural too. Lesson 6.

questions.q: Listen. Which did you hear?
questions.why: les enfants, with a z linking into the vowel. The singular would be l'enfant with no z at all. Lesson 6.

rounds.say: un, une, des. Un introduces it. Le assumes you already know it.
rounds.label: Lesson 7 · The indefinite articles

questions.q: Write the French for: I am a teacher
questions.why: Je suis professeur. Nothing at all after être in front of a job. The un is the single most common thing added here. Lesson 7.

questions.q: Which sentence is correct?
questions.why: C'est un professeur. After c'est the article comes back, and it is the one place it does. After être it never appears. Lesson 7.

questions.q: A learner says « J'achète pommes ». Fix it.
questions.why: J'achète des pommes. French has no bare plural noun, so the slot des fills is never left empty. Lesson 7.

questions.q: Turn « J'ai une voiture » negative.
questions.why: Je n'ai pas de voiture. Under a negative un, une and des all collapse to de. Lesson 7.

questions.q: Why does « Je n'aime pas le café » keep its le?
questions.why: The definite articles do not move under a negative. Only un, une, des and the partitives collapse to de. Lesson 7.
opts: Because le, la and les do not move under a negative
It is wrong, it should be de

rounds.say: du, de la, de l. Un is one of them. Du is some of it.
rounds.label: Lesson 8 · The partitive articles

questions.q: Write the French for: I eat bread
questions.why: Je mange du pain. Some of it, not one of them and not the whole category. French does not leave that slot empty. Lesson 8.

questions.q: You want coffee, not one cup of coffee. Which do you order?
questions.why: du café. Both un café and du café are correct French and they order different things: one is a cup, the other is coffee. Lesson 8.

questions.q: A learner says « beaucoup du café ». Fix it.
questions.why: beaucoup de café. After a quantity word the partitive flattens to plain de, every time. Lesson 8.

questions.q: Which is right for a bottle of water?
questions.why: une bouteille d'eau. A container behaves like a quantity, so it takes plain de, elided before the vowel. Lesson 8.

questions.q: Turn « Je mange du pain » negative.
questions.why: Je ne mange pas de pain. du, de la, de l' and des all become de under a negative. Lesson 8.
accept: Je ne mange pas de pain
questions.answer: Je ne mange pas de pain.

rounds.say: Nine pronouns. Six verb forms.
rounds.label: Lesson 9 · Subject pronouns

questions.q: Which verb form goes with « on »?
questions.why: On est. on means we and takes the il form, which is the mismatch that catches everyone. Lesson 9.

questions.q: A learner writes « On sommes d'accord ». Fix it.
questions.why: On est d'accord. on takes est however many people it means. Lesson 9.

questions.q: You are writing the closing line of a job application. Which do you use for we?
questions.why: nous. on is the spoken we and it is out of place in careful writing. Both are correct French, and only one is correct there. Lesson 9.

questions.q: A group of four women. Which pronoun?
questions.why: elles, for a group that is all women. One man in the room and it becomes ils. Lesson 9.

questions.q: In « Il pleut », who is il?
questions.why: Nobody. il is the empty subject French puts in front of weather, the clock and il y a, and looking for a person in it is what makes the sentence stall. Lesson 9.

rounds.say: No pattern. Six forms. Every conversation.
rounds.label: Lesson 10 · The verb être

questions.q: Write être for vous
questions.why: vous êtes, said [voo ZET] with a z linking in. It is the one form that looks nothing like the others. Lesson 10.

questions.q: Pointing at a man across the room, you say what?
questions.why: C'est Marc. A name takes c'est, never il est. Pointing is always c'est. Lesson 10.

questions.q: A learner writes « Je suis Français » about their nationality. Fix it.
questions.why: Je suis français, with a small f. As a nationality it is an adjective, and French does not capitalise those. The capital belongs to the noun, un Français. Lesson 10.

questions.q: Which is correct for « They are my parents »?
questions.why: Ce sont mes parents. More than one person turns c'est into ce sont. Lesson 10.

questions.q: Say it: « Je suis architecte. »
questions.why: No article in front of the job, ever, after être. Adding un is the most common error in this lesson. Lesson 10.

rounds.say: French has it. English is it.
rounds.label: Lesson 11 · The verb avoir

questions.q: Write the French for: I am twenty
questions.why: J'ai vingt ans. French HAS its age, and ans is never left off. Je suis vingt ans is the reflex to unlearn. Lesson 11.

questions.q: The room is warm and you want to say so about yourself. Which?
questions.why: J'ai chaud. Je suis chaud is real French about something else entirely, which is why nobody corrects it and everybody notices. Lesson 11.

questions.q: Which of these takes de after it?
questions.why: avoir besoin de. With avoir envie de and avoir mal à, it is one of only three that carry anything. The other eleven states take nothing at all. Lesson 11.

questions.q: A learner writes « Je n'ai pas de faim ». Fix it.
questions.why: Je n'ai pas faim. Nothing collapsed to de, because there was no article there to collapse. Lesson 11.

questions.q: Listen. Which did you hear?
questions.why: Ils ont, said [eel ZOHⁿ] with a z. Ils sont has an s sound and means they are. One consonant separates having from being. Lesson 11.

rounds.say: Le makes it every week.
rounds.label: Lesson 12 · Days of the week

questions.q: You are free every Saturday. Which do you say?
questions.why: Je suis libre le samedi. The le makes it every week. Without it you have offered exactly one Saturday. Lesson 12.

questions.q: Write the French for: Wednesday
questions.why: mercredi, [mehr-kruh-DEE], named after Mercury. Lowercase, like every day of the week. Lesson 12.

questions.q: A learner writes « On se voit sur samedi ». Fix it.
questions.why: On se voit samedi. A day name takes no preposition at all, and sur is the English on arriving where it is not wanted. Lesson 12.

questions.q: Which day of the week does a French calendar start on?
questions.why: lundi. The week runs lundi to dimanche, and le week-end sits at the end of the row rather than straddling it. Lesson 12.

questions.q: Which plural IS correct?
questions.why: tous les samedis. That is the one place the plural is right. For every Monday as a habit it is le lundi, singular. Lesson 12.
opts: tous les samedis, for every Saturday

rounds.say: En for a month, le for a date.
rounds.label: Lesson 13 · Months of the year

questions.q: Write the French for: in July
questions.why: en juillet, lowercase. A bare month takes en and never an article. Lesson 13.

questions.q: A learner says « Mon vol est en douze juin ». Fix it.
questions.why: le douze juin. Put a day in it and the frame changes: en names a month, le names a date. Lesson 13.
accept: Mon vol est le douze juin
questions.answer: Mon vol est le douze juin.

questions.q: Which is the first of January?
questions.why: le premier janvier. The first is the only ordinal in the whole system. Every other day is a plain counting number. Lesson 13.

questions.q: Listen. Which month is it?
questions.why: juillet, [zhwee-YEH], with a silent t. juin is [ZHWEHⁿ] and nasal. They are the pair that costs people flights. Lesson 13.

questions.q: Which of these is wrong?
questions.why: le douze de mars. Nothing goes between the number and the month. It still parses, which is why nobody corrects it. Lesson 13.

rounds.say: Weather makes, people have, things are.
rounds.label: Lesson 14 · Seasons and weather

questions.q: The sky is hot. Which shape?
questions.why: Il fait chaud. The weather MAKES. A person HAS, and a thing IS. Three shapes, one adjective. Lesson 14.

questions.q: Write the French for: in spring
questions.why: au printemps. It is the only season that takes au. The other three take en, and there is no reason behind it. Lesson 14.

questions.q: A learner says « Il fait pleut depuis ce matin ». Fix it.
questions.why: Il pleut. pleut is already the whole thing, so welding it to il fait produces two verbs and no sentence. Lesson 14.

questions.q: Which shape does « vent » take?
questions.why: il fait du vent, or il y a du vent. A weather THING takes du after il fait; a weather adjective takes nothing. Lesson 14.

questions.q: How is « automne » said?
questions.why: [oh-TONN]. Written with an m and said with none, and the n at the end is a real n you do pronounce. Lesson 14.

rounds.say: Il est says the time. À books it.
rounds.label: Lesson 15 · Telling the time

questions.q: Someone asks the time and it is eight. What do you answer?
questions.why: Il est huit heures. heures is never dropped, and à books an appointment rather than reporting the clock. Lesson 15.

questions.q: Write the French for: quarter to eight
questions.why: moins LE quart, with the article. It is one short unstressed word in the middle, which is why it goes missing. Lesson 15.

questions.q: A station board reads 20:30. A learner says « vingt heures et demie ». Fix it.
questions.why: vingt heures trente. The twenty-four hour clock takes plain minutes. Mixing it with et demie is the one that marks a beginner in a station. Lesson 15.

questions.q: Which is right?
questions.why: Il est midi. midi and minuit are the hour and the noun at once, so they take no heures and no article. And it is midi et demi, without the e. Lesson 15.

questions.q: Listen. What time is it?
questions.why: deux heures, [deu-ZUHR]. douze heures is [doo-ZUHR]. Both grow a z, so the vowel in front of it is the only difference. Lesson 15.
opts: Il est douze heures et demie.

rounds.say: Colours agree. Things that became colours do not.
rounds.label: Lesson 16 · Colours

questions.q: Write: a green skirt (une jupe)
questions.why: une jupe verte. The e is audible: [VEHR] becomes [VEHRT] and the t wakes up. Lesson 16.

questions.q: Which is correct for brown shoes?
questions.why: des chaussures marron. marron was a chestnut before it was a colour, so it never changes. Des marrons is a bag of chestnuts. Lesson 16.

questions.q: A learner writes « une porte blance ». Fix it.
questions.why: blanche. blanc changes more than its ending: the c turns into a ch, and you can hear it. Lesson 16.

questions.q: How do you write dark green eyes?
questions.why: des yeux vert foncé. Neither half moves: a two-word colour has stopped being a plain colour. Lesson 16.

questions.q: Which colour sounds identical in the masculine and the feminine?
questions.why: bleu and bleue are [BLUH] both ways, as are noir and noire. vert, gris and blanc all wake a consonant up. Lesson 16.

rounds.say: Colours follow the noun. These six come first.
rounds.label: Lesson 17 · Basic adjectives

questions.q: Write: a big house
questions.why: une grande maison. grand is one of the six that go in FRONT, which is the opposite of where a colour goes. Lesson 17.

questions.q: A learner writes « un beau homme ». Fix it.
questions.why: un bel homme. beau becomes bel in front of a vowel sound, because two vowels would collide. It is not the feminine. Lesson 17.

questions.q: What is the feminine of vieux?
questions.why: vieille. beau and vieux replace the word outright rather than adding to it. vieil is the masculine used before a vowel. Lesson 17.

questions.q: Which is the plural of « un vieux vélo »?
questions.why: des vieux vélos. vieux and mauvais already end in the letter the plural would add, so the masculine never changes. Lesson 17.

questions.q: Listen. Which did you hear?
questions.why: bonne, [BON], with a plain n. The masculine bon is [BOHⁿ] and nasal, so the doubling is audible. Lesson 17.

rounds.say: When in doubt, put it after.
rounds.label: Lesson 18 · Adjective placement

questions.q: Where does an adjective go if you have never met it before?
questions.why: After. The group in front is ten words and closed; the group behind is every other describing word in the language. Lesson 18.
opts: At the end of the sentence

questions.q: A learner writes « une rouge voiture ». Fix it.
questions.why: une voiture rouge. English puts the colour first and French puts it second, on every phrase. Lesson 18.

questions.q: Write the French for: beautiful paintings (using beaux)
questions.why: de beaux tableaux. des becomes de once one of the ten sits in front of a plural noun, and the adjective keeps its own plural ending. Lesson 18.

questions.q: The building itself is old. Which?
questions.why: C'est un hôtel ancien. In front, ancien means former: a place that used to be a hotel. Behind, it means old. Same word, two meanings, decided by position. Lesson 18.

questions.q: Which is correct for a small red dress?
questions.why: une petite robe rouge. One from each group with the noun in between. No new rule, just the two you already have. Lesson 18.

rounds.say: French has no apostrophe. Turn it around.
rounds.label: Lesson 19 · The family

questions.q: Write the French for: Paul's mother
questions.why: la mère de Paul. French has no apostrophe s, so the phrase turns around: the mother OF Paul. Lesson 19.

questions.q: How is « le fils » said?
questions.why: [LUH FEES]. Silent l and a sounded s, which is the reverse of what the spelling suggests. The thread, fil, is [FEEL] and behaves normally. Lesson 19.

questions.q: A learner writes « les grand-parents ». Fix it.
questions.why: les grands-parents. The grand takes the plural s here, though la grand-mère never changes shape. Lesson 19.

questions.q: Which article does « bébé » take?
questions.why: le bébé, for any baby at all. The word has one gender and the child has another, and they do not have to agree. Lesson 19.
opts: la for a girl, le for a boy

questions.q: Listen. Which did you hear?
questions.why: la cousine, [koo-ZEEN], with a real n because a vowel follows. The masculine is [koo-ZAⁿ], nasal, with no n sound at all. Lesson 19.

rounds.say: Ask what is owned, not who owns it.
rounds.label: Lesson 20 · Possessive adjectives

questions.q: Her father. Which?
questions.why: son père. son agrees with père, not with her. Ask what is owned, never who owns it. Lesson 20.

questions.q: Write the French for: my friend (a woman, using amie)
questions.why: mon amie. amie is feminine, and it still takes mon: ma would put two vowels together. Lesson 20.

questions.q: A learner writes « leurs enfants » about one child. Fix it.
questions.why: leur enfant. leur takes its s from the thing owned, not from the number of owners. Lesson 20.

questions.q: Which is wrong?
questions.why: le mon livre. A possessive replaces the article, so the two never appear together. Lesson 20.

questions.q: His mother. Which?
questions.why: sa mère. mère is feminine so it takes sa, whoever the owner is. This is the mirror of son père and the pair is the whole lesson. Lesson 20.

rounds.say: Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was.
rounds.label: Lesson 21 · Negation

questions.q: Turn « Il est là » negative.
questions.why: Il n'est pas là. ne and pas wrap the verb, and ne elides to n' in front of a vowel. Lesson 21.

questions.q: Turn « J'ai un frère » negative.
questions.why: Je n'ai pas de frère. After avoir, un, une and des collapse to de. Lesson 21.

questions.q: Turn « C'est un livre » negative.
questions.why: Ce n'est pas un livre. After être nothing collapses. The de rule belongs to avoir, and applying it here is the over-correction. Lesson 21.

questions.q: A learner writes « Je ne ai pas de temps ». Fix it.
questions.why: Je n'ai pas de temps. ne cannot sit unelided in front of a vowel. Lesson 21.

questions.q: Why does « Je n'aime pas le café » keep le?
questions.why: le, la and les do not move. Only un, une, des and the partitives become de. Lesson 21.
opts: Because it is a fixed phrase
Because the definite articles never collapse
It does not, it should be de café

rounds.say: Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices.
rounds.label: Lesson 22 · Yes and no questions

questions.q: Which way of asking is never wrong, spoken or written?
questions.why: Est-ce que. Your voice alone is spoken only, and inversion is for careful writing or formal speech. Lesson 22.
opts: Swapping the verb and the pronoun

questions.q: Write the inversion form of « Il a faim ? »
questions.why: A-t-il faim ? The t is inserted purely so two vowels do not collide, and it is joined by hyphens on both sides. Lesson 22.

questions.q: A learner writes « Est-ce que il est prêt ? ». Fix it.
questions.why: Est-ce qu'il est prêt ? The que elides in front of a vowel, exactly like ne and le. Lesson 22.

questions.q: Which uses two methods at once and so is wrong?
questions.why: Est-ce que es-tu prêt ? Pick one method. Stacking est-ce que on top of an inversion asks the question twice. Lesson 22.

questions.q: How do you ask « Am I hungry? »
questions.why: Est-ce que j'ai faim ? Inversion with je is avoided in speech, and reaching for Ai-je to complete the table is the trap. Lesson 22.

rounds.say: Your word, then est-ce que. That always works.
rounds.label: Lesson 23 · Question words

questions.q: You want to know WHEN the train leaves. Which word?
questions.why: quand gets you a time. où gets you a place, and asking the wrong one gets you a confident answer to a question you did not ask. Lesson 23.

questions.q: Write the French for: How many children do you have? (vous)
questions.why: Combien d'enfants. combien always carries de, and it elides in front of a vowel. Lesson 23.

questions.q: A learner writes « Quel heure est-il ? ». Fix it.
questions.why: Quelle heure. heure is feminine so quel agrees with it. All four forms sound identical, so only writing exposes this. Lesson 23.

questions.q: A learner writes « Ou est le train ? ». What is missing?
questions.why: où, with the accent. Without it, ou means or, and the accent is the only thing separating two very common words. Lesson 23.

questions.q: Which is right at the end of a spoken question?
questions.why: Tu fais quoi ? que cannot sit at the end. It becomes quoi there, and that is where you will hear it most. Lesson 23.

rounds.say: One word goes straight onto the noun. A phrase needs de first.
rounds.label: Lesson 24 · Prepositions of place

questions.q: Write the French for: The keys are on the desk
questions.why: sur le bureau. sur is one word and it goes straight onto the noun, with no de. Lesson 24.
accept: Les clés sont sur le bureau
les cles sont sur le bureau
questions.answer: Les clés sont sur le bureau.

questions.q: A learner writes « Le café est à côté la banque ». Fix it.
questions.why: à côté DE la banque. A multi-word preposition needs de before the noun. près de and loin de work the same way. Lesson 24.
accept: Le café est à côté de la banque
le cafe est a cote de la banque
questions.answer: Le café est à côté de la banque.

questions.q: What does « de + le » become?
questions.why: du. And de + les is des, à + le is au, à + les is aux. Only la and l' are left alone. Lesson 24.

questions.q: Which is wrong?
questions.why: sur de la boîte. sur is a one-word preposition, so the de is an over-correction borrowed from à côté de. Lesson 24.

questions.q: You are going to a friend's place. Which word?
questions.why: chez. It means at somebody's place and English has no single word for it. Lesson 24.

rounds.say: Learn the country with its article. Everything else follows.
rounds.label: Lesson 25 · Countries and nationalities

questions.q: Write the French for: I am going to Canada
questions.why: au Canada. le Canada is masculine, so à + le gives au. Store the article with the country and this falls out. Lesson 25.

questions.q: A learner says « Je viens du France ». Fix it.
questions.why: de France. A feminine country takes plain de coming from, and en going to. Lesson 25.

questions.q: Going to the United States. Which?
questions.why: aux États-Unis. les États-Unis is plural, so à + les gives aux. Lesson 25.

questions.q: Going to Iran. Which?
questions.why: en Iran. l'Iran is masculine, but it opens on a vowel, and a vowel takes en whatever the gender. Lesson 25.

questions.q: Which is right for a French woman describing herself?
questions.why: Je suis française. Lowercase, because it is an adjective here, and no article after être. Lesson 25.

rounds.say: Aimer takes the whole thing. Manger takes a part of it.
rounds.label: Lesson 26 · Food

questions.q: Write the French for: I like bread
questions.why: J'aime le pain. aimer points at the whole category, so it takes le, la or les. Lesson 26.

questions.q: Which verb takes du, de la or des?
questions.why: boire, with manger and prendre. Those three take an amount. aimer, adorer, détester and préférer take the whole category. Lesson 26.

questions.q: A learner writes « Je mange le pain ». Fix it.
questions.why: Je mange du pain. manger takes a part of it. Je mange le pain says you ate the whole loaf that was on the table. Lesson 26.

questions.q: Listen. Which food is it?
questions.why: le poisson, [luh pwah-SOHⁿ]. It is also the one -son noun that breaks the -tion feminine pattern. Lesson 26.

questions.q: Which is right?
questions.why: des pâtes. les pâtes is plural only. Une pâte is a dough or a paste, which is a different thing on a different shelf. Lesson 26.

rounds.say: The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les.
rounds.label: Lesson 27 · The body

questions.q: Write the French for: I have a headache
questions.why: J'ai mal à la tête. The person is already in j'ai, so the body part takes a plain article rather than a possessive. Lesson 27.

questions.q: A learner writes « Mon dos fait mal ». Fix it.
questions.why: J'ai mal au dos. French does not make the body part the subject. à + le gives au. Lesson 27.

questions.q: My teeth hurt. Which?
questions.why: J'ai mal aux dents. à + les gives aux, exactly as it did with countries. Lesson 27.

questions.q: Which is correct for brown eyes?
questions.why: les yeux marron. marron never agrees, here as everywhere. les yeux bleus and les yeux verts do take the silent s. Lesson 27.

questions.q: How do you say you have blue eyes?
questions.why: J'ai les yeux bleus. French HAS the eyes, with a plain article. Mes yeux sont bleus is understandable and it is not what anybody says. Lesson 27.

rounds.say: The parts of the day take le. Midi and minuit take nothing.
rounds.label: Lesson 28 · Daily routine

questions.q: Write the French for: I get up at seven
questions.why: Je me lève. se lever carries its me, and dropping it leaves a verb with nobody doing anything. Lesson 28.
accept: Je me lève à sept heures
je me leve a sept heures
questions.answer: Je me lève à sept heures.

questions.q: At noon. Which?
questions.why: à midi. Noon is a point on the clock, so there is nothing to mark as a habit. A stretch of hours takes le: le matin, le soir. Lesson 28.

questions.q: A learner writes « Je déjeuner le midi ». Fix it.
questions.why: Je déjeune à midi. Two things went wrong: the infinitive was left unconjugated, and midi took an article it never takes. Lesson 28.

questions.q: Which article does « après-midi » take here?
questions.why: l'après-midi. It is a stretch of hours so it takes an article, and the article elides before the vowel. Lesson 28.

questions.q: You mean THIS evening, not evenings in general. Which?
questions.why: Ce soir. le soir makes it a habit, every evening. It is the same le that made le samedi every week. Lesson 28.

rounds.say: Never say room. Say which room.
rounds.label: Lesson 29 · The house

questions.q: You need the toilet in a French home. What do you ask for?
questions.why: les toilettes, always plural. The salle de bain is where the bath is, and in most French homes that is a different room. Lesson 29.

questions.q: Write the French for: the kitchen
questions.why: la cuisine. The -ine ending is feminine ninety-six percent of the time, which is a lean you can use. Lesson 29.

questions.q: An advert says « trois pièces ». What are you being offered?
questions.why: Three rooms in total, and the kitchen and bathroom are not among them. Hearing it as three bedrooms is how people rent the wrong flat. Lesson 29.
opts: Three rooms in total, kitchen and bathroom not counted

questions.q: A learner uses « chambre » for the room they are sitting in. Fix it.
questions.why: le salon for the living room, or la pièce for a room in general. A chambre has a bed in it. Lesson 29.

questions.q: Which takes le because it is a verb plus a noun?
questions.why: le lave-vaisselle, like le sèche-linge and le micro-ondes. A verb plus a noun is masculine, so those three need no storing. Lesson 29.

sections.say: Read the round scores, not the total.
sections.body: The percentage at the top is the least useful number on that screen. What is worth reading is the list underneath it, because a round is a lesson and a low round is an afternoon of work rather than a verdict on your French. Two or three weak rounds after twenty-nine lessons is an ordinary result and the fix is specific: go back to those units, sit them again, and come back here. When the rounds are level, the exam is the next thing, and it is deliberately harder in one way only, which is that it will not tell you what it is asking about.
sections.title: Where You Are
points: A wrong answer names the half hour to sit again.
Read the round scores rather than the total. The total hides which lesson went.
A drill that fired is worth more than a round you passed. It caught something live.
The exam is a separate sitting, and it is the one that answers whether you have A1.

errorTriggers.description: Opens with the wrong register, or answers a formula with the wrong formula.
Loses a number to its shape: the et, the s on quatre-vingts, the comma in a price.
Reaches for the wrong little word. Le for du, un after être, des where de was wanted.
Uses être where French uses avoir, or picks the wrong form for on, ils and vous.
Drops the article that makes a day or a part of the day habitual, or mixes two clocks.
Puts the weather in the wrong frame: il est for il fait, or a person where the sky goes.
Fails to agree an adjective, or agrees one that never moves.
Puts the describing word on the English side of the noun.
Agrees the possessive with the owner rather than with the thing owned.
Collapses an article that does not collapse, or leaves one that does.
Stacks two question methods, or drops the hyphen, the t or the elision.
Omits the de a multi-word preposition needs, or picks the wrong contraction.

recorded.desc: THE THREE CONTRAST PAIRS, AND THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT TAKE IN THE LESSON. Each pair is ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, the two lines recorded back to back with the smallest gap the recording allows and no change of pitch, pace or weight between them: « C'est un beau sac. » then « C'est un bel arbre. »; « C'est un nouveau sac. » then « C'est un nouvel ami. »; « C'est un vieux sac. » then « C'est un vieil homme. » RECORDED APART, THE LEARNER COMPARES TWO PERFORMANCES INSTEAD OF TWO SOUNDS AND THE ENTIRE TEACHING IS LOST. The third pair matters most and is the hardest: the h of homme is silent, so the reader must NOT pause before it or aspirate it, and the l of vieil runs straight into the vowel exactly as it does in vieil ami. If the reader gives homme even a breath of a consonant, the take proves the opposite of the screen. What must be audible in every pair is the describing word and nothing else; the two nouns differ and that is not the point.

THE FIFTEEN CELLS, THREE TAKES, ONE PER WORD, EACH WORD'S FIVE IN ONE BREATH GROUP. Within each take the FIRST AND FOURTH lines must be acoustically identical, and so must the SECOND, THIRD AND FIFTH: « Il est beau. » and « Ils sont beaux. » differ on the page and not in the mouth, and a reader who knows the fourth is spelled with an x will lengthen something or put a fraction of a z on it, and that instinct destroys the screen. If a listener with their eyes shut can tell the first from the fourth, or the second from the third, the take is unusable. FIVE WRITTEN SHAPES MUST REACH THE EAR AS TWO. That is the whole claim of the lesson and this take is where it is either proved or lost.

THE FOUR LINES FOR THE LISTENING SCREEN, WITH AUDIO BEFORE TEXT, IN THIS ORDER: Il est beau, Ils sont beaux, Elle est belle, Elles sont belles. The first pair and the second pair are each ONE take and must be indistinguishable within the pair; the learner is being asked to fail to hear a difference and to notice that they failed. Between the pairs the difference is real and should be left exactly as large as the language makes it, with no help. Do not put anything on the end of beaux.

THE THREE FEMININE-AGAINST-SHORT PAIRS, WHICH ARE THE SAME SOUND TWICE. « belle » then « bel »; « nouvelle » then « nouvel »; « vieille » then « vieil ». Each pair is one take and the two members MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE. This is the only take in the lesson whose value is that nothing happens in it, and it is the one a reader will be most tempted to help with, because the two words look different on the page and a reader who can see the page will differentiate them without meaning to. If it is possible to record this take without the reader seeing the spelling of the second member, do that.

THE SIXTEEN DICTÉE LINES, ONE TAKE EACH, CLEAN AND UNHURRIED, WITH NO CONTRAST INTENT AT ALL. This is the opposite instruction to every other take in the lesson: here the learner is spelling rather than comparing, and any pair-reading would hand them the answer. Read each line as though it were the only line. The x on beaux and nouveaux and the s on belles and vieilles must be neither helped nor hidden; say the sentence the way somebody would say it, which is the whole difficulty the exercise exists to create.

THE BREAK CARD, AND IT IS THE ONE PLACE IN THIS LESSON A WRONG FORM IS SPOKEN. « un beau immeuble » then « un bel immeuble », one take, back to back. The first is NOT to be read as a mistake, with a wince or a rising edge or a pause: it must be read as somebody genuinely trying to say it, which means the two vowels grinding into each other and the phrase almost stopping. That difficulty IS the teaching, and a clean, confident reading of it would teach that the wrong form is perfectly sayable. The second should then arrive easily and at ordinary pace, and the contrast between the effort in the first and the ease of the second is the whole card.

OUTSIDE THE OFFICE IN NANTES. He is friendly, in a hurry, and asking to be polite rather than because he needs to know. « C'est un grand appartement ? » is quick and light. The learner's own line, « Oui, et c'est un beau... un beau... euh... », is the take that has to be right: two false starts and a stall, and the stall must sound like somebody whose mouth has stopped rather than like somebody who has forgotten a word. There is a difference and it is audible. His last line is cheerful and completely unbothered; nothing in the delivery should suggest he noticed anything, because he did not, and that is what makes it expensive.
clipIds: Oui, et c'est un bel immeuble.

lessons.intro: Three describing words in French have a fifth shape that nothing else has, and you use it in front of anything that starts with a vowel sound. It is not a new word to learn: it is the form you already use about a woman, with the last two letters taken off, and it sounds exactly the same. This lesson is about when to reach for it, why it is there at all, and the one mistake it causes that nobody can hear.

fiveForms.body: 5 ways to write each of these three, and 2 ways to say them. a2.03 gave you four of the five and this is the one it could not. Five ways to write it and two ways to say it. Three of the five are one sound and the other two are the other. The extra shape is the one you use in front of a word that starts with a vowel sound, and it is only ever used about a man or about a masculine thing. Everything else on the grid you already know how to build, because a2.03 taught you the system these three sit inside.
fiveForms.title: Three words that have one more shape than the rest

examples.note: The plain one.
The extra one, and the reason the other four are not enough.
And the one the extra one borrows its sound from.

theXPlural.body: beaux and nouveaux take an x. vieux already ends in one, so it takes nothing at all, and a1.14 and a2.03 both told you so. None of the three is audible: an x on the end of a describing word has never been pronounced in French, any more than an s has, so the plural of all three sounds exactly like the singular. That is the half of this you can only get by having seen it written.
theXPlural.title: Two of them take an x and one takes nothing

examples.note: An x. Not an s, and not for any reason you could work out.
The second one, same ending.
And the third, which is the same four letters as the singular. a1.14 told you about this word by name.

onlyForAMan.body: Nobody hears this mistake, including the person making it. The two forms are one sound, so only the page shows it. The short form exists to run into the word after it, so it only turns up in front of a thing. The woman form already ends in a consonant sound, so there is no collision for a short form to prevent and French never made one. Writing « une belle amie » is right and writing « une belle appartement » is not, and the two sound exactly the same, which is the whole difficulty. The only way to catch it is to know which word you are describing.
onlyForAMan.title: There is no woman version of the short one

examples.note: A masculine thing, so the short form.
And the full woman form, which is what goes in front of anything feminine, vowel or no vowel.
A masculine thing again. If this were feminine the word would be four letters longer and sound identical.

theShortOne.body: The form before a vowel is not a new word. It is the woman form two letters shorter, and it sounds the same. belle without the le is bel, nouvelle without the le is nouvel, vieille without the le is vieil. Three words, one operation. That is why it is worth knowing rather than memorising: you are not learning three new words, you are shortening three you already have. Say the woman form out loud, stop two letters early, and you have said the right thing. Before a vowel, say the feminine and drop its last two letters.
theShortOne.title: It is the woman form with two letters taken off

examples.note: Say this one.
Now say it two letters shorter. Same sound, and it is a different word on the page.
Third word, and the same two letters have come off again.

whereItGoes.body: Where these three go is a1.16 and it has not changed: they are three of the small set that stand in front of the thing. That is the one thing about placement worth saying here, and it is worth saying because it is the CAUSE: a describing word that comes after the thing never meets the sound that starts it, so it never needs a short form. These three come first, so they do. a2.17 is next and it is built on the woman form, which you have now used more than any other shape of these three. Nothing here expires when you get there.
whereItGoes.title: Not this lesson, and it is why this lesson exists

examples.note: In front of the thing, which is where all three of these live.
In front of the thing, and now the sound of the thing has changed the word.
After the verb, where nothing follows it and nothing has to happen.

aVowelIsComing.body: sons.07 put it this way: Two vowels collide, the little word gives way. It said that about the little words in front of a noun. This is the same pressure on the word after them. a1.17 taught you « mon amie » rather than « ma amie ». Same trade, other direction: a form borrowed from the other side so a consonant lands in front of the vowel. 3 of your lessons have made you do it already. What decides it is the SOUND at the front of the next word rather than the letter, which is why a silent h counts as a vowel and why you have to listen to the word rather than look at it. Nothing about the thing being described matters here: not what it means, not how long it is, only what noise it starts with.
aVowelIsComing.title: What sets the whole thing off

examples.note: A vowel at the front of the next word, so the short form.
A consonant at the front of the next word, so the plain form and nothing to do.
An h on the page and a vowel in the mouth. French listens to the mouth.

whatYouCanHear.body: You can hear the plain one against the one before a vowel, and that is the only difference here your ear will ever get. Five ways to write it and two ways to say it. Three of the five are one sound and the other two are the other. So the ear tells you one thing and one thing only: whether the speaker used the plain form or the short one. It will not tell you whether they meant one thing or several, and it will not tell you whether the short form or the woman form came out, because those two are the same noise. Everything else on this grid is a decision you make with your eyes and your grammar rather than your ears.
whatYouCanHear.title: Five shapes reaching your ear as two

examples.note: One sound.
And the other one. This is the whole of what is audible in this lesson.
Back to the first sound. The x makes no more noise than nothing would.

beats.text: A Tuesday evening in Nantes. A colleague you like but do not know well has asked where you have moved to, and you have been waiting all week for somebody to ask.

beats.en: Is it a big flat?
beats.speaker: Le collègue

beats.en: Yes, and it is a lovely... a lovely... er...
beats.fr: Oui, et c'est un beau... un beau... euh...
beats.stage: You know the word. You have said « beau » a thousand times. It went into your mouth, it hit the front of the next word, and it would not come out.
