items.ipa: lə ma.tɛ̃ | ʒə mə lɛv | e ʒə paʁ
items.respell: [luh ma-TAⁿ | zhuh muh LEHV | ay zhuh PAR]

items.fr: Ce soir, on mange tôt, puis on sort.
items.en: Tonight, we eat early, then we go out.
items.ipa: sə swaʁ | ɔ̃ mɑ̃ʒ to | pɥi ɔ̃ sɔʁ
items.respell: [suh SWAR | ohⁿ mahⁿzh TOH | pwee ohⁿ SOHR]

items.fr: En été, il fait chaud, même la nuit.
items.en: In summer, it is hot, even at night.
items.ipa: ɑ̃.n‿e.te | il fɛ ʃo | mɛm la nɥi
items.respell: [ahⁿ-n‿ay-TAY | eel feh SHOH | mem la NWEE]

items.fr: Le samedi, je lis, ou je marche.
items.en: On Saturday, I read, or I walk.
items.ipa: lə sam.di | ʒə li | u ʒə maʁʃ
items.respell: [luh sam-DEE | zhuh LEE | oo zhuh MARSH]

items.fr: Après le travail, il rentre, et il dort.
items.en: After work, he comes home, and he sleeps.
items.ipa: a.pʁɛ lə tʁa.vaj | il ʁɑ̃tʁ | e il dɔʁ
items.respell: [a-preh luh tra-VAY | eel RAHⁿTR | ay eel DOHR]

items.fr: À midi, on ferme, puis on rouvre.
items.en: At noon, we close, then we reopen.
items.ipa: a mi.di | ɔ̃ fɛʁm | pɥi ɔ̃ ʁuvʁ
items.respell: [a mee-DEE | ohⁿ FEHRM | pwee ohⁿ ROOVR]

items.fr: En hiver, la nuit tombe, et tout dort.
items.en: In winter, night falls, and everything sleeps.
items.ipa: ɑ̃.n‿i.vɛʁ | la nɥi tɔ̃b | e tu dɔʁ
items.respell: [ahⁿ-n‿ee-VEHR | la nwee TOHⁿB | ay too DOHR]

items.fr: Chaque jour, il attend, puis il repart.
items.en: Every day, he waits, then he leaves again.
items.ipa: ʃak ʒuʁ | il a.tɑ̃ | pɥi il ʁə.paʁ
items.respell: [shak ZHOOR | eel a-TAHⁿ | pwee eel ruh-PAR]

items.fr: Quel est le plat du jour ?

items.notes: The X is silent on its own. Before a vowel it comes back as a Z, joined on: deux heures.
The feminine of un, and the only number in French that changes for gender. The N is fully pronounced here; in un it is not.
No S on cent, because a number follows it. deux cents has one, because nothing does. Nothing about the sound changes either way.

items.fr: Mon numéro est le zéro six, quatre-vingt-douze, soixante-quinze, quatre-vingt-un, trente-trois.
items.en: My number is zero six, ninety-two, seventy-five, eighty-one, thirty-three.
items.ipa: /mɔ̃ ny.me.ʁo ɛ lə ze.ʁo sis ka.tʁə.vɛ̃ duz swa.sɑ̃t kɛ̃z ka.tʁə.vɛ̃ œ̃ tʁɑ̃t tʁwa/
items.notes: A French phone number is read as five two-digit numbers, never as ten single digits. This is the shape of every number anyone will ever give you.

items.fr: Ma sœur a soixante et onze ans.
items.en: My sister is seventy-one years old.
items.notes: Seventy-one takes et and drops its hyphens, because onze is standing where un would. Eighty-one and ninety-one do not.
million is a noun, so it needs de to reach what it counts. Before a vowel that de becomes d’. cent and mille need nothing at all.

items.fr: Cette application compte trois millions d’utilisateurs.
items.en: This app has three million users.
items.notes: Both halves of the noun rule in one line: the S on millions, and the de that reaches the thing counted, elided to d’ before a vowel.
The one place the article comes back. C'est points at a person; il est describes one.

items.fr: La France produit plus de deux milliards de bouteilles chaque année.
items.en: France produces more than two billion bottles every year.
items.ipa: /la fʁɑ̃s pʁɔ.dɥi ply də dø mi.ljaʁ də bu.tɛj ʃak a.ne/
items.notes: milliard behaves exactly like million: an S in the plural, and de before what it counts. A French milliard is a thousand million, which is the English billion.

items.fr: Ce billet de train coûte cent vingt-quatre euros quatre-vingts.
items.en: This train ticket costs one hundred twenty-four euros eighty.
items.ipa: /sə bi.jɛ də tʁɛ̃ kut sɑ̃ vɛ̃t.katʁ ø.ʁo ka.tʁə.vɛ̃/
items.notes: A price is one run at one speed. No word for centimes and no et: the cents arrive as a bare number after the currency, and quatre-vingts keeps its S because nothing follows it.
Any hotel. The listener does not yet know which one, and does not need to.

items.en: I am looking for a hotel.
items.notes: First mention. Un opens the question rather than pointing at an answer.
Second mention. Both people now know which hotel, so le takes over.
The room was introduced one line ago, so it is the room now.
English has nothing in front of croissants. French has des, and it is not optional.
They are on the table between you, so les. Des would ask about croissants in general.
Coffee as a whole, not a cup of it. English drops the article here and French cannot.
Negated, and le is untouched. Only un, une and des collapse to de.
English needs a. French forbids it after être. The gap is the grammar.

items.en: I do not have a car.
items.notes: Une becomes de. Not pas une, and not pas la: the negative eats the indefinite.

items.en: I do not have a pen.

items.fr: Il y a des livres sur la table.
items.en: There are books on the table.
items.ipa: /il ja de livʁ syʁ la tabl/
items.notes: Des in front of the new thing, la in front of the table you can both see.
The English has nothing where the French has des, so there is nothing to remind you.
Des goes the same way un and une do.
One loaf, the round kind, wrapped and paid for. Not a request for bread.
Bread, an amount nobody has measured. The same sentence with one syllable changed.

items.fr: Je ne mange pas de pain.
items.notes: Du becomes de. Not pas du pain, and not pas le pain: the negative eats the partitive.
The masculine form. English has no word here at all, which is why it goes missing.

items.en: I drink a lot of coffee.
items.notes: Name the quantity and the article goes. Never beaucoup du café.
Eau starts with a vowel sound, so de la shortens to de l' the way la shortens to l'.
De l' goes to d' under a negative, because de meets a vowel and shortens again.
Coffee, the substance. Not a cup of it, and not coffee in general.
One cup, served at a counter, on a saucer. You can count it.
Coffee rather than tea, or some of what is in the pot. Not one cup.
Invariable: works with countable and uncountable nouns. Always followed by de/d', never du/de la/des.
Un peu de suggests a small but sufficient amount; peu de (without un) suggests too little.
Marks a sufficient quantity; the opposite idea to pas assez de (not enough).
Marks an excessive quantity; pairs with pas assez de as its opposite.
Du is the masculine singular partitive article, used for an unspecified part of something.
De la is the feminine singular partitive article.
De l' replaces du/de la before a word starting with a vowel sound.
Des is the plural partitive article, used the same way for masculine and feminine nouns.

items.fr: Je voudrais du pain, s'il vous plaît.
items.en: I would like some bread, please.

items.fr: Elle met de la confiture sur sa tartine.
items.en: She puts jam on her toast.

items.fr: Tu veux de l'eau ou du jus d'orange ?
items.en: Do you want water or orange juice?

items.fr: Nous achetons des légumes au marché.
items.en: We buy vegetables at the market.

items.fr: Est-ce qu'il y a encore du café ?
Ils boivent du vin avec le dîner.
Je voudrais un peu de sucre dans mon café.
items.en: I would like a little sugar in my coffee.
items.ipa: /ʒə vu.dʁɛ œ̃ pø də sykʁ dɑ̃ mɔ̃ ka.fe/
items.notes: Un is a nasal vowel, do not pronounce the n separately.

items.fr: Tu mets trop de sucre dans ton thé.
items.en: You put too much sugar in your tea.
items.ipa: /ty mɛ tʁo də sykʁ dɑ̃ tɔ̃ te/
items.notes: Thé keeps a silent h that never affects the pronunciation.

items.fr: Je prends un café après le repas.
items.en: I'll have a coffee after the meal.

items.fr: Le serveur apporte du pain frais.
Je ne mange pas de viande.
L'addition arrive à la fin du repas.
items.en: The bill arrives at the end of the meal.
items.ipa: /la.di.sjɔ̃ a.ʁiv a la fɛ̃ dy ʁə.pa/
items.notes: 'La addition' is never written that way, the article must elide to l'addition before the vowel.

items.en: I am out on the terrace.
items.notes: je stays lowercase in the middle of a sentence, unlike the English I.
One person, and someone who has already offered you the closeness.

items.fr: Il est au comptoir du café.
items.en: He is at the café counter.
items.respell: eel eh oh kohⁿ-twar dü ka-FAY
items.notes: Pairs with .161. Only the verb tells you whether it is one man or several.

items.fr: Elle est en terrasse ce matin.
items.en: She is out on the terrace this morning.
items.respell: el eh ahⁿ teh-ras suh ma-TAⁿ
items.notes: Pairs with .162. Same shape, and elle and elles are the same sound.

items.fr: On est trois à la terrasse.
items.en: There are three of us on the terrace.
items.respell: ohⁿ neh trwa a la teh-RAS
items.notes: A we idea on a he form. That mismatch is the whole difficulty.

items.fr: Nous sommes trois à la terrasse.
items.en: There are three of us on the terrace.
items.respell: noo som trwa a la teh-RAS
items.notes: The same sentence as .158, one register up. Neither is wrong.

items.en: How many of you are there?
items.notes: The question at the door of every French restaurant. Here vous is plainly plural.

items.fr: Ils sont au comptoir du café.
items.en: They are at the café counter.
items.respell: eel sohⁿ oh kohⁿ-twar dü ka-FAY
items.notes: The plural of .156, and the S on ils is silent. sont is the only audible difference.

items.fr: Elles sont en terrasse ce matin.
items.en: They are out on the terrace this morning.
items.respell: el sohⁿ ahⁿ teh-ras suh ma-TAⁿ
items.notes: Every one of them a woman. One man and this becomes .161.
Said on its own, ils is the same sound as il. sont is the whole signal.
il faut is how French says one has to. It never has a subject you could point at.
ai starts on a vowel, so je drops its e. The same drop the learner already makes with le and la.

items.en: I am waiting for a friend.
Are you ready? (to one person you are close to)
Are you ready? (to one person, politely)
items.notes: One person, kept at a distance, and the verb still takes the plural form.
Identical out loud to .177. Only the silent S on prêts separates them.
The written twin of .167, and the line the opening scene puts in your mouth.

items.fr: Je suis ici pour la conférence.
items.en: I am here for the conference.
items.respell: zhuh swee ee-see poor la kohⁿ-fay-RAHⁿS
items.notes: suis. Said far more often than any other form, because most of what you say is about yourself.

items.fr: Tu es ici pour la conférence ?
items.en: Are you here for the conference?
items.respell: tü eh ee-see poor la kohⁿ-fay-RAHⁿS
items.notes: es. Two letters, and no S sound at the end of it.

items.fr: Il est ici pour la conférence.
items.en: He is here for the conference.
items.respell: eel eh ee-see poor la kohⁿ-fay-RAHⁿS
items.notes: est. The T is silent, so es and est are the same sound.

items.fr: Nous sommes ici pour la conférence.
items.en: We are here for the conference.
items.respell: noo som ee-see poor la kohⁿ-fay-RAHⁿS
items.notes: sommes. The doubled m really does sound, which is why it is not a nasal vowel.

items.fr: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?
items.en: Are you here for the conference?
items.respell: voo zet ee-see poor la kohⁿ-fay-RAHⁿS
items.notes: êtes, and the only form in the six that binds to its pronoun out loud: voo-ZET, never voo ETT.

items.fr: Ils sont ici pour la conférence.
items.en: They are here for the conference.
items.respell: eel sohⁿ ee-see poor la kohⁿ-fay-RAHⁿS
items.notes: sont. A nasal vowel and no T sound. Compare ils ont, which is the next lesson.
A name takes nothing in front of it. It is already as specified as a word can be.
Introducing somebody else. c est points at a person; il est would describe one.
ma is a little word in front of the noun, so the sentence takes c est.
The plural of c est. Nobody says ce est, and almost nobody remembers ce sont.
No un. English needs one and French forbids it, so the error is audible every time.
Being a student counts as a job here. The gap after es is the grammar.
The liaison and the missing article in one short question.

items.en: I am French. (said by a man)
items.notes: Lowercase f. The adjective is not capitalised in French the way the English is.

items.en: I am French. (said by a woman)
items.notes: The e wakes the s, and the two are audibly different. This is the agreement a1.01 taught on enchanté.
Plural group, plural adjective. The s is silent and the agreement is only on the page.
de plus a town. Nothing agrees with anything, whoever is saying it.
A woman, and de still does not move. Compare elle est espagnole, where the adjective did.
The question that gets you both origin answers. de plus où, elided.

items.en: I am tired. (said by a man)
I am tired. (said by a woman)
items.notes: Identical out loud to the masculine. The agreement is real and it is silent, exactly like désolé and désolée in a1.01.
Here the agreement IS audible: the e wakes the d. Compare fatiguée, where it stays silent.
un is the little word in front, so the sentence takes c est.
Same doctor, no little word, so il est. Il est un médecin is the sentence to unlearn.
le counts too. The test is any little word, not the indefinite one specifically.
Not a person at all. c est also points at a thing, a situation or an idea, which il est never does.
Two joins in four words, and the first one is the one nobody hears themselves miss.
The half of the ils sont / ils ont pair that belongs to this lesson. The other half is a1.07.

items.en: I have a present for Léa.
items.notes: ai. Said more often than the other five together, because most of what a beginner says is about themselves.

items.fr: Tu as un cadeau pour Léa ?
items.en: Do you have a present for Léa?
items.respell: tü ah uhⁿ ka-DOH poor lay-A
items.notes: as. Two letters, and the s is silent, so it sounds exactly like the a of il a.

items.fr: Il a un cadeau pour Léa.
items.en: He has a present for Léa.
items.respell: ee LA uhⁿ ka-DOH poor lay-A
items.notes: a. One letter, no accent on it, and the l of il runs straight into it.

items.fr: Nous avons un cadeau pour Léa.
items.en: We have a present for Léa.
items.respell: noo za-VOHⁿ uhⁿ ka-DOH poor lay-A
items.notes: avons, and the silent s of nous wakes up as a z in front of the vowel.
Same again at the feminine end. The ear gets nothing from the pronoun.
What gets said when a group walks in. Never « On sommes là ».
What you would write. Same meaning as .168 and a register higher.
on carries a suggestion the way English uses shall we.
Weather takes il, the same way English weather takes it.
Literally it makes beautiful. Nobody is making anything.

items.fr: Vous avez un cadeau pour Léa ?
items.en: Do you have a present for Léa?
items.respell: voo za-VAY uhⁿ ka-DOH poor lay-A
items.notes: avez, with the same join you already learned on vous êtes. One word out loud.

items.fr: Ils ont un cadeau pour Léa.
items.en: They have a present for Léa.
items.respell: eel ZOHⁿ uhⁿ ka-DOH poor lay-A
items.notes: ont, and the join makes a z. Ils sont opens on an s instead, and that is the whole difference.
Hunger, had. The English is "I am hungry" and there is no word for am anywhere in this sentence.
About the person. Il fait chaud is about the room, and the two are not interchangeable.
The rarest of the fourteen in this corpus: one row existed before this lesson, and it was the headword.
The question a French speaker asks before they open a window. The s of as is silent.
Avoir l'air is how French says somebody looks or seems. The corpus held no example of it at any level.
A real possession: one noun after the form, and no second verb behind it.

items.en: I do not have a car.
items.notes: Une became de. The same collapse you met on un, une and des one lesson ago.
Nothing collapsed, because faim never had a word in front of it. Never pas de faim.
Il a l'air content. About how somebody appears rather than how they are.
Literally: to have hunger. J'ai faim = I am hungry.
Literally: to have thirst. J'ai soif = I am thirsty.
Avoir phrase: J'ai sommeil, I am sleepy.
Avoir phrase: J'ai froid, I am cold.
Avoir phrase: J'ai chaud, I am hot.
Avoir phrase: Tu as raison, you are right.
Avoir phrase: J'ai tort, I am wrong.
J'ai honte means I am ashamed. Uses avoir, not être.

items.en: to feel like, to want to

items.notes: “a” (from avoir) sounds like “à” but takes no accent here because it's the verb.

items.fr: Elle a chaud dans la salle d'attente.
items.en: She is hot in the waiting room.
items.ipa: ɛl a ʃo dɑ̃ la sal da.tɑ̃t

items.fr: Il a froid dans le bureau.
items.en: He is cold in the office.
items.ipa: il a fʁwa dɑ̃ lə by.ʁo
items.notes: "froid" se termine par un d muet, on ne l'entend pas

items.fr: Elle a soif pendant la marche.
items.en: She is thirsty during the walk.
items.ipa: ɛl a swaf pɑ̃.dɑ̃ la maʁʃ
items.notes: "soif" se termine par un f qu'on prononce bien

items.en: We are afraid of the storm.
items.notes: l'apostrophe devant orage marque l'élision de la

items.fr: Nous avons faim après le travail.

items.en: She feels like having a coffee.

items.fr: Ils ont faim, ils veulent manger tout de suite.
items.en: They're hungry, they want to eat right away.
items.ipa: il.z‿ɔ̃ fɛ̃ il vœl mɑ̃.ʒe tu də sɥit
items.notes: "Ont" (they have) is the verb form, not the pronoun "on".
“vingt” links to “ans” with a silent t that becomes pronounced.
“vingt-huit” is written with a hyphen between the two numbers.
“âge” needs a circumflex accent on the a.
Leave a space before the question mark in “vous ?”.
This coming Monday, once. No article, and no preposition either.

items.en: Are you free on Wednesday evening?

items.fr: Le marché a lieu tous les samedis.
items.en: The market takes place every Saturday.
items.ipa: lə maʁ.ʃe a ljø tu le sam.di
items.notes: 'Tous les samedis' reinforces that the market happens every single Saturday.

items.fr: J'ai piscine le mardi et le jeudi.
items.en: I have swimming on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
items.ipa: ʒe pi.sin lə maʁ.di e lə ʒø.di
items.notes: 'Le mardi et le jeudi' marks a fixed weekly schedule for swimming lessons.
'Samedi prochain' needs no article, unlike the habitual 'le samedi'.

items.fr: Mercredi, nous allons au cinéma en famille.
items.en: On Wednesday, we're going to the movies as a family.
items.ipa: mɛʁ.kʁə.di nu za.lɔ̃ o si.ne.ma ɑ̃ fa.mij

items.fr: Le mardi matin, j'ai un cours de français.
items.en: On Tuesday mornings, I have a French class.
items.ipa: lə maʁ.di ma.tɛ̃ ʒe œ̃ kuʁ də fʁɑ̃.sɛ
items.notes: 'Le mardi matin' marks a fixed recurring class slot every week.

items.fr: Dimanche prochain, c'est la fête des mères.
items.ipa: di.mɑ̃ʃ pʁɔ.ʃɛ̃ sɛ la fɛt de mɛʁ
items.notes: 'Dimanche prochain' stays lowercase and needs no article.

items.fr: Elle a soufflé ses bougies un lundi soir.
items.en: She blew out her candles on a Monday evening.
items.ipa: ɛ.la su.fle se bu.ʒi œ̃ lœ̃.di swaʁ

items.fr: Je dois acheter un cadeau avant jeudi.
items.en: I need to buy a gift before Thursday.
items.ipa: ʒə dwa aʃ.te œ̃ ka.do a.vɑ̃ ʒø.di

items.fr: J'ai cours de yoga le lundi et le mercredi soir.
items.en: I have yoga class on Monday and Wednesday evenings.
items.ipa: ʒe kuʁ də jɔ.ga lə lœ̃.di e lə mɛʁ.kʁə.di swaʁ
items.notes: Naming both days with 'le' shows a fixed weekly schedule, every Monday and every Wednesday.

items.fr: Le docteur me reçoit uniquement le mardi.
items.en: The doctor only sees me on Tuesdays.
items.ipa: lə dɔk.tœʁ mə ʁə.swa y.nik.mɑ̃ lə maʁ.di
items.notes: 'Le mardi' here means every Tuesday is reserved for these appointments.

items.en: The shop is closed on Tuesday.
items.notes: One Tuesday, the next one. A handwritten note taped over the sign.
Every Wednesday. On means we, and takes the same form as il.
This Wednesday only. Nothing in front of the day, and nothing before it.

items.fr: Elle est à Paris le jeudi.
items.en: She is in Paris on Thursdays.
items.notes: Every Thursday, as a standing arrangement.
Every Monday, as a rule. The article is the only thing making it habitual.

items.fr: Le magasin est fermé le mardi.
items.en: The shop is closed on Tuesdays.
items.notes: Every Tuesday. This is what a sign on a door means.
After 'nous sommes', the day name 'lundi' stays lowercase.

items.fr: La pharmacie est fermée le dimanche.
items.en: The pharmacy is closed on Sundays.
items.ipa: la faʁ.ma.si ɛ fɛʁ.me lə di.mɑ̃ʃ
items.notes: 'Le dimanche' here means every Sunday, the pharmacy's regular closing day.

items.fr: Le samedi, je fais du sport avec mon frère.
items.en: On Saturdays, I do sports with my brother.
items.ipa: lə sam.di ʒə fɛ dy spɔʁ a.vɛk mɔ̃ fʁɛʁ
items.notes: 'Le samedi' indicates a weekly habit of exercising with his brother.
Masculine noun: 'zhoor'. Quel jour sommes-nous ? asks what day it is.
Feminine noun: 'suh-men'. Cette semaine = this week.
Masculine noun: 'ka-lahn-dree-yay'.
borrowed from English, written with a hyphen.

items.en: She is in Paris on Thursday.
items.notes: One Thursday. Whether it is the next one is decided by the conversation.

items.fr: Nous avons une réunion le vendredi.
items.en: We have a meeting on Fridays.
items.notes: Every Friday. The one in the diary that repeats.

items.en: We have a meeting on Friday.
items.notes: One meeting, this Friday. Drop the article and you have changed the diary.
Every Saturday. This is a fact about your week.
This Saturday. This is an answer to an invitation.

items.fr: La réunion est reportée à jeudi.
items.en: The meeting is postponed to Thursday.
items.ipa: la ʁe.y.njɔ̃ ɛ ʁə.pɔʁ.te a ʒø.di

items.fr: Le musée est gratuit le dimanche.
items.en: The museum is free on Sundays.
items.notes: Every Sunday. Worth knowing before you buy a ticket.

items.en: The museum is free on Sunday.
items.notes: This Sunday only, because of something happening that week.
This Saturday. An arrangement for one day, which is what makes it a plan.

items.fr: Elle prend le train le vendredi soir pour rentrer chez ses parents.
items.en: She takes the train on Friday evenings to go back to her parents' house.
items.ipa: ɛl pʁɑ̃ lə tʁɛ̃ lə vɑ̃.dʁə.di swaʁ puʁ ʁɑ̃.tʁe ʃe se pa.ʁɑ̃
items.notes: 'Le vendredi soir' describes a regular weekly routine, not a single trip.

items.fr: Le cours de cuisine a lieu un mercredi sur deux.
items.en: The cooking class takes place every other Wednesday.
items.ipa: lə kuʁ də kɥi.zin a ljø œ̃ mɛʁ.kʁə.di syʁ dø

items.fr: Elle arrose ses plantes le mercredi et le samedi.
items.en: She waters her plants on Wednesdays and Saturdays.
items.ipa: ɛ.la.ʁoz se plɑ̃t lə mɛʁ.kʁə.di e lə sam.di
items.notes: 'Le mercredi et le samedi' describes a fixed watering routine every week.
Say 'mar-dee'. From Mars, like English Tuesday comes from a god of war.

items.en: We see each other on Saturdays.
items.notes: Every Saturday. Not a plan at all, a description of how things are.

items.fr: Lundi, je commence un nouveau travail.
items.en: On Monday, I'm starting a new job.
items.ipa: lœ̃.di ʒə kɔ.mɑ̃s œ̃ nu.vo tʁa.vaj
items.notes: 'Lundi' is capitalized here only because it opens the sentence; day names are otherwise always lowercase.

items.fr: Le lundi, je vais à la bibliothèque après les cours.
items.en: On Mondays, I go to the library after class.
items.ipa: lə lœ̃.di ʒə vɛ a la bi.bli.jɔ.tɛk a.pʁɛ le kuʁ
items.notes: 'Le lundi' (with the article) means every Monday, a repeated habit, not a single Monday.

items.en: We have an appointment on Tuesday morning.

items.fr: Le mardi, ma sœur fait du yoga.
items.en: On Tuesdays, my sister does yoga.
items.ipa: lə maʁ.di ma sœʁ fɛ dy jɔ.ga
items.notes: 'Le mardi' means every Tuesday; without the article, 'mardi' alone would mean just one Tuesday.

items.fr: Mercredi, je dois aller chez le dentiste.
items.en: This Wednesday, I have to go to the dentist.
items.ipa: mɛʁ.kʁə.di ʒə dwa a.le ʃe lə dɑ̃.tist

items.notes: Vin rouge, vin blanc, vin rosé.
Feminine noun. The classic long French bread loaf.
The final c is silent, unlike in English pork.
The f is pronounced in the singular but silent in the plural bœufs.

items.fr: Tous les jeudis, elle prend son cours de yoga à dix-huit heures.
items.en: Every Thursday, she has her yoga class at six in the evening.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Tous les jeudis,","t":"every thursday,"},{"w":"elle prend","t":"she takes"},{"w":"son cours de yoga","t":"her yoga class"},{"w":"à dix-huit heures.","t":"at six in the evening"}]}

items.fr: Tous les mardis, je vais à la bibliothèque après le travail.
items.en: Every Tuesday, I go to the library after work.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Tous les mardis,","t":"every tuesday,"},{"w":"je vais","t":"i go"},{"w":"à la bibliothèque","t":"to the library"},{"w":"après le travail.","t":"after work"}]}

items.fr: Le mercredi, mon fils a son cours de musique à seize heures.
items.en: On Wednesday, my son has his music class at four in the afternoon.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Le mercredi,","t":"on wednesday,"},{"w":"mon fils","t":"my son"},{"w":"a son cours de musique","t":"has his music class"},{"w":"à seize heures.","t":"at four in the afternoon"}]}

items.fr: Le mercredi après-midi, les enfants n'ont pas école.
items.en: On Wednesday afternoons, children don't have school.
items.ipa: lə mɛʁ.kʁə.di a.pʁɛ mi.di le zɑ̃.fɑ̃ nɔ̃ pa ze.kɔl
items.notes: 'Le mercredi' signals a repeated Wednesday habit, unlike a single 'mercredi'.

items.fr: Le lundi est souvent difficile après le week-end.
items.en: Monday is often hard after the weekend.
items.ipa: lə lœ̃.di ɛ su.vɑ̃ di.fi.sil a.pʁɛ lə wik.ɛnd

items.fr: Mardi, il y a une grève des trains.
items.en: On Tuesday, there's a train strike.
items.ipa: maʁ.di il i a yn gʁɛv de tʁɛ̃

items.fr: Le jeudi soir, mes cousins viennent dîner.
items.en: On Thursday evenings, my cousins come for dinner.
items.ipa: lə ʒø.di swaʁ me ku.zɛ̃ vjɛn di.ne
items.notes: 'Le jeudi soir' is a recurring weekly visit, not a one-time event.

items.fr: Nous partons jeudi et nous revenons dimanche.
items.en: We're leaving on Thursday and coming back on Sunday.
items.ipa: nu paʁ.tɔ̃ ʒø.di e nu ʁə.və.nɔ̃ di.mɑ̃ʃ
items.notes: Both 'jeudi' and 'dimanche' stay lowercase mid-sentence here.

items.fr: Jeudi prochain, nous partons en voyage.
items.en: Next Thursday, we're leaving on a trip.
items.ipa: ʒø.di pʁɔ.ʃɛ̃ nu paʁ.tɔ̃ ɑ̃ vwa.jaʒ
items.notes: Day names like 'jeudi' stay lowercase even when followed by 'prochain'.

items.fr: Le jeudi, il joue au foot avec ses amis.
items.en: On Thursdays, he plays soccer with his friends.
items.ipa: lə ʒø.di il ʒu o fut a.vɛk se za.mi
items.notes: 'Le jeudi' describes a weekly habit; drop the article and 'jeudi' means just one specific Thursday.

items.fr: Le vendredi, la boulangerie ferme plus tôt.
items.en: On Fridays, the bakery closes earlier.
items.ipa: lə vɑ̃.dʁə.di la bu.lɑ̃.ʒʁi fɛʁm ply to
items.notes: 'Le vendredi' here means every Friday, a recurring closing time, not one Friday.

items.fr: Samedi, je fais les courses au marché.
items.en: This Saturday, I'm doing the shopping at the market.
items.ipa: sam.di ʒə fɛ le kuʁs o maʁ.ʃe

items.fr: Le samedi matin, mes parents dorment tard.
items.en: On Saturday mornings, my parents sleep in.
items.ipa: lə sam.di ma.tɛ̃ me pa.ʁɑ̃ dɔʁm taʁ
items.notes: 'Le samedi matin' means every Saturday morning, a routine, not a single occasion.

items.fr: Dimanche, toute la famille se retrouve chez grand-mère.
items.en: On Sunday, the whole family gets together at grandma's.
items.ipa: di.mɑ̃ʃ tut la fa.mij sə ʁə.tʁuv ʃe gʁɑ̃.mɛʁ
items.notes: 'Dimanche' stays lowercase mid-sentence; only a capital D at the very start of a sentence is correct.

items.fr: Le dimanche, nous ne travaillons jamais.
items.ipa: lə di.mɑ̃ʃ nu nə tʁa.va.jɔ̃ ʒa.mɛ
items.notes: 'Le dimanche' with the article means every Sunday, contrasted with a single 'dimanche'.
'Vendredi dernier' needs no article and no capital letter.

items.fr: Le professeur donne un contrôle le lundi et le jeudi.
items.en: The teacher gives a quiz on Mondays and Thursdays.
items.ipa: lə pʁɔ.fɛ.sœʁ dɔn œ̃ kɔ̃.tʁol lə lœ̃.di e lə ʒø.di
items.notes: Using 'le' before both days shows this happens every Monday and every Thursday, not just once.

items.fr: Ce n'est pas lundi, c'est mardi.
items.ipa: sə nɛ pa lœ̃.di sɛ maʁ.di

items.fr: Mon cours de piano est le mercredi à seize heures.
items.en: My piano lesson is on Wednesdays at four o'clock.
items.ipa: mɔ̃ kuʁ də pja.no ɛ lə mɛʁ.kʁə.di a sɛ.zœʁ
items.notes: 'Le mercredi' here marks a fixed weekly time slot, repeated every week.

items.fr: Nous fermons le dimanche et le lundi.
items.en: We are closed on Sundays and Mondays.
items.ipa: nu fɛʁ.mɔ̃ lə di.mɑ̃ʃ e lə lœ̃.di
items.notes: 'Le dimanche et le lundi' means every Sunday and every Monday, a permanent weekly closure.

items.fr: Le facteur passe le mardi et le vendredi.
items.en: The mailman comes on Tuesdays and Fridays.
items.ipa: lə fak.tœʁ pas lə maʁ.di e lə vɑ̃.dʁə.di
items.notes: 'Le mardi et le vendredi' describes the mail carrier's regular weekly route.

items.fr: Elle a les cheveux châtain clair.

items.notes: The final s is silent.

items.en: Monday or Tuesday, does that work for you?

items.fr: Cette année, mon anniversaire tombe un mardi.
items.en: This year, my birthday falls on a Tuesday.
items.ipa: sɛ.ta.ne mɔ̃ na.ni.vɛʁ.sɛʁ tɔ̃b œ̃ maʁ.di
items.notes: 'Mardi' stays lowercase here since it is not the first word of the sentence.

items.fr: Nous avons une réunion d'équipe tous les vendredis.
items.en: We have a team meeting every Friday.
items.ipa: nu za.vɔ̃ yn ʁe.y.njɔ̃ de.kip tu le vɑ̃.dʁə.di
items.notes: 'Tous les vendredis' emphasizes that the meeting repeats every single Friday.

items.fr: Tous les jeudis soir, nous regardons un film en famille.
items.en: Every Thursday evening, we watch a movie as a family.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Tous les jeudis soir,","t":"every thursday evening,"},{"w":"nous regardons","t":"we watch"},{"w":"un film","t":"a movie"},{"w":"en famille.","t":"as a family"}]}
Three syllables: 'mair-kruh-dee'. The middle e is very light.
The middle e is usually dropped in speech: 'sam-dee'.
One syllable: 'yair'. The h is silent, as always in French.
Say 'duh-man' with a nasal ending. A demain ! means see you tomorrow.
Say 'suh-men proh-shen'. On se voit la semaine prochaine, see you next week.
Say 'suh-men dair-nyair'. Dernière is the feminine of dernier, last.
Say 'too lay zhoor'. The s of tous is silent here. Je travaille tous les jours.

items.fr: Le musée est ouvert le samedi.
items.en: The museum is open on Saturdays.
items.ipa: lə my.ze ɛ u.vɛʁ lə sam.di
items.notes: 'Ouvert' follows 'être' describing the museum.

items.fr: Le cinéma est fermé le lundi.
items.en: The cinema is closed on Mondays.
items.ipa: lə si.ne.ma ɛ fɛʁ.me lə lœ̃.di

items.notes: Days are not capitalized in French. Le lundi means every Monday, lundi alone means this Monday.
Say 'zhuh-dee' with a soft j, like the s in 'measure'.
Say 'vahn-druh-dee'. The first syllable is nasal.
Say 'dee-mahnsh'. In France the week starts on lundi, so dimanche closes the week.

items.fr: Mon anniversaire est le premier janvier.
items.en: My birthday is on the first of January.
items.notes: A day inside a month, so le plus a number. premier is the only ordinal a date ever takes.
The month on its own, so en and nothing else. The same frame that gives the date takes no number here.

items.fr: La fête du Travail est en mai.
items.ipa: /la fɛt dy tʁa.vaj ɛ ɑ̃ mɛ/
items.notes: Which May day is not said, so the month alone is enough and en carries it.
Somewhere in June. True, and not enough for anybody to meet you at an airport.

items.fr: Mon vol est le douze juin.
items.en: My flight is on the twelfth of June.
items.notes: One day inside June. The number comes first and the le cannot be dropped.
The month alone. Note the le in front of concert is the noun's own, not the date frame.

items.fr: Le concert est le quatorze juillet.
items.en: The concert is on the fourteenth of July.
items.notes: A plain cardinal, quatorze, with no ordinal ending and no de before the month.

items.fr: Le magasin est fermé en août.
items.en: The shop is closed in August.
items.notes: The whole month, which is what a sign on a French shop door usually means in August.

items.fr: Le magasin est fermé le premier août.
items.en: The shop is closed on the first of August.
items.ipa: /lə ma.ɡa.zɛ̃ ɛ fɛʁ.me lə pʁə.mje ut/
items.notes: One day, so a date. Same sentence, same shop, and a week of your shopping between them.

items.fr: L'anniversaire de mon père est le trois octobre.
items.en: My father's birthday is on the third of October.
items.ipa: /la.ni.vɛʁ.sɛʁ də mɔ̃ pɛʁ ɛ lə tʁwa ɔk.tɔbʁ/
items.notes: trois, not troisième. Every day but the first takes a plain counting number.

items.en: I have an exam in December.
items.notes: Sometime in December. Enough to plan a holiday around and not enough to revise for.

items.fr: J'ai un examen le douze décembre.
items.en: I have an exam on the twelfth of December.
items.notes: One day. The number goes in front of the month, which is the opposite of the English order.

items.fr: Les journées sont chaudes en juillet.
items.en: The days are hot in July.
items.ipa: le ʒuʁ.ne sɔ̃ ʃod ɑ̃ ʒɥi.jɛ

items.fr: La rentrée scolaire est en septembre.
items.en: The start of the school year is in September.
items.ipa: la ʁɑ̃.tʁe skɔ.lɛʁ ɛ ɑ̃ sɛp.tɑ̃bʁ
items.notes: 'Septembre' is lowercase here, only sentence-initial month names take a capital letter.

items.fr: En décembre, les vitrines sont magnifiques.
items.en: In December, the shop windows are beautiful.
items.ipa: ɑ̃ de.sɑ̃bʁ le vi.tʁin sɔ̃ ma.ɲi.fik
items.notes: 'Décembre' needs its accent aigu on the é, and no capital letter mid-sentence.

items.fr: L'anniversaire de mon père est en octobre.
items.en: My father's birthday is in October.
items.ipa: la.ni.vɛʁ.sɛʁ də mɔ̃ pɛʁ ɛ ɑ̃ nɔk.tɔbʁ

items.fr: Le concours a lieu tous les ans en novembre.
items.en: The competition takes place every year in November.
items.ipa: lə kɔ̃.kuʁ a ljø tu le zɑ̃ ɑ̃ nɔ.vɑ̃bʁ

items.fr: La fête du Travail est le premier mai.
items.en: Labor Day is on May first.
items.ipa: la fɛt dy tʁa.vaj ɛ lə pʁə.mje mɛ
items.notes: Even inside a fixed holiday name, 'mai' is never capitalized in French.
The final l is pronounced: 'ah-vreel'. En avril = in April.
Say 'ok-tobr'. The final -bre is one quick sound, no extra vowel.
The s in tous and mois both stay silent here.
Swap mois for an or semaine to change the frequency.
One nasal syllable: 'zhwan'. Careful not to confuse with juillet.
Say 'sep-tahnbr'. En septembre = in September, back-to-school month in France.
Say 'noh-vahnbr' with a nasal middle syllable.
Say 'day-sahnbr'. En décembre = in December.

items.en: Excuse me, what time is it?

items.fr: Le magasin ouvre à huit heures et demie.
items.en: The store opens at half past eight.
items.ipa: lə ma.ga.zɛ̃ u.vʁ a ɥi.tœʁ e də.mi
items.notes: The t of "huit" is silent alone but liaises before "heures".
"Est" (is) sounds close to "et" (and) but they are never interchangeable in writing.

items.fr: Il est huit heures moins le quart.

items.notes: Plural is irregular: les genoux.
Almost always plural in French.
The only singular hour. Une and heure run together into one sound, so nothing marks where the number ends.
The x of deux is silent on its own and says z here. This and douze heures are the pair the ear actually fails on.
The silent s of trois says z before the vowel, exactly as the x of deux does.
No new consonant appears. The r of quatre simply carries straight on into the vowel.
The q of cinq is sounded here. The vowel before it stays nasal and never becomes a separate n.
The x says z, the same join as deux and trois. Six alone ends in an s sound and here it does not.
The p of sept is silent always. The t is silent alone and sounded here.
The t of huit is silent alone and sounded here. Huit opens on a sound English has no letter for.
The one genuine exception. The f of neuf becomes a v, and it does that before heures and before ans and nowhere else in the language.
The feminine of bleu, and it sounds exactly the same. Ma veste est bleue. The e is written and never heard, which is why learners refuse to believe the spelling.
The feminine of noir, and it sounds exactly the same. Ma veste est noire. Nothing in the sound tells you the e is there.

items.fr: Le magasin ferme à dix-huit heures.
items.en: The store closes at six pm.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Le magasin","t":"the store"},{"w":"ferme","t":"closes"},{"w":"à dix-huit heures.","t":"at six pm"}]}
Added after the hour: trois heures et demie is half past three.
The feminine of gris. The silent s at the end of gris wakes up as a z: GREE becomes GREEZ. This one you can hear.
The feminine of violet. The silent t wakes up and the spelling doubles it: violet becomes violette, not violete.
The plain form, and the t at the end is silent.
The noun is feminine, so the colour adds an e. Here you HEAR it: the sleeping t wakes up.
The x says z. Dix alone ends in an s sound, so the consonant both appears and changes.
The z is already there in the spelling and simply carries over. The o stays nasal.
Said for a length of time and not for a time of day: the twelfth hour on a clock is midi or minuit.

items.fr: Le film commence à huit heures et demie.
items.en: The film starts at half past eight.
items.ipa: /lə film kɔ.mɑ̃s a ɥi.tœʁ e də.mi/
items.notes: The same showing as the listing that reads vingt heures trente. One clock is what you say and the other is what is printed.

items.fr: Le train part à quatre heures dix.
items.en: The train leaves at four ten.
items.notes: The same train as the board that reads seize heures dix. Past twelve the two clocks stop agreeing on the number.

items.fr: Le magasin ferme à six heures du soir.
items.en: The shop closes at six in the evening.
items.ipa: /lə ma.ɡa.zɛ̃ fɛʁm a si.zœʁ dy swaʁ/
items.notes: The spoken clock has only twelve hours, so it says which half of the day it means. The printed one says dix-huit heures and does not need to.

items.fr: Le rendez-vous est à deux heures de l'après-midi.
items.en: The appointment is at two in the afternoon.
items.notes: The one of the four built on être, so it is the pair a learner can be asked to produce. The card it faces reads quatorze heures.

items.fr: Quelle heure est-il, s'il vous plaît ?
Vous avez l'heure, s'il vous plaît ?
items.en: Do you have the time, please?

items.fr: Il est huit heures et demie.

items.notes: « demie » agrees with the feminine « heure », but « demi » stays masculine after « midi » and « minuit ».

items.fr: Le musée ouvre à dix heures.

items.notes: Liaison links "une" and "heure" so you hear one linked syllable; don't write an extra word between them.
The x in "deux" is silent alone but liaises as a z sound before "heures".

items.fr: Il est cinq heures moins dix.
items.notes: "Cinq" holds a nasal vowel sound, not a separate n consonant like in English.

items.fr: Il est sept heures du matin.
items.notes: The p in "sept" is always silent, and the final t liaises into the next word.

items.fr: Il est huit heures du soir.
items.notes: The t of "huit" is silent alone but is pronounced here through liaison.
"Neuf" is an exception where the final f sound changes to v before heures.

items.fr: Nous avons rendez-vous à dix heures.
items.en: We have an appointment at ten o'clock.
items.notes: The x of "dix" liaises to a z sound right before "heures".
"Une" and "heure" link into one sound, don't write "une" as if it stood alone.

items.fr: Le rendez-vous est à quatorze heures.
items.en: The appointment is at two PM.
items.notes: The final t of "est" is silent alone but is pronounced here before the vowel of "à".

items.fr: La réunion commence à seize heures trente.
items.ipa: la ʁe.y.njɔ̃ kɔ.mɑ̃s a sɛ.zœʁ tʁɑ̃t
items.notes: "Réunion" and "trente" both contain nasal vowels that are easy to under-spell.

items.fr: Il travaille de neuf heures à dix-sept heures.
items.en: He works from nine to five.
items.ipa: il tʁa.vaj də nœ.vœʁ a diz.sɛ.tœʁ
items.notes: "Neuf" again shifts its final sound to v before the vowel of "heures".

items.fr: Le cours de français dure deux heures.
items.en: The French class lasts two hours.
items.ipa: lə kuʁ də fʁɑ̃.sɛ dyʁ dø.zœʁ
items.notes: The x of "deux" liaises into a z sound right before "heures".

items.fr: La bibliothèque ouvre à neuf heures et demie.
items.en: The library opens at half past nine.
items.ipa: la bi.bli.jɔ.tɛk u.vʁ a nœ.vœʁ e də.mi
items.notes: "Neuf" shifts to a v sound before the vowel of "heures" once again.
"Cinq" holds a nasal vowel that liaises smoothly into "heures".

items.fr: Il est huit heures et quart.
items.notes: The liaison in “huit heures” makes the final “t” of “huit” pronounced.

items.fr: Le bus arrive à sept heures moins le quart.
items.en: The bus arrives at a quarter to seven.
items.ipa: lə bys a.ʁiv a sɛ.t‿œʁ mwɛ̃ lə kaʁ
items.notes: The final “t” of “quart” stays silent.

items.fr: Il est trois heures et quart.

Added after the hour: quatre heures et quart is quarter past four.
With midi and minuit, demi has no final e in writing.
Minuit is midnight. The pattern mirrors midi et demi.
Trois heures pile means three o'clock sharp.
Vers before a time means approximately, around.
Use à before a time to say when something happens.
[kel-uhr eh-teel] · quelle and heure glue together
Rendez-vous covers doctor visits, meetings and dates alike.

items.fr: Ça marche, on se voit à dix-huit heures.
items.en: Sounds good, we'll see each other at six.
items.ipa: sa maʁʃ ɔ̃ sə vwa a di.zɥi.t‿œʁ

items.notes: Ask this outside any shop, museum or bakery.
The twin of ça ouvre à quelle heure. Worth asking, French lunch closures are real.
Cinq heures moins le quart means quarter to five, literally five minus the quarter.
Six heures moins dix means ten to six. Works with any minute count.
The s is written and never said. This is the same sound as the singular.
Feminine and plural, so both endings are there. It sounds exactly like the singular verte.
The plain form.
The e is there in writing and changes nothing in the sound. This is the spelling learners refuse to believe.
Still the same sound. Nothing in this sentence tells your ear it is plural except the words around it.
Two endings written, neither of them said. All four bleu sentences sound identical on the colour.
The plain form, and the only form there is.
No e. Marron is a chestnut being used as a colour, and a noun borrowed this way keeps its own shape.
No s either. Writing marrons here would be the one error a French reader always notices.
Feminine and plural and still unchanged. All four marron sentences are spelled the same way.
Set this beside "Les chaussures sont rouges." Same shoes, same sentence, and only one of the two colours took the s.
Same form for masculine and feminine: un sac rouge, une voiture rouge. Sounds like 'roozh'.
Feminine: bleue (same sound). The vowel is like 'uh' with rounded lips, not 'oo'.
Feminine: verte, and you hear the final t: /vɛʁt/. The t is silent in the masculine.
Feminine: noire (same sound). Sounds like 'nwahr'.
Feminine: grise /ɡʁiz/. The s is silent in the masculine: 'gree'.
Same form for masculine and feminine. Also the noun for the flower: une rose.
Feminine: violette /vjɔ.lɛt/. The final t is silent in the masculine: 'vyoh-leh'.

items.fr: Le ballon des enfants est violet.
items.ipa: lə ba.lɔ̃ de zɑ̃.fɑ̃ ɛ vjɔ.lɛ

items.notes: "Violet" becomes "violette": the silent t is now pronounced.

items.fr: Les fleurs des champs sont violettes.
items.ipa: le flœʁ de ʃɑ̃ sɔ̃ vjɔ.lɛt
items.notes: "Violette" agrees with the feminine plural "fleurs".

"Blanc" becomes "blanche" for a feminine noun; the silent c turns into a pronounced ch.
"Gris" adds an e for the feminine "chemise"; the silent s becomes a pronounced z.
"Rouge" adds an s to agree with the plural "chaussures".

Invariable: des chaussures marron. Named after the chestnut. For hair, French uses brun instead.
Invariable as a color: des sacs orange, no extra ending. Named after the fruit, une orange.

Weather uses « faire », not « être » : il fait froid.

items.en: It rains a lot in autumn.

After « il fait », the weather adjective stays masculine and invariable : chaud, never chaude.

Weather can use il y a plus a noun.
The opposite of il fait beau. Weather phrases use il fait plus an adjective.
Pleasantly warm, not hot. Doux also means soft or gentle.

items.en: it is cool, it is chilly
items.notes: Between mild and cold. Frais also describes fresh food.

items.fr: Il pleut depuis ce matin, et le ciel est gris.

items.fr: Il fait du brouillard ce matin.
items.ipa: il fɛ dy bʁu.jaʁ sə ma.tɛ̃

items.notes: "froid" se termine par un d muet.
“souvent” ends in a silent “t”, not pronounced as in “vent”.

items.fr: Fait-il beau à Paris en ce moment ?
items.en: Is the weather nice in Paris right now?
items.ipa: fɛ.til bo a pa.ʁi ɑ̃ sə mɔ.mɑ̃

items.fr: Est-ce qu'il y a du vent aujourd'hui ?
items.ipa: ɛs kil ja dy vɑ̃ o.ʒuʁ.dɥi

items.fr: Il fait beau et il y a du soleil.

items.notes: Spring is the only season that takes au instead of en.
Liaison links en and été, sounding like one smooth phrase.
Because hiver starts with a mute h, en liaises into it.
Liaison connects en to the vowel-initial automne.
The feminine of vieux, and it is a different word rather than an added ending: vieille, never vieuxe. Ma grand-mère est vieille. Before a vowel the masculine is vieil.
The feminine of mauvais: add the e and the sleeping s wakes up as a z. Cette idée est mauvaise. The masculine plural is still mauvais, because the s is already there.
Beau becomes bel in front of a word starting with a vowel sound: un bel homme, un bel arbre. It sounds exactly like the feminine belle and it is used with the un kind of thing.
Vieux becomes vieil in front of a word starting with a vowel sound: un vieil ami, un vieil immeuble. It sounds exactly like the feminine vieille and it is used with the un kind of thing.
Feminine: mauvaise. Opposite: bon. Un mauvais jour.
Feminine: belle. Becomes bel before a vowel: un bel homme.
Feminine: vieille. Becomes vieil before a vowel: un vieil homme. Opposites: nouveau, jeune.

items.fr: Mon grand-père a un vieil ami à Lyon.
items.en: My grandfather has an old friend in Lyon.
items.ipa: mɔ̃ ɡʁɑ̃.pɛʁ a œ̃ vjɛj a.mi a ljɔ̃
items.notes: 'Vieil' replaces 'vieux' before a vowel-starting masculine noun.
'Vieux' precedes the noun 'château'.

items.fr: Elle habite dans une grande maison.
items.en: She lives in a big house.
items.ipa: ɛl a.bit dɑ̃z yn ɡʁɑ̃d mɛ.zɔ̃
items.notes: Feminine 'grande' pronounces the d clearly.

items.fr: Elle porte une petite robe rouge.
items.en: She is wearing a small red dress.
items.ipa: ɛl pɔʁt yn pə.tit ʁɔb ʁuʒ
items.notes: Feminine 'petite' pronounces the final t.

items.fr: Elle porte une belle robe bleue.

items.ipa: ɛl pɔʁt yn bɛl ʁɔb blø
items.notes: 'Beau' becomes 'belle' in the feminine.

items.en: I have a small white dog.
items.notes: The masculine 'petit' ends in a silent t.
The final “d” in “grand” stays silent when nothing follows it.
“grand” takes a feminine e to agree with “table”.
The plural “grands” still sounds like singular “grand”, the s stays silent.
The feminine of “beau” is the irregular form “belle”.
Feminine: petite. Opposite: grand. Goes before the noun: un petit chat.
English puts the owner first and adds an apostrophe. French puts the relationship first and joins it with de. The two names come out in the opposite order.
The relationship first, then de, then the owner.
In front, grand is about importance rather than height. Nothing about the man's size is being said.
Behind, grand is a measurement. Same three words, same order of everything else, and the two sentences describe two different men.
In front, ancien means it used to be one and is not one now. It could be flats today.
Behind, ancien means old. It is still a hotel and you can still book a room in it.
In front, pauvre is sympathy. It says nothing at all about money.

items.en: He is a man with no money.
items.notes: Behind, pauvre is about money and nothing else. English uses the one word poor for both of these, which is why the position has to do the work.
Pairs with .235: same owner, different relationship, so only the first word moves.
Pairs with .236: same owner, different relationship.
Daughter, not girl. With de and a name behind it, la fille is a relationship.
The l in fils is silent and the s is said: FEES, not FEELS.

items.fr: Marie est la sœur de Paul.
items.notes: Half of the pair. Only the name after de changes between this and .242, and the meaning changes with it.

items.fr: Paul est le frère de Marie.
items.notes: The other half. The same two people, and de now points at Marie.
Voici puts somebody in front of the person you are talking to. a1.01 already used it at fr.a1.salutations.073.
The same frame with a longer relationship word in it. Nothing about the order changes.

items.fr: J'ai un frère et deux sœurs.
items.en: I have one brother and two sisters.
items.notes: avoir plus a number. a1.07 owns the verb and a1.02 owns the numbers, so this sentence needs nothing new.

items.en: I do not have a brother.
items.notes: After a negative, un and une flatten to de. The same frame as fr.a1.famille.233, « Je n'ai pas de voiture. »

items.fr: Tu as des frères et sœurs ?
items.en: Do you have any brothers and sisters?
items.notes: The question you will be asked. Rising intonation, no inversion, which is how it is really said.
Learn it as one word. Mon goes with the words that take le.
Ma goes with the words that take la.
Mes goes with anything plural, whichever kind of word it is.
Masculine plural, whatever mix of boys and girls it covers. The theme holds the singular l'enfant and has never held the plural.
La fille is girl or daughter. With de and a name behind it, only one reading is available, and that is what de buys you.
Also means woman; context decides.
Same form for boys and girls.
Note the s on grands.
Several people own him, and leur carries no s because he is one brother.
Still leur. The kind of thing has not mattered for three rows now.
Several people, one daughter, and no s on leur.

The plural of notre, and it is the same word whatever the things are. Nos parents, nos filles. Nothing about who is doing the owning changes it and nothing about the kind of thing changes it either. Only how many.
The plural of votre. Vos parents, vos livres. This is the one form of the fifteen that was absent from the corpus in every article form before this lesson, and a grid looks complete without it.

The plural of leur, and the s counts the THINGS rather than the owners. The owners were already several before the s arrived. Leur fille is one daughter belonging to several people; leurs filles is more than one daughter belonging to the same several people.
A man friend. The n of mon arrives on the front of ami and is fully pronounced, which is why this sounds like moh-na-mee rather than mon, ami.

A woman friend, and the word for her is the une kind: une amie. It still takes mon rather than ma, because ma amie would put two vowel sounds against each other. Said out loud this is the same as mon ami, sound for sound, and only the page can tell you which one was meant.
And her parents. Same sentence, and only what is around it decides.
From here the kind of thing stops mattering.
A brother is the un kind, so the word for my is mon.
In front, propre means it belongs to me and I do not share it.
Behind, propre means clean. Same room either way, and only one of the two sentences is about tidying.
Every word correct, and it does not mean what the learner in the opening scene meant by it. In front, ancien is always former.
Feminine: ancienne. Opposite: moderne. Before the noun it means former: mon ancien travail.
Feminine: grande. Opposite: petit. Un grand arbre, une grande maison.
Feminine: bonne. Opposite: mauvais. Un bon film, une bonne idée.
A sister is the une kind, so the same my becomes ma. Nothing about the speaker changed between this sentence and the one before it.
More than one thing, so the question about the kind is never asked and mes covers both.
The owner changed and the ending on the possessive did not. Compare the row above.
Same speaker as the sentence before, and the word changed because the thing did.
The plural, and it looks exactly like mes with a different first letter.
This also means her brother. French does not say whose it is, only what it is.
This also means her sister, word for word. The sentence carries no information about the owner at all, and the English has to pick one.
The same word as the sentence above it, in front of a une word. This row asks nothing.
The only change this row ever makes, and it is about how many.
The polite or plural your, and it behaves exactly like notre.
Unchanged again.
vos. This is the form most courses leave out of the table without anybody noticing.
The s arrives because there are two parents, not because there are several owners. The owners were already several in all three of these sentences.

items.en: He is talking with his sister.
items.notes: The owner is a man and the possessive is sa, because a sister is the une kind.

items.en: She is talking with her sister.
items.notes: The owner is a woman and the possessive is still sa. One word changed between these two sentences and it was not the possessive. The English had to change twice as much.
A woman friend, and the word for her is the une kind. It takes mon anyway, because ma amie would put two vowel sounds against each other and French will not have it.

items.fr: Ma sœur et mon amie sont ici.
items.en: My sister and my friend are here.
items.notes: Both of these are the une kind and one takes ma while the other takes mon. The only difference between them is the letter the second one starts with.
The s of mes wakes up as a z in front of the vowel. Say it beside the next sentence.
And her friends. The only thing separating this from the sentence above is the vowel in the first syllable, which is the one place in this lesson where listening carries real work.
The same several people and more than one daughter. The s counts the daughters. Out loud these two sentences are identical, so this is a difference you read rather than hear.
There is no le in this sentence and there cannot be one. The possessive is standing where the article would have stood, so the two never appear together.
before a feminine noun: ma soeur
before any plural noun: mes amis
informal, before a feminine noun: ta maison
informal, before any plural noun: tes parents
agrees with the noun, not the owner: sa mère
before any plural noun: ses enfants
same form for masculine and feminine: notre chat
polite form: votre nom
same form for masculine and feminine: leur chien
before a masculine noun: mon frère
informal, before a masculine noun: ton livre
agrees with the noun, not the owner: son père
Plural; covers both mother and father.
The sentence before the negative arrives. Its negative is 044.
Two words arrived and nothing else in the sentence moved. Ne went in front of suis and pas went behind it.
The sentence before the negative arrives. Its negative is 046.
The same wrap, and ne has lost its e because est starts on a vowel. That is the elision rule from sons.07, not a new one.
The sentence before the negative arrives. Its negative is 048.
The wrap goes around the conjugated verb whatever person it is in. Sommes is one word, so ne and pas sit either side of it.
The sentence before the negative arrives. Its negative is 050.
France is the la kind, so the word for to is en. Nothing else in this sentence changes when the country does.

items.fr: Bien sûr que non, ce n'est pas grave.
items.en: Of course not, it's not a big deal.
items.ipa: bjɛ̃ syʁ kə nɔ̃, sə nɛ pa gʁav
items.notes: “Grave” ends in a silent final “e” that does not change its pronunciation.

items.en: I am going to the United States.
items.notes: The country is plural, so the word for to is aux, and the x wakes up as a z in front of the vowel. Said out loud this is one long word rather than two.

items.en: I come from the United States.
items.notes: The same plural country, coming the other way, and des does exactly what aux did. The s wakes up as a z for the same reason.
Iran is the le kind and still takes en, because au Iran would put two vowel sounds against each other. The n of en arrives on the front of Iran and is fully pronounced.
Coming the other way the exception is over: this is the ordinary de of a le country, cut short in front of a vowel exactly as le and la were.
Mexique ends in an e and takes le anyway, so the word for to is au. The ending is a hint rather than a rule, and this is the country most likely to catch you out.
No article in front of the nationality. The last sound is a nasal vowel with no n behind it.
The e on the end wakes the n up. The nasal vowel collapses into a plain one with a real n after it, which is the same thing that happens between brun and brune.
A capital F, because here the word is the name of a person rather than a description of one. Out loud this is identical to the sentence without the capital.
au Portugal (in or to Portugal).
Feminine: portugaise.
Soif never had a word in front of it, so the negative had nothing to take away. It is pas soif and never pas de soif.
The sentence before the negative arrives. Its negative is 052.

items.en: I do not have a brother.
items.notes: Two things changed. The wrap went round ai, and then the un became de. A learner who does only the first says Je n ai pas un frère.
The sentence before the negative arrives. Its negative is 054.

items.en: I do not have a car.
items.notes: De agrees with nothing. Une became de, exactly as un did, and there is no de feminine to remember.
The sentence before the negative arrives. Its negative is 056.
Des became de like the other two, and then de lost its e in front of the vowel. The same elision, arriving on the other side of the sentence.
The sentence before the negative arrives. Its negative is 058.

items.en: I do not have a book.
items.notes: Un became de. This is the rule you already have, on the noun the next two cards use as well.
The sentence before the negative arrives. Its negative is 060.

items.en: I do not have the book.
items.notes: Same verb, same noun, and le did not move. Only un, une, des, du and de la ever collapse. Le, la and les stay exactly where they were.
The sentence before the negative arrives. Its negative is 062.
The un survived, and the only thing different from the first card is the verb. After être nothing collapses at all.
The sentence before the negative arrives. Its negative is 064.
Une survived as well. If this had been avoir it would have been de, and the only thing telling you otherwise is the verb.
The sentence before the negative arrives. Its negative is 066.

items.fr: Ce ne sont pas des amis.
items.notes: Des survived too, and ne kept its e because sont starts on a consonant. The exception reaches every person of être, not just ce n est pas.
The sentence before the negative arrives. Its negative is 068.

items.en: I do not have a dog.
items.notes: The written form, with both halves of the wrap in place. This is what you write and what you will be marked on.

items.en: I do not have a dog. (spoken French, with the ne dropped)
items.notes: The same sentence as Je n ai pas de chien, said the way it is actually said. Dropping the ne is not slang and not careless: it is what ordinary spoken French does with a negative, and a learner who has only met the written form will hear this and register agreement rather than refusal. Recognise it. Do not write it, and do not say it while you are still learning which half you would be dropping.
'Méchant' follows 'n'est pas' describing the dog.
Familier for c'est cher, it is pricey. Literally: it is not given away.

items.fr: Nous n'avons pas de fruits frais.
items.en: We do not have any fresh fruit.
items.ipa: nu na.vɔ̃ pa də fʁɥi fʁɛ
items.notes: "frais" ends in a silent s, homophone trap with "frai".

items.fr: Je n'aime pas le café. Moi non plus.
items.en: I don't like coffee. Me neither.
items.ipa: ʒə nɛm pa lə ka.fe mwa nɔ̃ ply
items.notes: "Non plus" pairs with a negative statement; it never follows a positive one.

items.fr: Il n'est pas triste, au contraire il est très content.
items.en: He's not sad, on the contrary he's very happy.
items.ipa: il nɛ pa tʁist o kɔ̃.tʁɛʁ i.lɛ tʁɛ kɔ̃.tɑ̃
items.notes: "Au contraire" oppose totalement deux idées, plus fort que "par contre".

items.en: We do not live in Lyon.
items.notes: Ne becomes n' before a vowel sound.
The elided n' before ai must be written even though it almost disappears in fast speech.

items.fr: Elle ne mange pas de viande.
items.notes: The ne before mange is barely audible but still required in writing.
Faim ends in a nasal vowel sound with no audible consonant, so listen for the nasal quality rather than a final letter.
N'aime elides ne before the vowel of aime, so remember the apostrophe when writing.

items.en: I do not have any children.
items.notes: “de” elides to “d'” before the vowel in this negative sentence.

items.fr: Je ne suis pas espagnol, je suis portugais.
items.notes: négation ne...pas + correction

items.fr: Non, je ne suis pas mariée, je suis fiancée.
items.en: No, I'm not married, I'm engaged.
items.notes: accord féminin : mariée, fiancée

items.fr: Non, ce n'est pas mon mari, c'est mon frère.
items.en: No, that's not my husband, that's my brother.
items.notes: ce n'est pas / c'est, correction
Nasal vowel, do not pronounce a hard n at the end.
The same en as en France, on a different la country. The choice was made by the article and by nothing else.
And the same de. Belgium and France take the same two words as each other and nothing about either country decided it except which article it carries.
au Canada (in or to Canada).
en Belgique (in or to Belgium).
Same form for masculine and feminine: belge.
aux États-Unis (in or to the United States). Always plural.
au Sénégal (in or to Senegal).
Feminine: sénégalaise.
en Allemagne (in or to Germany).
en Espagne (in or to Spain).
Feminine: espagnole.
en Italie (in or to Italy).
Feminine: française. Nationality adjectives are lowercase in French.
Feminine: japonaise.
au Mexique (in or to Mexico). Masculine even though it ends in e.
“du” is used before a masculine country like “le Canada”.
“de” alone is used before a feminine country like “la France”, not “du”.

items.en: He comes from the United States.

items.fr: La France est un pays d'Europe.
items.en: France is a country in Europe.
items.notes: La liaison 'est_un' sonne comme 'ɛtɛ̃', facile d'oublier le t de liaison à l'écrit.

items.fr: Le Canada est un grand pays.
items.notes: 'Grand' se termine par un d muet, ne pas ajouter de lettre en trop.
'États-Unis' prend un trait d'union et deux majuscules.

items.fr: J'habite au Canada depuis deux ans.
items.en: I have been living in Canada for two years.

items.notes: en France (in or to France).
Feminine: canadienne.
Feminine: américaine.
Feminine: allemande.
Feminine: italienne.
au Japon (in or to Japan).
Feminine: mexicaine.

items.fr: Le chat est sur la boîte.
items.en: The cat is on the box.

items.fr: Le chat est sous la boîte.
items.en: The cat is under the box.

items.fr: Le chat est dans la boîte.
items.en: The cat is in the box.

items.fr: Le chat est devant la boîte.
items.en: The cat is in front of the box.

items.fr: Le chat est derrière la boîte.
items.en: The cat is behind the box.

items.fr: Le chat est à côté de la boîte.
items.en: The cat is next to the box.
items.ipa: /lə ʃa ɛ a ko.te də la bwat/

items.fr: Le chat est près de la boîte.
items.en: The cat is near the box.
items.ipa: /lə ʃa ɛ pʁɛ də la bwat/

items.fr: Le chat est loin de la boîte.
items.en: The cat is far from the box.
items.ipa: /lə ʃa ɛ lwɛ̃ də la bwat/

items.fr: Le chat est en face de la boîte.
items.en: The cat is opposite the box.
items.ipa: /lə ʃa ɛ ɑ̃ fas də la bwat/

items.notes: à + le = au. The two words are gone and one has replaced them.
à + les = aux. Said out loud it is the same sound as au; the difference is written.
à + la does NOT contract. Both words stay, exactly as written.
à + l' does NOT contract either. The l' is the noun's own article, already shortened.

items.notes: Three words, and the third is the one that gets dropped. À côté la banque is the most common thing an A1 learner says wrong here.
The same shape again. Absent in every form: en face, en face de and en face du all return nothing as a headword.
Silent t. Sounds like 'duh-vahn'.
Identical sound to a. The mark is doing grammar, not sound.
Nasal start, like 'ahntr'. Entre nous: between us.
Loin sounds like 'lwan' with a nasal ending. Opposite of près de.
The same question as Tu es prêt ?, with the two words swapped and a hyphen holding them together. The hyphen is not decoration: Es tu prêt ? without it is a typo rather than a question.
No t is added here, because est already ends in one. Compare A-t-il faim ?, where a has no consonant to lend and one is put in.
prête rather than prêt, because the word is describing a woman. The question form did not cause that: it would be prête in the statement too.
The safe form of the vous question. Notice that est-ce que did not care that the pronoun changed: you bolt the same three words onto the front of anything.
The nous form, and it is the longest of the twelve. Nothing special happens to it.
The one of the twelve you will hear most often, because vous is already the careful pronoun and inversion is the careful form. The two travel together.
The t on the end of sont is silent in the statement Ils sont prêts, and inversion wakes it up: this comes out as sohⁿ-TEEL.
The same question as Tu as faim ?, swapped. Said to a friend across a table it sounds oddly stiff, which is the whole subject of this lesson rather than a fault in the sentence.
A ends in a vowel and il starts with one, so a t is put between them. There is no such word as a-il. The t means nothing at all and is there only to keep the two vowels apart.
The same insertion with elle. If you can say A-t-il you can say A-t-elle, and those are the only two places in this lesson it happens.
No t is inserted, because avons already ends in a consonant. The rule only fires when a vowel would meet a vowel.
The avoir form you will meet most, and the corpus agrees: avez-vous turns up in shops, restaurants and waiting rooms far more than any other inversion on this list.
Like sont-ils, the silent t wakes up. Ils ont is said eel-ZOHⁿ and Ont-ils is said ohⁿ-TEEL, so the same two words rearrange their sounds completely.
Est-ce que loses its e in front of il. This is the fourth time you have watched French refuse to let two vowel sounds meet, and the third different way it has got out of it.
The same cut in front of elle. In fast speech ess-KEEL and ess-KEL are close enough to be worth listening for, and they are the only pair in this lesson your ear has real work to do on.
And in front of on. Two things happen at once here: que loses its e, and the n of on carries over onto est, so the middle of this comes out as kohⁿ-NEH.

A statement, and it is the same four words as the question. On the page one full stop separates them. Out loud one is a voice going down and the other is a voice going up, and nothing else differs at all.
Oui on its own is a complete answer. The rest is only there if you want to say more.
Non, then a reason. Nothing here needs a negative: saying why is friendlier than saying not.
The answer to the avoir question, and j'ai rather than je ai for the same reason est-ce qu'il is not est-ce que il.
A negative statement with a rising voice on the end, which makes it a question. The negation is the one the previous lesson taught, doing exactly what it did there; only the contour is new.
Not oui. When somebody asks you a question with a not in it and you want to disagree with the not, French has a separate word for that, and this is the only job it does.
Also the standard word for 'if'. This 'si' answers yes to a negative question or statement; used at every register but essential in casual argument.
“prêt” agrees in gender: use “prête” for a feminine subject.
“faim” ends in a nasal vowel spelled “aim”, don't confuse it with “fin”.

The S of les is silent everywhere else in French. A vowel follows, so it sounds, as a Z.
Same S, same determiner. A consonant follows, so nothing wakes and both S sounds stay away.
The T of petit is written and never said. Here a vowel follows it, so it says itself.
Same adjective, same T. A consonant follows, so it goes back to being written only.
H muet, so the word opens on a vowel sound and the plural S wakes.
H aspiré. Nothing on the page differs from les hôtels, and the liaison is blocked anyway.
The X of deux comes back as a Z, which is what an X does in liaison.
H aspiré blocks it, so both X stay silent and a small gap opens where the Z would have been.
Two syllables. The S of ils sounds, and ont is one nasal vowel with no T at the end of it.
Two syllables again, and the only audible difference between them is the Z.
The D wakes as a T. A liaison consonant is not always the letter you see.
Same D, asleep. The vowel of grand stays nasal either way.
The N does two jobs at once: it keeps the vowel nasal AND it links. It is not spent on either.
Three nasal vowels and not one audible N. The N only surfaces when a vowel needs it.
One S links and one does not. A noun subject closes its group before the verb, and no join crosses that edge.
A pronoun subject does not close a group, so here the S does link.
The S of amis is followed by a consonant anyway, so two separate reasons keep it quiet.
Two sleeping T, both woken, in one short sentence.
The same two T, both asleep: an h aspiré blocks the first and a consonant blocks the second.
Three rules on four words: ne elides, the S of pas wakes as a Z, and mangé keeps its silent E.
Remove one word and the Z disappears with it. The elision is untouched: it never depended on encore.

items.en: Have a large glass of water.

Two elisions, then two vowels meeting with nothing to join them. French tolerates that gap: no rule applies.
Four written words, one unbroken run of syllables. Every join in it is compulsory.
Three liaisons in four words, and not one of the linking letters is audible on its own.
Three liaisons, then a stop: the T of accent has a consonant after it and stays down.
Four written words and four spoken syllables. Two elisions took two of them away.
An S and an X, both silent as written, both saying Z here.
The same words rearranged, and the X of deux goes quiet because nothing follows it.
Four nasal vowels and two N doing double duty. Say it as one word or it falls apart.
Four nasal vowels in three words, joined by two N that belong to neither side.
Two joins, then two vowels sitting side by side untouched. a has no sleeping consonant to lend.

items.en: It is a very nice flat.

Three different linking consonants, one sentence. The ée at the end contributes nothing at all.
habitent ends in four written letters that make no sound. The Z in front of it makes plenty.
Three words, three final consonants, and exactly one of them is heard.

items.fr: Quand il arrive, tout le monde est content.
items.en: When he arrives, everyone is happy.
items.notes: The D of quand says T and the D of monde says D. One was asleep and one was already awake.

items.fr: On arrive à l'heure, comme d'habitude.

Three plural S. The first one sounds and the other two do not.
Five words, five silent endings, one nasal vowel, and no join available anywhere in it.

Four words, two joins, and a final D that nothing can wake because the sentence stops there.
